# PROLOGUE.

<image-desc>The text begins with a small Greek cross symbol. The letter 'I' of the first word "I have learned" is a decorative initial.</image-desc>

**I** have learned from pious and elder men, from whom this tradition has come down to me: that <margin>1 Samuel 16:7; 2 Chronicles 6:30; John 2:25; Revelation 2:23.</margin> God alone is the inspector of hearts, who searches the hearts and the minds <note>original: "corda & renes," literally "hearts and kidneys." In biblical Latin, the kidneys/reins were considered the seat of the deepest emotions and sincerity.</note>, and knows the thoughts of men. No other creature, whether rational <note>Refers to humans.</note> or intellectual <note>Refers to angels.</note>, can know the secrets and hidden things of human hearts; only He who formed their hearts individually. And because this is said to be the unique property of God alone, it is held that Angels and any other celestial powers recognize the movements and affections of the mind and heart only through some outward demonstration, or from certain signs, hints, or movements of the body. Likewise, demons perceive the internal and hidden things of men from these same signs. Even if it is found written anywhere in Holy Scripture that Angels or Demons know the thoughts of men, it is said that this must be understood not as referring to those things which are hidden in the depths of the heart and still dwell in the mind alone, but as those which have already been brought forth, in a way, through outward signs or movements of the body. However, there is an opinion held by some <margin>Jerome in the letter to Paulinus, which is the first in the Bible.</margin> that just as we see bodies and discern them with our physical eyes, so Angels and Demons, being spirits, thoroughly see and recognize our spirits, our minds, and whatever is within them. Nevertheless, what I feel about this matter can easily be understood from what will be said below.

While I was turning these things over in my mind, and was leaning more toward the view that it is the unique property of God alone to search the secrets and hidden depths of human hearts, it happened that a certain small book came into my hands. In it, many things were told concerning the miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary. Among these was one story that brought me no small amount of wonder and made me wonder whether this, too, among other miracles, had been divinely granted to the Virgin Mother of God <note>original: "Deiparae Virgini." This is a Latin translation of the Greek "Theotokos," a title for Mary emphasizing her role in giving birth to the divine.</note>: that she might perceive those things which lie hidden in the depths of the heart. For it was told there that a certain devotee of the Mother of God, who held great devotion to her and greeted her frequently in his mind, uttering the <term>Hail Mary</term> <note>original: "Ave Maria." The primary prayer of the rosary.</note> along with other prayers, was one day reciting the <term>Hail Mary</term> in his heart only, without any utterance of the voice and without any outward sign, in his mind alone... <meta>The text cuts off here due to the catchword "con-", which would begin the word "contemplating" or "continuing" on the next page.</meta>

<term>Hail Mary (Ave Maria)</term> — A traditional Catholic prayer asking for the intercession of the Virgin Mary.
<term>Mother of God (Deipara)</term> — A theological title for Mary, asserting that Jesus is both fully human and fully divine.

<summary>In this prologue, the author explores whether angels, demons, or the Virgin Mary can read human thoughts, initially concluding that only God possesses this power before encountering a book of miracles that challenges his view.</summary>

# ON THE DIVINE NAMES.

<margin>How the names of Angels are gathered.</margin>
The Hebrews say there are two Angels: one benign and merciful, the other severe and avenging. They say the name of the former ends with the letters **ia** <note>This refers to a suffix associated with the divine name "Yah."</note>, while the name of the latter ends in **el** <note>Associated with "El," meaning God/Power.</note>; hence we have Michael, Gabriel, etc.

<margin>The Names of God.</margin>
## THE TEN AND DAILY NAMES.

1. **Eheie** <note>original: "Eheie"</note>. That is, the Divine Essence.
2. **Jehovah** <note>original: "Iehovah"</note>. That is, Essence.
3. **Elohim** <note>original: "Elohim"</note>. That is, Judgment and Power.
4. **El** <note>original: "El"</note>. That is, the Mighty God.
5. **Eloah** <note>original: "Eloah"</note>. That is, the Blessed God.
6. **Tsebaoth** <note>original: "Tſebaoth"</note>. That is, the God of Hosts <note>Literally "God of Armies."</note>.
7. **Shaddai** <note>original: "Schaddai"</note>. That is, the Almighty.
8. **Adonai** <note>original: "Adonai"</note>. That is, the Lord.
9. **Jah** <note>original: "Iah"</note>. That is, God.
10. **Ehieh** <note>original: "Ehieh"</note>. That is, I will be what I will be <note>A reference to God's revelation to Moses in Exodus 3:14.</note>.

There are also other names attributed to God, such as <term>Iod, He, Vau, He</term> <note>These are the four letters of the Hebrew alphabet: Yod, He, Waw, and He.</note>, which are called the <term>Tetragrammaton</term>. Likewise, <term>Agla</term> and <term>Amen</term>.

<margin>The Name of 12 letters.</margin>
## THE NAME OF 12 LETTERS.

**Iod, He, Vau, He: Iod, He, Vau, He: Iod, He, Vau, He.** That is, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit <note>The author is interpreting the 12-letter name through a Christian Kabbalistic lens by repeating the four-letter name three times to represent the Trinity.</note>.

<margin>The Name of 42 letters.</margin>
## THE NAME OF 42 LETTERS.

Ab, gita, tza'k, basch, ko tzit, na gad, ieche, schatzit, batait, rache, itacka, tzech, betho, vach, schake, vitz, korech, dathani, hamneke, phithchana, iace, lieveth, barot, tatztha <note>These are phonetic transliterations of a 42-letter name of God, traditionally derived from the medieval Hebrew prayer 'Ana B'Koach'.</note>.

<margin>The Shemhamphoras. Exodus 14.</margin>
## THE NAME OF 72 LETTERS.

This is extracted from three verses of the 14th chapter of Exodus: namely, *And the Angel of God moved.* [v. 19] *And it came between the camps of the Egyptians.* [v. 20] *And Moses stretched out his hand.* [v. 21]. From the letters of these verses (each of which contains 72 letters), seventy-two names are gathered.

<header>SECOND SECTION</header>

# BOOK ONE
## On the Elements in General

<margin>Aristotle, *On Generation and Corruption*, Book 2, chapter 3</margin>
Since the Elements are the material building blocks of natural things, from which things are composed and into which they are **ultimately** broken down, we must discuss them first.

<margin>Aristotle, *Meteorology*, Book 4, chapter 1</margin>
The Element is defined by Aristotle in this way: *An element is the primary thing from which something is composed; it exists within that thing, and its form cannot be divided into another type of form.* <note>original: "Elementum est primum, ex quo aliquid componitur, & inest, & est specie indiuisiile in aliam speciem."</note>

It is called *Primary* because it is not made of other bodies, but rather other bodies are made of it.

It is said to be *that from which something is composed* because it is not the "trigger" (efficient cause) or the "purpose" (final cause), but the actual material.

It is said to *exist within* because it differs from transitory matter. For example, bread is made from wheat, but the wheat does not remain wheat once it is bread. However, the Elements remain themselves within any compound thing.

<margin>Seneca, *Epistle* 117</margin>
It is called *indivisible in its form* because an Element cannot be divided into bodies of a different kind. For instance, water can only be divided into water, and air into air. However, compound bodies can be divided into different kinds of matter; wood, for example, can be separated into fire, air, water, and earth <note>referring to smoke, steam, and ash produced by burning wood</note>.

<margin>Plato, *Timaeus*</margin>
In this definition, the "material" distinguishes an Element from the spiritual or purposeful aspects of a thing. Its "simplicity" distinguishes it from mixtures. Its "permanence" distinguishes it from seeds <note>which change into plants and do not remain as seeds</note>.

Furthermore, Elements are called by different names depending on their role. They are called *Elements* insofar as they are what things are made of. They are called *Principles* insofar as they are the starting point of creation. They are called *Initials* because they are first. They are called *Ultimates* because they are the **final** state when something is broken down.

<header>SECOND PART: OF CHEMISTRY</header>

# CHAPTER ONE
## On the Matter and Form of the Elements

<margin>Aristotle, *Physics*, Book 1, text 74</margin>
In the Elements, two things must be considered: Matter and Form. These are related in such a way that the essence found in air can also become present in water.

<margin>Aristotle, *On the Soul*, Book 1, chapter 1</margin>
The *Matter* of the elements is "Prime Matter," which is called the most universal <term>Subject</term> <note>the underlying "stuff" of the universe</note> from which all bodies consist. It is a thing without any specific shape, quality, size, or property; it is neither a specific "what," nor a "how much," nor a "what kind."

<margin>Scaliger, *Exoteric Exercises*, 6, section 2</margin>
The *Form* of the elements is twofold: *Substantial* and *Accidental*.

*Substantial* form is that by which water is water, and fire is fire. This is hidden from us; it is known only through its qualities and effects.

*Accidental* forms are the primary qualities: Heat, Cold, Moisture, and Dryness. Through these, the Elements act upon one another and are acted upon.

<margin>Seneca, *Epistle* 65</margin>
In the Elements, matter and form are not of equal importance. For Matter by itself is inert and idle, possessing only <term>Potency</term> <note>the potential to become something</note>. Form, however, gives "Being" and moves the matter. **Hence**, the *Active* is more excellent than the *Passive*, and *Form* is more excellent than *Matter*.

Therefore, the Chemists divide these four Elements into <term>Active</term> and <term>Passive</term> categories based on the relationship between their matter and form. The <term>Active</term> ones are Fire and Air, in which form dominates over matter. The <term>Passive</term> ones are Water and Earth, in which matter dominates over form. These latter two are even called <term>Matter</term> in relation to the former.

Phlegm (or Water) is called *Matter* in relation to Spirit; because Spirit is something subtle, fiery, and "formal" which hides within the Phlegm as if inside a container.

<term>Caput Mortuum</term> <note>literally "Dead Head"; the useless solid residue left after distillation or chemical reaction</note> (or Earth) is called *Matter* in relation to Salt; because Salt is a certain "terrestrial form" that hides within the Dead Head.

# Preface to the Newly Compiled Essence of the Taoist Canon

## By Xiao Tianshi, the Hermit of Wenshan

### ->The Way connects the tradition of all under Heaven; Virtue initiates the transformation of all generations.<-

Long ago, the <term>Grand Historian</term> <note>original: "Tai Shi Gong," referring to Sima Qian (c. 145–86 BCE), the foundational historian of early China</note> discussed the essential aims of the Six Schools of thought. Regarding the other schools, he had various criticisms, but for the Taoists—known in antiquity as the **School of the Way and Virtue**—he stated: "The Taoist school enables a person's spirit to be unified, their actions to harmonize with the formless, and their provisions to suffice for all things. Their method follows the great natural flow of <term>Yin and Yang</term>, adopts the best of the Confucians and Mohists, and captures the essentials of the Legalists and the School of Names. They shift with the times and change in response to things. In establishing customs and performing tasks, nothing is unsuitable; their instructions are concise and easy to grasp, their tasks are few, yet their achievements are many." The Grand Historian was not far removed from antiquity, and he was still able to witness the profound and vast nature of Taoism. Thus, his words of praise were uniquely numerous, ranking them at the head of all schools and stating that they could encompass all diverse currents of thought.

He further stated: "Taoism practices **non-action** <note>original: "wu-wei," a core Taoist concept of acting in harmony with the natural flow without forced or artificial effort</note>, yet it is also said that *there is nothing left undone*. Its reality is easy to practice, but its words are difficult to understand. Its method takes emptiness and nothingness as its root, and follows along with nature as its application. It has no fixed momentum and no constant form, therefore it can understand the essence of all things. It does not place itself before things, nor after them, and thus it can be the master of all things. Whether there are limits or no limits, it harmonizes with things as they are. Thus it is said: The Sage is immortal because he holds to the changes of the times." From this, one can see the reasons why Taoism has been able to endure through a thousand ages without decaying.

However, since the Han Dynasty followed the **fires of the Qin** <note>referring to the infamous "burning of books and burying of scholars" under the first emperor of China, which destroyed many philosophical texts</note>, the "hundred schools" were suppressed and Confucianism was exclusively honored. Confucianism thus became the <term>Prominent Learning</term>, and from that point on, Taoism no longer flourished! 

Now, I do not hesitate to offer my humble efforts, wishing to spend my entire life engaged in the "Revival of Chinese Culture." By this, I hope to turn back the raging tide and support the mansion that is about to fall! My goal in revealing the essential principles of the various schools of the pre-Qin era is to ensure the sacred lineage of the Taoists is not severed, so that the Taoist tradition can continue to be carried forward for thousands of generations. Furthermore, through the promotion and expansion of Taoist culture and academic thought, I hope to lead all of humanity to advance together toward the **Way** <note>Tao</note>!

<summary>This preface by Xiao Tianshi argues for the historical superiority and practical flexibility of Taoism, citing the praise of the ancient historian Sima Qian. The author positions his work as a vital cultural rescue mission to restore Taoist wisdom to a world where it has been overshadowed by Confucianism.</summary>

<keywords>Taoism, Sima Qian, Wu-wei, Chinese Philosophy, Xiao Tianshi, Taoist Canon, Cultural Revival, Han Dynasty, Yin and Yang</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Xiao Tianshi's preface, moving from the historical endorsement of Taoism by Sima Qian to a broader claim: that Taoism is the foundational root of all Chinese civilization, science, and governance. It categorizes Taoist thought into eight distinct functional branches to show its practical utility.</meta>

<page-num>11</page-num>

...aiming for the "**Taoization of human life**" and the "**Taoization of the world**": this is truly his desire to use the Way to save the world and to save humanity. By spreading the **Light of Virtue** <note>original: "dao de zhi guang," referring to the radiance of the Way and its manifestation in moral power</note>, he perhaps reveals his hidden purpose in uniquely honoring the Taoists above all other "Hundred Schools" of thought!

The academic traditions of the Taoists are extremely ancient. Since **Fuxi** <note>A mythical cultural hero credited with creating the I Ching (Book of Changes) and the first writing</note> drew the trigrams, he opened the fountainhead of culture. When the **Yellow Emperor** <note>Huangdi, the legendary ancestor of the Chinese people; Taoism is often called the "Learning of Huang-Lao" after him and Laozi</note> established the nation, he set the celestial majesty of the Chinese people. Every establishment made was rooted entirely in the Way. 

Consider the vast array of human knowledge: astronomy and calendrical math, the harmony of <term>Yin and Yang</term> and musical scales, military strategy and criminal law, metallurgy and alchemy, medicine and painting, architecture and carving, and even the diplomatic arts of political maneuvering. In every instance of observing signs to create tools, or "opening up nature to accomplish tasks," most were products of the Taoist school. Its greatness is sufficient to encompass the specific focuses of all other schools and to oversee all the affairs of the world. Therefore, people say that where there is China, there is Taoism. The reason China became "China" is because the Taoists helped to form it. Before the **pre-Qin era** <note>the period before 221 BCE, considered the golden age of Chinese philosophy</note>, there was only Taoist culture. The various philosophers and the "Hundred Schools" all emerged from Taoism; like branches of a river drawing from the same water, each took one part to establish themselves. Therefore, without Taoist culture, there would be no Chinese culture. After the pre-Qin era, as various thinkers competed and a hundred schools Harmonized, if one examines their lineage, they ultimately do not stray from Taoism. A careful study of historical facts shows: when the Way flourishes, the nation prospers; when the Way declines, the nation is in peril! For thousands of years, the cycles of order and chaos, prosperity and decay, survival and ruin, have indeed followed this pattern without exception.

The academic teachings of Taoism, in summarizing their content, can be divided into eight lineages:

1. The <term>Lineage of Statecraft</term> <note>Jingshi Zong: focused on managing the world and social order</note>
2. The <term>Lineage of Nature and Life</term> <note>Xingming Zong: focused on spiritual cultivation and inner alchemy</note>
3. The <term>Lineage of Yin and Yang</term> <note>Cosmology and natural cycles</note>
4. The <term>Lineage of Diplomacy</term> <note>Zongheng Zong: the art of political maneuvering and alliances</note>
5. The <term>Lineage of Military Strategy</term>
6. The <term>Lineage of Jurisprudence</term> <note>Fashu Zong: the "methods" and "standards" of governance</note>
7. The <term>Lineage of Penal Law and Logic</term> <note>Xingming Zong: relating to the "rectification of names" and legal punishments</note>
8. The <term>Lineage of Science and Technology</term>

Whether it is the principles of the birth and transformation of all things in the universe; the methods of governing the state and bringing peace to society; the cultivation of the sacred achievements and divine transformations of human life; the arts of astronomy, geography, and the changes of Yin and Yang; the strategies of diplomatic maneuvering; the applications of military plans, legal methods, and penal names; or the benefits of industry, agriculture, technology, and the chemistry of the forests and waters—all are encompassed within it. Thus, whether one speaks of the Confucians, Mohists, Cosmologists, Logicians, Legalists, or Diplomats, it can be said they all emerged from this source. 

Modern people sometimes seize upon the theory of **"pure emptiness and non-action"** <note>qingxu wu-wei</note> and criticize it as being "passive" or "negative." This is because they do not understand the highest universal and political principle: **"to act through non-action, so that nothing is left undone."** Within this principle, there exists an even more "active" and "positive" spirit!

<summary>Xiao Tianshi argues that Taoism is the singular source of all Chinese cultural and scientific achievements, from medicine to military strategy. He organizes Taoist thought into eight practical lineages to prove its relevance to statecraft and active life, rather than just passive meditation.</summary>

<keywords>Fuxi, Yellow Emperor, Eight Lineages of Taoism, Wu-wei, Chinese Cultural Origins, Pre-Qin Philosophy, Statecraft, Science and Technology in Taoism</keywords>

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument for Taoism’s practical utility. While the previous page categorized Taoism into eight functional branches to demonstrate its breadth, this page delves into the philosophical justification for "non-action" (wu-wei). It refutes the idea that Taoism is merely passive, arguing instead that "non-action" is a method for both internal self-cultivation and effective external governance, modeled on the spontaneous patterns of nature.</meta>

<page-num>3</page-num>

Furthermore, the Taoist principle of **"non-action and yet nothing is left undone"** is the Way of Heaven itself. Did not Confucius also say: "Does Heaven speak? The four seasons run their course, and the hundred things are born. What does it say?" <note>A quote from the Analects of Confucius, illustrating that the highest power operates through silent, natural processes rather than overt command.</note> Heaven and Earth practice non-action, yet the four seasons move on their own, the hundred things are born of themselves, the sun and moon shine of their own accord, and cold and heat complete themselves—it is essentially nothing more than purely allowing nature to take its course! Therefore, **"non-action through following nature"** is the Way of Heaven. To establish the Way of Man based on the Way of Heaven, to establish the Way of the World based on the Way of Heaven, and to establish the Way of Governance based on the Way of Heaven—there is nothing for which this is not suitable.

To put it simply, **"non-action"** is the means by which one governs the <term>inner nature</term> <note>xin-xing: a term referring to the union of the heart-mind and the essential nature of a human being</note>; while **"non-action and yet nothing is left undone"** is the means by which one governs external affairs and objects. If the inner nature is not governed, then one's actions will struggle to find their proper fit, and affairs will consequently fall into disorder. This principle is perfectly clear and requires no further debate. 

Therefore, it is said that "non-action and yet nothing is left undone" also carries the meaning of "wishing to be established oneself, one seeks to establish others; wishing to be successful oneself, one seeks to help others be successful." <note>This is a famous Confucian quote, here used by the author to show that Taoist "non-action" actually fulfills the highest social ethics.</note> This is the principle of extending oneself to others, and it is the essential achievement of **"Inner Sageliness and Outer Governance"** or <term>Inner Sageliness and Outer Kingship</term> <note>nei-sheng wai-wang: the ideal of a ruler who possesses the internal virtue of a saint and the external skill of a monarch</note>. The *Book of Changes* says: "Exhaustively study principles, completely fulfill one's nature, and thereby reach the core of destiny." The mind and nature are the root of the person; the person is the root of the world and the nation. 

Thus, when the **Grand Historian** <note>Sima Qian, the legendary historian who first categorized the philosophical schools of China</note> discussed the essential tenets of the Six Schools, he also stated: "The spirit is the root of life; the physical form is the tool of life. If one does not first settle the root, yet claims to have the means to govern the world, by what means can they do so?" **Yi Yin** <note>A legendary sage-minister of the early Shang Dynasty</note>, when answering King Tang’s question about "how to take the world," also said: "The root of every matter must first be the cultivation of the person. Be frugal with the great treasure <note>Referring to one's vital energy and spirit</note>, utilize what is renewed, and discard the stale." 

From this, we know that the "non-action" of the Taoists consists in following the Way of Heaven to establish the Way of Man. On a large scale, it is used to govern the world and the state; on a small scale, it is the means of **nourishing life**. The essential point of nourishing life lies in internally governing the body, mind, nature, and life, and externally governing the world and the state. It is not merely about an individual transcending the mundane to become a sage, or transcending the sage to become divine! 

Therefore, the reason Taoists emphasize the **"dual cultivation of nature and life"** and the **"simultaneous nourishment of the internal and external"** is the hope of advancing in virtue and cultivating one's work, and "opening up nature to accomplish tasks." It involves harmonizing with the divine to transform, transforming to generate life, growing and nurturing it—constantly changing without remaining fixed, with a divine way that is unfathomable, yet suitable for everything. 

It is only that **"when the superior man finds his time, he drives forth; if he does not find his time, he remains in seclusion."** Whether to serve or to withdraw, whether to act or to hide, he follows only the Way; he is not anxious to be used by the world, nor does he scramble for fame and profit! People of the world fail to observe this, often regarding Taoists as individualists or practitioners of passivity. Their distance from the core of Taoism...

It moves from the philosophical justification of "non-action" to a historical and syncretic argument, asserting that Taoism, Confucianism, and Buddhism share a common root and ultimate goal: the elevation of human character and the preservation of life.</meta>

<page-num>4</page-num>

intent is off by thousands upon thousands of miles; furthermore, it is no different from cutting off the very foundation by which one establishes oneself, others, the nation, and the world—as well as the grand enterprise of establishing a **"Taoist Universe"** for a thousand autumns and ten thousand generations.

In antiquity, the *Bibliographical Treatise of the Book of Han* <note>The *Hanshu Yiwenzhi*, the earliest surviving catalog of Chinese literature, which categorized various schools of thought.</note> described the Taoists as "grasping the essentials and holding to the root, maintaining themselves through clarity and void, and upholding themselves through humility and weakness." It noted that they were "in accord with the yielding and modesty of the sage-kings Yao and Shun, and the 'Modesty' hexagram of the *Book of Changes*." It is clear, then, that Taoism does not focus solely on passivity as its goal, nor is it concerned only with the perfection of the self. Furthermore, while the Confucians trace their lineage to Yao and Shun, and the Taoists trace theirs to the **Yellow Emperor and Laozi**, if one investigates their ultimate purpose, there is actually no difference. All things come from one root though they have ten thousand variations; ten thousand variations return to one root. Whether exploring the source or tracing the stream, Confucianism is Taoism, and Taoism is Confucianism. Likewise, Confucianism and Taoism are Zen Buddhism, and Zen Buddhism is Confucianism and Taoism. Within that which can be divided, there remains that which cannot be divided; this is precisely what **Zhuangzi** <note>The influential Taoist philosopher known for his wit and focus on spontaneity.</note> meant by "perceiving the divided as one." Those who distinguish between "you" and "me" based on external forms are merely small-minded men! The world occasionally slanders the Taoist doctrine of **"Divine Immortality"**, but in reality, this is merely a name. Like the "Sage" of the Confucians or the "Buddha" of the Buddhists, these are all ways to represent the highest state of human cultivation. Because it is human nature to love life and hate death, the Sages utilized this inclination to guide people toward the cultivation of their body, mind, <term>inner nature and life-force</term> <note>xing-ming: the dual focus of Taoist practice, involving both spiritual temperament and physical vitality</note>, and morality, thereby elevating their human character.

> Thus, when the *Bibliographical Treatise of the Book of Han* introduced the School of Divine Immortals, it stated: "The practitioners of Immortality are those who preserve the truth of nature and life to wander in the external world. They do so to soothe the will and calm the heart, equalizing the realms of life and death so that no fear or anxiety dwells within the breast." It further noted: "If the confused make this their sole preoccupation, then deceitful and strange writings will multiply, which is not what the Sages intended to teach."

Viewed from this perspective, it is evident that the true meaning lies elsewhere! This is something today's scholars must clearly distinguish so that they do not miss the target. I often say: "The study of Immortality uses the study of Sageliness as its starting point. The Way of the Immortal uses the Way of the Human as its foundation." If one wishes to cultivate the Way of the Immortal, one must begin by cultivating the path of the **Sage**! After transcending the mundane and entering sageliness, one then practices the work of divine transformation, aiming to enter the realm of "Unity with Heaven" and "Unity with the Tao." This is the core principle of the **"New Taoist Studies"** that I advocate: the revival of Chinese Taoist culture to save the world and humanity.

<meta>This page provides a historical overview of the compilation and expansion of the Taoist Canon (Daozang) from the Han Dynasty through the early Republican era. It emphasizes the sheer volume of these works and laments that their complexity and the tradition’s secrecy have caused Taoist scholarship to fall behind Confucianism and Buddhism in the modern age.</meta>

<page-num>5</page-num>

Upon examining the Taoist classics recorded in the *Bibliographical Treatise of the Book of Han*: the Taoist school—ranging from the **Yellow Emperor**, Yi Yin, Jiang Ziya, and **Laozi** downwards—consisted of only thirty-seven families and nine hundred and ninety-three volumes. The discourse on "Divine Immortals" comprised only ten families and two hundred and five volumes. These numbers increased successively in later eras. By the time of the *Treatise of the Sui Dynasty* <note>The *Suishu Jingjizhi*, a major 7th-century bibliographic record.</note>, the collection had already reached as many as three hundred and seventy-seven categories and 1,216 volumes. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang Dynasty, the superfluous was removed and the weeds were cleared to organize the books into a formal "Treasury" (Canon), titled the <term>Three Caverns and Precious Records</term> <note>Sandong Qionggang: an early name for the organized Taoist Canon</note>, which reached 3,744 volumes.

In the Song Dynasty, the collection once grew to over seven thousand volumes. After the scholars Xu Xuan and others performed a critical collation to remove redundancies, 3,737 volumes remained. The general outline was divided into the **"Three Caverns, Four Supplements, and Twelve Categories."** <note>The traditional structural classification of the Taoist Canon.</note> In the early years of the Dazhong Xiangfu era, Emperor Zhenzong ordered the Hanlin Scholar Chen Yaozuo and others to specialize in its revision and proofreading; combining these with newly recorded works, the total reached 4,359 volumes. Later, Zhang Yunfang further evaluated the details and categorized the differences, arranging them into a complete Canon totaling 4,565 volumes. By the Chongning and Daguan eras, the Great Canon had increased again to 5,387 volumes. The *Comprehensive Examination of Literature* <note>The *Wenxian Tongkao*, a massive encyclopedia compiled by Ma Duanlin.</note> describes the volumes of the Song Dynasty Taoist Canon in great detail. 

Later, during the Yuan Dynasty, the monk Piyunzi carved the Taoist Canon in Pingyang Prefecture, totaling over 7,800 volumes. Moving to the Zhengtong and Wanli eras of the Ming Dynasty, the collection was compiled and revised successively, totaling five hundred and twelve cases and 5,485 volumes. Aside from these two editions, the Ming Canon also featured a "pocket-sized" edition newly carved during the sixth year of the Tianqi era <note>1626 CE</note>. These are all rare and secret texts seldom seen by book collectors. Scholars of the Qianlong and Jiaqing periods in the Qing Dynasty mostly relied on these to proofread and correct common editions. During the Tongzhi era, another round of repairs and supplements was undertaken. Finally, in the early years of the Republic, when **Xu Shichang** served as President, he ordered the Minister of Education, **Fu Zengxiang**, to borrow the Taoist Canon from the <term>White Cloud Temple</term> <note>Baiyun Guan: a prominent Taoist temple in Beijing</note> in Tianjin. It was reduced to a lithographic six-page format for reprinting; the transition from the "Sutra-style" concertina binding to the "Square-book" format <note>Transitioning from traditional scrolls/folded sheets to modern bound books.</note> actually began here. 

This is a general summary of the origins and development of the **Taoist Canon**. One can catch a glimpse of the richness of these books from this account. Even regarding the *Essentials of the Taoist Canon* <note>The *Daozang Jiyao*, a refined selection of the most important texts.</note>, although it reaches as many as two hundred and eighty-two types and over eight hundred volumes, it still fails to exhaust the profound mysteries! Even if a reader puts in years and months of effort, they would have no way to distinguish the refined from the crude or to grasp the orthodox lineage. Consequently, people collectively fear the difficulty and shrink back, "gazing at the ocean and stopping" in frustration. Coupled with the traditional habit of keeping teachings secret and being self-enclosed, the promotion of Taoist academic study has fallen far behind that of Confucianism and Buddhism. This is truly a great cause for sorrow.

At this time, when human desires are overflowing and the nation is no longer a nation, the high development of Western science, technology, and material civilization is such that it makes humanity daily...

It is especially noted for the heights of the spiritual realms it marks, which surpass those of the ancients. It integrates the changes of past and present, converges the origins of a myriad of schools, exhausts the transformations of the human and the divine, and connects the tradition of the "One Thread." <note>A reference to a unified, consistent truth or lineage underlying diverse teachings.</note> If one views this with the "Eye of the Dao," its divine utility—though it may pass through ten thousand generations—can still be "renewed daily" and remain immortal.

As formal historians have said, "The words of Huang-Lao filled the world" and "The followers of Huang-Lao filled the world." Tracing back to before the Pre-Qin period, what was called "Chinese Culture" was, in fact, "Taoist Culture." Examining previous histories...

By using Laozi’s words: **"Great completion seems incomplete, yet its use is never exhausted. Great fullness seems empty, yet its use is never-ending. Great straightness seems crooked. This means that to <gloss>cling</gloss> is to die, while not clinging is to live. Can the Way be easily described? Because it is that by which Heaven is Heaven and the Universe is the Universe—and because it was born before Heaven and Earth and can be the Mother of Heaven and Earth—it cannot be shaped by words or writing. # Preface to Xiao’s Compendium of Daoist Essentials

### Cao Zheshi

The Daoist philosophers <term>Daojia|The philosophical tradition associated with figures like Laozi and Zhuangzi</term> take their name from the Dao; the Daoist religion <term>Daojiao|The organized religious tradition involving rituals and deities</term> establishes its teachings upon the Dao; Daoist scholarship <term>Daoxue|The academic and theoretical study of Daoist principles</term> centers its study on the Dao; and the Daoist scriptures <term>Daojing|The vast body of written works and canons</term> name their collection after the Dao. Everything, without exception, is centered upon the Dao. 

Expanding upon this, the academic and spiritual thoughts of China’s "Three Teachings"—Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism—as well as those of other major world religions, may use different terminology and profess different beliefs, yet their ultimate destination and final realm, when unified through the Dao, are largely the same. All take the "Dao" <note>The Way</note> as their core, with the primary aims of believing in the Dao, practicing the Dao, transmitting the Dao, and preaching the Dao. Adherents follow this throughout their lives, remaining committed even unto death without regret! The intent is to remain consistent from beginning to end, using the Dao to establish a lineage, to transform the world, to transform humanity, and to transform all living beings under heaven for ten thousand generations. 

Laozi <note>The legendary founder of Daoism and author of the Dao De Jing</note> said: "Within the realm, there are four greats, and humanity dwells as one of them." These four greats are: "The Dao is great, Heaven is great, Earth is great, and humanity is also great" (Note 1). He also said: "Humanity follows Earth, Earth follows Heaven, Heaven follows the Dao, and the Dao follows nature <term>ziran|Literally "self-so," referring to the spontaneous and natural state of the universe</term>." 

These five—Dao, Heaven, Earth, Humanity, and Nature—are "unified by a single thread." Furthermore, that which "was born before Heaven and Earth" and yet "can be the mother of Heaven and Earth" (Note 2) is truly the "ineffable" <note>original: "bukeshuo bukeshuo," a term used to describe truths that exceed the capacity of language</note> "Primordial Unified Breath" <term>Hunyuan Yiqi|The undifferentiated, original energy of the universe before the division into Yin and Yang</term>, which is also the "Pre-celestial Breath" <term>Xiantian Qi|The vital energy existing before physical form or birth</term>. 

This thing-less thing, this formless form, this breath-less breath, this void-less void—it cannot be named, so it is forced to be called "○": zero, nothingness, the "Limitless" <term>Wuji|The ultimate state of nothingness before the creation of the universe</term> that existed before things, before Heaven and Earth began. This is exactly what the ancient realized masters <term>Guzhen|Literally "Ancient True Ones," referring to perfected or immortal beings</term> meant by: "There is a thing that preceded Heaven and Earth, continuously generating and returning to Primordial Chaos." 

This refers to the pre-celestial realm <term>Xiantian Jingjie|A state of existence prior to physical manifestation or ego</term> of the "self" as it was before all things were born, before all thoughts moved, and even before one's parents were born. This "selfless self, this formless form," along with "the thing-less thing, the image-less image, the thought-less thought, and the heart-less heart," is the pre-celestial realm. It is what the ancient realized masters called: "There is a thing that preceded Heaven and Earth; it is formless and inherently silent; it can be the master of all things, and does not wither with the passing of the four seasons." It transcends Heaven and Earth, transcends—

<summary>In this preface, Cao Zheshi introduces the "Dao" as the ultimate, ineffable source of all religion and philosophy, describing it as a pre-celestial state of nothingness (Wuji) that precedes the creation of the universe.</summary>

<keywords>Dao, Laozi, Hunyuan Yiqi, Wuji, Pre-celestial realm, Cao Zheshi, Three Teachings</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "Dao" from the previous page, moving from its cosmic origins to the internal "heart-ground" of the practitioner. It discusses the necessity of transmitting this wordless truth through generations.</meta>

<page-num>11</page-num>

...cosmic realm. In Daoist terms, this is the pre-celestial heart-ground realm <term>Xiantian Xindi Jingjie|The fundamental, original state of the mind before it is influenced by external perceptions or desires</term>, also known as the "○" zero realm, the realm of the "no-realm." When one cultivates until "the single heart is clear and unmoving, and the ten thousand thoughts are silent and unborn," then Immortals, Buddhas, Sages, God, and the ten thousand spirits cannot exert any power over you. At that moment, you can "stand alone and be uniquely honored!" 

In the past, Mencius <note>A foundational Confucian philosopher</note> took the "unmoving heart" as his teaching, and the Sixth Patriarch <note>Huineng, a pivotal figure in Chan/Zen Buddhism</note> of the Chan School took "no-thought" as his principle. This realm of the "eight nothings"—no heart, no thought, no desire, no person, no self, no thing, no form, and no realm—is precisely the realm of "Unifying with the Dao" <note>original: "Yu Dao He Yi"</note> that the Hermit Elder <note>A pseudonym for the author or his teacher</note> proclaims and advocates. 

This realm of "Unifying with the Dao" stands far above the realms of "Unity of Heaven and Humanity" or "Unity of God and Humanity." This pre-celestial heart-ground realm is also "the Heaven and Earth where there is no Heaven and Earth, the realm where there is no realm." It is at once nothingness and existence, existence and nothingness. This can only be understood in silence and realized through the heart and soul; it cannot be described or discussed through language or writing. To open one's mouth is to err; to deliberate is to stray. This is why the Buddha preached the Law for forty-nine years, yet in the end claimed he had not spoken a single word. This is because any "Law" that can be spoken is not the eternal Law <note>original: "Fei Fa," a reference to the Diamond Sutra stating that fixed teachings are not the ultimate truth</note>. 

Understand it in silence, connect to it in silence, transmit it in silence, and receive it in silence. This "untransmitted transmission" and "unreceived reception" is also "no transmission and no reception." This is truly the supreme heart-method of the "heart-to-heart imprint" <term>Xinxin Xiangyin|A direct, non-verbal transmission of spiritual truth from master to student</term> passed down by the sages since ancient times. 

Does the *Book of Changes* <note>The text attributes this to the I Ching, though it famously appears in the Analects of Confucius</note> not say: "What does Heaven say? The four seasons move, and the hundred things are born! What does Heaven say?" This is the sacred teaching of Confucius, who taught people "no-speech" and "non-action" <term>wuwei|The Daoist principle of effortless action or acting in alignment with the natural flow</term>, allowing them to awaken themselves, act for themselves, grow themselves, and do for themselves, while leaving everything to "nature" <term>ziran|Spontaneity or the "self-so" state of the universe</term>. 

However, since ancient times, the thousands of worthy ones and sages still could not refrain from speaking. This is because the Law cannot be allowed to vanish, and the Dao cannot go untransmitted. We must inherit from what came before and pass it to what comes after. Since I have inherited something from those before me, I must provide an account for those who follow. If I do not transmit it, and the lineage of the Dao is broken by me, then "what will later generations have to recount?" <note>A quote from the Book of Songs</note> My sin would be great indeed. To inherit from those above and open the way for those below—to make the sacred lineage continue for millions of years without end—is this not a joy! 

This is why the Hermit Elder of Wenshan once changed a few words of a famous poem by Chen Zi'ang <note>A Tang Dynasty poet</note> so that the flavor of the Dao shines through. It says: "Above, I can connect with the ancients; below, I can connect with those yet to come; mindful of the vastness of Heaven and Earth, I alone am tranquil and find joy within." (Note: the word "connect" here refers to the continuity of transmission...)

<summary>This page describes the "pre-celestial heart-ground" as a state of "nothingness" that transcends religious boundaries, emphasizing that while the Dao is wordless, it must be recorded and transmitted to ensure the continuity of the sacred lineage.</summary>

<keywords>Heart-ground, Zero Realm, Eight Nothings, Heart-to-heart imprint, Wuwei, Ziran, Lineage Transmission, Chen Zi'ang</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the transmission of the Dao, contrasting the Daoist approach with Confucianism and Buddhism. It moves from the concept of spiritual continuity to the specific practical stages of Daoist internal alchemy.</meta>

<page-num>13</page-num>

...to connect with them.) <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page regarding the poet Chen Zi'ang's work.</note> If you study and savor this carefully, you will understand the difference between the Daoist school and the Confucian school, as well as the difference between the Buddhist school and the hundreds of other teachings. When I connect with those above and below, past and present, uniting ten thousand generations into **"one consistent thread,"** <note>original: "Yi Yi Guan Zhi," a famous phrase from the Analects of Confucius, meaning a single principle that unifies all knowledge</note> then what joy could compare to that?

Laozi <note>The legendary founder of Daoism</note> once said: "He who dies but does not perish enjoys longevity." 

The Hermit Elder also often says:

->“Even if one lives a thousand years, who can escape death? Better to leave behind a divine light to illuminate the past and present!”<-

This should be contemplated carefully, for there is a deep meaning within it.

As for what is called <term>Daojia Gongfu|The specific practices, disciplines, and internal arts associated with the Daoist path</term>, among the hundred schools of thought it can be described as "the most vast and most high-minded, the most simple and most profound." Among the hundred schools, none can compare. To speak plainly of its initial purpose, it lies in—saving oneself to save others, establishing oneself to establish others, transforming oneself to transform others, and delivering oneself to deliver others. One cannot establish others without first establishing oneself; one cannot deliver others without first delivering oneself; and one cannot transform others—let alone transform the world for ten thousand generations—without first transforming oneself! 

Based on this fundamental principle, the highest realm of life cultivation and practice held by the Daoist school is the "Heaven-Human realm" and the "Divine-Human realm," which stand above the realm of the Sages or the Bodhisattvas <note>Enlightened beings in Buddhism who delay their own nirvana to help others</note>. It is exactly what the world calls: 

->"To be great and transformed is called a Sage; to be a Sage and yet be unknowable is called Divine."<-

This is the realm of the Immortals <term>Xian|Transcendent beings who have achieved longevity and spiritual perfection through cultivation</term>: "When a person can communicate with the divine, and the divine transformation has no fixed direction, unpredictable to all spirits, appearing and disappearing at will, and perfectly penetrating the universe." A person in this realm is not only "a companion to Heaven" and "a companion to the Divine," but is also **"Unified with the Dao"** and **"Unified with Nature,"** becoming the "Mother of Heaven, Earth, all things, spirits, and humanity." This is why the Daoist school can encompass ten thousand schools with a single "Dao," for the ten thousand schools have always been walking within the Dao from the beginning.

The reason the Daoist school can reach this realm is by no means through empty words or "Utopian" ideals; it is because "He who dies but does not perish enjoys longevity"—the spirit lives eternally with the Dao. Furthermore, in its practice of cultivation, there exists the "unpredictable and divine" realm of the Immortals. To put it simply, these are the five great stages of cultivation and realization known to the world as: 

1. **Refining Essence into Breath-Energy** <note>original: "Lian Jing Hua Qi"</note> 
2. **Refining Breath-Energy into Spirit** <note>original: "Lian Qi Hua Shen"</note>
3. **Refining Spirit to return to Emptiness** <note>original: "Lian Shen Huan Xu"</note>
4. **Refining Emptiness to join with the Dao** <note>original: "Lian Xu He Dao"</note>
5. **Unifying with the Dao** <note>original: "Yu Dao He Yi"</note>

This is not merely a theoretical claim. Moreover, this skill goes far beyond the Confucian concept of "transforming one’s temperament" <note>The Confucian goal of refining one's character and physical disposition through study and ritual</note>...

<summary>This page distinguishes Daoism from other schools by its pursuit of the "Immortal" realm and outlines the five practical stages of internal alchemy required to unify with the Dao.</summary>

...and it stands above the realm of **"Sanctifying Human Life,"** as well as above the Buddhist realm of <term>Nirvana|The state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth</term>. If a student can move beyond the realm of mere language and text, and instead keep their heels firmly on the ground—practicing the cultivation step-by-step—then during the process of the **"Realm of Transformation"** <note>original: "Huajing." The author notes this is not a term used in the Zen school, but specific to this internal alchemical process</note>, they will naturally experience a spiritual journey of "self-knowing and self-clarification, self-seeing and self-realization, self-awakening and self-attainment, self-transformation and self-deliverance." As the saying goes, it is **"like a person drinking water; only they know if it is cold or warm."** <note>A famous Buddhist idiom expressing that spiritual experience must be felt personally and cannot be fully described to others</note> Unless one has personally traveled this path, it is difficult to truly affirm it. This is because it is not a "castle in the air," something to be gazed at but never reached. In this realm, the heart knows itself, the original nature sees itself, and the spirit illuminates itself.

->“Uniting Heaven and Earth, making life and death as one! Exhausting the universe, leaving behind a single stream of light!”<-

Truly, words and writing cannot describe even a ten-thousandth part of this state.

I and <term>Dun Sou|The Hermit Elder; a respectful title for Xiao Tianshi (1909–1986), a prominent scholar and the founder of the Freedom Press</term> have jointly managed the **Freedom Press** <note>A significant publishing house in Taiwan dedicated to preserving traditional Chinese philosophy and Daoist texts</note>, laboring silently and remaining committed to the Dao from beginning to end. For thirty years, we have worked as if it were a single day, without a single word of discord. Did the ancient sages not say:

->“Seek the Dao, not a salary; seek the Dao, not profit; seek the Dao, not fame; seek the Dao without needing others to know.”<-

For those who seek the Dao are "disciples of Heaven" and "disciples of the Dao." They must be able to transcend the mundane world and, as Laozi did, "make their business to remain hidden and nameless." How could they be willing to drift with the tide of the world, bowing to the times, or competing for wealth, rank, and fame? Though they live in the world, they are able to transcend it: **"The person is a person of the world, but the heart is a heart of the world beyond."** They remain unstained by a single speck of dust, silent and unmoving. Although occasionally a "mind of weeds" <note>An idiom for messy thoughts or worries</note> may arise, it is only out of concern that the Dao is not being practiced, that the Dao is not being spread, or that the lineage of the Dao is not being continued! 

The Hermit Elder is not only like this, but he also possesses a heart that **"worries for the Dao, but does not worry about life or death."** For the sake of the "Revival of Chinese Culture," the Hermit Elder edited the *Great Collection of Masterworks of Chinese Philosophy*, a massive set of one hundred volumes containing several hundred types of rare editions and precious texts. For over four years, he worked without sleep or rest, which violated the health preservation principle that <term>The Dao follows Nature|Dao Fa Zi Ran; the fundamental Daoist principle that one should act in accordance with the spontaneous flow of the natural world</term>. This resulted in a serious illness lasting over a year, in which he nearly died twice. He believed that preserving the <term>Daotong|The 'Orthodox Lineage' or 'Sacred Pulse' of the Dao; the continuous transmission of spiritual truth through the ages</term> for a thousand generations was far more important than an individual’s hundred-year lifespan. He once said:

->“A thousand-year-old fox, even if it does not die, is still just a thousand-year-old fox.”<-

If a person merely lives a stolen life, seeking only to prolong their days and achieve immortality for their own sake, how are they any different from a thousand-year-old fox? The Hermit Elder has always taken the historical mission of organizing, preserving, and reviving Chinese culture as his personal responsibility, and because of this, he is able to set aside...

<summary>The author describes the "Realm of Transformation" as a personal spiritual experience and praises his colleague, the Hermit Elder, for sacrificing his health to publish and preserve the sacred lineage of Chinese philosophy.</summary>

...he sets aside his own concerns of life and death. If he were to merely use Daoist techniques to prolong his years or achieve longevity—clinging to a "stolen life" or a shameful existence—it is not that he does not know how to do so, but rather that he refuses to do so. This is exactly what the Hermit Elder meant when he said:

->“One should set aside natural, physical life, and allow the cosmic life to flow into the infinite. Use the brilliance of cultural life to shine the light of historical life into eternity.”<-

How profound these words are! Because of this conviction, even while he was just beginning to recover from a major illness and was not yet fully restored to health, he was still willing to put all his effort into working with me at the **Freedom Press** to complete the organization, supplementation, and revision of this peerless masterpiece: the **"Newly Edited Essentials of the Daoist Canon"** <note>original: "Xinbian Daozang Jinghua." A massive compilation of the most important texts from the Daoist Canon, curated by Xiao Tianshi to make them more accessible to modern scholars.</note>. He did this so that these books, which have not been transmitted for ages, could be **"stored in famous mountains and passed to the right person"** <note>A traditional Chinese expression meaning to preserve sacred knowledge in a safe place until a worthy student or successor is found</note> without the lineage being broken. This is truly a great fortune. Life and death are a "great matter"; when it comes to the moment of choosing one's path, how could one not be careful? Since he is willing to sacrifice his own body for the Dao, what more can I say?

Readers might say: “The selection of this collection is so strict, its scope so rich, and its quality so broad and excellent that, since ancient times, it is truly a sight to behold. However, because the source editions vary, it could truly be called: **‘Xiao’s Patchwork Edition of the Essentials of the Daoist Canon’** <note>original: "Bainaben." This refers to a "patchwork" or "monk’s robe" edition, which is a scholarly term for a book compiled from various different historical editions to create the most complete version possible.</note> to match its reality.”

These words are very appropriate. When the Hermit Elder heard this, he also deeply agreed. Furthermore, if one examines the content of the entire collection, although it covers a hundred schools and ten thousand sects, omitting nothing great or small, a detailed audit of its contents confirms what <term>Wang Bi|Also known by his courtesy name Fusi (226–249 CE); a brilliant young philosopher who revolutionized the study of the I Ching and the Dao De Jing</term> wrote in the preface to his classic work, **"General Remarks on the Changes"**:

->“The many cannot govern the many; the one who governs the many is the most singular. Motion cannot control motion; the one who controls the motion of the world is the one who remains steadfast in the One. Therefore, the reason the many are able to exist together is that their master must reach the One. The reason motion is able to operate is that its source must be non-dual.”<-

He continued, saying:

->“To unify them there is a principle; to gather them there is an origin. Therefore, they are complex but not chaotic, numerous but not confusing.”<-

How profound are these words! Although the Hermit Elder’s *Essentials of the Daoist Canon* records every school and misses no branch, he clearly understands the intent of Fusi (Wang Bi). By remaining steadfast in the **"One"** and attaining the "One," then <term>Maintaining the One|Shou Yi; a fundamental Daoist meditation practice involving focusing the mind on a single point or the primordial unity of the Dao</term> allows one to govern the ten thousand things, and staying in the center allows one to control the circle.

Moreover, if one can be steadfast in the One, they can naturally **“unify with a principle and gather with an origin.”** Thus, the work is **“complex but not chaotic, numerous but not confusing.”** Fusi was deeply versed in the *Changes* <note>The I Ching or Book of Changes</note>; his method of "sweeping away the images" was derived from the principle of "simplicity" found in the *Changes*, as well as the Teacher’s <note>Referring to Confucius</note> instruction: **“My Way is bound together by one thing.”** To be "bound by one thing" means to use the "One" to thread through everything. (Note 4)

...the Orthodox Lineage of Chinese Culture, from the great **"Book of Changes"** downward, can all be **“bound together by one thing”** <note>original: "Yi yi guan zhi." A famous phrase from the Analects of Confucius, suggesting that a single principle underlies all his teachings.</note>. This is also true of **“Xiao’s Patchwork Edition of the Essentials of the Daoist Canon.”** The reason it is able to be **“complex but not chaotic, numerous but not confusing”** is that it is **“unified by a principle and gathered at the origin.”** Therefore, even though the stars are scattered across a million scrolls and broadly encompass all categories, there is nothing that does not ultimately return to the **Dao**. I ask the brilliant scholars at home and abroad: do you agree with this assessment or not? This concludes the preface.

**Note 1**: In the common and widely circulated versions of the **"Laozi"** <note>The Dao De Jing</note>, it says: **“The Dao is great, Heaven is great, Earth is great, and the King is also great.”** However, in the Hermit Elder’s work, **“The Sacred Interpretation of Laozi’s Dao De Jing,”** he cites it as: **“Man is also great.”** The "Great" section of the **"Explaining Graphs and Analyzing Characters"** <note>The Shuowen Jiezi, the first Chinese dictionary</note> states: **“Heaven is great, Earth is great, and Man is also great.”** The commentary by <term>Duan Yucai|A famous Qing dynasty philologist (1735–1815) known for his exhaustive commentary on the Shuowen Jiezi</term> also says: **“Laozi says: The Dao is great, Heaven is great, Earth is great, and Man is also great... Man follows Earth, Earth follows Heaven, Heaven follows the Dao, and the Dao follows Nature.”** Thus, we follow the version found in the Hermit Elder's **“Sacred Interpretation.”**

**Note 2**: Common versions of the **"Laozi"** say: **“[The Dao] can be the Mother of the world.”** However, the **“Sacred Interpretation of the Dao De Jing”** says: **“[The Dao] can be the Mother of Heaven and Earth.”** According to the **“Collected Commentaries on the Dao De Jing”** (which includes notes from the Tang Emperor Xuanzong, Heshang Gong, Wang Bi, and Wang Pang), it cites Wang Bi’s note: **“Therefore, it can be the Mother of Heaven and Earth.”** Jiang Xichang also recognized that the ancient Wang Bi version used the word **“Earth.”** Fan Yingyuan’s edition is the same. For details, refer to the Hermit Elder’s **“Sacred Interpretation of the Dao De Jing.”**

**Note 3**: The **“Zero Realm”** <note>original: "〇零境界." This refers to the concept of the primordial void or the "Wuji" (Limitless), often represented by an empty circle (〇).</note> is a technical term within the **"Innate Daoist Studies."** This lineage stretches back to <term>Fuxi|The legendary first sage of China, credited with creating the Eight Trigrams</term> and **Laozi**. The Master of Innate Studies, <term>Shao Yong|Also known as Shao Yaofu (1011–1077); a Song dynasty philosopher who developed complex cosmological systems based on the I Ching</term>, and the Hermit Elder of Wenshan <note>Xiao Tianshi</note>, who is famous for transmitting **“Innate Daoist Studies”** in our time, both possess secret realizations of this concept. To explain it in detail is beyond the reach of language and writing; it is something that can be transmitted, but only through silent recognition and mental connection—then the Dao will naturally become clear.

**Note 4**: Refer to the book **“Elaborating the Subtle Meanings of the Chinese Daoist Orthodox Lineage”** written by the Hermit Elder of Wenshan.

# Explanatory Notes for the Newly Edited Essentials of the Daoist Canon

## The Hermit Elder of Wenshan, Xiao Tianshi

1. The primary objectives for selecting and publishing the **"Essentials of the Daoist Canon"** are twofold: first, to preserve our inherent cultural heritage to ensure its wide distribution; second, to organize and revitalize this heritage, aiming to restore **Daoist Culture**—one of the primary currents of our Chinese civilization. We hope to see it flourish in the coming century, allowing the Daoist spirit to reform the world and humanity, aiming for the "Dao-ification" <note>Transforming through the principles of the Dao</note> of life and the world. Regarding Daoist culture, we place particular emphasis on its academic thought and its <term>Separate Transmission|Esoteric or specialized lineages passed down outside of standard institutional religious structures</term>. Our criterion is to avoid the common or vulgar, aligning instead with the spirit of **"New Daoist Studies."**

The "Separate Transmission" of Daoism refers to the **Study of Immortality** practiced by the **School of Immortals**, which holds a unique banner in the history of world culture. It is also known globally as the **Alchemical Path** <note>original: "Dandao Xue"</note> of the **Golden Elixir School**, and is variously called the **Alchemical School**, the **Mysterious Sect**, or the **True Sect**. Its philosophical foundations originate from the **Study of the Changes** <note>The I Ching</note> dating back to <term>Fuxi|The legendary creator of the Eight Trigrams</term>. Within the various schools of the *I Ching*, the Daoist interpretation has long been lost to time; its remaining thread, "thin as a single strand of silk," can only be found preserved within the books of the Alchemical Sect.

Next in importance is the **"Method-Immortal Dao"** <note>original: "Fangxian Dao," an early form of Daoism focused on recipes, formulas, and techniques for longevity</note> which flourished from the time of the **Yellow Emperor** through the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods. Since the time of **Qin Shi Huang** and **Emperor Wu of Han**—who were both fond of the study of immortals and sought the path to immortality—this field has shared an indissoluble bond with imperial families, literati, scholars, and folk recluses alike. The aim of this study focuses entirely on an individual’s **"Inner Sagely Cultivation,"** <note>The process of internal spiritual and moral refinement</note> hoping to allow one to "flow with Heaven and Earth above and below, and share the same light as the sun and moon." Furthermore, it tasks the practitioner with "self-concealment and namelessness," transcending life, death, and the mundane world to "commune solely with the spirit of the universe" in the **"Limitless Realm."** <note>The Wuji realm</note>

Therefore, this study is truly the supreme philosophy of cultivation for human life. It could also be called a **"Sacred Philosophy of Life,"** enabling the brilliance of an individual’s life to reach its absolute peak. By beginning cultivation from the heart, one can truly ensure that **"the universe is in my hands, and the myriad transformations are in my heart."** How could it only be that the upper...

This includes the **Dual Cultivation of the Internal and External**, the simultaneous nourishment of virtue and the Dao, and the combination of active and still practices. ## 3. The Alchemical Classics of Various Sects Selected for This Book Are All Comprehensive and Complete.

From the orthodox lineage of Donghua <note>Refers to the lineage of the "Eastern Wall," tracing back to the primordial origins of the Dao</note> and the two patriarchs Zhong and Lü <term>Zhong-Lü|Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin, the legendary figures who refined the internal alchemy system</term> downwards, this collection includes everything essential to the Dao. It covers the Southern and Northern lineages, the Eastern and Western sects, and all other schools' teachings on the **Lesser Vehicle**, **Middle Vehicle**, and **Higher Vehicle** <note>These terms, borrowed from Buddhism, refer to the scope of practice: from personal health to universal spiritual liberation</note> of alchemy. Nothing has been omitted. The "thousand sects and ten thousand schools" are all contained within.

This ensures that those who only practice the Lesser Vehicle can still reap the benefits of health, longevity, and the healing of illness. Meanwhile, those who practice the Middle and Higher Vehicles may, through repeated study and reflection, attain the realms of "transcending the mundane to enter the sacred," "transcending the sacred to enter the divine," and "transcending the divine to enter the realm of transformation." Once one has merged with this transformation, one can become "One with the Void" and "wander with the Creator" <note>A reference to the philosopher Zhuangzi's idea of ultimate spiritual freedom</note>. As for the specific lineages and branches of the Daoist alchemical schools, I shall provide a detailed table and explanation elsewhere in this book; I will not dwell on them further here.

## 4. The Selection and Editing of This Book Followed the Strictest Standards, Regarding Both the Choice of Commentaries and the Verification of Source Texts.

The former was done to ensure a correct interpretation, while the latter was done to obtain the most authentic original texts. We have pruned away the redundant and removed the confused or contradictory elements, aiming to "strip away the skin to preserve the marrow" <note>To remove superficial layers to get to the core essence</note>. Our goal has been extreme refinement, ensuring that every word is a "pearl or jade" and every sentence contains supreme principle. 

Although the methods are secret transmissions, their formulas must be scientific and applicable—capable of being used, practiced, and cultivated. They serve as a "ladder and boat" <note>A metaphor for the tools needed to reach spiritual realization</note> for the study of the Dao and as a standard for the Sacred Teachings. Furthermore, they align with the Confucian goal of "rectifying the heart and making the intentions sincere to cultivate the self" and "exhausting principle and nature to reach one's destiny," ultimately attaining the sage-like state of "**Unity of Heaven and Humanity**." 

In Daoist terms, this can be called the realm of the **Immortal** <term>Shenxian|A perfected spiritual being who has achieved longevity or eternal life</term> or the realm of the **Realized Person** <term>Zhenren|A 'True Person' who has reached the pinnacle of Daoist cultivation</term>. At the ultimate level, the realm of the "Divine Person" stands even above the realms of the Sages and the Buddhas. Thus, the writings of the more than one hundred authors selected here represent the Great Way of the world, the most extraordinary literature of the world, the supreme principles of the world, and the most righteous meanings of the world.

## 5. The Cultivation of Body, Mind, Nature, and Life Discussed in This Book Is Entirely Based on "Taking Virtue as the Foundation and Practice as the Application."

Both virtue and **Practice** <term>Gongfu|The dedicated effort, skill, and time invested in spiritual or physical cultivation</term> rely entirely on self-cultivation—that is, they rely completely on vigorous, practical action. Devoting oneself to this morning and night, month after month, and year after year, one must persist without ceasing. Like a hen sitting on her eggs <note>A classic Daoist metaphor for the constant, gentle "warmth" of meditative focus required for spiritual gestation</note>, when the time is right, one can naturally "refine iron into steel," "shed the mortal womb," and "release the spirit." One must understand that there is absolutely nothing impossible in this world; it only depends on how one puts it into practice! Otherwise, even if one’s innate potential is sharp and powerful, there will be no way to "attain the fruit" <note>Achieve the final result of practice</note>; even if one’s intellectual understanding is penetrating, there will be no way to enter the Dao. 

The myriad realms of experience rely entirely on one’s own personal realization. If one merely reads the words of others or listens to their talk—even if one seems to see it, understand it, or even "awaken" to it—one is still separated from the truth by ten thousand heavy mountains. The **Alchemy** <term>Liandan|The process of "refining the elixir," which in this context refers to Internal Alchemy (Neidan) rather than external chemistry</term> of the Daoist school focuses on refining life-force, refining the heart-mind, refining the inner nature, refining the breath, and refining the spirit. The word "**Refine**" <note>original: 煉 (liàn)</note> is chosen with the utmost precision; it is most worthy of deep appreciation and contemplation! In cultivating the mind, the nature, the life-force, and the state of the Immortal, the most critical work lies in this single step. One must move forward one step at a time; not the slightest bit can be skipped over. In these matters, there is only the achievement that comes from following the sequence and practicing gradually; there is absolutely no logic by which "instant enlightenment" can lead to immediate success. Remember this! Remember this!

The practice taught in this book resides entirely within the single heart-mind. At the beginning of cultivation, one must first give rise to a heart of sincerity, strengthen one's faith, establish perseverance, and nurture patience. Basing one’s efforts on the spirit of "the Old Fool who moved the mountains" <note>A famous Chinese fable about a man who, through sheer persistence, moved two great peaks that blocked his path</note>, persisting to the very end and progressing without ceasing, the highest realms of becoming an Immortal, a Buddha, or a Sage can finally be achieved. Only when a person’s alchemical practice reaches the realm of "miraculous transformation" do they truly witness that there is "another heaven and earth" beyond the mundane world.

## 7. The List of Titles Selected for This Book Includes Over a Thousand Works, Generally Chosen from Rare and Precious Volumes of Chinese Culture and Ten Thousand Volumes of Alchemical Scriptures. 

Among these, many consist of several types of texts compiled and published together under a new title; in other cases, a primary work is used as the title. ## 8. The Daoist Classics Selected for This Book Are Mostly "Secret Scriptures Not Transmitted for a Thousand Years, and Extraordinary Books Undying for Ten Thousand Generations." 

The standard for selection is based entirely on whether a work can provide "actual Dao and actual cultivation, actual learning and actual application, actual contemplation and actual refinement, and actual experimentation and actual proof." Among the ten thousand volumes of **Alchemical Scriptures** <term>Danjing|Textual records detailing the methods of Daoist alchemy and spiritual transformation</term>, the very first step is simply to teach people to "be a decent and honest person in their proper role." Only after completing this **Sagely Work** <note>original: 聖功 (shènggōng)</note> does one begin to cultivate from the level of a Sage upward; only then can one achieve the result of "returning to simplicity and perfecting the authentic self." Therefore, the ancient realized masters often said:

-> "Only a Sage is permitted to become an Immortal, <-
-> Yet even after reaching Sagehood, one is still separated by the gate of the One Vehicle." <-
<note>This couplet emphasizes that moral perfection (Sagehood) is the necessary foundation for spiritual transcendence (Immortalhood), but they are distinct stages of development.</note>

Because of this, all the Daoist books selected here can be read entirely as works of **Sagely Learning** <term>Shengxue|The study of the path to becoming a Sage, often overlapping with Confucian and Daoist ethics</term>; furthermore, they are works that everyone can learn, everyone can practice, and everyone can succeed in.

### 10. The books selected for this publication make no distinction between various sects and schools, provided they align with the true purpose of the teachings and reach the "Superior Vehicle." All are published together with equal status. This is to enable the reader to achieve a comprehensive understanding and see the thread that connects them all. Furthermore, within these various schools, the alchemical methods <term>Danfa|Internal alchemical practices involving the cultivation of essence, energy, and spirit</term> of the Superior, Middle, and Lower Vehicles are all included—excluding only those heterodox or "side-door" practices that might offend refined sensibilities. Our hope is that those with deep understanding can utilize the profound teachings, while those with a simpler grasp can utilize the basic ones; we leave the choice of what to adopt or discard to the readers themselves.

### 11. The books selected for this publication represent a breadth of collection, a variety of schools, and a rigor of editorial review that far surpasses any previous collection of Daoist scriptures. Chronologically, it spans from the Pre-Qin period through the Han, Tang, Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing dynasties, up to the present Republic era; any work of lasting renown has been selected. Finally, we intend to compile a *Dictionary of Daoist Studies*, using the most clear and concise language possible to explain the highly mystical terminology of Daoism and alchemical scriptures. This is intended to reduce the hardship of readers searching blindly in the dark, allowing them to achieve "understanding without a teacher." We hope they can investigate, cultivate, and realize the truth for themselves, thereby preventing the sacred lineage <term>Shengmai|The 'Sacred Pulse' or spiritual transmission of Daoist wisdom</term> from being extinguished.

### 12. Because the editor lives in a remote coastal corner, secluded in Wenshan <note>Literally "Literary Mountain"; likely a reference to a specific library or a poetic name for his place of retreat</note>, the scriptures that could be gathered are naturally limited. Some "lost pearls" may inevitably have been missed. Furthermore, as the materials have arrived, been reviewed, and undergone facsimile printing <term>Jingyin|A high-quality photographic reproduction process used to preserve the appearance of the original woodblocks or manuscripts</term> in successive batches, we have adopted the method of publishing in separate collections and volumes.

<summary>This page outlines the editorial philosophy of the collection, emphasizing a non-sectarian approach to "Superior Vehicle" alchemy and the compiler's intent to create a Daoist dictionary to aid self-study. It also notes the logistical reality of publishing the works in stages as rare manuscripts were acquired from remote locations.</summary>

<keywords>Maoshan, internal alchemy, Danfa, sectarianism, Superior Vehicle, Daoist Dictionary, sacred lineage, Wenshan, facsimile printing, editorial principles</keywords>
