# Essentials of the Daoist Canon, Series 7 (Third Edition Fine Print)

## The Seven Slips from the Cloudy Satchel: Ming Dynasty <term>Zhengtong</term> Daoist Canon Edition ⋯⋯⋯⋯ Authored and Compiled by the <term>Perfected</term> Zhang Junfang of the Song Dynasty. <note>The "Zhengtong" Canon refers to the definitive collection of Daoist texts compiled in 1445 during the Ming Dynasty. The "Seven Slips" is often called a "Miniature Daoist Canon" because it summarizes the most important knowledge of the era.</note>

## Essentials of the Song Dynasty Daoist Canon

1. This book was created by Mr. Zhang Junfang, the chief editor of the "Great Song Heavenly Palace Treasure House." He spent several decades of focused effort to extract the essence from the more than 4,500 volumes of the Daoist Canon that he personally helped compile. The entire Canon was compiled by imperial decree during the reign of Emperor Zhenzong and presented to the throne in the third year of the Tianxi era (1019 AD). Subsequently, he gathered the "Excellence of the Seven Sections of the Cloudy Slips" to form this book, which was presented for the imperial inspection of Emperor Renzong. The volumes are rich in content and cite a vast array of sources. From the profound mysteries of the <term>Three Grottoes and Four Supplements</term> to the esoteric secrets of transformative arts, it encompasses almost everything. Whether through abridged records or complete texts, it preserves lost writings and gathers secret methods, making it a rare and miraculous collection of classic texts unparalleled throughout history. Now, it is specifically published via photostatic reproduction of the Ming Dynasty <term>Zhengtong</term> edition, allowing these secret books—once reserved only for the Emperor’s eyes—to be studied and practiced by everyone today. <note>The "Three Grottoes and Four Supplements" is the traditional seven-part classification system used to organize the thousands of texts in the Daoist Canon.</note>

2. For a reader to possess a copy of the *Seven Slips from the Cloudy Satchel* is equivalent to owning a condensed version of the entire Daoist Canon; furthermore, it saves a great deal of time and energy. For scholars and practitioners who are unable to purchase or store the full Canon, or who cannot manage a comprehensive reading of it, this is truly a rare opportunity encountered once in a thousand years. Therefore, one must not look upon this as an ordinary matter or an ordinary book.

3. This work consists of 122 volumes in total, categorized as follows:
> Section on Virtue and the Way; Section on Primal Chaos, the Great Void, and the Cycles of Kalpas; Section on the Origins of Daoism; Section on the Transmission of Daoist Scriptures;
> Section on the Transmission of Methods; Section on the Lineage of Scriptural Teachings; Section on the Scriptural Teachings of the <term>Three Grottoes</term>; Section on Heaven and Earth; Section on the Sun, Moon, and Stars; Section on the Ten Continents and Three Islands; Section on <term>Grotto-Heavens</term> and Blissful Realms; <note>Grotto-Heavens and Blissful Realms refer to sacred sites on earth believed to be inhabited by immortals or acting as portals to other realms.</note>
> Section on Geography; Section on the Twenty-Eight Jurisdictions; Section on Bestowed Life and Mandates; Section on Miscellaneous Cultivation and Preserving Life; Section on Fasts and Precepts; Section on Miscellaneous Methods of the Seven Slips; Section on Visualization and Meditation; Section on Secret Essential Formulas and Methods; Section on the Soul and Spirits; Section on Various Schools' <term>Qi</term> Methods; Section on Methods of the Golden Elixir (Internal and External Alchemy); Section on Prescriptions and Medicines; Section on Talismans and Diagrams.

### Essentials of Daoist Life-Cultivation, Integrated with Confucianism and Buddhism (Five Versions)

->Reading this book is equivalent to reading an abridged Daoist Canon; reading this book is equivalent to reading all ten thousand volumes of alchemical scriptures.<-

This book is a masterpiece by Mr. Xiao Tianshi <note>pseudonym: Wenshan Dunshou, "The Hermit of Mount Wen"</note>. Mr. Xiao exhaustively researched secret texts from the Daoist Canon for decades. While in Mainland China, he traveled to famous mountains and <term>grotto-heavens</term> <note>sacred sites believed to be inhabited by immortals</note>, visiting and studying under more than a dozen famous masters of Daoism and Buddhism. He received the authentic transmission of both the Northern and Southern lineages <note>The "Northern" (Quanzhen/Complete Perfection) and "Southern" (focusing on internal alchemy) schools represent the two major branches of later Daoism</note>, and possesses many unique secrets. After coming to Taiwan, he selected and published over 100 volumes of the *Essentials of the Daoist Canon*, including more than 800 types of secret texts—yet this represents less than one-tenth of his total collection. 

At the request of readers, he has specially written this volume, revealing much that predecessors left unsaid and elucidating what was previously unexpressed. Not only can it be used to <term>ward off illness and strengthen the body</term> <note>original: "quebing qiangshen"</note> for health and longevity, but it can also be used to transcend the mundane and enter holiness, transforming into a divine immortal. Although titled "Essentials of Daoist <term>Life-Cultivation</term>," <note>original: "Yangsheng Xue," a traditional system of health and spiritual refinement</note> it actually reveals the supreme secret tenets of the <term>Three Schools</term> <note>Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism</note>. The book is written in separate chapters, all extremely concise, and mostly in an aphoristic style, making it accessible, clear, and easy to understand and practice. Any reader who has purchased books from our publishing house should have a copy to assist their research; even those who haven't should use this to glimpse the ultimate truths. — The appended "Mystic Gate Taiji Long-Life Gong" is a particularly secret technique of the <term>Qingcheng School</term> <note>A major Daoist lineage based at Mount Qingcheng in Sichuan</note> that was previously untransmitted.

# General Bibliography of the Essentials of the Daoist Canon

Following the previous volume, this is yet another immortal new work; it can also be viewed as a collection of his teachings on the development of <term>New Daoist Studies</term> <note>A modern movement seeking to revitalize Daoist philosophy and practice for the contemporary world</note> over the past twenty years. The methods of <term>Sacred Achievement and Divine Transformation</term> <note>original: "shenggong shenhua," referring to the highest stages of spiritual attainment and manifestation</note> and the <term>Longevity Alchemy Methods</term> <note>original: "changsheng danfa"</note> advocated within can be traced directly back to the lineages of <term>Fu Xi, the Yellow Emperor, Laozi, and Zhuangzi</term> <note>The foundational figures of Chinese civilization and Daoist philosophy</note>. The author harmonizes the <term>Three Schools</term> <note>Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism</note> and integrates the teachings of a hundred different sects while establishing a unique new tradition. Its scope is as vast and deep as the ocean, with nothing else that can compare! 

Among all those throughout the ages who have spoken of sacred achievement and divine transformation to reach the "Supreme Vehicle" of the Great Dao, there has truly been no second person like him in a thousand years. Practicing these methods can literally enable a person to "transcend heaven and earth and exist independently." The book contains authentic traces of the <term>Dunhuang Daoist Manuscripts</term> <note>Ancient scrolls discovered in the Dunhuang caves, containing lost or early versions of sacred texts</note>, as well as the <term>Daoist internal work</term> and <term>sleeping exercises</term> <note>original: "shuigong," a specialized form of reclining meditation</note> of the <term>Primordial Dao Limitless Sect</term> <note>original: "Xiantian Dao Wuji Menpai"</note>. These are secret principles that were never transmitted by the thousands of previous sages <note>A common saying: "no matter who you are, half your life is spent in bed; who then has met the 'Sleeping Immortal'?"</note>. 

The entire book consists of six volumes and includes sixty-four illustrations, totaling over five hundred thousand words and more than seven hundred pages. Each volume can stand alone as its own book. It can be read as a guide to <term>life-cultivation</term>, or as a work of philosophy or literature, as the writing is beautiful, the concepts are fresh, and every opening of the book brings benefit. ### General Introduction to Daoist Studies ............................................................................ 1

This volume is drawn from the book *Daoist Life-Cultivation* written by Mr. Xiao Tianshi (the Recluse of Wenshan). It selects four articles from his discussions on <term>Daoist Studies</term> <note>original: "daoxue," referring to the academic and philosophical study of Daoist principles</note>, the <term>Daoist Canon</term> <note>the "Daozang," the massive collection of all sacred Daoist scriptures</note>, and the <term>Daoist Religion</term>. These are: 1. Essentials of Daoist Scholarly Principles; 2. Overview of the Origins and Development of Daoist Studies; 3. A Brief Description of the Daoist Canon and the "Essentials of the Daoist Canon" collection; 4. Overview of the Essentials of the Daoist Religion. Through these, one can gain a glimpse into the <term>New Daoist Studies</term> <note>A movement to adapt ancient Daoist wisdom for the modern era</note> that he promotes. His goal is not merely "long life and lasting vision," but <term>Sacred Achievement and Divine Transformation</term> <note>original: "shenggong shenhua," the highest levels of spiritual mastery</note> and the promotion of orthodox Daoist scholarly thought.

### Record of Cultivating Nature and Extending Life ........................................................ 31

Authored by <term>Tao Hongjing</term> <note>A legendary physician and alchemist (456–536 CE) who helped organize the Daoist pantheon</note> of the Liang Dynasty; recorded in the Bibliographic Treatise of the *History of the Song Dynasty*. This book gathers the rules for longevity followed by realized masters found in the scriptures of the immortals. It records the longevity teachings of <term>Pengzu</term> <note>The Chinese "Methuselah," said to have lived over 800 years</note> and <term>Laozi</term>. Spanning from the eras of <term>Shennong and the Yellow Emperor</term> <note>The mythical ancestors of Chinese civilization</note> down to the Wei and Jin dynasties, it collects everything that is beneficial for <term>life-cultivation</term> <note>original: "yangsheng," the practice of nourishing health and spirit</note> and the cultivation of the body, mind, and essence.

### Methods of Absorbing Qi for Longevity and Grain Abstinence ................................ 39

Methods of Abstaining from Grains through Ingesting Qi <note>original: "bigu," the practice of replacing physical food with spiritual energy</note>. Several of these were recorded in the *History of the Song Dynasty*. What past sages did not transmit is now transmitted here; what past sages did not reveal is now revealed here.

# Three Essentials of Maintaining Health ......................................... 47

Written by Yuan Huang (styled Kunyi) of Jiashan during the Ming Dynasty, who is popularly known as <term>Mr. Liaofan</term> <note>Yuan Liaofan (1533–1606) was a famous official and scholar best known for his work "Four Lessons of Liaofan," which taught that one could change their destiny through merit and meditation</note>. The text consists of three essays: 1. **Gathering Essence**; 2. **Nourishing Qi**; 3. **Preserving Spirit**. Every essay is extremely refined and essential. The core principle of the <term>Daoist School</term> is to use the boundless, empty void as the <term>Primordial Aperture</term> <note>original: "yuan qiao," a subtle, non-physical center used as a focal point in meditation</note>, to use "knowing without clinging" as the rule, and to use "not a single thought arising" as the primary practice. If one were to examine all ten thousand volumes of alchemical scriptures, they would not escape this profound mechanism. The essentials of maintaining health are entirely contained within this.

# Tianyinzi’s Book of Life-Cultivation ................................... 55

This method serves as the wondrous gateway of the "Five Gradual Steps." It means that once the first step is completed, one proceeds to the second, following through to the fifth. There are five sections in total: 1. **Fasting and Precepts**; 2. **Peaceful Dwelling**; 3. **Visualization** <note>original: "cunxiang," the practice of mentally focusing on internal deities or cosmic energies to stabilize the mind</note>; 4. **Sitting in Forgetfulness** <note>original: "zuowang," a classic Daoist state of deep meditative absorption where the ego and physical awareness are "forgotten"</note>; 5. **Spiritual Liberation**. The language is concise and the meaning is comprehensive, reaching the heights of the wondrous and the depths of the mysterious. It points out the path from the shallow into the deep and opens the door from the gradual to the sudden. Through <term>Faith, Stability, Closure, and Wisdom</term>—the four gates that connect with the divine—the body is liberated and the spirit is transformed.

# Chapter on Maintenance and Protecting Life ...................................... 59

This is divided into seven sections. The first is called **Supplementing Clarity**, which involves absorbing <term>qi</term> and refining strength to supplement the body; practiced over time, it makes the skin radiant. Next is **Prohibitions**, which discusses the necessity of practicing quiet contemplation to prevent and suppress the flare-ups of desire; this is the method for maintaining and gathering essence to nourish oneself, and for <term>returning essence to nourish the brain</term> <note>original: "huanjing bunao," a famous internal alchemical technique intended to reverse the flow of essence to promote longevity</note> to achieve the path of immortality. The following sections are: **Expedient Means**, **The Method of Manifesting the Body and Sitting in Forgetfulness**, **Embryonic Breathing** <note>original: "taixi," a refined form of internal breathing so subtle it resembles that of a fetus in the womb</note>, **The Shadow Man**, and finally **The Method of Swallowing the Purple Clouds**. These are all top-tier methods for maintaining the physical form and essential rules for extending one's years.

At the highest level, these can serve as the foundation for ascending to the state of a <term>Perfected Being</term> <note>original: "zhen," a fully realized or enlightened immortal in Daoist tradition</note>.

## Commentary on Guangchengzi ..................................................................... 183

This book contains the answers given by Guangchengzi <note>A legendary figure said to have lived over 1,200 years and served as a teacher to the Yellow Emperor, representing the source of ancient Daoist wisdom</note> to the Yellow Emperor regarding the inquiry into the ultimate Way. It reaches into the obscure and the profound, making it one of the most refined and ancient texts in the Daoist tradition. The original text was extracted from the *Zhuangzi* <note>A foundational Daoist scripture attributed to the philosopher Zhuang Zhou (c. 4th century BCE)</note>. This specific version uses the compilation and commentary of Su Shi from the Song Dynasty <note>Su Shi (1037–1101), also known as Su Dongpo, was a preeminent poet and statesman who often integrated Daoist and Buddhist insights into his scholarly work</note>. It is truly a precious record for achieving the ultimate Way and <term>Perfecting Truth</term> <note>original: "quanzhen," a state of complete spiritual integrity</note>.

## Record of Seeking Correction ..................................................................... 187

Written by Lu Shichen, this work contains his lifelong insights into learning, which he shared with Yuan Zhiwu. "Seeking Correction" is a modest expression <note>A traditional humble phrasing used by authors to suggest they are presenting their work for criticism and refinement by others</note>. It elaborates on the "Learning of the Heart" and contains many unique perspectives. Furthermore, every part of it aligns with the heart-to-heart transmissions of both Confucius and Laozi; one should not view it merely as a technical manual for <term>Alchemical Practice</term> <note>original: "dan jia," referring to the practitioners of Internal Alchemy</note>.

## Treatise on the Learnability of Immortality ......................................................... 201

Written by Wu Yun of the Tang Dynasty <note>Wu Yun (died 778) was a famous Daoist priest and poet who argued that immortality was a result of practice and study rather than mere fate</note>. It is recorded in the *Bibliographic Treatise of the History of the Tang* and the *General Examination of Literary Remains*; it was also included in volume 926 of the *Complete Tang Writings* and was added to the <term>Daoist Canon</term> during the Northern Song Dynasty. Its arguments are upright and grand, praising both Confucianism and Daoism. It serves as a guiding light for students of immortality. Appended to it are essays on "The Nature of the Way," "The Three Aspects," "The True Aspect," and "Yin-Yang and the Five Elements." It elucidates the wondrous application of the mutual generation of being and non-being, providing a profound and unchanging truth that is perfectly penetrating and without obstacles.

## The Master of Nourishing Life ..................................................................... 209

Written by Zhuang Zhou, this is extracted from the "Inner Chapters" of the *Zhuangzi*. It represents the correct aim of Daoist longevity practices. By taking the Way as the guideline and following the middle path as the constant, it uses harmony with nature as its fundamental law. It also warns against "nourishing" to an extreme where the practice itself begins to damage the life force. It is truly the master principle of <term>Nourishing Life</term> <note>original: "yang sheng," the traditional Chinese practice of cultivating health and longevity</note>.

# Treatise on Nourishing Life ................................................................................................. 111

Written by Ge Hong <note>Ge Hong (283–343 CE), also known by his pseudonym Baopuzi or "The Master Who Embraces Simplicity," was a minor official and famous alchemist of the Jin Dynasty whose works synthesized early medicine, ethics, and alchemy</note> of the Jin Dynasty. # An Introduction to the Academic Thought of Chinese Taoism
## Xiao Tianshi, the Hermit of Wenshan <note>The author, Xiao Tianshi (1908–1986), was a prominent 20th-century scholar of Taoism and traditional Chinese culture. "Hermit of Wenshan" is his literary pseudonym.</note>

### I. The Essentials of Taoist Academic Thought
### 1. Inheriting the Tradition of the Yin and Zhou Dynasties and Penetrating the Changes of All Ages

Chinese culture achieved a magnificent scale by the time of the Zhou Dynasty <note>c. 1046–256 BCE</note>; thus, Confucius remarked:
> "The Zhou surveyed the two preceding dynasties. How glorious and refined is its culture! I follow the Zhou." <note>original: 「周監於二代，郁郁乎文哉」. Confucius refers here to the Xia and Shang (Yin) dynasties, praising the Zhou for its sophisticated synthesis of their cultural achievements.</note>

From the Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods through the Qin Dynasty, the <term>Hundred Schools of Thought</term><note>A period of great intellectual expansion where various philosophical schools competed for influence.</note> bloomed together. Academic thought reached its pinnacle, marking what can be called the Great Liberation and the Golden Age of Chinese culture. In a broad sense, the culture existing prior to this era can generally be termed <term>Taoist culture</term><note>original: 道家文化 (Dàojiā wénhuà). The author suggests that "Taoism" represents the original, unified root of Chinese thought before it fractured into different schools.</note>; therefore, those of the Taoist school often claim, "Without Taoist culture, there is no Chinese culture." After the rise of Confucius, <term>Confucianism</term><note>original: 儒 (Rú)</note> branched off from the <term>Tao</term><note>The "Way" or the ultimate principle of the universe.</note>. During the Warring States period, the hundred schools vied for supremacy, each taking a single branch of knowledge to establish its own authority and system of thought. Consequently, the historian Sima Tan wrote his treatise on the *Essentials of the Six Schools*. In reality, except for the Confucian, Mohist, and the School of Names <note>Logicians</note>, all other schools can generally be classified under the umbrella of Taoism.

From the Spring and Autumn period to the early Han Dynasty, the reason academic thought rose in such fierce competition was that the era was one of great upheaval. Everyone felt an urgent desire for order, and thus each scholar presented their own vision of the truth as they saw it. As <term>Mencius</term><note>A major Confucian philosopher who defended and expanded upon Confucius's teachings.</note> said:
> "Sage-kings do not arise, the feudal lords act with abandon, and scholars in retirement indulge in wild discussions." <note>original: 「聖王不作，諸侯放恣，處士橫議。」</note>

<term>Zhuangzi</term><note>A foundational Taoist philosopher known for his wit and use of allegory.</note> observed:
> "The world is in great disorder, the sages and saints are obscured, and Virtue is no longer unified. Many in the world grasp only a single facet of the truth to satisfy themselves." <note>original: 「天下大亂，賢聖不明，道德不一，天下多得一察焉以自好。」</note>
> "The people of the world each follow their own desires to create their own methods." <note>original: 「天下之人，各為其所欲焉，以自為方。」</note>

As the house of Zhou faltered and the "Royal Way" withered, the feudal lords each governed for themselves, and scholars likewise sought to use their ideas to gain influence in the world...

<summary>This opening page argues that Taoism is the foundational "root" of Chinese culture, predating the split into various schools like Confucianism during the Warring States period.</summary>

<keywords>Taoism, Confucianism, Hundred Schools of Thought, Zhou Dynasty, Confucius, Mencius, Zhuangzi, Sima Tan, Chinese Philosophy, Golden Age</keywords>

--- Page 64 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Hundred Schools of Thought," transitioning from their origins in social chaos to their eventual suppression under the Han Dynasty’s adoption of Confucianism as the state ideology. It emphasizes the practical governance of "Huang-Lao" Taoism during the early Han as a high point of the tradition's political application.</meta>

...this is why the <term>Hundred Schools</term><note>The various philosophical movements that flourished from the 6th century to 221 BCE.</note> were established in competition with one another. When Qin Shihuang <note>The First Emperor of Qin, reigned 221–210 BCE.</note> followed the advice of Li Si to burn the books, he forbade the people from hiding the "Songs, Documents, and the words of the Hundred Schools." That the words of these schools were enough to shake the First Emperor is proof of their great influence. Although Sima Tan <note>A Han Dynasty historian and father of Sima Qian.</note> only categorized six schools, the *Zhuangzi* in its "Under Heaven" chapter uses the phrase "the learning of the hundred schools," and the "Treatise on Literature" in the *Book of Han* classifies those that could be verified into ten categories.

> The text states: "The various schools of the masters numbered ten, of which nine are worthy of consideration. They all arose after the <term>Royal Way</term><note>original: 王道 (Wángdào). The idealized moral and political order of the ancient sage-kings.</note> had already withered and the feudal lords ruled by force; the rulers of those times had no consistent standard for their likes and dislikes. Consequently, the techniques of the nine schools emerged together like a swarm of bees, each drawing upon a single principle and exalting what they deemed good. With these, they traveled about to persuade and find favor with the feudal lords."

Because their aim was to "find favor with the feudal lords," they emphasized practical utility, with their main goal being the correction of the times and the curing of societal ills. Because they "followed only a single principle," they generally lost sight of the whole and neglected the root. They were far inferior to the <term>Taoist school</term><note>original: 道家 (Dàojiā)</note>, which is capable of "inheriting the tradition of a thousand generations and penetrating the changes of all ages." Therefore, the Grand Historian <note>Sima Tan or his son Sima Qian.</note> highly praised the Taoist school as the highest among all schools. During the early Han Dynasty, Taoism was also very popular. For example, Emperor Wen's <note>Reigned 180–157 BCE.</note> love for the "words of Huang-Lao," his governance based on compassion, frugality, and <term>non-action</term><note>original: 無為 (wúwéi). The principle of acting in harmony with the natural flow rather than through forced interference.</note>, Gai Gong’s teaching of Cao Can on how to govern the state through "purity and stillness," and Ji An's practice of <term>Huang-Lao techniques</term><note>original: 黃老術 (Huáng-Lǎo shù). A school of thought named after the Yellow Emperor and Laozi that focused on statecraft and natural order.</note>—all of these provide a glimpse into its influence. These "Huang-Lao techniques" were the "art of the ruler facing south" <note>An ancient idiom for the art of governance, as the ruler sat on a throne facing south.</note> within Taoist academic thought. This is also what is called "the study of the sovereign" or "the study of emperors and kings." History records that the prosperity of the "Rule of Wen and Jing" <note>A period of peace and prosperity under Emperors Wen and Jing of Han (180–141 BCE).</note> was essentially brought about by these "Huang-Lao techniques."

Ever since Emperor Wu of Han <note>Reigned 141–87 BCE.</note> adopted the strategy of Dong Zhongshu to **exalt Confucianism and suppress the hundred schools**, the emperors of successive dynasties followed suit, using it as a tool for governance. Consequently, <term>Confucianism</term><note>original: 儒學 (Rúxué)</note> flourished day by day while Taoist studies gradually declined. The *Book of the Former Han* states:

> "From the beginning of Emperor Wu's reign, the Marquises of Weiqi and Wu'an were made Chancellors, and Confucianism was elevated. When Dong Zhongshu submitted his response to the imperial inquiry, he praised the teachings of Confucius and suppressed the hundred schools. The establishment of official schools and the recommendation of <term>Abundant Talent</term><note>original: 茂材 (Mào-cái)</note> and <term>Filial and Incorrupt</term><note>original: 孝廉 (Xiào-lián). Two primary categories for selecting government officials based on talent and virtue.</note> candidates by the prefectures and commanderies all originated with Dong Zhongshu."

From this point forward, the atmosphere of extreme intellectual freedom that existed from the end of the Qin until the unification of the six states was lost. I have once remarked, "Since Emperor Wu exalted Confucianism and suppressed the hundred schools, he strangled the hundred schools, and he also strangled Confucianism. Thus, after Laozi and Zhuangzi, there were no more like Laozi and Zhuangzi; after Confucius and Mencius, there were no more like Confucius and Mencius." Looking at it from a historical perspective, although it seems that after Emperor Wu's elevation of Confucianism, the entire landscape was dominated by the influence of the **Confucian school**, in reality, this was not the case. For example, during the transition between the Eastern Han and the Three Kingdoms...

<summary>This page describes how Taoism, particularly the "Huang-Lao" style of governance, led to a golden age in the early Han Dynasty before being officially sidelined by Emperor Wu's decree making Confucianism the state ideology.</summary>

Page 3

The <term>Taoist school</term><note>original: 道家 (Dàojiā)</note> of thought once again gradually gained influence. The <term>Dark Learning</term><note>original: 玄學 (Xuánxué). A metaphysical movement in the 3rd–4th centuries CE that reinterpreted Confucianism through a Taoist lens.</note> of the Northern and Southern Dynasties—led by figures such as He Yan, Wang Bi, Ruan Ji, Xi Kang, Xiang Xiu, and Guo Xiang—primarily took <term>Laozi and Zhuangzi</term><note>original: 老莊 (Lǎo-Zhuāng). The two foundational figures of Taoist philosophy.</note> as their ancestral source. These thinkers exerted a profound and lasting influence on the scholarship of both their own time and later generations. At the same time, since the <term>Tang Dynasty</term><note>original: 李唐 (Lǐ-Táng). The ruling family of the Tang (618–907 CE) claimed descent from Laozi, whose surname was also Li.</note> honored Laozi as their ancestor, Taoist studies surged once more. Furthermore, <term>Buddhism</term><note>original: 佛學 (Fóxué)</note> took advantage of the intellectual void during the transition between the Northern and Southern Dynasties and the Sui and Tang periods to enter China, reaching a peak of prosperity. In light of this, <term>Confucianism</term><note>original: 儒學 (Rúxué)</note> could not truly maintain an exclusive position of supreme authority or represent the whole of Chinese thought.

I have often remarked that the scholarship of the Taoist school is profound, vast, and peerless. From the perspective of its highest clarity, it encompasses the strengths of the <term>Hundred Schools</term>. From the perspective of its immense breadth, it contains the essentials of all intellectual streams. From the perspective of its perfect adaptability, it can be applied anywhere without obstruction. From the perspective of its profound mystery, its transformations are divine and unpredictable. If one employs its spiritual essence, then "purity, stillness, and <term>non-action</term>" can bring about peace and order. If one employs its hidden yielding, then one can suppress tyranny, quell disorder, and return the world to the correct path. If used for self-reflection and cultivation, one can transcend the mundane to become a sage or a "True Person." If used for self-preservation, one can be wise and retreat from the world without inner distress. As for its techniques of strategic maneuvering and the diplomatic arts of "opening and closing," these are but secondary applications. Upon detailed and deep investigation, these are truly not empty words.

It is a pity that among later scholars who dedicated themselves to this study, those with deep insight and realization are few. Those capable of carrying it forward, continuing this "lost learning," sustaining the "sacred lineage," and rectifying the orthodox tradition are as rare as <term>phoenix feathers and unicorn horns</term><note>An idiom for something extremely rare and precious.</note>! This is why Laozi said: "Those who know me are few; those who follow me are honored." And why Zhuangzi sighed: "To meet one who understands this after ten thousand generations is like meeting someone at dawn whom you just saw the previous evening."

## II. The Tao Encompasses the Essentials of Yin and Yang; Virtue Combines the Strengths of the Hundred Schools

In the past, the <term>Grand Historian</term><note>original: 太史公 (Tàishǐ Gōng). Referring to Sima Qian, though quoting the work of his father, Sima Tan.</note>, when discussing the essential tenets of the <term>Six Schools</term><note>The primary philosophical categories of ancient China: Yin-Yang, Confucianism, Mohism, Logicians, Legalists, and Taoists.</note>, highly praised the Taoist school. He wrote:

> "The 'Great Commentary' of the <term>Book of Changes</term><note>original: 易大傳 (Yì Dàzhuàn)</note> says: 'In the world there is one goal, though there are a hundred paths of thought; the destination is the same, though the routes are many.' Now, the <term>Yin-Yang</term>, Confucian, Mohist, Logician, Legalist, and Taoist schools all strive for good governance. It is simply that they follow different paths in what they say, and some are more insightful than others."

The Grand Historian continued: "I have observed that the arts of the Yin-Yang school are overly detailed and full of taboos, making people feel constrained and fearful; however, their sequence of the four seasons' natural flow must not be ignored. The Confucians are broad in learning but lack focus..."

<summary>The author highlights how Taoism survived through "Dark Learning" and Tang Dynasty patronage, even as Buddhism entered China. He argues that Taoism is a comprehensive system for governance and personal life, quoting the Grand Historian Sima Qian to show how Taoism integrates the best of all other philosophies.</summary>

<keywords>Dark Learning (Xuanxue), Laozi, Zhuangzi, Tang Dynasty, Buddhism, Sima Qian, Six Schools, Yin-Yang School, Book of Changes, Non-action (Wu-wei)</keywords>

...[the Confucians] work hard but achieve little; for this reason, their tasks are difficult to follow in their entirety. However, their <term>etiquette</term><note>original: 禮 (Lǐ). Refers to the ritual decorum and social hierarchy central to Confucian thought.</note> regarding the relationship between ruler and subject, father and son, and the distinctions between husband and wife or elders and youths, cannot be changed. The <term>Mohists</term><note>Followers of Mozi, known for "universal love" and extreme frugality.</note> are so frugal that their way is difficult to obey, and thus their practices cannot be followed by everyone; however, their emphasis on strengthening the production of essentials and being thrifty with resources cannot be discarded. The <term>Legalists</term><note>original: 法家 (Fǎjiā). A school focused on strict laws, rewards, and punishments to maintain state power.</note> are strict and lack kindness, yet their role in correcting the distinctions between ruler and subject, or superior and inferior, cannot be altered. The <term>Logicians</term><note>original: 名家 (Míngjiā). Also known as the School of Names, they focused on the relationship between language (names) and reality.</note> make people feel constrained and often lose sight of the truth; however, their method of correcting the relationship between "names" and "realities" must be examined. 

The <term>Taoist school</term> allows a person's spirit to be concentrated and unified, so that their actions move in harmony with the formless and provide for all things. As a method of governance, it follows the great natural cycles of <term>Yin and Yang</term>, adopts the virtues of the Confucians and Mohists, and extracts the essentials of the Logicians and Legalists. It shifts with the seasons and responds to the changes of the world. In establishing customs and managing affairs, there is nothing it cannot accommodate. Its principles are concise and easy to grasp; it requires little effort but achieves great results.

From this, it is proven that the scholarship of the Taoist school truly encompasses the strengths of every other school without their weaknesses. Furthermore, it can move with the times—flexible and never stagnant. It responds to change with a perfect, unobstructed versatility. This is why it is regarded as both the most vast and the most profound, the most brilliant and yet the most simple. There is no situation where its application is not suitable. The "Tao" is the root of all things and all affairs. If one holds onto the root, then affairs will naturally govern themselves, things will naturally align, and the underlying principles will naturally reside within them. The Grand Historian, living not far from ancient times, was still able to grasp the subtle essence of each school. He offered a fair and impartial discourse; thus, while he offered both praise and criticism for the other schools, he gave only words of the highest praise for the Taoist school—and this was not without good reason.

He further stated: "Taoism practices <term>non-action</term><note>original: 無為 (Wúwéi). Often misunderstood as "doing nothing," it refers to acting in a way that is so natural and aligned with the Tao that it requires no forced effort.</note>, yet it is also said that there is nothing left undone. Its reality is easy to practice, but its words are difficult to understand. Its method takes 'emptiness and non-being' as its root and 'following nature' as its application. It has no fixed momentum or permanent form; thus, it can grasp the true essence of all things. It does not place itself before things, nor does it lag behind them; thus, it can act as the master of all things. Whether there are rules or no rules, it simply aligns itself with the nature of things. Thus it is said: 'The Sage is immortal because he remains in harmony with the changes of the times.'" 

The Grand Historian lived in an age not far from antiquity; his vast learning regarding the <term>Hundred Schools</term> was unsurpassed throughout the ages, and his judgments are extremely fair, as recognized by scholars of later generations. This is why I have also claimed that the scholarship of the Taoist school is truly the essential substance of the universe and the crown of the Hundred Schools, remaining immortal throughout a thousand generations.

The <term>Treatise on Literature</term><note>original: 藝文志 (Yìwén Zhì). A famous bibliography of ancient texts found within the *Book of Han*.</note> in the *Book of Han* also describes the essentials of the Taoist school:

> "The Taoist school likely originated from the <term>official historians</term>. They recorded the path of success and failure, survival and ruin, disaster and fortune, from ancient times to the present. Only then did they learn to grasp the essentials and hold onto the root—maintaining themselves through purity and emptiness, and conducting themselves with humility and yielding. This is the art of the ruler who sits facing south <note>In ancient China, the Emperor sat facing south; this refers to the art of leadership.</note>, which accords with the self-control of the legendary Emperor Yao..."

The author reinforces this by citing the Book of Han, which traces the origins of Taoism to the wisdom of ancient court historians.</summary>

...[yielding], which is the 'humility' mentioned in the *Book of Changes*. To be humble once brings four-fold benefits—this is its strength." This refers to the Taoist school as being purely the **"art of the ruler facing south"** <note>A traditional Chinese metaphor for the art of governance, as the Emperor's throne always faced south.</note>. Subsequently, its scope gradually widened, many disparate elements were attached to it, and its content became increasingly complex and diverse.

The modern scholar <term>Liang Qichao</term><note>1873–1929; a pivotal intellectual and reformist in modern Chinese history.</note> discussed Taoist scholarship by dividing it into four branches: 

1.  The **Orthodox Metaphysical Branch**, comprising the metaphysical principles of He Yan, Wang Bi, Xiang Xiu, Guo Xiang, and others. 
2. 3.  The **Talisman and Register Branch**, comprising the "Orthodox Oneness" school <note>Zhengyi Dao</note> following the tradition of Celestial Master Zhang. 
4.  The **Divination and Omen Branch**, comprising the arts of hexagram reading and fortune-telling. 

In truth, however, classifying Taoist scholarship in this manner carries the risk of being too narrow and superficial.

### 3. Taoist Scholarship and Thought: Expanded, it Encompasses the Universe; Contracted, it Rests in Secrecy

Let us attempt to discuss this: Taoist learning began with the mythical rulers <term>Fu Xi and Shen Nong</term>, took the <term>Yellow Emperor</term> as its ancestor, was synthesized by <term>Laozi</term>, and evolved through the masters Peng Meng, Tian Pian, and Shen Dao. It flowed into the works of Yin Xi, Zhuangzi, and Liezi. 

*   When its application changed to **Legalism**, it produced the legal school of Shang Yang and Han Fei. 
*   When its application changed to the **School of Diplomacy**<note>original: 縱橫家 (Zònghéngjiā). Philosophers focused on political alliances and rhetoric during the Warring States period.</note>, it produced the strategic schools of Guiguzi and Huang Shigong. 
*   When its application changed to the **Military School**, it produced the martial theories of Sunzi and Wuzi. 
*   When its application changed to the **Way of Governance**, it produced the statecraft of Yi Yin, Jiang Ziya, and Zhang Liang. 
*   When its application changed to **Withdrawal from the World**, it produced the hermit school of the Gatekeeper of Shimen, the Morning Gatekeeper, Jie Yu, and Jie Ni. 
*   When its application changed to **Philosophy**, it produced the metaphysical school of He, Wang, Xiang, and Guo. 
*   When its application changed to the **Way of the Elixir**, it produced the **Science of Cultivating Life** <term>Immortal Arts</term>—including the lineages of Ge, Tao, Boyang, Zhong, Lü, Qiu, and Zhang—as well as the external alchemy branch of smelting and refining. 
*   When its application changed to the **Way of Medicine**, it produced the school of medical sciences. 
*   When its application changed to **Religion**, it produced the Taoist religion and theology of Celestial Master Zhang. 
*   When its application changed to **Yin and Yang**, it produced the school of naturalists, as well as the fields of astronomy, calendars, and geography. 
*   When its application changed to **Divination Arts**...

...[Divination Arts], there emerged the branch of **Prophecy and Apocrypha** <note>original: 讖緯 (Chanyi/Wei). These were mystical texts during the Han Dynasty that interpreted omens and predicted the future through a theological lens.</note> during the transition between the Western and Eastern Han dynasties, as well as the **"Image and Number" School** <note>Xiangshu; a branch of I Ching studies focusing on the mathematical and cosmological patterns of the universe.</note> represented by figures like **Chen Xiyi** and **Shao Kangjie** <note>Shao Yong (1011–1077); a famous Song dynasty philosopher known for his complex cosmological diagrams.</note> during the Han and Song dynasties. 

*   When its application changed to **Occult Arts**, it produced the schools of divination, clairvoyance, physiognomy <note>The art of judging character or destiny from facial features or landforms (Feng Shui).</note>, and the arts of supernatural transformations, such as the lineages of Yu Ji, Guan Lu, and Zuo Ci. 
*   When its application changed to **Eclecticism**, it produced works like the *Heguanzi* and the *Huainanzi*. 

All of these evolved from Taoist academic and philosophical thought; they can all be regarded as offshoots of the Taoist school. From this, one can see how vast the scope of Taoist learning truly is. Indeed, by grasping even a single branch of it, one can establish a separate school and stand alone as a master. This is because the "Way" of the Taoists is broad, profound, and possesses both **substance and function** <note>A core concept in Chinese philosophy where "substance" (Ti) is the internal reality and "function" (Yong) is its external application.</note>. 

When holding onto the essentials and grasping the root, it is **"rolled up into one"**; when applied according to what is appropriate, it is **"scattered to become ten thousand things."** As the saying goes: **"Expanded, it fills the six directions of the universe; contracted, it rests in secrecy."** It nets the hundred schools of thought and is broad enough to encompass them all; it harmonizes the various philosophers and covers all the "ten thousand streams" of thought. Aside from the Taoist school, there is truly nothing else capable of this.

At the same time, regarding traditional Chinese history, culture, and academic thought: prior to the Qin dynasty <note>The "Pre-Qin" era (before 221 BCE), the foundational period of Chinese philosophy.</note>, almost everything can be categorized under Taoism—this is beyond dispute. From the Han and Tang dynasties down through the Song and Ming, it may appear at first glance that **Confucianism** was the sole honored tradition. Most of those who governed were Confucian figures, and the most prominent scholars were Confucians. 

However, upon closer inspection, the most brilliant rulers of every era were invariably Taoist in their approach; the most profound scholars were also, without exception, deeply influenced by Taoism. They were either **"Confucian on the outside but Taoist on the inside"** or **"Exoterically Confucian but esoterically Taoist."** All those who achieved great things used the Taoist spirit as their core essence. The two schools served as the "surface" and the "interior" of the culture, and neither was ever truly discarded. 

Furthermore, whenever there was a change of dynasties, a period of an Emperor founding a new state, or an era when civil and military achievements flourished, it was always a time when Taoist figures were at their peak and the Taoist spirit was quietly expanding! Conversely, when a period declined, it was always caused by the fading of Taoist figures and the slackening of the Taoist spirit. If one can open-mindedly and carefully examine the pulse of history, they will believe my words are not empty. Therefore, the ancient sages said: **"When the Tao flourishes, the nation flourishes; when the Tao declines, the nation declines."** How could they have been deceiving us?

## 2. Overview of the Origins and Evolution of Taoist Academic Thought

From the above, we can see that Taoist academic thought was originally extremely vast, profound, and high-minded. However, because later generations attached "supernatural arts" and "strange theories" to it, the school became cluttered and disorganized. Consequently, the influence of these secondary elements has, in a sense, "overpowered the host" <note>A Chinese idiom (xuan bin duo zhu) meaning the guest outshines the host; here, it refers to the superficial magic overshadowing the core philosophy.</note>, causing the orthodox and great principles of Taoism to become obscured and fail to shine. 

The famous scholar of the Qing Dynasty, **Ji Xiaolan** <note>Ji Yun (1724–1805), the chief editor of the *Siku Quanshu*.</note>, once wrote in the "Summary of the Taoist Category" in the **Complete Library of the Four Treasuries** <note>original: *Siku Quanshu Zongmu Tiyao*. This was the largest collection of books in Chinese history, compiled by imperial decree.</note>:

> "In later generations, traces of the supernatural and strange were mostly attached to the Taoist school, and the Taoists themselves took pride in these oddities. Examples include the *Biographies of Immortals* and the *Records of Daoist Miracles*. Yet, if we examine its origins, the school was primarily centered on **'quietude and self-preservation'** <note>original: 清靜自持 (qingjing zichi). This refers to the practice of maintaining internal peace and moral integrity.</note>, assisted by the power of **'fortitude and endurance,'** using **'softness to overcome hardness'** and **'retreat as a means of progress.'** 
> 
> Because of this foundation, the teachings of **Shenzi** and **Hanzi** <note>Shen Buhai and Han Fei, the primary philosophers of the Legalist school.</note> evolved into the **Study of Names and Laws** <note>original: 刑名之學 (Xingming zhi xue). An early form of political science and jurisprudence focused on matching titles to actual performance.</note>, and the **Classic of the Hidden Talisman** <note>original: 陰符經 (Yinfujing). A short, cryptic work often interpreted as a manual for military strategy or internal alchemy.</note> could be applied to military affairs. 
> 
> Later, the theories of **longevity** were merged with the School of Immortals, bringing in the practices of **ingesting medicinal herbs** <note>term: 服餌 (Fuer). The consumption of minerals or herbs to achieve immortality.</note> and **guided breathing and stretching** <note>term: 導引 (Daoyin). Ancient physical exercises, a precursor to modern Qigong.</note>. The 'Bedchamber' school <note>Sexual longevity practices.</note>, being close to the School of Immortals, was also incorporated. The 'Great Treasure' books <note>original: 鴻寶 (Hongbao). Refers to ancient texts on alchemy and the supernatural.</note> appeared, and **alchemical smelting** <note>term: 燒煉 (Shaolian). The practice of laboratory alchemy, specifically trying to turn base metals into gold or elixirs.</note> was added. When **Zhang Lu** <note>A grandson of Zhang Daoling and a leader of the Celestial Masters sect during the late Han dynasty.</note> established the organized religion, **talismans and registers** <note>term: 符籙 (Fulu). Written charms and sacred mandates used in religious Taoism to command spirits.</note> were introduced. During the Northern Wei dynasty, **Kou Qianzhi** and others further added **liturgical rituals and offerings** <note>term: 齋醮 (Zhaijiao). Elaborate public ceremonies and sacrificial rites.</note>. 
> 
> Most of what has been transmitted to the world consists of these later additions, rather than the original intent of the school. Even the practitioners themselves cannot distinguish between them, and there is no need to differentiate them now. However, if one observes the remaining records, the reasons for the evolution and changes in the school's lineage can still be traced one by one."

Therefore, if we speak today of promoting Taoist academic thought and glorifying the Taoist lineage, we must first begin with the **"Great Root and Great Foundation"** rather than pointlessly pursuing research into the "side branches and minor details."

From a purely academic perspective, one might argue that there is no need to deeply investigate these "strange and supernatural" theories. However, from the perspective of a nation's history and culture, all the elements mentioned above possess their own value for preservation and study. Nevertheless, given our current circumstances, if we wish for the "Learning of the Way" to be glorified and expanded, we must start by **organizing and clarifying the early academic thought of the Taoist school**. Only then can we achieve the effect of "getting twice the result with half the effort" and "continuing the past to open the way for the future." This will allow this "lost learning" to flourish in the days to come, serving as a foundation upon which our nation and people can rely.

He argues that reviving Taoism requires focusing on its philosophical roots rather than its supernatural branches.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general evolution of Taoism to a detailed chronological lineage. It identifies the "Huang-Lao" tradition (Yellow Emperor and Laozi) as the foundational core and traces its development through the Jixia Academy in the State of Qi, the rise of mystical practices under Zou Yan, and the eventual shift from political "Huang-Lao" thought to the more metaphysical "Lao-Zhuang" philosophy of the Jin Dynasty.</meta>

<page-num>8</page-num>

The Taoist school of our nation follows the lineage of **Huang-Lao** <note>A portmanteau of the Yellow Emperor (Huangdi) and Laozi. This school was the dominant form of Taoism in the early Han dynasty, focusing on both statecraft and self-cultivation.</note> and prizes **nature** <note>original: 自然 (ziran). In Taoist philosophy, this refers to the spontaneous, self-so-ing state of the universe, rather than just the "outdoors."</note>; it is the earliest school of academic thought in our country. Although the works of **Zhuangzi** <note>The second most influential Taoist philosopher (c. 4th century BCE).</note> contain legends with mystical tones—such as the Yellow Emperor seeking the Way from **Guangchengzi** <note>A mythological immortal said to have lived in a cave on Mount Kongtong.</note> while balancing warfare with the study of immortality—for thousands of years, the Yellow Emperor has generally been regarded as the founding ancestor of Taoism, while Laozi is seen as its Great Master. The essence of their thought can be simply titled the **School of Naturalism**. 

In the early period following the Yellow Emperor, there were figures such as **Yi Yin**, **Yu Xiong**, and **Lü Shang** <note>These were all famous advisors to founding kings, emphasizing the early Taoist connection to successful governance.</note>. Later, Laozi appeared and produced the five-thousand-word *Classic of the Way and Virtue* <note>The *Tao Te Ching*.</note>, bringing the school to its great fruition. In terms of inheriting the past and opening the way for the future, his role was similar to that of **Confucius** in relation to the sage-kings **Yao and Shun**. After Laozi, the masters **Guan Yinzi**, **Zhuangzi**, and **Liezi** were all giants in the academic arena of Taoism. 

Meanwhile, among the various thinkers of the pre-Qin period, scholars from the **Jixia Academy** <note>A famous center of learning in the State of Qi where scholars of all schools gathered to debate.</note> such as **Peng Meng**, **Shen Dao**, **Huan Yuan**, **Jie Zi**, and **Tian Pian** were all branches of the "Huang-Lao" school of virtue. Their primary aim was to achieve the Taoist ideal of **"transformation through non-action"** <note>term: 無為之化 (Wuwei zhi hua). The concept that a ruler who aligns with the Way can govern effectively by not interfering with the natural order.</note>. (The books of these Jixia masters are mostly lost today, but the outlines of their thought can be seen in the *Zhuangzi* and the *Spring and Autumn Annals of Master Lü*. Regarding Shen Dao, fragments of his work, the *Shenzi*, still exist for study.) 

The writings of Master **Zou Yan** <note>A philosopher famous for developing the theories of Yin-Yang and the Five Elements.</note> were numerous. These scholars held the Yellow Emperor in high esteem. The *Records of the Grand Historian* states that Zou Yan's books "first sequence the present and then go back to the Yellow Emperor, which is the common practice of scholars." Based on the ancient concepts of **Yin and Yang** and the **Five Elements** <note>term: 五行 (Wuxing). Metal, wood, water, fire, and earth; the five phases of universal energy.</note>, Zou Yan strongly advocated for a deep observation of the "waxing and waning" of these forces. However, he also introduced strange transformations and mystical interpretations, promoting the **"Way of the Fangshi Immortals"** <note>term: 方仙道 (Fangxiandao). An early movement of "method-masters" who sought physical immortality through alchemy and magic.</note> and the "Apocryphal Texts" of later generations. Because Zou Yan’s mystical explanations and theories of the Five Elements cycle became extremely popular among the feudal lords, the practitioners of magic and seekers of immortality became very prevalent. 

When the **Han Dynasty** unified the world, the study of Huang-Lao flourished during the Western Han era. The **"Rule of Wen and Jing"** <note>The reigns of Emperor Wen and Emperor Jing (180–141 BCE), characterized by peace, low taxes, and minimal government interference—the practical application of Taoist "non-action."</note> was achieved through this philosophy. Commentators on the *Laozi*, such as Mr. Lin, Mr. Fu, Mr. Xu, **Heshang Gong**, Muqiu Wangzhi, and Yan Zun, were all figures from the Western Han or earlier. 

From the end of the Han through the Northern and Southern Dynasties, the trend shifted toward valuing **"Dark Mystery"** <note>term: 玄虛 (Xuanxu). Referring to *Xuanxue* or "Neo-Taoism," which focused on metaphysical and ontological questions.</note>. Scholars began to shift from talking about "Huang-Lao" (political Taoism) to "Lao-Zhuang" (philosophical/literary Taoism). The poet-philosopher **Ji Kang** especially favored pairing Laozi and Zhuangzi together. Consequently, after the **Jin Dynasty**, the study of Zhuangzi flourished and many commentaries were written. All of these movements represent pure Taoist academic thought.

# I. The Study of Longevity and the School of the Way of the Immortals

From King Wei and King Xuan of the State of Qi and King Zhao of Yan, to the First Emperor of Qin and Emperor Wu of the Han, every one of these rulers sent envoys across the seas to seek out divine immortals and the methods of **attaining longevity without death**. 

Later, during the Western Han, **Liu An**, the Prince of Huainan, emulated the famous "Four Lords" of the Warring States by hosting thousands of guests, including men of extraordinary talent and practitioners of the occult arts. Together, they authored twenty-one chapters of "Inner Books," a vast collection of "Outer Books," and eight volumes of "Middle Chapters" which totaled 200,000 words and discussed the **"arts of the yellow and white"** <note>term: 黃白之術 (Huangbai zhi shu). An early term for alchemy, specifically the transmutation of base metals into gold (yellow) and silver (white) to create elixirs of immortality.</note>. (According to the *Biography of the Prince of Huainan* in the *Book of the Han*, the Inner Books are what we know today as the *Huainanzi*, while the Outer and Middle books have been lost.) 

According to the *Biography of Liu Xiang* in the *Book of the Han*: Emperor Xuan revived interest in the arts of immortals and magic. Liu Xiang presented the Emperor with two works: the **"Pillow Secrets of the Garden of Great Treasures"** <note>original: 枕中鴻寶苑秘 (Zhenzhong Hongbao Yuanmi). A "pillow secret" refers to a text so precious and private that it was kept inside one's pillow for safekeeping.</note>—which his father, Liu De, had discovered while overseeing the Huainan legal cases—and Zou Yan’s *Two Books on the Way of Extending Life*. Liu Xiang claimed that immortality could be achieved and gold could be manufactured. 

The writings of Huainan represent a monumental collective work in our history. They gathered the theories of various schools but used the philosophy of Laozi as the central theme. Furthermore, they blended Laozi’s study of "The Way and Virtue" with the practical techniques of the **Fangshi** <note>term: 方士. "Masters of Methods"—specialists in alchemy, astrology, and the occult who were precursors to later Taoist priests.</note> of the "Way of the Immortals." 

This blending is distinct from the classification found in the **"Treatise on Literature"** <note>term: 藝文志 (Yiwenzhi). The bibliographic section of the *Book of Han*, which provides the first systematic classification of Chinese literature.</note> in the *History of the Former Han*. In that record:
*   **Laozi** is categorized under the **"School of the Tao"** <note>Taoist philosophers.</note>.
*   The **"School of Immortals"** is listed separately under "Technical Arts."
*   The **"School of Bedchamber Arts"** <note>term: 房中家 (Fangzhongjia). Practices involving sexual yoga and hygiene intended to preserve vitality and prolong life.</note> is also listed as its own category rather than being part of the Immortals or the Taoists.

The "Treatise on Literature" lists only thirty-seven schools of Taoist thought (including the Yellow Emperor, Yi Yin, Laozi, Zhuangzi, etc.), totaling 993 volumes. The "School of Immortals" lists ten schools with 205 volumes. The "School of Bedchamber Arts" lists eight schools with 186 volumes. 

This proves that in the early Han Dynasty, the "Immortals" and the "Bedchamber" practitioners were **not yet considered part of the Taoist school**. Although Taoist academic thought certainly valued **"nurturing life"** <note>term: 養生 (Yangsheng). A broad tradition of health and self-cultivation practices including diet, exercise, and meditation.</note> and the methods of "long life and lasting vision," it was not as narrow or specialized as those latter groups. Moreover, while the Bedchamber practitioners had their own methods of health cultivation that possessed their own internal logic, they were also distinct from the "Way of the Immortals" of that era.

<summary>This page describes how the quest for physical immortality and alchemy, championed by figures like the Prince of Huainan, began to merge with philosophical Taoism, despite being categorized as separate disciplines in early Han Dynasty bibliographies.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the discussion on the historical separation of Taoist schools and describes the consolidation of these traditions into a formal religion and a standardized "Taoist Canon" during the Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties. It introduces the pivotal figures of Wei Boyang, Ge Hong, and Zhang Daoling.</meta>

<page-num>10</page-num>

...otherwise, the emperors of successive dynasties would not have needed to seek the divine medicine of immortality from far across the seas. The inclusion of the two aforementioned schools <note>Referring to the Schools of Immortality and the Bedchamber from the previous page.</note>, along with the "technical arts" and various other groups concerned with **nurturing life**, into the single category of "Taoism" was a later development. This synthesis occurred during the Kaiyuan era of the Tang Dynasty <note>713–741 CE; a golden age of Tang culture.</note> when the **Taoist Canon** <note>term: 道藏 (Daozang). The massive collection of all Taoist scriptures, rituals, and philosophical texts.</note> was first compiled, bringing together every sect and school of thought under one umbrella.

Since the Jin Dynasty, when **Wei Boyang** authored the three volumes of the **"The Seal of the Unity of the Three"** <note>original: 參同契 (Cantong qi). Often called the "ancestor of all alchemical texts," it uses the symbolism of the I Ching (Book of Changes) to explain the chemical and meditative processes of alchemy.</note>, the path has been clear. By using the symbols of the hexagrams and the laws of the changes to reveal the true source of "nature and life," he explained the "Pre-heaven" school of the *Book of Changes* and unveiled the subtle transmission of alchemical methods. His work shines as brightly as the sun and stars, illuminating the entire world; it has been revered by practitioners of alchemy throughout the ages as the **"Holy Scripture of Cultivation."** 

Furthermore, during the Jin Dynasty, **Ge Hong** <note>Also known by his pen name Ge Zhichuan or "The Master Who Embraces Simplicity."</note> wrote the **"Master Who Embraces Simplicity"** in two parts: the Inner and Outer Chapters. The Inner Chapters focus exclusively on the arts of the divine immortals and long life. This work gathered the knowledge of the ancients and opened the way for a hundred generations to follow, making it a primary text that every student of alchemy must study. 

The actual worship of Laozi as a deity began at the end of the Han Dynasty. However, the formal establishment of Laozi as the **Ancestral Founder** of the Taoist religion—deifying him and transforming the philosophy into a religious institution—began with **Zhang Daoling**. 

Zhang Daoling was a descendant of the famous statesman Zhang Liang in the eighth generation. He was originally a scholar of the Grand Academy, well-versed in the Five Classics. However, he later realized that such studies did not benefit one's lifespan. He turned to the study of the Way of Longevity, obtaining the alchemical methods of the **"Nine Tripods of the Yellow Emperor."** He practiced the Way at Crane Cry Mountain in Sichuan, where he refined the **"Great Elixir of the Dragon and Tiger"** and received the newly revealed "Way of Orthodox Oneness and Covenanted Authority." Consequently, later generations of religious Taoists typically focused on **jiao rituals** <note>term: 醮 (Jiao). Elaborate communal rituals of renewal and offerings to the deities.</note>, worshipping gods, and using **talismans** <note>term: 符籙 (Fulu). Sacred diagrams or symbols believed to have magical power to command spirits or heal the sick.</note> to cure illness. This branch became quite distinct from the "Elixir Tripod" branch of the Alchemical practitioners.

During the Tianbao era of the Tang Dynasty <note>742–756 CE.</note>, the Taoist Canon was compiled. It was organized into the **"Three Caverns"** <note>term: 三洞 (Sandong). The primary division of the Taoist Canon, representing three different spiritual lineages.</note>, which were further divided into the "Four Supplements" and "Twelve Divisions," a structure similar to that of the Buddhist scriptures. It is worth noting that the date of the first printing of the Taoist Canon was actually over two hundred years earlier than the compilation of the Buddhist *Tripitaka*. This Taoist Canon, which represents the great synthesis of Taoist academic and spiritual achievement, was continually revised through the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties. 

The extant photographic reproduction of the Canon we have today is based on the version held at the **White Cloud Temple in Beijing**. Its compilation date reaches back to the Zhengtong era of the Ming Dynasty <note>1436–1449 CE.</note>; hence, it is also known as the "Zhengtong Edition of the Canon." Including the supplementary collection added during the Wanli era, it totals 512 cases and 5,485 volumes. Today, if one wishes to promote Taoist studies or illuminate the subtle principles of the Taoist art of nurturing life, there is no way to gain a complete understanding of the subject without turning to this collection.

## II. The Realm of the Realized Person in the Alchemical Path and the Dual Cultivation of Inner Nature and Life Force

<meta>This page transitions from the historical overview of the Taoist Canon to the specific philosophical foundations of the Alchemical Path. It defines the goal of Taoist practice—attaining the state of a "Realized Person"—and distinguishes these spiritual practices from mere physical longevity or religious superstition.</meta>

<page-num>11</page-num>

The Alchemical Path of the Taoist school, also known as the **Elixir Tripod School** or the **School of the Immortal Way**, does not contain the slightest hint of religious superstition. Its fundamental philosophy is to enable a person, through cultivation, to transcend the mundane and enter sagehood, to transcend sagehood to enter the divine, and to transcend the divine to reach a state of transformation. The goal is to reach the **"Realm of the Realized Person"** <note>term: 真人 (Zhenren). Literally "True Person." In Taoism, this refers to an enlightened being who has mastered the laws of nature and achieved a state of spiritual perfection beyond the reach of decay.</note>, a state characterized by **"boundless spiritual transformation."** This is the ultimate efficacy of the path. On a smaller scale, one can use these practices to extend their lifespan; on a larger scale, one can reach toward the infinite. Therefore, one must absolutely not compare this to contemporary **"longevity studies"** <note>Refers to the biological or medical study of life extension/gerontology.</note>. While the two share minor similarities, they are vastly different—separated by a distance as great as that between the heavens and the earth. As for the so-called **"Realm of the Realized Person,"** it is effectively the state of **"Unity of Heaven and Humanity."** If one delves deeply into its philosophical content, its ontology, cosmology, and theory of life are all profoundly subtle, rigorous, and expansive. One must not merely cling to the literal idea of "living forever" or judge it by superficial appearances, nor should one recklessly disparage it. The concept of longevity first appeared with Laozi. However, Laozi only spoke of **"long life and long vision"** <note>original: 長生久視 (Changsheng jiushi).</note>; he did not say "long life without death." "Long life and long vision" means one can extend their life and sustain their perception, not necessarily live forever in a physical sense. Thus, Laozi also said:

> "To die but not be forgotten is true longevity." <note>original: 死而不亡者壽 (Si er bu wang zhe shou). This suggests a form of spiritual or cosmic persistence where the "true self" remains even after the physical body passes.</note>

The reason one "does not perish" lies in being able to **"dwell in tranquility alone with the divine,"** to **"coexist with Heaven and Earth,"** to **"share the same light as the sun and moon,"** and to **"commune alone with the spirit of the universe."** This is the most crucial point to recognize and experience.

The Alchemical Path generally advocates for the **Dual Cultivation of Inner Nature and Life Force** <note>term: 性命雙修 (Xingming shuangxiu). A central Taoist practice balancing the cultivation of the mind/spirit (Nature) and the physical body/vitality (Life Force).</note>. This is based on the sacred words from the *Book of Changes* (I Ching): **"Exhausting the principles of the world and fully developing one's nature to reach the core of one's destiny."** Its outlook on life emphasizes **"nurturing the heart and inner nature"** as the primary aim—the goal of entering sagehood and attaining truth. Simultaneously, it uses **"refining the external physical form"** to **"nurture health and extend life"** as a supporting practice. However, "nurturing the inner nature" is the absolute first priority. Because it emphasizes internal cultivation and views the Sage or the Realized Person as the highest realm of human existence, it strongly advocates for **"inward restraint"** and strictly warns against **"outward pursuit."** All external human desires—what the mundane world calls wealth, status, fame, and profit—should first be set aside and severed with a single stroke. When human desires are completely purified, <term>Primordial Breath</term> <note>original: 元炁 (Yuanqi). The fundamental, vital energy of the universe that exists before physical form; the root of life and vitality in the body.</note> will naturally overflow, and the Principles of Heaven will flow freely. Even if one were as noble as an emperor or as wealthy as the four seas, it would have no connection to the completion of one's "True Self." Having these things adds nothing; lacking them subtracts nothing. Only the internal...

Through the cultivation of the heart and inner nature, one can become filled with radiance, finally enabling them to share the same light as the sun and moon and to flow in harmony with the movements of Heaven and Earth. In this state, the human is Heaven and Heaven is the human; they are one and the same. Only when spiritual cultivation and the sublimation of character reach this realm of **"Unity of Heaven and Humanity"** <note>term: 天人合一 (Tianren heyi). A core Chinese philosophical concept suggesting that the individual and the cosmos share the same fundamental principles and can exist in a state of perfect resonance.</note> can one truly achieve immortality and endure for ten thousand eons.

For the practitioner, the inner world is a separate heaven and earth, a distinct universe. It is by no means something that the "eye-sockets" of mundane people—who only see the external world of physical forms and the visible universe—can hope to investigate, judge, or even begin to imagine in the slightest degree. It is precisely a kind of "spirit of Heaven and Earth" or "spirit of the universe" that **"wanders above with the Creator, and below makes friends with those who are outside of life and death, having no end or beginning."** <note>This is a famous quote from the *Zhuangzi*, describing the absolute freedom of the enlightened mind.</note> The essence lies in the ability to **"respond to things yet be detached from things"** and to **"respond to the world yet transcend the world."** 

Those within the **School of the Alchemical Path** must understand: **"When the mundane heart dies, the spirit lives; when the mundane heart lives, the spirit dies."** Also: **"When the heart is empty, the spirit is divine; when the heart is full, the spirit is obscured."** <note>In this context, "full" means cluttered with worldly desires and intellectual preoccupations, whereas "empty" refers to a state of receptive, clear stillness.</note> Therefore, this heart must not only break through the barrier of wealth and status, the barrier of fame and profit, and the barrier of lust and emotion, but it must also break through the barrier of life and death itself. 

If one does not dwell on wealth and status, only then can one break through the **"cages"** <note>term: 樊籠 (Fanlong). Literally "birdcage," used metaphorically to describe the traps of social and material attachments.</note> of wealth and status. If one does not dwell on fame and profit, only then can one break through the cages of fame and profit. If one does not dwell on lust and emotion, only then can one break through the cages of lust and emotion. If one does not dwell on life and death, only then can one break through the cages of life and death. If a single thought dwells on wealth, one is enslaved by wealth; if a single thought dwells on fame, one is enslaved by fame; if a single thought dwells on life and death, one is enslaved by life and death; if a single thought dwells on lust, one is enslaved by lust. How could such a person possess even a fraction of self-mastery or true freedom? Furthermore, if one treats "attaining longevity" as a preoccupied task, one will never actually achieve longevity. 

Wait until the point where the myriad things do not enter my heart, and I have no heart for the myriad things; then, from that moment, the heart is perfectly clear, the entire being is filled with spiritual luminosity, and one is united with the heights of Heaven and Earth. This is a lofty and expansive philosophy of life and a grand worldview. If one does not first recognize and adopt this as their foundation, then even if the results of your cultivation allow you to live for eighty thousand eons, how would you differ from a **"spiritually-connected, immortal donkey or pig"**? <note>A pointed Taoist critique: physical longevity without spiritual wisdom or character is seen as meaningless, reducing a human to the level of a long-lived animal.</note> Only by using this fundamental mindset to pursue higher cultivation can one hope to enter the realm of the Sages and the Realized.

Regarding what the Immortals call "immortality," one aspect is **"preserving the form"** and the other is **"preserving the spirit."** Regardless of whether one remains in the world through the form or through the spirit, that which...

For those who are able to reach this state, the emphasis then shifts to **Cultivation and Refinement** <note>term: 修煉 (Xiulian). A Taoist term for the process of transforming the self through disciplined mental and physical practices to achieve spiritual perfection or immortality.</note>. There are many methods of cultivation, but they are essentially divided into two branches: **Internal Work** (*Neigong*) and **External Work** (*Waigong*). 

Internal work emphasizes nurturing the **Inner Nature** (*Xing*), while external work emphasizes nurturing the **Physical Life-force** (*Ming*). The former is called the **Work of Inner Nature** (*Xinggong*), and the latter is called the **Work of Life** (*Minggong*). The former inherits the methods of **Laozi** <note>The legendary founder of Taoism, traditionally associated with the *Tao Te Ching* and the philosophy of non-action.</note>, while the latter adopts the methods of the **School of Immortality** <note>term: 神仙家 (Shenxian jia). An ancient school of thought focused on dietary, respiratory, and alchemical techniques to prolong life and achieve divinity.</note>. 

Some refer to those who practice the **"Method of Clarity, Stillness, and Non-action"** as practicing the Work of Inner Nature, and those who practice the **"Method of Grafting Yin and Yang"** <note>term: 陰陽栽接法 (Yinyang zaijie fa). A technical alchemical term for techniques used to replenish vital energy, often metaphorically compared to grafting a branch onto a tree to restore its life.</note> as practicing the Work of Life. Because of this, there is a common saying: *"The Work of Inner Nature is easy to transmit, but the Work of Life is difficult to transmit."* However, this is merely a convenient way of speaking for a particular context and must absolutely not be seen as two separate things. 

In the internal work of nurturing nature, there are also external methods for nurturing the form; and in the external work of nurturing the form, there are even more internal methods for nurturing the nature. The difference between the two is only a matter of sequence and priority. The primary aim of the School of Immortality is to prioritize the **"Simultaneous Nurturing of Nature and Life,"** where the Way (the philosophy) and the Law (the technique) work together, and the spirit and the physical form blend into one. Only in this way can one hope to achieve a state where **"the object and the self are forged into one"** and **"humanity and heaven are forged into one,"** thereby entering the realms of:
*   Transcending the mundane to enter the Sage-like;
*   Transcending the Sage-like to enter the Divine;
*   Transcending the Divine to enter the Transformative.

Therefore, the "Treatise on Literature" in the *History of the Han Dynasty* <note>original: 漢書藝文志 (Hanshu Yiwen Zhi). One of the earliest records of Chinese bibliography and intellectual history, compiled around 111 CE.</note> says of the School of Immortality: **"The followers of the Way of Immortality are those who preserve the truth of inner nature and physical life, and roam outside the mundane world. They do so to wash the will and calm the heart, unifying the realms of life and death so that there is no fear or trembling in their minds."** 

It further states: **"If those who are deluded treat this only as a preoccupied task, then deceptive and strange writings will only increase, which is not what the Sages intended to teach."** From this, it is clear proof that the School of Immortality never intended for "long life" to be their only pursuit! 

In summary, the essentials of the Taoist art of nourishing life can be simplified into these four phrases: 
->**"The Way to nourish Inner Nature,
the Law to extend Life;
the Way to complete the Spirit,
the Technique to complete the Form."**<-

Those whose ambition is for greatness will concern themselves with the great; those whose ambition is for small things will concern themselves with the small. Over thousands of years, when the **School of the Alchemical Path** has passed down its teachings from master to disciple, the "laws" and "techniques" have often been kept secret and not easily shared, and it is even rarer to receive the true transmission. Perhaps this is the main reason why these teachings have remained obscure and have not flourished openly?
