He certainly performed the meritorious service of inheriting the wisdom of the past and opening the way for the future.)

Primary credit must also be given to **Tao Hongjing** <note>Tao Hongjing (456–536 CE) was a key figure of the Liang dynasty, a physician, and a collector of Taoist scriptures who helped organize the Shangqing school.</note> of the Liang dynasty. However, the figure who truly established the foundation for the **School of the Immortal Alchemical Path** for later generations, broadly expanding the spiritual realm, creating a thriving community, and establishing a lineage that continues unbroken to this day, was **Ancestor Lü, the Transcendent of Pure Yang** <note>term: 呂祖純陽眞人 (Lü Zu Chunyang Zhenren). Better known as Lü Dongbin, one of the most famous of the Eight Immortals, revered as a primary ancestor of the internal alchemical tradition.</note>. The later North, South, East, and West Sects...

...and others all regard him as their foundational ancestor. These four sects, in particular, consider the spiritual teachings directly transmitted from Ancestor Lü as their sacred lineage. Other significant contributors include:
*   **Ancestor Wang Chongyang** and **Ancestor Liu Haichan**;
*   The **Seven Perfected** <note>term: 七眞 (Qizhen). The seven main disciples of Wang Chongyang who founded various branches of the Quanzhen school.</note> of the North Sect, including **Qiu Chuji** and **Ma Danyang**;
*   The **Seven Perfected** of the South Sect, including **Zhang Ziyang** and **Bai Yuchan**;
*   **Lu Qianxu** and **Fu Jinquan** of the East Sect;
*   **Li Hanxu** of the West Sect;
*   **Zhang Sanfeng** <note>A legendary figure often credited with the creation of Tai Chi Chuan.</note> of the Sanfeng Sect;
*   **Wu Chongxu** and **Liu Huayang** of the Wu-Liu Sect;
*   Female practitioners such as **Sun Bu’er** and **Cao Yiwen**;
*   And those who practiced the combined paths of Confucianism and Taoism, such as **Chen Zhixu**, **Liu Wuyuan**, **Li Daochun**, **Zhu Yunyang**, **Huang Yuanji**, **Tao Susi**, **Min Yide**, and **Xiao Dening**;
*   As well as **Zhang Junfang**, the editor of the Song dynasty Taoist Canon.

All of these individuals performed truly great deeds.

In summary, the study of alchemical refinement within the Alchemical Path is by no means limited to the task of nurturing and extending physical life. Its primary purpose is to **"cultivate inner nature"** in order to transcend the mundane and enter the divine. This is exactly what **Zhang Ziyang** <note>A Southern Song dynasty alchemist known for his emphasis on the "Internal Elixir."</note> meant when he wrote:
> **"A halo behind the head is still an illusion;**
> **clouds rising beneath the feet do not yet make one an Immortal."**
<note>original: 頂後有光猶是幻，雲生足下未為仙. This verse warns that external "miracles" or psychic phenomena are distractions from true spiritual attainment.</note>

True mastery is only reached when one can **"harmonize with the light and join with the dust"** <note>A phrase from the *Tao Te Ching* meaning to be in the world but not of it, staying humble and unpretentious.</note>; when one can **"place life and death outside oneself and communicate with the creation of the universe"**; when one is **"pure, empty, peaceful, and indifferent"**; and when one **"exists without beginning or end, alongside Heaven and Earth."** Only then has one reached the ultimate goal!

## 1. A Brief Overview of the Taoist Canon

The two works that represent the greatest synthesis of our nation’s inherent culture and academic thought are the **Complete Library of the Four Treasuries** <note>term: 四庫全書 (Siku Quanshu). A massive 18th-century collection of Chinese literature commissioned by the Qianlong Emperor.</note> and the **Taoist Canon** <note>term: 道藏 (Daozang). The comprehensive collection of Taoist scriptures, rituals, and philosophical texts.</note>. The books of the *Four Treasuries* represent Confucian culture; the books of the *Taoist Canon* represent Taoist culture. Positioned between these two is the collection representing Buddhist culture, known as the **Buddhist Canon** (also called the *Tripitaka*). However, while the latter has Indian Buddhist thought as its root, the former two are pure treasures of our national cultural heritage, entirely free from the infiltration of foreign academic thought.

The Taoists trace their origins back to the Yellow Emperor and Laozi <note>term: 黃老 (Huang-Lao). A major school of thought named after the mythical Yellow Emperor and the philosopher Laozi.</note>, while the Confucians trace theirs to the sage-kings Yao and Shun. When investigating their ultimate purpose, there is initially no difference between them. Therefore, among the books collected in the *Taoist Canon*, if one were to strictly define boundaries, there are also books from various other philosophical schools included within it. Critics have occasionally mocked the collection for being a miscellaneous jumble; however, in a broad sense, there is not a single volume that is not essentially a Taoist book.

The followers of Taoism assert that Chinese culture originates from Taoism; if one sets aside Taoist culture, one cannot truly speak of Chinese culture. Branches such as the School of Military Strategy, Legalism, the School of Agriculture, the School of Diplomacy, the School of Yin-Yang, the School of Medicine, the School of Alchemy, Architecture, the Miscellaneous schools, the **Nine Schools of Thought** <note>term: 九流 (Jiu Liu). The various philosophical branches of the Warring States period.</note>, Astronomy, and Geography—all of these, without exception, originate from Taoism. Upon examining historical facts, this is actually not an overstatement.

Therefore, when discussing Chinese culture today, if one excludes Taoism and treats only Confucianism as the basis of governance, it is no different from **"counting the records while forgetting the ancestors"** <note>A Chinese idiom meaning to be well-versed in details but forgetting the fundamental source or origin.</note>; it is to voluntarily abandon half of one’s own heritage. The late **President Chiang Kai-shek** <note>original: 蔣公 (Jiang Gong). Refers to Chiang Kai-shek, leader of the Republic of China.</note> was far-sighted and recognized this. He recently and very solemnly issued an instruction that Taoist culture is an integral part of China's inherent culture. 

Unfortunately, for thousands of years, Taoist scriptures have been viewed by those within the sect as family treasures and precious jade, not to be easily shared with others. Although many of these are immortal and extraordinary books for all generations, they have been treated as secret texts never to be transmitted. This self-imposed isolation has meant that the world not only has no way to glimpse the "inner sanctuary" of this knowledge, but even those who wish to find the entrance find no way to begin their journey!

## 2. The Origins and Evolution of the Taoist Canon

When examining the Taoist classics recorded in the *Treatise on Literature* of the **Book of Han** <note>term: 漢書藝文志 (Hanshu Yiwen Zhi). The earliest extant catalog of Chinese literature, compiled by Ban Gu in the 1st century AD.</note>, beginning with the Yellow Emperor, Yi Yin, Taigong, and Laozi, there were only thirty-seven schools of thought, totaling 993 volumes. Regarding the "Theories of Immortality" <note>term: 神僊 (Shenxian). Refers to the practices and philosophies of becoming a transcendent or immortal being.</note>, there were only ten schools and 205 volumes. The "Chamber Arts" <note>term: 房中 (Fangzhong). Taoist sexual yoga and health practices aimed at longevity.</note> consisted of seven schools and 186 volumes. These numbers increased incrementally over time. Scholars such as Hou Kang, Yao Zhenzong, and Zeng Pu provided supplements and research for the *Book of the Later Han: Treatise on Literature*; Qian Daxin supplemented the *Continued Book of Han*; Ding Guojun supplemented the *Book of Jin*; and the *Book of Wei* included a *Treatise on Buddhism and Taoism*. All of these historical records added to the collection across successive generations.

By the time of the *Treatise on Classics and Documents* in the **Book of Sui**, the records showed 377 categories and as many as 1,216 volumes. During the Kaiyuan era of the Tang Dynasty <note>713–741 AD, a golden age of Tang culture under Emperor Xuanzong.</note>, a widespread search and collection effort was undertaken. After pruning redundancies and discarding the superficial, the books were arranged as a "Canon" <note>term: 藏 (Zang). A "storehouse" or "treasury," used here to denote a complete, sanctioned collection of sacred scriptures.</note> titled the **Jade Guide of the Three Grottoes** <note>original: 三洞瓊綱 (Sandong Qionggang). This marked the first formal attempt by the state to organize Taoist texts into a unified system.</note>, which reached 3,744 volumes. It was from this point onward that Taoist books began to be formally referred to as a "Canon."

According to the **Comprehensive Examination of Literature** <note>term: 文獻通考 (Wenxian Tongkao). A massive 13th-century encyclopedia documenting Chinese institutional history.</note>, during the Song Dynasty, the collection once increased to over 7,000 volumes. After being edited and cross-referenced by Xu Xuan and others to remove duplicates, 3,737 volumes remained. The general outline was divided into the "Three Grottoes," the "Four Supplements," and twelve categories <note>The Three Grottoes (Sandong) and Four Supplements (Sifu) are the traditional seven-part division of the Taoist Canon, reflecting different levels of initiation and scriptural lineages.</note>.

At the start of the Dazhong Xiangfu era [1008 AD], Emperor Zhenzong ordered the Privy Councilor Qi Lun, the Hanlin Scholar Chen Yaozuo, and the Taoist Master of Profound Purity [Chongsu Dashi], along with Zhu Yiqian and Feng Dezhi, to dedicate themselves to the revision and editing of the works. The Minister of Education, Wang Qinruo, was appointed as the General Director to oversee its completion. Following the old conventions, they expanded and supplemented the sections for the *Grotto of Truth, Grotto of Divinity, Grotto of Mystery, Great Mystery, Great Peace, Great Purity,* and *Orthodox Unity*. Combined into a new record and presented to the throne, it was granted the title **Bao-wen Comprehensive Records** <note>original: 寶文統錄 (Baowen Tonglu).</note>, totaling 4,359 volumes.

Subsequently, **Zhang Junfang** received imperial orders to reorganize the collection once more. He compiled authentic versions of the Taoist Canon sent from various provinces across the empire, carefully categorizing them by rank and standard, collating differences, and arranging them into a final Canon. It totaled 4,565 volumes and was titled the **Great Song Tiangong Treasure Canon** <note>original: 大宋天宮寶藏 (Da Song Tiangong Baozang).</note>. Zhang Junfang also extracted the essential points to create a 122-volume work; this is the famous **Seven Slips from a Cloudy Satchel** <note>term: 雲笈七籤 (Yunji Qiqian). A highly influential anthology that summarizes the most important philosophical and meditative texts of the entire Canon.</note>.

During the Chongning era [1102–1106 AD], the Canon was re-edited and increased to 5,387 volumes. During the Zhenghe era [1111–1118 AD], a decree was issued once more to collect Taoist books, which were compiled and carved into printing blocks. It was named the **Wanshou Taoist Canon** <note>original: 萬壽道藏 (Wanshou Daozang). Also known as the *Eternal Life Taoist Canon*.</note>, consisting of 540 cases and 5,481 volumes. This marked the beginning of the printing of the entire Taoist Canon in woodblock format. By the Yuan Dynasty...

### 3. The Contents of the Taoist Canon

... [Master] Piyun, Song Defang, carved a version of the Taoist Canon at Pingyang Prefecture <note>During the Yuan Dynasty, c. 1244 AD</note>, which reached a massive size of more than 7,800 volumes. Later, during the Zhengtong [1436–1449] and Wanli [1573–1620] eras of the Great Ming Dynasty, the collection was successively compiled and edited again, totaling 512 cases and 5,485 volumes. They utilized the **Thousand Character Classic** <note>term: 千字文 (Qianziwen). A classic Chinese poem used as a primer for teaching characters; here used as a traditional filing system where each character represents a volume number.</note> for numbering. (The volumes collected during the Zhengtong era were labeled with characters from "Heaven" [*Tian*] to "Hero" [*Ying*]; the *Supplemental Canon* added during the Wanli era was labeled from "Du" to "Tassel" [*Ying*]). One set of this Canon was bestowed by imperial decree to be enshrined at the **White Cloud Monastery** <note>term: 白雲觀 (Baiyun Guan). The most prominent Taoist temple in Beijing and the seat of the Quanzhen school.</note>. Xu Bin, a scholar of the Hanlin Academy, once carved a stone tablet to commemorate this event.

In addition to the two Ming printings mentioned above, there was also a pocket-sized edition newly carved in the *Bing-Yin* year of the Tianqi era [1626 AD]. These were all secret texts rarely seen by book collectors and were extremely precious, though they have unfortunately been lost to time. Although the various ancient philosophical works <note>term: 子書 (Zishu). "Masters' Literature," referring to the writings of early Chinese philosophers such as Zhuangzi or Liezi.</note> included in the Taoist Canon were printed during the Ming, most were actually based on older engravings from the Song and Yuan dynasties. During the Qianlong and Jiaqing eras of the Qing Dynasty, scholars frequently used these for textual criticism <note>term: 考據 (Kaoju). A school of philology focused on rigorous evidential research and the restoration of ancient texts.</note>. They regarded every word and phrase as a rare, vanished echo of the past, as the saying goes: "The records of the Zhou and Qin provide the basis for critical study; they are valued no less than precious green jade" <note>original: 周秦載籍資考訂，貴之不翅青琅玕. This poetic line compares the ancient texts to "langgan," a mythical green gemstone.</note>. This is because these versions were not only superior to the common editions sold in markets, but also often more accurate than the versions included in the imperial **Complete Library of the Four Treasuries** <note>term: 四庫全書 (Siku Quanshu). The largest collection of books in Chinese history, compiled by order of the Qianlong Emperor.</note>.

The White Cloud Monastery in Peiping [Beijing] kept a complete Taoist Canon in the **Sutra-leaf format** <note>term: 梵筴本 (Fanceben). A binding style where long strips of paper are stacked between boards, mimicking ancient Indian palm-leaf manuscripts.</note>. Each half-page contained five lines, with seventeen characters per line. By the Daoguang era [1821–1850], many parts had become damaged or missing. A gentleman named Wang Tingbi provided the funds to borrow scriptures from various mountain temples and hired scholars to respectfully transcribe imperial editions to repair the set. Only then was it restored to its "perfect jade" <note>meaning: a state of complete integrity.</note> status; this is the **Zhengtong Taoist Canon** that survives today as a rare treasure. The White Cloud Monastery in Shanghai also possesses a complete set, the repairs for which were completed during the Tongzhi era [1862–1874]; it too is a Ming-era Zhengtong edition.

In the early Republican period, while **Mr. Xu Donghai** <note>Xu Shichang (1855–1939), who served as President of the Republic of China from 1918 to 1922.</note> served as President, he borrowed the Taoist Canon from the Beijing White Cloud Monastery and had it reduced into a lithographed six-leaf small-format edition. For this edition, every two leaves of the original sutra-style text were combined into a single page. He appointed the Minister of Education, **Fu Yuanshu** [Fu Zengxiang], to oversee the project. The initiators of this effort were more than ten famous scholars, including **Kang Youwei**, **Liang Qichao**, **Zhang Jian**, and **Huang Yanpei**. The transition from the "Sutra-leaf" format to the **"Square-volume" format** <note>term: 方册本 (Fangceben). Modern book-style binding.</note> began with this edition.

This concludes the general overview of the origins and development of the Taoist Canon. The richness of the collection can be clearly seen from this summary.

### 3. The Contents of the Taoist Canon (Continued)

The general table of contents for the existing **Taoist Canon** <note>term: 道藏 (Daozang). The collective body of Taoist scriptures.</note> is divided into the **Three Caverns**, the **Four Supplements**, and **Twelve Categories**.

The **Three Caverns** <note>term: 三洞 (Sandong). The primary division of the Canon, originally representing different Taoist traditions.</note> are:
1. The Cavern of Perfection (*Dongzhen*)
2. The Cavern of Mystery (*Dongxuan*)
3. The Cavern of Spirit (*Dongshen*)

The **Four Supplements** <note>term: 四輔 (Sifu). Developed later to complement and categorize texts not included in the Three Caverns.</note> are:
1. The Great Mystery (*Taixuan*)
2. The Great Peace (*Taiping*)
3. The Great Purity (*Taiqing*)
4. The Orthodox One (*Zhengyi*)

The **Twelve Categories** <note>term: 十二類 (Shi'er lei). A sub-classification system applied to each of the Three Caverns to organize texts by genre or function.</note> consist of:
1. Original Texts, 2. Divine Talismans, 3. Jade Instructions, 4. Divine Diagrams, 5. Genealogies and Registers, 6. Precepts and Discipline, 7. Ceremonial Rituals, 8. Methods, 9. Various Arts, 10. Records and Biographies, 11. Eulogies and Hymns, and 12. Petitions and Memorials.

The details are as follows:

① The **Cavern of Perfection** (*Dongzhen*) within the Taoist Canon represents the "Supreme Method of the Great Vehicle" <note>This implies the highest level of spiritual teachings.</note> and the Way of the Nine Sages. It was issued by the **Celestial Worthy of Primordial Beginning** <note>term: 元始天尊 (Yuanshi Tianzun). The highest deity in the Taoist pantheon, representing the beginning of the universe.</note>, the Supreme King of the Law, and is called the *Dongzhen Scripture*. This section is divided into twelve categories:

1.  **Original Texts** (*Benwen*): This includes writings such as the "Three Origins and Eight Assemblies" and prose accounts of origins. These are different names for the scriptures and represent the foundation from which the Law is born.
2.  **Divine Talismans** (*Shenfu*): Once the Law is born, it must be supported and nurtured. Examples include texts written in "Dragon Scripts and Phoenix Seals" <note>A poetic term for the stylized, calligraphic script used in celestial talismans.</note> or spiritual traces and talismanic characters.
3.  **Jade Instructions** (*Yujue*): Without study and practice, it is difficult to gain benefit; thus, these are commentaries. Examples include **Heshang Gong's** commentary on the *Dao De Jing* <note>Heshang Gong is a legendary figure said to have lived during the Han Dynasty; his commentary is one of the oldest and most important for understanding the "Way and Its Power."</note> or the "Explanations of the Golden Book." These explain the underlying principles and practical applications.
4.  **Divine Diagrams** (*Lingtu*): These aid in understanding through visuals. Examples include images of the Five Emperors' shadows or diagrams of the forms of the "Three Ones" <note>term: 三一 (Sanyi). Refers to the three essential energies or deities within the human body according to Taoist meditation.</note>.
5.  **Genealogies and Registers** (*Pulu*): These highlight the achievements of the sages. Examples include the accounts of the original deeds of the Three Lords or the manifestations of the Five Emperors.
6.  **Precepts and Discipline** (*Jielü*): These are used to prevent evil and stop errors, such as rules for restraining the "six emotions and seven desires" and the "ten evils and ten thousand vices," allowing one to ascend to the realm of the Sages and Perfected.
7.  **Ceremonial Rituals** (*Weiyi*): These provide solemnity to the sacred. Examples include the liturgical formats for retreat rituals and the protocols for requesting scriptures.
8.  **Methods** (*Fangfa*): These demonstrate power and communication with the divine. Examples include "Preserving the Three and Guarding the One" <note>A core Taoist meditation practice involving focusing the mind on the three "Cinnabar Fields" of the body.</note>, subduing the souls, commanding ghosts and spirits, praying for rain or sunshine, and delivering the spirits of the dead and the living.
9.  **Various Arts** (*Zhongshu*): These are the technical means to transcend the mundane. Examples include self-cultivation, alchemy, transforming the spirit, concealment, yin-yang calculations, herbal medicine, and the nourishment of the body, mind, and life-destiny.
10. **Records and Biographies** (*Jizhuan*): These track the past to guide the future. Examples include the original careers and historical traces of **Laozi** <note>The legendary founder of Taoism.</note> and the "Yellow Emperor's Teacher" (Huangren).
11. **Eulogies and Hymns** (*Zansong*): These are used to respect the sages and honor their virtues, such as the ancient verses of the Nine Heavens.
12. **Petitions and Memorials** (*Biaozou*): These are used to communicate with the celestial bureaus, such as the opening addresses for the "Six Retreats" or the petitions for the "Three Assemblies."

Whenever a text originates from the Celestial Worthy of Primordial Beginning, it is categorized into one of the twelve categories above.

② The **Cavern of Mystery** (*Dongxuan*) within the Taoist Canon represents the "Middle Method of the Middle Vehicle"...

Upon reviewing the entire **Taoist Canon**, a total of 1,473 different works are collected. The breakdown is as follows:
*   **Cavern of Perfection** (*Dongzhen*): 12 categories, totaling 323 works.
*   **Cavern of Mystery** (*Dongxuan*): 12 categories, totaling 300 works.
*   **Cavern of Spirit** (*Dongshen*): 12 categories, totaling 360 works.
The Three Caverns and their Thirty-Six Supreme Scriptures comprise 983 works in total.

The number of works collected in the **Four Supplements** is as follows:
*   **Great Mystery** (*Taixuan*): 110 works.
*   **Great Peace** (*Taiping*): 66 works.
*   **Great Purity** (*Taiqing*): 24 works.
*   **Orthodox One** (*Zhengyi*): 238 works.
The Four Supplements comprise 438 works.

The combined total for the Three Caverns and Four Supplements is 1,421 works. When including the 52 works from the *Supplement to the Taoist Canon* <note>Compiled during the Wanli reign of the Ming Dynasty (1573–1620).</note>, the existing Taoist Canon contains a total of **1,473 works**, spanning **5,485 volumes**.

Upon examining the nature of these collected works, the majority fall under the categories of philosophy, metaphysics, theology, the **Internal Alchemy Sect** (*Dandao Pai*), and Taoist religion. The health-preservation theories of the Alchemical Sect are centered on the **"Dual Cultivation of Nature and Life"** <note>term: 性命雙修 (Xingming shuangxiu). A core concept in Taoist internal alchemy. Its "Nature-work" (*Xinggong*) consists of using the **Way** to permeate the supreme essentials of both **Confucianism** and **Buddhism**; this is the study of becoming an **"Inner Sage and Outer King"** <note>term: 內聖外王 (Neisheng waiwang). A phrase describing the ideal person: someone who possesses the internal spiritual cultivation of a sage and the external capability to govern or act in the world.</note>. Its "Life-work" (*Minggong*) emphasizes the internal refinement and nourishment of our own body, mind, nature, and destiny. This aligns perfectly with modern scientific principles and is not merely concerned with the task of extending one's lifespan. To view it only as longevity is to see it too narrowly! 

People in the world have many misunderstandings regarding this. If one were to ask them about the "Jade Writings and Beautiful Texts" <note>Metaphorical terms for the profound and precious alchemical scriptures.</note> found within the Alchemical Sect's books in the Canon...

Consequently, many of these are supreme masterpieces that even the most famous scholars of past generations rarely had the chance to see. In terms of Chinese culture, it possesses truly immense value and contribution; its preservation, circulation, promotion, and study are absolute necessities.

# The Essentials of the New Edition of the Taoist Canon: Selected from a Scholarly Perspective

## 1. An Overview of the *Essentials of the New Edition of the Taoist Canon*

China’s *Taoist Canon* is a rare masterpiece that stands unique in the field of global scholarship. Any scholar who delves even slightly into its depths will discover that it possesses a distinct cosmic philosophy, a philosophy of life, a moral philosophy, and a religious philosophy. It places particular emphasis on the cultivation of the individual's body, mind, nature, and life-destiny <note>term: 性命 (Xingming). A core Taoist concept referring to the dual cultivation of inner nature and physical vitality.</note>. 

It balances **internal nourishment** and **external practice**, theory and application, in a manner that is holistic and complete, without the flaw of being one-sided. 
*   The **Superior Sages** can use it to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred. 
*   The **Average Sages** can use it to clarify their virtue and cultivate their character. 
*   The **Lesser Sages** can use it to nourish their health and live out their natural years. 

At its peak efficacy, on a small scale, it can rectify the trends of the current age; on a large scale, it can correct the hearts of people for a hundred generations. One must never view it merely as a catalog of health and longevity manuals. Those who speak of "immortality" or "long life" do so because they wish to appeal to the common people's love of...

Because the collection is so vast and the books were once treated as secret treasures, their brilliance has been entirely obscured, causing the world to hesitate and refrain from deep research and exploration. 

Seeing this in recent years, and unwilling to let these works be scattered and destroyed, we have followed the mission of **preserving cultural heritage**. We have put all our effort into collecting, strictly editing, collating, and selecting texts for publication in separate volumes, titled the **Essentials of the Taoist Canon** <note>original: *Daozang Jinghua*</note>. Our goal is to promote Chinese Taoist scholarship and preserve our national cultural heritage. Many of the books selected are out-of-print or unique "orphan" copies from domestic and foreign collections; the Northern Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasty editions are especially precious. Even regarding the various Qing dynasty Taoist books we have published, they are often "books never before seen in the human world." However, limited by manpower and financial resources, collection has been difficult, and some "pearls left in the sea" <note>A Chinese idiom referring to overlooked or lost masterpieces.</note> are perhaps unavoidable!

## 2. The Origins of the *Essentials of the New Edition of the Taoist Canon*

In history, the precedent for distilling the "essentials" of the Canon was the **Seven Tablets in a Cloudy Satchel** <note>original: *Yunji Qiqian*. Compiled around 1029 CE, this is often called the "Mini-Taoist Canon."</note>. Totaling 120 volumes, it was compiled by the Song dynasty Minister **Zhang Junfang** after he completed the imperial task of organizing the entire Taoist Canon. The selections in that work lean heavily toward religious and **Alchemical Sect** <note>term: 丹鼎派 (Danding Pai). The branch of Taoism focused on laboratory alchemy (External) or meditative alchemy (Internal) to achieve immortality.</note> themes. Nevertheless, scholars throughout the ages who wished to avoid the overwhelming bulk of the full Canon have generally used it as their primary source for research. 

This marked the beginning of selecting the "essentials" from the Canon for public circulation. Later, the *Collected Essentials of the Taoist Canon* <note>original: *Daozang Jiyao*</note> was compiled and published; it contained far more books than the *Seven Tablets* and possessed a richer scholarly character. Afterward, **Shouyizi** <note>The pseudonym of Xiao Tianshi (1908–1986), the primary editor of this modern "Essentials" series.</note> again felt that the *Taoist Canon*...

### 3. Contents of the New Edition of the *Essentials of the Taoist Canon*

The "Essentials of the Taoist Canon" referred to here is the edition selected and published by **Linsou** <note>A pseudonym for Xiao Tianshi (1908–1986), the primary editor of this series.</note>. Its scope is far broader than the four works mentioned above. It primarily uses the five thousand-plus volumes of the **Ming Dynasty Zhengtong Canon** <note>original: *Zhengtong Daozang*. The definitive Taoist collection printed in 1445 during the Ming Dynasty.</note> as its core, supplemented by the **Wanli Continuation of the Canon** <note>original: *Xu Daozang*. An expansion printed in 1607.</note>, lost Taoist texts from the **Dunhuang Manuscripts** <term>敦煌卷子 (Dunhuang Juanzi). A cache of ancient documents discovered in the Mogao Caves, containing many lost religious texts.</term>, and the "Continuation of the Taoist Canon" from the **Longmen Sect** <term>龍門派 (Longmen Pai). The "Dragon Gate" branch, a major lineage of the Complete Reality school of Taoism.</term> published at Mount Jingai during the early Qing Dynasty (at the time, only two hundred copies of this work were printed). It also includes the two major abridged versions—the *Seven Tablets in a Cloudy Satchel* and the *Collected Essentials of the Taoist Canon*—while also reaching out to Taoist writings from the Ming and Qing dynasties and the Republican era that were never included in the formal Canon. We have removed the redundant and the trivial, selecting only the finest and most essential. The selection standards are extremely rigorous, and the review and collation have been exceptionally precise.

Although this collection includes materials for the **Upper, Middle, and Lower Vehicles** <note>Refers to the three levels of spiritual cultivation: the "Upper" for spirit/emptiness, "Middle" for energy, and "Lower" for the physical body.</note>—allowing the advanced seeker to recognize depth and the beginner to understand the basics—its primary goal remains rooted in an academic and scholarly stance. At first glance, the contents might seem to consist mostly of charts and texts regarding "life-nourishing" (longevity) practices. In reality, this edition includes works on the **Book of Changes** <note>original: *Da Yi* (The Great Change)</note>, the teachings of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi, and the philosophers Zhuangzi, Liezi, and Guan Yinzi, which were originally distinct from what later generations called "immortality arts." Even the various "Supreme Secret Instructions," the Northern and Southern lineages, and the **Alchemical Arts** <term>丹道 (Dandao). The "Way of the Elixir," referring primarily to Internal Alchemy (Neidan) techniques.</term> of the Eastern and Western traditions included here all transcend mere physical health. Practices focused purely on physical effort—such as **Guided Stretching** <term>導引 (Daoyin). Ancient physical exercises combining movement and breath, a precursor to Qigong.</term>, massage, and breathing techniques—account for less than one percent of the content! Originally, after the Song and Yuan dynasties, orthodox Taoism largely transformed the "tales of immortals" passed down from the Han and Jin dynasties, harmonizing them with **Confucianism and Buddhism** <note>original: 儒釋 (Ru-Shi)</note>. ...the teachings of these schools are generally categorized as the **Upper Vehicle** <note>Refers to the highest level of spiritual practice, focusing on direct realization rather than preparatory or physical exercises.</note> and the highest methods. They rely upon the principles of the **Book of Changes** <note>original: *Da Yi*</note> and the *Kinship of the Three* <note>original: *Cantong*. Referring to the *Zhouyi Cantong Qi*, the "Ancestor of Alchemical Books," which uses the hexagrams of the *I Ching* to explain alchemy.</note> to discuss **Internal Alchemy** <term>內丹 (Neidan). A system of Taoist meditation and spiritual chemistry where the "elixir" is created within the practitioner's own body.</term>. Occasionally, if a trace of these lineages remains, it is only to preserve a record of the more orthodox branches of that school to provide a general overview. Furthermore, we have invariably included introductory essays at the beginning of such volumes to refute their errors, ensuring that future students do not wander down the wrong path!

## 4. Synthesis and Cultivation of the Three Schools

The various orthodox lineages of **Alchemical Arts** recorded in this book have completely broken free from the constraints of primitive Taoism and "Lesser Vehicle" immortal arts. Instead, they are able to integrate the "Upper Vehicle" essentials of **Confucianism, Buddhism, and Zen** <note>original: 儒、佛、禪宗 (Ru, Fo, Chanzong)</note>, synthesizing them into a unified whole. Consequently, many of the key works included are based on the "Synthesis of Confucianism and Taoism," the "Synthesis of Immortality Arts and Buddhism," or the "Dual Cultivation of Zen and Taoism." 

Upon examining the intent of these works, the emphasis is clearly on the **"Synthesis and Joint Cultivation of the Three Schools"** (Confucianism, Buddhism, and Taoism). This ensures that the entire collection aligns with the principles of the *Book of Changes* and the *Kinship of the Three* at the highest level, investigates the mechanics of Yin and Yang and the creation of nature at the middle level, and integrates the logic of Zen and Buddhism throughout. These are used to discuss the "Way of the Cauldron and the Elixir" <note>Metaphors for the body and the refined spirit.</note> and serve as a standard for the joint nourishment of the mind, inner nature, and morality. The contents are subtle, profound, vast, and complete. 

The writings of figures such as **Qiu Chuji**, **Ma Danyang**, **Zhang Ziyang**, and **Bai Ziqing**—representing the "Seven Northern Patriarchs" and the "Five Southern Patriarchs"—are particularly prominent examples. Generally, they teach practitioners that the primary goal of cultivating the Way is to focus on clarity, stillness, and non-action; to sever greed and eliminate desire; to return to simplicity and truth; and to return to one's roots to reclaim life. They emphasize "wandering the mind in the placid" and "merging one's energy with the vast void," ensuring that external things—such as fame, wealth, right and wrong, or likes and dislikes—do not internally damage one's vital life. 

The same holds true for the theoretical cultivation methods of **Li Hanxu** of the Western School, as well as **Zhu Yunyang** and **Liu Wuyuan** during the Qianlong and Jiaqing eras of the Qing Dynasty. As for **Lu Qianxu** of the Eastern School, he is considered the founder of the orthodox "Dual Cultivation" branch. His methods are similar to the "Great Bliss of Fixed Meditation" found in the Supreme Yoga of **Vajrayana Buddhism** <note>original: 密宗 (Mizong)</note>, although his specific techniques are...

## Conclusion

The compilation of the **Taoist Canon** <term>道藏 (Daozang). The comprehensive collection of Taoist scriptures, rituals, and philosophical texts.</term> can be roughly divided into five historical periods:

**The First Period** begins with the first recorded listings in the "Bibliographical Treatise" of the *Book of Han* and continues through the successive additions and revisions by masters such as **Ge Hong**, **Lu Xiujing**, Master Meng, **Tao Hongjing**, Ruan Xiaoxu, Wang Yan, and Yin Wencao. This phase culminated in the Tang Dynasty during the Kaiyuan era with the compilation of the **Jade Framework of the Three Caverns**, which was the first to use the formal title of a "Canon."

**The Second Period** starts with the Tang Dynasty Canon (consisting of 3,744 scrolls) and moves through the reigns of Emperors Taizong and Zhenzong of the Song Dynasty. During this time, officials such as Xu Xuan and Wang Qinruo performed imperial collation, and **Zhang Junfang** continued the refinement to produce the **Great Song Tiangong Treasure of Taoism**. This edition organized the volumes according to the sequence of the *Thousand Character Classic* <note>A traditional Chinese primer used here as a filing system, similar to an alphabetical or numerical index.</note>, beginning with the character "Heaven" (*Tian*) and ending with "Palace" (*Gong*), totaling 4,565 scrolls.

**The Third Period** began during the Chongning era of the Song Emperor Huizong. An imperial decree was issued to search for lost Taoist texts, which were then professionally edited. The collection grew to 5,387 scrolls across 540 cases. Crucially, woodblocks were carved for printing and distribution under the name **The Longevity Taoist Canon**. This marked the beginning of the entire Canon being printed and circulated via woodblock carving.

**The Fourth Period** occurred during the reign of Emperor Zhangzong of the Jin Dynasty. Because many printing blocks had been lost or damaged, Sun Mingdao was ordered to search for missing scriptures to patch the holes. This expanded the collection to 6,455 scrolls, titled the **Great Jin Xuandu Treasure of Taoism**. Later, during the Yuan Dynasty, **Song Defang** followed the dying wishes of his master **Qiu Changchun** <note>Also known as Qiu Chuji, the famous leader of the Quanzhen school.</note> and widely sought out lost books. After eight years of carving and collation, the collection grew to over 7,800 scrolls, retaining the name *Xuandu Treasure of Taoism*. However, during the reigns of Emperors Munkhe and Kublai Khan, a fierce debate broke out between Buddhists and Taoists regarding the authenticity of the *Scripture of Converting the Barbarians* <note>original: *Huahu Jing*. A controversial Taoist text claiming Laozi traveled to India to teach the Buddha, essentially arguing Buddhism was a branch of Taoism.</note>. An imperial decree was issued to burn Taoist scriptures, and the collection suffered further devastation during the chaos of the late Tang and the Five Dynasties period, leaving it incomplete.

**The Fifth Period** arrived during the Zhengtong and Wanli eras of the Ming Dynasty. With the empire at peace, imperial decrees were once again issued to re-compile the entire Canon. This massive undertaking began in the tenth year of the Zhengtong era and was not completed until the thirty-fifth year of the Wanli era. This version remains...

Using the **Thousand Character Classic** <note>A traditional Chinese primer used as a filing system. Each volume was assigned a character in sequence to keep them in order, much like a modern library's call numbers.</note> as the filing sequence, from the character *Tian* (Heaven) to the character *Ying* (Tassels), the collection totaled 512 cases and 5,485 scrolls, which were carved into woodblocks and circulated throughout the world. Separately, there was a pocket-sized edition newly published in the *Bingyin* year of the **Tianqi** era <note>equivalent to the year 1626</note>; this was considered a "secret treasury" among people, seen by very few, and has long since been lost. Today, the version that allows the people of this world to once again study these secret scriptures from several millennia is none other than the **Zhengtong Taoist Canon**! This constitutes the **Fifth Period**.

Up until the **Qing Dynasty**, there were occasional efforts to patch and repair missing parts of the scriptures held in various temples, but these were generally just borrowing and hand-copying to fill gaps, rather than formal restoration or re-editing. Since the **Republic era** <note>The period following the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1912.</note>, the world has been plagued by frequent chaos. Furthermore, with the eastward spread of European influence and the loud clamor of modern science, very few have paid any attention to these ancient books of philosophy, metaphysics, and Taoist studies dedicated to spiritual cultivation!

The publication of the **Essentials of the Taoist Canon** <term>道藏精華 (Daozang Jinghua). A curated selection of the most important texts from the vast Taoist Canon, intended for modern practitioners and scholars.</term> may perhaps contribute a tiny fraction to the preservation and promotion of our nation’s inherent Taoist culture. Ultimately, it is a matter of "looking far back to spiritual connections, while observing the decaying waves of the present," acting to prevent the true teachings from being buried and the **Great Way** from perishing.

->Revised and expanded by the **Old Recluse of Wenshan** at the **Wenshan Vihara** in January of the 72nd Year of the Republic of China <note>January 1983</note>.<-

# Overview of the Essential Tenets of Taoism

->Xiao Tianshi, the Old Recluse of Wenshan<-

Taoism is China’s inherent religion. Its aim is to follow Heaven and practice the Way, establishing the religion through the Way and transforming people through the religion. It inherits the traditions of a thousand generations and connects to the changes of ten thousand future generations. Its supreme guiding principles are always to honor the Way <term>道 (Dao). The fundamental, nameless principle that is the source of all existence.</term> and prize Virtue <term>德 (De). The inner power or manifestation of the Dao within a person or thing.</term>, and to benefit all things and save the masses. Its state of "Complete Perfection" <note>The author uses the term "Quanzhen," which is both a major sect of Taoism and a term for a state of spiritual wholeness.</note> is to harmonize Heaven and humanity and to merge with the Great Void. Its ultimate goal is to purify human life and sanctify the world.

Originally, the **Great Way** began from the Limitless <term>無極 (Wuji). The primordial state of non-being before the universe was formed.</term> and the Beginningless, manifesting its forms in the Supreme Ultimate <term>太極 (Taiji). The source of all things, characterized by the interplay of Yin and Yang.</term> and the Supreme One. From the One it divided into the Three Origins <note>The Three Origins (San Yuan) refer to the primordial breaths of Heaven, Earth, and Water.</note>, and from the Three Origins it transformed and nurtured all things, generating life endlessly. In ancient times, Fuxi received the Diagram <note>The Hetu, or Yellow River Map, a cosmological diagram.</note>, the Yellow Emperor received the Talismans, Gaoxin received the Heavenly Scriptures, and Yu the Great received the Luo Book <note>The Luoshu, a mathematical and divinatory grid.</note>, until the time of **Laozi**, who brought these teachings to their great synthesis. Laozi inherited the past and opened the way for the future, silently wielding spiritual wisdom to compose the **Tao Te Ching** <note>The *Classic of the Way and Its Virtue*, the foundational text of Taoism.</note>. Based on the subtle principles of nature and following the great harmony of Yin and Yang, he taught "non-action yet nothing left undone," non-arising yet nothing not arising, non-being yet nothing not being, and non-utility yet nothing not utilized. From the perspective of its highest clarity, it penetrates the mysteries of creation; from the perspective of its greatest breadth, it encompasses the strengths of all schools of thought. Containing profound and extensive meanings, it is truly an immortal sacred scripture for all eternity.

In the Han Dynasty, **Zhang Daoling** <note>The founder of the Way of the Celestial Masters, the first organized Taoist religious institution.</note> took Laozi as his ancestral source and followed the laws of the various ancient sages. Through purification rituals, offerings, and talismans, he transmitted the "Way of the Five Bushels of Rice." From the **Orthodox One** <term>正一 (Zhengyi). The "Orthodox Oneness" sect, known for its focus on talismans, rituals, and household practice.</term> sect, the Talismanic branch was opened. This branch then stood alongside the other major lineages that trace back to the sacred pulse: the School of Accumulating Goodness, the School of Scriptures, the School of the Alchemical Cauldron <term>丹鼎派 (Danding Pai). The branch focused on internal and external alchemy to achieve immortality.</term>, and the School of Divination. Together, these constitute the **Five Great Taoist Schools**.

If distinguished by their theoretical doctrines, there are four lineages: the **Scriptural Lineage**, which encompasses Metaphysics; the **Nature and Life Lineage**, which encompasses the Alchemical Way; the **Statecraft Lineage**, which encompasses governance and peace; and the **Yin-Yang Lineage**, which encompasses the mantic arts <term>術數 (Shushu). Traditional Chinese systems of calculation, including astrology, numerology, and divination.</term>. 

From the compilation of the **Taoist Canon** in the Tang Dynasty, through the Song, Yuan, Ming, and Qing Dynasties, the continuous editing has never ceased. Organized into the **Three Caverns, Four Supplements, and Twelve Divisions** <note>The traditional structural classification of the Taoist Canon, similar to how the Buddhist Tripitaka is organized.</note>, it is so vast it is difficult to exhaust and its mysteries are unfathomable. It is truly the great treasury of Taoist culture and the jewel house of Taoist scriptures. From the celestial texts of the Three Origins and Eight Meetings, to the proclamations of the Golden Tablets and Jade Chapters, the books of divine talismans and secret mantras, and the classics of spiritual writings and true instructions—all serve to receive Heaven's mandate and proclaim its transformation. They are vast and comprehensive, providing benefits and blessings to the ten thousand... <note>The text on this page ends mid-sentence.</note>

# The School of Accumulating Goodness

The main purpose of the School of Accumulating Goodness <note>The *Jishan Pai*, which focuses on ethical conduct and social service as a path to spiritual attainment.</note> lies in embracing compassion and practicing righteousness. Through the accumulation of personal merit and virtue <term>功德 (Gongde). Spiritual "credit" earned through good deeds, believed to improve one's destiny or spiritual standing.</term>, one aims to provide relief to the world and deliver others from suffering. This, in turn, influences the masses so that all may understand the supreme principle that "The Way of Heaven is ultimate goodness; defying Heaven brings misfortune," leading everyone to joyfully perform good deeds.

The Most High <note>Referring to *Taishang Laojun*, the deified form of Laozi.</note> said: "Fortune and misfortune have no gates; they are invited only by oneself." Whether one performs good or evil, the retribution is clear; it follows a person like a shadow follows a form, without the slightest error. Generally, when a person commits evil, the Great Way may strip away their "periods" and "calculations" <note>Traditional terms for units of time subtracted from one's lifespan as divine punishment.</note>, while smaller offenses invite slander or legal punishment. If one can accumulate goodness and store up merit, the great result is an increase in blessings and longevity, while the smaller result is the invisible avoidance of calamity.

The essence of doing good is to follow only the Way: if a path accords with the Way, advance; if it does not, retreat. Do not deceive the spirits of Heaven, and do not behave in a way that would make you feel ashamed even in the privacy of your own home. Diminish yourself to serve others, and give of yourself for the sake of others. Pity the wickedness of men and rejoice in their goodness; help those in urgent need and rescue those in danger. Treat the misfortunes of others as if they were your own; treat the sins of others as if you had committed them yourself. Extend a heart of mercy to all living things and manifest the law of cause and effect in even the smallest, hidden matters. If one practices goodness without ceasing, the Way of Heaven will protect them and disasters will stay far away. 

Therefore, the ancient perfected masters said: "One who wishes to become a Heavenly Immortal <term>天仙 (Tianxian). The highest grade of immortal who ascends to the celestial realms.</term> must establish one thousand three hundred good deeds; one who wishes to become an Earthly Immortal <term>地仙 (Dixian). An immortal who remains on earth to assist humanity.</term> must establish three hundred good deeds." This is not only the primary task for cultivating the path of immortality, but also the level road for entering the gates of the sages. From the time of Fuxi and the Yellow Emperor onward, all have held this in high esteem.

# The School of Scriptures

The main purpose of the School of Scriptures lies in participating in the study of metaphysics and investigating the classics to realize the principles of harmonizing Heaven and humanity. Through the chanting of scriptures and the performance of repentance rituals <note>Liturgy involving the confession of sins and seeking divine forgiveness.</note>, one seeks to liberate the body and mind from internal and external transgressions. 

Those who engage in study and research encompass the "Three Caverns" <note>The three main divisions of the Taoist Canon (*Daozang*).</note> and extend their reach to a hundred other branches. Their work in textual criticism, compilation, annotation, and explanation lies in promoting the origin of nature, observing the mysteries of the universe, exploring the subtle principles of the Three Origins <note>Heaven, Earth, and Water.</note>, and magnifying the sacred lineage of Virtue. Once a scripture is thoroughly understood, one "returns to simplicity and reverts to the truth" <term>返樸歸真 (Fanpu Guizhen). A core Taoist concept of shedding artificiality to return to one's original, primordial nature.</term>. At the highest level, such a person can govern the world; at the practical level, they can save humanity.

For those who engage in chanting and ritual, there are no complex requirements; they take sincerity and earnest faith as the supreme practice. They clear the heart and purify the thoughts, keeping every reflection fixed on the scripture; they maintain a solemn and respectful bearing, keeping every breath in harmony with the spirit. When their merit is complete and their "fruit" is ripe, a mutual resonance between the divine and the human will naturally occur. The boundary between the self and the external world dissolves; transformation happens without being sought, and success is achieved without being forced. At the ultimate peak, one becomes suddenly vast and transcendent, achieving total liberation of the entire being and reaching the realm of **Pure Emptiness and Great Harmony**.

## The School of the Alchemical Cauldron

The main purpose of the School of the Alchemical Cauldron <note>The *Danding Pai*, often referred to as the school of Internal and External Alchemy.</note> is founded upon three great tenets: to transcend the ordinary and enter the realm of the sacred, to transcend the sacred and enter the realm of the divine, and to transcend the divine and enter the realm of transformation. Its specific method is the dual cultivation of nature and life-force <term>性命雙修 (Xingming Shuangxiu). The simultaneous refinement of one's spiritual temperament (*Xing*) and one's physical vitality and lifespan (*Ming*).</term>. Its ultimate goal is to "ascend like a feathered immortal" <note>A traditional term for achieving immortality and flying to heaven.</note> and to achieve oneness with the Great Void. Therefore, the study of the Alchemical Cauldron is essentially the study of the body, mind, nature, and life.

As a Path, it is subtle, mysterious, and all-encompassing. As an explanation, it uses "mysterious pearls and secret whispers" <note>Metaphorical language used in alchemy to describe the hidden processes of spiritual transformation.</note> that possess infinite applications. Generally, one must cut off greed and discard desire, purifying the thoughts to preserve the truth, thereby nourishing the heart. One seeks a state of clear emptiness and profound stillness, remaining tranquil and practicing non-action <term>無為 (Wuwei). "Non-doing" or effortless action that aligns with the natural flow of the universe.</term> to suit one's inner nature. By refining and nourishing the Yin and Yang, and by securing the "essence" and "qi" <note>The fundamental energies of the body.</note>, one makes the life-force everlasting. Finally, by letting the divine light shine everywhere, one transcends the material world to make the spirit wondrous. 

Nature is established through the life-force, and the life-force is made divine through nature; if separated, they conflict, but if they rely on each other, they become spiritually efficacious. All things—the Yin and Yang, the Five Elements, the Cauldrons and Furnaces, the Fire and Medicines, the River Map and the Luo Scroll <note>Ancient cosmological diagrams used in divination and alchemy.</note>, the Ultimate Nothingness and the Supreme Ultimate—are all wondrous applications of alchemical methods. The starting point of the work lies in the cultivation of the body, mind, and intent, alongside the refinement of essence, qi, and spirit. 

Some practitioners incorporate Confucianism into the Way, others apply Buddhist concepts to the mysterious, some engage with Zen, and others combine the "arts of numbers" <note>Techniques related to destiny and divination.</note>. This school blends a hundred schools of thought into a single thread and unites the Three Religions <note>Taoism, Buddhism, and Confucianism.</note> into one origin. To summarize its essential secret: it lies in "Complete Perfection" <note>Referring to the *Quanzhen* school of Taoism.</note>. Though there are thousands of sects, their orthodox purpose never departs from two lineages: "Clear Stillness and Solo Cultivation" or "Yin-Yang Dual Cultivation." Both aim for the highest goal of breaking free from the shackles of the world to move in harmony with the formless. Whether through the Alchemy of Heaven, Earth, or Humanity <note>The "Three Primordials" (*Sanyuan*) of alchemical practice.</note>, all regard this as the unsurpassed, supreme, and ultimate Path of Truth.

## The School of Talismans and Registers

The main purpose of the School of Talismans and Registers <note>The *Fulu Pai*, the branch of Taoism focused on ritual, exorcism, and communication with the celestial bureaucracy.</note> lies in using talismans and registers to communicate with the divine heavens and to influence worldly affairs. It is the study of the resonance between Heaven and humanity and the mutual communication between the divine and the human. 

Talismans are the secret scripts of Taoism. A talisman <term>符 (Fu). Sacred diagrams or sigils.</term> consists of curved strokes resembling ancient seal and "star-and-thunder" scripts; they are the language used to communicate with the spirits. While humans do not recognize them, the spirits alone understand them. Registers <term>籙 (Lu). Religious certificates or "passports."</term> are documents written on plain silk that list the names of the various celestial officials and their subordinates; they are the pathways for sending petitions to the heavens.

Those who believe in the Way wear talismans and registers as a sign of total devotion. If they can further discipline themselves through self-cultivation, perform good deeds, and pray sincerely for divine protection, they can invite heavenly assistance and enter the sacred city. Important methods of this school also include praying for the removal of disasters, assisting the souls in the underworld, cleansing impurities, and absolving sins. Rituals such as "submitting petitions to the heavens," "stepping the Big Dipper" <note>A ritual dance where the priest mimics walking among the stars of the Dipper.</note>, "refining souls," and "meditative visualization" are also vital components. 

Historically, the arts of Talismans and Registers flourished through the Way of Orthodox Unity <note>The *Zhengyi* sect.</note>. The *Book of Sui* records seventeen sections and 103 volumes of Talismans and Registers. The *Book of Wei* records that Zhang Ling <note>Zhang Daoling, the founder of the Celestial Masters school.</note> authored 1,200 volumes of celestial petitions. Everything—the Three Origins, the Nine Palaces, the 120 officials, and all the various deities—is under their command and governance. Their arts range from transforming gold and melting jade to commanding waters with talismans, encompassing thousands of wondrous techniques and miraculous methods.

When taking up the brush to draw a talisman, one must first purify the heart and silence all stray thoughts, offering devout reverence to the divine spirits. From this state—where the heart and spirit are unmoving—one places the first dot; this is what is called "the opening of the primordial chaos." Furthermore, with one's vital breath connected to the heavenly spirits and in a state of no-thought or worry, the talisman is drawn in a single, fluid stroke. Only then will the talisman possess spiritual power. Essentially, this is a case where "complete sincerity can split even gold and stone" <note>A traditional Chinese idiom meaning that absolute sincerity can overcome any obstacle.</note>; it is the principle that when the mind is unmoving, one can resonate with Heaven and Earth. However, upholding morality, honoring goodness, and abstaining from evil are still considered the primary merits; one does not rely solely on magical arts.

## The School of Divination and Prognostication

The main purpose of the School of Divination and Prognostication <term>占驗派 (Zhanyan Pai). The branch of Taoism focused on observing natural signs, calculation, and verifying outcomes to predict the future.</term> lies in the deep observation of the cycles of growth and decay of **Yin and Yang**, the alternating patterns of fullness and emptiness, the cause and effect within human affairs, and the calculations of the **Five Elements** <note>Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water.</note>. By examining the minute, they understand the prominent; by observing signs, they know what is to come. Their predictions of good and bad fortune, and of the transformations from beginning to end, are as responsive as an echo.

Whether observing astrology, inspecting the qualities of Yin and Yang, calculating the hexagrams and lines of the *I Ching*, relying on tortoise shells or stalks for divination, consulting the Five Virtues, studying geomancy <term>堪輿 (Kanyu). More commonly known today as Feng Shui, the study of how the environment affects human fortune.</term>, researching the "Hidden Gates" <note>original: "遁甲" (Dunjia), a complex form of ancient Chinese divination.</note>, or exhausting the "Six Ren" <note>original: "六壬" (Liuren), one of the three most prestigious mantic arts in China.</note>, as well as prophecies and diagrams—all means used to predict natural disasters, human calamities, good or bad fortune, and the rise and fall of national or personal destiny are encompassed within the School of Divination and Prognostication. 

The purpose of foretelling fortune and misfortune is ultimately to encourage people to "realize that practicing good brings blessings, while practicing evil brings calamity." In this way, people are moved toward virtue and cautioned against vice, remaining vigilant at all times to seek the auspicious and avoid the harmful. Historically, the *Rites of Zhou* <note>An ancient text detailing the bureaucracy of the Zhou Dynasty.</note> established official positions for diviners and prognosticators. Successive generations followed this example, continuing through the Ming and Qing dynasties without ceasing. Although science is flourishing today, the study of divination is rooted in the principles of numbers and logic <note>original: "理數" (Lishu).</note>; it will continue to exist alongside human affairs as a means of foretelling the future.

In summary, Chinese Taoism follows the way of Heaven to aid humanity, permeating all matters. Taoist learning is vast, profound, and subtle; it is transcendent and ethereal, yet leaves out no physical thing. It serves as the framework for all categories of life, and its applications are infinite. As for its deeper mysteries, they are truly difficult to exhaust. I, Tianshi, recognize my own foolishness and mediocrity; how could I dare to wag my tongue or cling to mere words? As soon as one falls into interpretation, one deviates from the mysterious truth. However, I am deeply alarmed by the current prevalence of heterodox theories <note>False or misleading spiritual teachings.</note> and saddened by the potential disappearance of the ancient spiritual connection. Therefore, without considering my own lack of talent and speaking from the bottom of my heart, I offer these humble contributions, hoping they may assist in the promotion of the Way and the salvation of the world. Because I have written this in haste, omissions and errors are inevitable; I respectfully hope that the eminent scholars abroad and the elders of our Path will correct and instruct me.

***

->January 1983 (Year 72 of the Republic), Xiao Tianshi, the Recluse of Wenshan, at the Wenshan Hermitage<-

# Record of Nourishing Nature and Extending Life
### Recorded in the Bibliography of the History of the Song Dynasty

->Composed by Tao Hongjing<- <note>Tao Hongjing (456–536 AD) was a prominent Daoist, alchemist, and physician of the Liang Dynasty, known for his work in organizing the Taoist canon and Chinese pharmacology.</note>

Among all beings endowed with vital breath <term>氣 (Qi). The fundamental life force or energy that flows through all things.</term> and spirit, humans are the most precious. What is precious about humans is the fact that they possess life. Life is the root of the spirit, and the physical form is the tool of the spirit. If the spirit is used excessively, it will be exhausted; if the physical form is over-labored, it will perish. If one can allow the mind to wander in void-like stillness, quiet one's worries through non-action <term>無為 (Wuwei). "Non-doing" or effortless action; a central Taoist concept of aligning with the natural flow of the universe.</term>, observe the primordial breath after the hour of midnight, and regularly practice guiding the breath <term>導引 (Daoyin). Ancient Chinese physical exercises and breathing techniques, ancestors of modern Qigong.</term> in a quiet room—maintaining one's health without deficiency while also taking refined medicines—then reaching a century of life is a common expectation. However, if one indulges in desires and becomes addicted to music and sex, exhausts one's wisdom in the pursuit of wealth and status, allows gains and losses to entangle the heart, remains restless and unable to find peace, ignores the rules of propriety, and eats and drinks without moderation—how can such a person avoid the calamity of a premature death?

During a moment of leisure from my official duties, I have perused various "Collections of Essential Life-Nourishing Arts." These collections were compiled by former worthies such as the followers of Zhang Zhan and Daolin, and individuals like Zhai Ping and Huangshan—all of whom were extraordinary figures with a shared goal of preserving and nurturing life. Some gathered the rules for longevity from the Immortal Scriptures and Realized Beings, while others collected the long-life techniques of Pengzu and Laozi. From the era of the Divine Farmer and the Yellow Emperor down to the Wei and Jin dynasties, I have recorded all methods that benefit life-nourishing <term>養生 (Yangsheng). The traditional Chinese practice of self-cultivation for health and longevity.</term> and cause no harm. Now, I have selected the most essential methods, pruned away the redundant or confusing parts, and organized them into chapters under the title *Record of Nourishing Nature and Extending Life*. It is my hope that this will assist those with whom it resonates and serve as a means of aiding others.

The *Scripture of the Divine Farmer* says: Those who eat grain possess wisdom and intelligence; those who eat stones <gloss>This refers to the "Refinement of the Five Stones," an early alchemical practice of consuming mineral compounds.</gloss> will be stout, sleek, and ageless. Those who eat the *Zhi* mushroom will enjoy longevity and never die; those who consume the primordial breath cannot be buried by the Earth nor killed by Heaven. Therefore, those who consume such medicines shall endure as long as Heaven and Earth and stand alongside the Sun and Moon.

The *Tao Te Ching* of Laozi says: The Valley Spirit <note>A metaphor for the receptive, empty, and life-giving power of the Tao.</note> never dies <gloss>Heshang Gong says: "Valley" means to nourish. One who can nourish the spirit does not die. The "Spirit" refers to the spirits of the five viscera. The liver stores the ethereal soul (Hun), the lungs store the corporeal soul (Po), the heart stores the spirit (Shen), the kidneys store the essence (Jing), and the spleen stores the will (Zhi). If the five viscera fail, the five spirits depart.</gloss>. This is called the Mysterious Female <gloss>This refers to the "Path of Immortality" residing within the "Mysterious Female." "Mysterious" (Xuan) represents Heaven; in humans, this corresponds to the nose. "Female" (Pin) represents Earth; in humans, this corresponds to the mouth. Heaven feeds humans with the five breaths, which enter through the nose and are stored in the heart. These five breaths are clear; they become the essence, spirit, intelligence, voice, and the five natures. Their spirit is called the Hun; the Hun is masculine. It exits and enters through the nose to communicate with Heaven; thus, the nose is "Mysterious." Earth feeds humans with the five flavors, which enter through the mouth and are stored in the stomach. These five flavors are turbid; they become the physical frame, bones, flesh, blood, and the six emotions. Their spirit is called the Po; the Po is feminine. It exits and enters through the mouth to communicate with Earth; thus, the mouth is "Female."</gloss>. The gate of the Mysterious Female is called the root of Heaven and Earth <gloss>"Root" means the origin. This suggests that the gates of the nose and mouth are where the primordial breath of Heaven and Earth originates.</gloss>. Softly, softly, as if it remains <gloss>The breathing through the nose and mouth should be soft and subtle, as if it barely exists, or as if it were not there at all.</gloss>. Use it without exertion <gloss>The use of breath should be relaxed and comfortable; it should not be hurried, forced, or laborious.</gloss>.

The *Te Ching* of Laozi says: Life comes forth, and death enters <gloss>Remove desires from the five internal organs so that the Hun (ethereal soul) is settled and the Po (corporeal soul) is still.</gloss>

# The Way of Life and Death

Coming into life and entering into death. <gloss>This refers to the way passions and desires enter into the breast and mind.</gloss>

The followers of life are thirteen; the followers of death are thirteen. <gloss>In ancient times, the categories of life and death were each considered thirteen. This refers to the nine orifices <note>The eyes, ears, nostrils, mouth, and the two lower openings.</note> and the four "gates" or limbs. Regarding life: the eyes do not look recklessly, the ears do not listen recklessly, the nose does not smell recklessly, the mouth does not speak recklessly, the hands do not grasp recklessly, the feet do not walk recklessly, and the emotions are not unsettled recklessly. Regarding death, the opposite is true.</gloss>

In human life, the actions that lead to the land of death are also thirteen. <gloss>While people desire life, their actions often go against it, thereby driving them toward the thirteen ways of the land of death.</gloss>

And for what reason? It is because of the intensity with which they pursue life. <gloss>The reason they are driven to the land of death is that they pursue the pleasures of living too intensely. This violates the Way and goes against Heaven, leading to reckless actions and the loss of harmony.</gloss>

I have heard that one who is good at preserving life <term>攝生 (Shesheng). The practice of maintaining health by protecting one's vital energy.</term> encounters no rhinoceros or tiger when traveling by land and is not harmed by weapons when entering a battle. <gloss>This is because such a person does not clash with the natural order.</gloss>

The rhinoceros finds no place to thrust its horn; the tiger finds no place to fix its claws; the weapon finds no place to admit its blade. And for what reason? Because there is no land of death within them. <gloss>Meaning they have eliminated the thirteen avenues of death mentioned above.</gloss>

### From the "Nourishing the Lord of Life" Chapter of *Zhuangzi*

**Zhuangzi** says: My life has a limit, but knowledge has no limit. <gloss>Xiang Xiu says: Desiring without deliberation is the movement of one's inner nature. However, the urge to know everything is the application of the intellect. Those whose nature moves naturally find contentment in meeting things as they are. But the intellect pursues things relentlessly and becomes exhausted. Thus, the troubles of the world usually lie in the use of the intellect, not in the natural movements of our nature.</gloss> <note>Xiang Xiu (c. 227–272 AD) was a scholar of the "Seven Sages of the Bamboo Grove" known for his commentary on the Zhuangzi.</note>

To pursue the limitless with the limited is perilous indeed. <gloss>Xiang Xiu says: The intellect has its own limits. Guo Xiang says: If one uses a finite nature to seek infinite knowledge, how can one avoid being distressed? To persist in being "clever" is simply dangerous.</gloss> <note>Guo Xiang (d. 312 AD) was a key philosopher of the "Neo-Daoist" movement who edited and finalized the standard version of the Zhuangzi.</note>

**Zhuangzi** says: Those who understand the reality of life do not strive for what is unnecessary for life. <gloss>Xiang Xiu says: Things "unnecessary for life" are those matters that lie outside of one's inherent nature. Zhang Zhan says: The principle for those whose lives end naturally is that the mechanics of life are self-sufficient; one should not be acted upon by external influences. To do otherwise is to pursue the limitless with the limited.</gloss>

Those who understand the reality of destiny do not strive for what the intellect cannot control. <gloss>Xiang Xiu says: If one follows the principles of life's natural flow and exhausts only the portion one was born with, how could the intellect ever be frustrated?</gloss>

### From the *Liezi*

**Liezi** says: In youth, do not be over-diligent in your conduct; in maturity, do not compete for time; in old age, be content with simplicity and have few sorrows. Let the mind be idle while the body labors—this is the formula for nourishing life.

**Liezi** says: The filling and emptying, the waxing and waning of a single body are all connected to Heaven and Earth and correspond to the ten thousand classes of things. <gloss>Zhang Zhan says: If humans harmonize with this—harmonizing at the beginning and harmonizing at the end—quieting the spirit and extinguishing thoughts is the way of life.</gloss>

### From the *Scripture of the Wondrous Truth of the Old Lord*

The **Miaozhen Jing** says: Humans constantly lose the Way; it is not the Way that loses humans. Humans constantly abandon life; it is not life that abandons humans. Therefore, those who nourish life should be careful not to lose the Way; those who practice the Way should be careful not to lose life. Let the Way and life guard each other, and life and the Way preserve one another.

### From the *Scripture of Huang-Lao*

The **Huanglao Jing** further says: The Way of Heaven bestows transformation and is infinite alongside the ten thousand things; the Way of Humans bestows transformation and the physical form perishes. If one redirects the spirit and expends the essence <term>精 (Jing). Vital essence or seed; the concentrated physical energy of the body.</term>, the essence will be exhausted and the body will decline. The physical form is the root that produces essence, and essence is produced from the spirit. By not expending the essence, one can unite their virtue with Heaven. By not transforming along with the spirits, one can share the same pattern as the Way.

### From Master Xuan He

**Xuan He** says: Those who transform through the physical form belong to the category of "corpse-liberation" <term>尸解 (Shijie). A Daoist concept of immortality where the practitioner appears to die but leaves behind a physical object (like a sword or staff) while the spirit ascends.</term>. In this case, the spirit and form are separated and the two are not united. It is like the phenomenon where birds enter the sea and become clams <note>An ancient Chinese biological myth based on seasonal appearances.</note>, following the Yin and Yang energies of late autumn. Transformation through breath <term>氣 (Qi)</term> allows for the hope of life; transformation through the physical form is something to be greatly feared.

### From the *Essentials of the Old Lord* by Yan Junping

**Yan Junping** says: Wander the mind in void-like stillness, fix the will upon the subtle and profound, entrust your worries to the state of no-desire, and return your aims to non-action <term>無為 (Wuwei)</term>. Thus, you can circulate life and extend your destiny, lasting as long as the Way itself.

### From the *Scripture of Great Existence*

The **Dayou Jing** says: Some doubters say that we all begin together from the "Outside of Nothingness," eventually receiving our breath from Yin and Yang, carrying our physical forms and souls between Heaven and Earth, and drawing the resources for our growth from food and breath.
