...yet there are those who are foolish and those who are wise, those who are strong and those who are weak, those who live long and those who die young. Is this the work of Heaven? Those who understand human nature say: The physical form, wisdom, and folly are granted by Heaven. However, strength, weakness, longevity, and premature death are determined by the person. The Way of Heaven is natural; the Way of Humans is within one's own control. If, at the beginning, the fetal breath <term>胎氣 (Taiqi). The primordial energy or "breath" one is born with.</term> is full and solid, and after birth, the nursing and diet are sufficient, and as one grows, one does not overindulge in rich flavors, and in one's prime, one regulates sexual desire—then such a person will be strong and long-lived. If, at the beginning, the fetal breath is depleted, and after birth, nursing is insufficient, and as one grows, one overindulges in rich flavors, and in one's prime, one is reckless with sexual desire—then such a person will be weak and die young. Even if one's growth is fully sufficient, if one adds to it the practices of "guiding and nourishing" <note>Referring to Daoyin, ancient physical and breathing exercises similar to Qigong.</note>, then the years of their life will be beyond measure.

> **The *Mechanism of the Way* says:** That the lifespan of a human is long or short is not a matter of nature alone. It is entirely due to a lack of caution in handling one's body, excessive eating and drinking, unrestrained lust, and violating the balance of Yin and Yang. When the soul and spirit are not guarded, the essence is exhausted and the life-force declines, and a hundred illnesses sprout. Thus, they do not live out their natural lifespan.

> **The *River Map: The Emperor's View of the Sprout* says:** Those who ignore the principles of Heaven and Earth will meet misfortune; those who follow the seasons of Heaven will find good luck. In spring and summer, find joy in high mountains; in autumn and winter, dwell in low, secluded places. This brings great luck and many blessings, and longevity without end. <note>The "River Map" (Hetu) is a foundational mystical diagram in Chinese cosmology, often associated with the origins of the I Ching.</note>

> **The *Luo Script: Treasure My Life* says:** The ancient method for treating illness involved harmonizing with sweet springs and moistening with the "Original Breath" <term>元氣 (Yuanqi). The foundational life energy of the universe and the body.</term>. Use medicines that are neither pungent nor bitter, but sweet and full of flavor. If one can take these regularly, the fluids will flow through the five organs <term>五藏 (Wuzang). The heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys.</term> and be linked to the lungs. Throughout life, one will have no illness.

> **The *School Sayings of Confucius* says:** Those who eat meat are brave and fierce. <gloss>Like tigers and wolves.</gloss> Those who eat "breath" are divine and long-lived. <gloss>Such as the Immortals and the spiritual tortoise.</gloss> Those who eat grain are wise but die young. <gloss>This refers to ordinary humans.</gloss> Those who do not eat at all do not die and become spirits. <gloss>They rely directly on breathing without worrying about food.</gloss>

> **The *Commentary* says:** Those who eat a variety of foods are shackled by a hundred diseases and demonic influences. The less one eats, the more the heart opens and the years increase. The more one eats, the more the heart becomes blocked and the years decrease.

> **The *Discourse of Sima Qian, the Grand Historian*, says:** The spirit is the root of life; the physical form is the tool of life. If the spirit is used excessively, it becomes exhausted; if the form is overworked, it perishes. If the spirit and form wither early, then the desire to live as long as Heaven and Earth is unheard of. Therefore, that which gives life to a person is the spirit. That which the spirit relies upon is the form. When the spirit and form separate, death occurs. The dead cannot be brought back to life, and that which has departed cannot return. Therefore, the Sages value this unity. <note>Sima Qian (c. 145–86 BC) was the definitive historian of early China; this quote emphasizes the Daoist influence on his philosophy regarding the body-soul connection.</note>

In the Way of Nourishing Life, there are grand principles and major themes. For those who cannot master every detail, they should simply think of doing the opposite of whatever is common or "secular." By doing so, they will unknowingly walk the path of the victors and achieve more than half the merit.

> **The *Scripture of Lesser Existence* says:** Have few thoughts. Have few ruminations. Have few desires. Have few affairs. Have few words. Have few laughs. Have few sorrows. Have few joys. Have few pleasures. Have few angers. Have few likes. Have few dislikes.

Practicing these "Twelve Fewnesses" is the master key to nourishing life. Too much thinking withers the spirit; too much rumination scatters the will; too many desires damage wisdom; too many affairs exhaust the body; too much speech causes the breath to struggle; too much laughter harms the internal organs; too much sorrow makes the heart fearful; too much joy leads to an over-flowing mind; too much happiness leads to forgetfulness and confusion; too much anger leaves the hundred vessels unstable; too many "likes" lead to obsession and lack of self-control; too many "dislikes" lead to bitterness and a lack of joy. If these "Twelve Excesses" are not removed, they are the root of losing one's life. He who has no excesses is nearly a Realized Person <term>眞人 (Zhenren). An enlightened Daoist who has achieved perfect harmony with the Way.</term>. Generally, those who are easy-going and relaxed live long; those who are stingy...

Those who die young do so because of the differences in how they dissipate their energy and toil. The fact that a farmer lives on coarse food while others indulge in fine meats and rich grains is a testament to the effects of desire. A scholar living in seclusion has few illnesses, while a traveler has many worries—this is the distinction between a simple life and a complex one.

Therefore, secular people compete for profit, while the Daoist practitioner rarely strives for it. **Hu Zhao** <note>Hu Zhao (186–250 AD) was a famous scholar and calligrapher who lived as a recluse during the Three Kingdoms period.</note> said: The eyes should not wish to see improper colors; the ears should not wish to hear foul words; the nose should not wish to smell rank odors; the mouth should not wish to taste pungent or toxic flavors; and the heart should not wish to plot deceitful schemes. First, cast away those anxieties and quiet the reflections that disturb the spirit and violate one's nature. This is one of the arts of "Nourishing the Spirit."

> **The *Yellow Court Scripture* says:** The clear water of the Jade Pool <term>玉池 (Yuchi). A Daoist term for the mouth or the area under the tongue.</term> irrigates the spiritual root; if one can truly cultivate this, one may live forever. This is called "Feeding on the Natural." That which is "Natural" is the Flower Pool. The Flower Pool is the saliva in the mouth. If one breathes according to the method and swallows it, one will not feel hunger. <note>The "Spiritual Root" often refers to the tongue or the source of life energy in the throat.</note>

> **The *Inner Explanation of Lord Lao to Yin* says:** Saliva, when rinsed in the mouth, becomes the "Sweet Spring"; when gathered, it becomes "Jade Fluid"; when it flows, it becomes the "Flower Pool"; when scattered, it becomes "Refined Essence"; when it descends, it becomes "Sweet Dew." Therefore, it is said that within the Flower Pool lies a Sweet Spring. If one rinses and swallows it, it irrigates the internal organs, moistens the body, allows the hundred vessels to flow smoothly, and transforms to nourish the myriad spirits. The limbs, joints, and even the hair rely upon it to grow.

> **The *Classic of the Center* says:** He who is quiet lives long; he who is restless dies young. If one is quiet but does not know how to nourish life, his lifespan will decrease; if one is restless but knows how to nourish life, his years will be extended. However, it is easy to be quiet and difficult to control restlessness. For those who truly wish to follow the suitability of nourishment, one can find nourishment in quietude, and one can also find nourishment in restlessness.

> **Han Rong (Yuanzhang) says:** Wine is the flower of the five grains and the pinnacle of flavor, yet it can also harm a person. Fine things are difficult to manage and easy to overindulge in; those who nourish their nature should be cautious of this.

> **Shao Zhongkan says:** The five grains fill the flesh and body but cannot increase the lifespan; the hundred medicines treat illness and extend years but are not sweet to the palate. That which fills the flesh and pleases the palate is what secular people treasure; that which is bitter to the mouth but extends life is the treasure of the Daoist.

**The *Basic Questions* says:** The Yellow Emperor asked Qi Bo: "I have heard that the people of ancient times lived to be over a hundred years old, yet their movements did not falter. <gloss>This means their blood and energy were still strong.</gloss> Today, people are only fifty when their movements become weak. Is it because the world has changed, or is it the fault of the people?" 

Qi Bo replied: "The people of ancient times knew the Way. They modeled themselves on Yin and Yang and lived in harmony with the 'Arts and Numbers.' <gloss>This refers to the methods of sexual health and internal cultivation.</gloss> Their eating and drinking were moderated; their rising and resting had a regular schedule. They did not engage in reckless actions. Thus, their physical forms and spirits remained unified, allowing them to complete their natural lifespan and live past a hundred years. 

People today are not so. They use wine as if it were water and make recklessness their constant habit. They enter the bedchamber while drunk, exhausting their essence through lust and scattering their true energy through their cravings. They do not know how to maintain a state of fullness or how to manage their spirits. They strive only to please their hearts, acting contrary to the harmony of Yin and Yang. Their lifestyle and routines have no moderation or limit. Therefore, they wither by the age of fifty."

**Laozi says:** The great term of a human life is limited to a hundred years. Those who moderate and protect it can reach a thousand years—it is like a lamp using a small wick versus a large one. The common multitude...

While others speak much, I speak little. While the masses are filled with worries, I remember little. While others are fierce and violent, I am not moved to anger. I do not allow human affairs to burden my intentions, nor do I obsess over the formal duties of lords and ministers. Remaining indifferent and practicing "non-doing" <note>The Daoist concept of *Wuwei*, or effortless action in harmony with the natural world.</note>, my spiritual energy naturally becomes full. This is the medicine of immortality, yet no one in the world recognizes it in me. 

Do not say that the heavens are dim and do not know human feelings; do not say that the darkness is absolute and spirits cannot see the human form. Even the softest whisper of the heart is heard by the ghosts as a loud voice. If one violates the sacred prohibitions a thousand times, the Earth will reclaim the person’s form. 

When a person performs "Visible Good," <term>陽善 (Yang Shan). Good deeds done openly, which are rewarded by society.</term> righteous people will reward them. When a person performs "Hidden Good," <term>陰善 (Yin Shan). Good deeds done in secret, which are rewarded by the spiritual realm.</term> the ghosts and spirits will reward them. Conversely, when a person commits "Visible Evil," righteous people will punish them; when a person commits "Hidden Evil," the ghosts and spirits will punish them. Thus, Heaven does not deceive man, for it follows him like a shadow; Earth does not deceive man, for it follows him like an echo.

**Lord Lao** <note>Laozi, the deified founder of Daoism.</note> said: If a person practices goodness and accumulates virtue yet encounters calamity, it is because they are suffering from the "lingering misfortunes" of their ancestors. If one violates the prohibitions and commits evil yet encounters good fortune, they are receiving the "lingering blessings" of their ancestors.

The ***Treatise on Diseases by Famous Physicians*** says: Those in this world who do not live out their natural lives, and those who die prematurely, all perish because they do not love or cherish themselves. They engage in angry disputes to satisfy their whims, and they chase after fame and profit. This gathers poison within their bodies, injuring the bones and marrow from the inside and exhausting the muscles and flesh from the outside. Their blood and energy are depleted, and their "meridians" <note>Channels through which life energy, or Qi, flows.</note> become blocked. Their internal courage is emptied, inviting a multitude of illnesses. Their "Righteous Energy" <note>The body's natural defense and vitality.</note> declines daily, while "Evil Energy" <note>Pathogenic influences or disease-causing factors.</note> flourishes. This is no different from trying to fill the vast ocean into the tiny flame of a lamp, or crumbling a Great Mountain to stop a tiny trickle of water. To speak of the ease of their decline—it is swifter than even these examples.

**Peng Zu** <note>A legendary figure in Chinese mythology said to have lived over 800 years through Daoist practices.</note> said: The Way does not lie in complexity. One simply must not obsess over clothing, food, sound, color, victory, defeat, loss, gain, glory, or shame. If the heart is not overworked and the physical form is not pushed to the limit, and if one constantly guides the internal energy and breath—simply by doing this, one can live for a thousand years. Those who wish for infinite long life should take the "Superior Medicine" <note>Likely referring to internal cultivation rather than herbal drugs.</note>.

**Zhongchang Tong** <note>A Han dynasty philosopher known for his "Treatise on Spontaneity."</note> said: To cleanse the "Six Emotions," one may have a heart but should not use it for anxious thought; one may have a mouth but should not use it for excessive speech; one may have a body but should not use it merely for comfort. If one finds comfort, one should be able to move on from it; if one finds joy, one should not become attached to it. By planning one's life this way, one will not even notice the daily benefits or how things around them change.

Regarding **Peng Zu**, he was nearly equal to **Laozi**. If not, why would he be of the same species as other men but possess such a different lifespan?

**Chen Ji (Yuanfang)** <note>A scholar of the Eastern Han period.</note> said: Most illnesses and premature deaths are caused by diet. The dangers of eating and drinking exceed even those of "sound and color" <note>A common metaphor for sensory and sexual indulgences.</note>. One can abstain from sensory pleasures for over a year, but one cannot go a single day without food. Thus, the benefit of food is great, but its harm is also acute. <gloss>Excessive intake causes sharp injury, while eating little increases one's benefit.</gloss>

**Zhang Zhan** <note>A Jin dynasty scholar and commentator on the *Liezi*.</note> said: Those who hold extreme status and power, even if they are not struck by "external evils," <note>External pathogens like wind or cold.</note> suffer internal damage to their spirit, leading to the death of heart and body. <gloss>This is not due to external omens or spirits, but simply because of internal conflict—like ice and hot coals searing within—leading to internal collapse and the vomiting of blood.</gloss> Those who were once wealthy but become poor, even if not struck by external illness, will find their skin withered and their muscles protruding, leading to paralysis. <gloss>The transition between poverty and wealth affects a person like the shifting stakes of a gambling game. Thus, the distress in the chest damages the physical frame.</gloss>

Movement overcomes cold; stillness overcomes heat. Being able to balance movement and stillness is the way to long life. When the "Essence and Energy" are pure and quiet, one becomes one with the Way.

**Zhuangzi** <note>The influential Daoist philosopher.</note> said: The "True Person" <term>真人 (Zhenren). An enlightened Daoist who has transcended worldly attachments.</term> does not sleep and does not dream.

**Shenzi** <note>Shen Dao, a philosopher who blended Legalist and Daoist ideas.</note> said: He who has no worries during the day will have no dreams at night.

**Master Zhang**, who was over one hundred and seventy years old, still appeared as robust as a young man. He said: The Way of nourishing nature is to never walk for too long, sit for too long, or lie down for too long.

It features advice from sages like Peng Zu and Zhuangzi on avoiding the internal "burning" caused by stress and attachment.</summary>

Wearing clothes that are too heavy or using thick quilts makes the body unable to endure hardship, leading to diseases caused by wind and cold. Eating rich meats and fats and indulging in heavy drinking and gluttony leads to diseases of internal blockage. Obsessing over beautiful women and filling one's house with concubines leads to the disaster of "Depletion and Damage." Listening to licentious or mournful music to please the ears leads to the confusion of indulgence. Galloping about for sightseeing or hunting in the wilderness leads to the loss of self in wild frenzy. Plotting for victory and taking advantage of the weak leads to the ruin of pride and excess. The Sages and Worthies warned against losing these principles. The tools for nourishing life are like water and fire—one must not lose the proper balance, or they will instead become harmful.

Therefore, it is said that when one's power and influence reach their absolute peak, one cannot do without the wisdom of Lord Yang; and to maintain a state of fullness and preserve success, one cannot do without the insight of Lord Wang.

# The Method of Absorbing Vital Energy for Longevity and Abstaining from Grains <gloss>This text was transcribed from the Daoist Canon of the Song Dynasty and is recorded in Zhang Junfang’s *Seven Tablets in a Cloudy Satchel* <note>A major Daoist anthology compiled around 1019 AD.</note>.</gloss>

## Absorbing Vital Energy to Cure Illness

The **Scripture of Original Yang** <note>original: "元陽經" (Yuanyang Jing)</note> says: Regularly inhale through the nose. Hold the breath and rinse the mouth with it <note>This refers to mixing the breath with saliva, a practice known as "swallowing the jade fluid."</note>, moving it across the tongue and coating the lips and teeth, then swallow it. If one can do this a thousand times in a single day and night, it is excellent. One should eat little; if one eats too much, the **Vital Energy** <term>Qi (氣). The fundamental life force or "breath" that flows through all living things.</term> will flow backward, and the **Hundred Vessels** <note>The network of meridians or pathways through which energy flows in Traditional Chinese Medicine.</note> will become blocked. When the vessels are blocked, the Vital Energy cannot circulate, and when it cannot circulate, illness arises.

**Yuan Wei** <note>Likely referring to an early Daoist commentator or a specific lineage text.</note> said: The **Will** is the commander of the Vital Energy. The Vital Energy is the filler of the body. Those who are skillful in this use it to pursue life; those who are wicked use it to destroy their physical form. Therefore, in the method of circulating Vital Energy, one must eat little and practice self-restraint. Move the physical form to harmonize the internal energy. Let the will and intention be focused as one, firmly guarding the internal and external. Close both the upper and lower gates <note>Referring to the bodily orifices</note>, so the spirit may permeate the entire frame and the flow of energy may spread smoothly in all directions. Cultivate and guard the **Gate of Origin** <term>Guan Yuan (關元). A primary energy center located about three inches below the navel, also known as the lower Dantian.</term> until it is full and solid. By doing this, any lurking "evil influences" <note>Pathogenic factors like wind, cold, or stagnant energy.</note> will depart on their own.

**Peng Zu** <note>A legendary long-lived figure in Chinese mythology, said to have lived over 800 years.</note> said: Regularly hold the breath and take in new air. From dawn until noon, sit in a kneeling position. Wipe the eyes, massage the body, lick the lips, and swallow the saliva. After absorbing Vital Energy dozens of times, one may then stand up to walk, speak, or laugh. If one occasionally feels fatigued or uneasy, use **Guided Stretching** <term>Daoyin (導引). Ancient physical exercises combining movement and breath control, a precursor to modern Qigong.</term> and breath retention to attack the specific ailment. One must visualize the body—from the head and face, the nine orifices, the five internal organs, and the four limbs, down to the very tips of the hair—and make the Vital Energy felt in every location. Visualize the energy moving through the body like clouds, rising from the nose and mouth and reaching down to the tips of the ten fingers. This will clarify and harmonize the **True Spirit**, making acupuncture, medicine, or moxibustion unnecessary. 

Whenever using Vital Energy to eliminate the "hundred illnesses," direct your thoughts to wherever the pain resides. If the head aches, think of the head; if the feet ache, think of the feet. Harmonized energy will go there to attack the ailment, and from one hour to the next, it will dissipate naturally. If suffering from a seasonal cold, one can hold the breath to induce sweating; once sweat breaks out across the body, the illness is resolved.

Circulating and holding the breath are the essentials of governing the body, yet one must first understand the underlying principles. Furthermore, one should be "empty and hollow" <note>referring to an empty stomach</note>; one must not be full. If the energy becomes stagnant and cannot flow freely, it may cause sores or carbuncles. It is like a spring of water: it must not be forcibly suppressed. If one craves raw fish, raw vegetables, or fatty meats, or if one cannot eliminate feelings of joy, sorrow, worry, or anger, then practicing the circulation of energy will instead cause the energy to rush upward. 

Anyone wishing to learn how to circulate Vital Energy must do so gradually. **Liu An** <note>The Prince of Huainan (c. 179–122 BC), a Han Dynasty polymath and patron of Daoism.</note> said: "By inhaling the living and exhaling the dying, one can exist forever." This refers to the air taken in through the nose being "living." If a person cannot fully practice the absorption of Vital Energy, they should at least supervise their breathing from morning to night without ceasing, exhaling slowly and gently. Simply let the nose inhale and the mouth exhale; this is what is called **"Expelling the old and taking in the new."**

The **Scripture of Absorbing Vital Energy** says: The **Way** <note>original: "道" (Dao)</note> is Vital Energy. By preserving energy, one attains the Way; by attaining the Way, one exists forever. **Spirit** is the **Essence**. By preserving the Essence, the Spirit becomes enlightened; through an enlightened Spirit, one achieves longevity. **Essence** is the flowing river of the blood vessels and the numinous spirit that guards the bones. When Essence departs, then the bones... <note>The text fragment ends here.</note>

...become withered bones. If the bones wither, then death follows. Therefore, in practicing the **Way** <note>The Dao</note>, one must make it a priority to treasure their **Essence** <term>Jing (精). The foundational energy of the body, often associated with vitality and reproductive health.</term>.

From midnight until noon is the time of **Living Energy** <note>original: "生氣" (Shengqi). This is when Yang energy is rising.</note>; from noon until midnight is the time of **Dead Energy** <note>original: "死氣" (Siqi). This is when Yin energy dominates.</note>. During the time of Living Energy, one should lie flat on the back, close the eyes, and perform the technique of **Holding the Fist** <gloss>To "hold the fist" means to fold the hand like an infant, pressing the four fingers over the thumb.</gloss>. By doing this, the spirits of the body will be complete and the **Five Organs** <note>Heart, Liver, Spleen, Lungs, and Kidneys.</note> will be at peace. 

If one can hold the breath for two hundred and fifty counts, the **Luminous Canopy** <term>Huagai (華蓋). A poetic and anatomical term for the Lungs, which cover the other organs like a royal umbrella.</term> will become bright. When the Luminous Canopy is bright, the ears and eyes become sharp, the entire body is free of disease, and "evil influences" cannot take hold of the person.

## The Method of Long Breathing and the Six Sounds

In all practice of **Conducting Energy** <term>Xingqi (行氣). The art of directing the breath through the body's meridians.</term>, one should take energy in through the nose and expel it through the mouth. Draw it in subtly and deeply; this is called "Long Breathing." There is one way to take energy in, but six ways to expel it. The one way of taking it in is simply called "Inhaling." The six ways of expelling it are called **Chui** (blowing), **Hu** (exhaling), **Xi** (sighing), **He** (puffing), **Xu** (hissing), and **Si** (breathing out). These are all methods of exhalation.

Every person's natural breath consists of one inhalation and one exhalation, following a set count. If you wish to practice Long Breathing, use these methods of exhalation:
*   When it is cold, you may use **Chui** <note>To expel cold or clear heat.</note>.
*   When it is warm, you may use **Hu** <note>To harmonize wind.</note>.

These sounds are used with nuance to treat illness:
*   **Chui** to remove heat.
*   **Hu** to remove wind.
*   **Xi** to remove vexation.
*   **He** to move energy downward.
*   **Xu** to disperse stagnation.
*   **Si** to resolve extreme fatigue.

Generally, people who are exhausted will naturally use **Xu** and **Si** sounds often. However, Daoist practitioners of energy cultivation usually prefer not to use **Xu** or **Si** unnecessarily, as these sounds are the core of the Long Breathing method used for recovery. This is a method for both men and women to preserve life, derived from the **Immortal Scriptures**. 

Before practicing the conduction of energy, one must first remove the hair from inside the nose; this is what is called "clearing the path to the spirits." If the weather brings fierce winds, or during times of extreme cold or extreme heat, do not practice the intake of energy.

## The Theory of the Five Labors and Seven Injuries

The **Treatise on Illustrious Medicine** says: All illnesses arise from the **Five Labors**. Once the Five Labors are exerted, two organs are damaged first. The heart and kidneys receive the "evil influence," and subsequently all the organs and viscera become ill.

**The Five Labors are:**
1.  **Labor of the Will** (excessive ambition)
2.  **Labor of Thought** (overthinking)
3.  **Labor of the Heart** (emotional strain)
4.  **Labor of Worry** (anxiety)
5.  **Labor of Fatigue** (physical overexertion)

The Five Labors give rise to the **Six Extremities** (exhaustion of Qi, Blood, Sinews, Bones, Essence, and Marrow). These Six Extremities then lead to the **Seven Injuries**, which transform into the **Seven Pains**. These pains cause a person to have an abundance of "evil energy" and a deficiency of "upright energy." One becomes prone to sudden swings of joy, anger, or sadness; one loses the pleasure of eating, fails to build muscle or skin, loses the luster in their complexion, and their hair becomes white and withered. 

In severe cases, this leads to "great wind" <note>Often referring to stroke or paralysis in ancient texts</note>, wasting of one side of the body, contraction of the sinews, stiffness of the limbs, blockages in all the joints, emaciation, shortness of breath, and pain in the waist and legs. This is caused by marrying too young, excessive loss of essence, deficiency of blood and energy, and the results of extreme overwork.

All illnesses that arrive are rooted in the Five Organs; one must recognize their signs. If you do not recognize them, do not attempt to treat them blindly.
*   **For Heart Illness:** The body feels alternating cold and heat; use inhalation and exhalation to treat it.
*   **For Lung Illness:** The chest and diaphragm feel swollen and full; use the **Xu** sound to expel it.
*   **For Spleen Illness:** There is "wandering wind" on the body, a feeling of floating, itching, pain, or stuffiness; use the **Xi** sound to expel it.
*   **For Liver Illness:** Pain in the eyes, or feelings of sorrow and gloom; use the **He** sound to expel it.

The above are part of the twelve types of energy-tuning methods. One should always draw energy through the nose and expel it through the mouth, making the sound of the breath follow the specific words: *Chui, Hu, Xu, He, Xi, Si*. # The Supreme Clarity Secret Formula for Preserving the Spirit and Refining Energy through the Five Stages and Seven Symptoms

<note>original: "太清存神鍊氣五時七候訣" (Taiqing cunshen lianqi wushi qihou jue). "Supreme Clarity" refers to one of the highest heavens in Daoist cosmology, signaling the divine origin of this method.</note>

The body is the dwelling place of the **Spirit** and **Energy**. If the Spirit and Energy remain within, the body is healthy and strong. If the Spirit and Energy scatter, the body withers away. If you wish to preserve the body, you must first stabilize the Spirit and Energy. 

**Energy** is the mother of the **Spirit**; **Spirit** is the child of **Energy**. When both Spirit and Energy are complete, one achieves long life and does not die. If you wish to stabilize the Spirit, you must refine the **Primal Energy** <term>Yuanqi (元氣). The innate energy one is born with, which must be preserved to prevent aging.</term>. When Primal Energy is within the body, the Spirit settles in the **Sea of Energy** <term>Qihai (氣海). An acupuncture point and energy center located below the navel.</term>. When the Sea of Energy is full, the heart is at peace and the Spirit is stable. When the Spirit and Energy do not scatter, the body and mind become still. When stillness reaches the point of total meditative absorption, the body is preserved and the years are prolonged. By constantly dwelling in the source of the **Way** <note>The Dao</note>, one naturally becomes a sage. 

As Energy flows through the spiritual realm, the Spirit achieves innate wisdom. When the life-force is focused and the body is preserved, one aligns with their **True Nature**. Then, one's lifespan will equal that of the sun and moon, and the achievement of the Way is complete.

According to the inscriptions on refining energy: those who wish to learn this art must first **Abstain from Grains** <term>Bigu (絕粒/辟穀). A Daoist fasting practice where one stops eating common grains to clear the body of "turbid" energy and rely on "refined" energy.</term>. Center the mind on the Sea of Energy and preserve the Spirit in the **Cinnabar Field** <term>Dantian (丹田). The "elixir field," the primary focus point for internal alchemy located in the lower abdomen.</term>. Restrain the heart and purify your thoughts. Once the Sea of Energy is full, you will naturally feel satiated. 

For those who practice with a single-minded focus, a "minor success" is achieved in one hundred days, and a "great success" in three years. First, you will enter the **Five Stages**, and later you will master the **Seven Symptoms**. The Spirit will then become capable of divine transformations, appearing and disappearing at will. You could traverse a thousand miles of sheer cliffs, coming and going without any obstacle. If the Energy does not scatter, the Sea of Energy remains full. When the Spirit is still in the Cinnabar Field, the body and mind are eternally firm. Your countenance will naturally be restored to youth, your complexion maintained, and your physical form transformed into that of an **Immortal**. You will be free to remain hidden or revealed, possessing spiritual powers that never fade. Such a person is called a **True Immortal**; the world calls them a **Perfected Person** <term>Zhenren (真人). A human being who has achieved the highest level of spiritual cultivation and union with the Dao.</term>. They are as old as Heaven and Earth, and their lifespan is equal to the sun and moon. 

This method does not require the forced swallowing of air or saliva, nor is it a path of hardship. Eat when you need to eat, rest when you need to rest; it is a path of freedom, spontaneity, and lack of obstacles. The Five Stages and Seven Symptoms are simply the process of entering the "embryonic state" of meditative observation.

## The Five Stages

**The First Stage:** The mind moves a lot and is still only a little. Thoughts are drawn to ten thousand different environments; the mind chooses and discards without consistency. Thoughts and calculations are like a "wild horse" <note>A common metaphor in meditation for an untrained, wandering mind.</note>. This is the state of the ordinary person's heart.

**The Second Stage:** The mind is still for a little while, but moves a lot. One attempts to restrain the movement and bring it back to the heart, but the mind remains scattered and elusive, difficult to subdue. Continually applying effort to restrain it is the beginning of entering the Way.

**The Third Stage:** Movement and stillness are balanced. The mind seems to be restrained, but it cannot yet maintain constant stillness. Stillness and scattering are equal; by applying diligent effort, one gradually becomes practiced and refined.

**The Fourth Stage:** The mind is still a lot and moves only a little. The restraint of the heart has become familiar. As soon as movement occurs, one restrains it, remaining focused on a single state. Even if focus is lost, it is quickly regained.

## The Seven Symptoms

**The First Symptom:** All chronic illnesses are eliminated. The body feels light and the mind is cheerful. As the mind is kept focused within, the Spirit becomes quiet and the Energy becomes peaceful. The **Four Elements** <term>Sida (四大). A term referring to the physical body, composed of earth, water, fire, and wind.</term> are in harmony, and the **Six Emotions** <term>Liuqing (六情). The sensory and emotional attachments: joy, anger, sorrow, delight, love, and hate.</term> fall into deep silence. With the mind resting in the primal realm, one **Embraces the One and Guards the Center** <note>A classic Daoist meditation practice of maintaining unified focus on the source of life.</note>. A sense of joy is renewed daily. This is called "Attaining the Way."

**The Second Symptom:** One surpasses ordinary human limits. The complexion returns to that of a youth, the physical form is joyful, and the heart is at peace. One gains **Spiritual Perception** <term>Tongling (通靈). The ability to communicate with the divine or perceive the supernatural.</term> and "Clairvoyant Vision." At this stage, one should move to a different district and choose a new place to settle, ensuring that neighbors and old acquaintances do not recognize you. <note>Ancient Daoists often suggested moving away as one's appearance stopped aging, to avoid unwanted attention or accusations of sorcery.</note>

**The Third Symptom:** The lifespan is extended to a thousand years. At this point, one is called an **Immortal** <term>Xianren (仙人). A being who has transcended mortality through self-cultivation.</term>. One travels among famous mountains and flies through the air with ease. Served by **Azure Youths** and serenaded by **Jade Maidens** <note>Divine attendants in the Daoist celestial bureaucracy.</note>, one treads upon the mist and rosy clouds, with colorful clouds supporting the feet.

**The Fourth Symptom:** The physical body is refined into pure Energy, and a halo of light surrounds the person. One is now called a **Perfected Person** <term>Zhenren (真人). One who has achieved the highest truth and transformed their physical nature into spiritual essence.</term>. One can exist or vanish at will. Their own inner light shines forth, keeping them in constant brightness day and night. They travel to the various **Cave-Palaces** <note>Sacred grotto-heavens where the Immortals reside.</note>, and other immortals stand in attendance.

**The Fifth Symptom:** Energy is refined into Spirit. One is called a **Divine Person** <term>Shenren (神人). A being of pure spirit who has transcended the limitations of energy and form.</term>. Their powers of transformation are limitless, and their actions are inexhaustible. Their strength can move heaven and earth, relocate mountains, or dry up the seas.

**The Sixth Symptom:** Spirit is refined to merge with Form. One is called an **Ultimate Person** <term>Zhiren (至人). The highest realization of humanity, where spirit and matter are no longer separate.</term>. Since the Spirit has achieved total divine power, the physical form is no longer fixed; it changes according to circumstances and manifests different shapes to guide and transform others.

**The Seventh Symptom:** One transcends the material world entirely and rises far above the common crowd. One dwells with the **Great Way** and the **Jade Emperor** <note>The supreme ruler of the heavens in Chinese popular and Daoist religion.</note> in the spiritual realms. There, the sages and saints assemble to expound the ultimate truth. One understands all the mysteries of creation and the wandering souls. Only by practicing to this point does one reach the **Source of the Way**. All striving and practice then cease; this is called the "Ultimate State." 

People of the present age study the Way only shallowly. They have not even achieved the First Symptom, so how could they attain spiritual powers? They merely cling to their foolish emotions and preserve their "filthy shells." As the four seasons pass, their forms wither and their complexions fade; their bodies decay and return to the void. Yet they still claim to have "attained the Way"—this is a great error. This method of **Embryonic Breathing** <term>Taixi (胎息). A deep, internal breathing technique that mimics the way a fetus is said to breathe in the womb.</term> and **Fixed Observation** <term>Dingguan (定觀). A meditative state of intense, unmoving internal focus.</term> is the secret to retaining the Spirit and halting the aging of the form. It has been passed down from the **Primal Ancestor** to this day. It was first transmitted by a **Perfected Person**. The skill lies in oral instructions, while the general principles are written in texts. Only a person of virtue and resolve will encounter this method. If you study it in detail and keep it in your heart, success is certain. The wise and the noble will surely grasp these sacred writings.

Once the **Primal Chaos** <term>Hunyuan (混元). The state of the universe before the separation of Heaven and Earth.</term> was divided, Heaven and Earth took their respective positions. Humans and the myriad things each received a portion of the **Primal Energy** <note>original: "Qi"</note> to form their physical shapes. Those that move take their patterns from Heaven; those that are still follow the laws of Earth. Between Heaven and Earth, humans are the most spiritual beings. What sustains the human form is only **Energy** and **Spirit** <term>Shen (神). The divine or conscious spark within a person.</term>. "Spirit" is the word for that which acts mysteriously upon all things. "Energy" is used by borrowing from the **Great Void** <note>The infinite, empty space from which all existence arises.</note>. 

In the words of the **Ultimate Person**, nothing takes precedence over Energy. In the practice of the Ultimate Person, nothing is more wondrous than Spirit. My Master attained the Way of the Ultimate Person and saw the hidden mechanism of life and death. He often "tasted the tasteless," "used the useless," "acted through non-action," and "managed affairs by doing nothing." <note>These are classic Daoist paradoxes from the *Tao Te Ching*, suggesting that true power comes from aligning with nature rather than forcing one's will.</note>

Knowing that Spirit and Energy can preserve the physical form, he guarded the state of Emptiness and Non-existence to nourish them. Knowing that the **Profound Darkness** <note>original: "Yaoming". A state of deep meditation where external senses are shut off.</note> leads to true realization, he entered that darkness to observe the **Ultimate Essence**. Is the space between Heaven and Earth not like a **Bellows**? <note>A famous metaphor from Laozi: the universe is like a bellows—empty yet inexhaustible; the more it moves, the more it yields.</note> Does the immortality of the Ultimate Person not resemble the **Valley Spirit**? <note>The "Valley Spirit" refers to the receptive, female principle of the universe that never dies.</note>

The Master said: "In the midst of Emptiness, there is a thing called Spirit. In the midst of the Profound Darkness, there is a thing called Energy." Energy coalesces within the Void to create wonder. Thus, the **Perfected Person of the Great Cavern** <note>A high-ranking immortal in the Shangqing school of Daoism.</note> said: "For three months, practice internal vision, focusing the mind on a single Spirit. Then, the spiritual light will be born and wrap around the five internal organs." The principle is clear!

Furthermore, Energy is the **Mother of Spirit**, and Spirit is the **Child of Energy**. If you wish to reach the child, you must first cultivate the mother. If the Spirit does not receive "nourishment" from Energy, then Energy has no way to communicate with the divine. If the child does not seek "food" from the mother, then the mother has no way to achieve harmony. 

The **Scripture of the Way** <note>The *Tao Te Ching*.</note> says: "Once you have the mother, you can know the child; once you know the child, return and guard the mother." The **Jade Script of the Eastern Flower** says: "When the mother is bound to the child, the heart is at peace and the flow is eternal." These are all essential words for cultivating the truth. Additionally, the ears and eyes are the "doors" of the Spirit. The *Scripture of the Way* asks: "Can you concentrate your Energy and reach such suppleness that you are like a newborn infant?" The **Yellow Court Scripture** <note>A central text of Daoist internal alchemy focusing on the "deities" residing within the body's organs.</note> says: "Immortals and Daoists are not born with divinity; they achieve it by accumulating Essence and focusing on harmony and benevolence." This is exactly what is meant.

Later students sometimes try to "inhale the energy of the four seasons" or "consume the essence of the stars." They clench their fists to mimic the shape of a fetus or hold their breath to perform **Embryonic Breathing**. These methods deviate significantly from the wondrous intent of the Perfected Persons! These are merely the secondary, superficial practices of the ancients. People of this sort only confuse their Primal Energy and cause even more harm to their form and spirit.

The Ultimate Person allows the mind to wander in tranquility, drinks from the **Primal Spring** <note>Likely a metaphor for the saliva generated during meditation, considered a "divine fluid."</note>, and practices embryonic breathing in the realm of the tasteless. Then, the spiritual light shines within, and the "Five Energies" give birth to the divine. Naturally, purple mist floats upward, and jade-like colors reflect upon one another. I respectfully transmit the Master’s intent: transform the white into the crimson, accumulate Essence to complete the form, and hold the **Spirit Mushroom** <note>original: "Lingzhi". A symbol of immortality.</note> in the mouth as it descends into the body. This is called the Art of the True Immortal: **Guard the Center and Embrace the One**. If you embrace the One and do not lose it, you will endure as long as Heaven and Earth.

# The Method of Consuming Energy and Abstaining from Grains

Face the directions associated with the six calendar cycles. <gloss>This applies to all four seasons as well.</gloss> Perform the breathing cycles starting from nine-times-nine (eighty-one breaths), then eight-times-eight, seven-times-seven, six-times-six, and five-times-five, until you feel full. # The Book of the Later Han: Biographies of Magicians
## The Account of Fei Changfang

**Fei Changfang** was a man from Ru’nan <note>A region in present-day Henan Province, historically associated with many tales of the supernatural.</note> who served as a minor **Market Official** <term>Shiyuan (市掾). A low-level bureaucrat responsible for overseeing trade and order in the local marketplace.</term>. In the market, there was an old man selling medicine who kept a single gourd hanging at the front of his stall. Whenever the market business concluded, the old man would immediately leap into the gourd. No one in the market saw this happen, except for Changfang, who observed it from an upper floor and found it extraordinary. Consequently, Changfang went to the man, bowed twice, and offered him wine and dried meat. 

The old man realized that Changfang recognized his divine nature and said to him, "Come again tomorrow." Changfang returned to visit the old man day after day. Finally, the old man invited him to enter the gourd together. Once inside, they saw only jade halls of magnificent beauty, with fine wine and sweet delicacies overflowing within. After they finished drinking together, they exited. The old man warned him not to tell anyone. 

Later, the old man waited for Changfang on the upper floor and said, "I am a being of the **Celestial Realms** <note>original: "Shenxian zhi ren" (神仙之人). A person who has achieved immortality and spiritual transcendence.</note>. Because of a past mistake, I was punished and sent here, but now my task is complete and I must depart. Would you be able to follow me? There is a little wine downstairs; let us have a farewell drink." Changfang sent men to fetch the wine vessel, but they could not lift it. He then ordered ten men to carry it, yet they still could not move it. Hearing this, the old man laughed and came down the stairs. He lifted it with a single finger and brought it up. The vessel looked like it held only about one liter, yet the two of them drank from it all day without ever emptying it. 

Changfang then desired to seek the Way, but he was worried about his family. The old man cut a piece of green bamboo to the same height as Changfang and told him to hang it behind his house. When his family saw it, it looked exactly like Changfang’s body—they believed he had hanged himself. In great shock and lamentation, the family held a funeral and buried him. Meanwhile, Changfang stood right beside them, but no one could see him. 

He then followed the old man into the deep mountains. He trod through brambles and thorns and was left alone in the midst of a pack of tigers, but Changfang felt no fear. Later, he was made to lie in an empty room where a ten-thousand-pound stone was suspended above him by a rotting rope. A swarm of snakes competed to gnaw at the rope until it was nearly severed, yet Changfang did not move. The old man returned, patted him, and said, "You are indeed teachable." 

Next, the old man told him to eat feces. Within the waste were three worms, and the stench was particularly foul. Changfang felt a deep revulsion in his heart. The old man said, "You were so close to attaining the Way, but it is a pity you have failed at this final step. What can be done?" 

Changfang resigned himself to return home. The old man gave him a bamboo staff and said, "Ride this to go wherever you wish, and you will arrive instantly. Once you have arrived, you may throw the staff into the **Kudzu Pond** <note>original: "Gepi" (葛陂).</note>." He also created a **Talisman** <term>Fu (符). A ritual command or seal used in Daoism to summon or control spiritual entities.</term> for him, saying, "Use this to command the ghosts and gods of the earth." 

Changfang mounted the staff and returned home in an instant. He believed he had only been away from home for about ten days, but in the human world, ten years had already passed. He threw the staff into the pond as instructed; looking back, he saw it was actually a dragon. His family believed he had been dead for a long time and did not believe it was him. Changfang told them, "The one you buried previously was merely a bamboo staff." They opened the grave and split the coffin—indeed, the staff was still there. 

Thereafter, he was able to heal all kinds of illnesses, whip and lash the hundred ghosts, and command the local **Earth Gods** <note>original: "Shegong" (社公). Tutelary deities of a specific plot of land or community.</note>. Sometimes, while sitting with others, he would suddenly become furious; when asked why, he would say, "I am merely reprimanding a demon who has violated the law."

<summary>This page recounts the legend of Fei Changfang, a market official who becomes the apprentice of an immortal living in a gourd. It details his miraculous journey, his failure of the final test of revulsion, and his eventual career as a master of spirits and healing.</summary>

# The Three Essentials of Health Preservation

->By Yuan Huang (Kunyi) of Jiashan, Ming Dynasty<-

## 1. Gathering Essence

The classics state: "The kidneys are the storehouse where essence is kept." They also state: "Each of the five internal organs has its own stored essence." Blood does not remain stationary in any single location. Before a person engages in sexual union, the **Essence** <term>Jing (精). Often translated as "Essence," it refers to the concentrated life-force of the body, which manifests physically as reproductive fluids and energetically as the basis for health.</term> is contained within the blood and has no distinct shape. Once union occurs and the "fire of desire" is stirred to its peak, the blood circulating throughout the entire body reaches the **Life Gate** <term>Mingmen (命門). A vital point between the kidneys considered the source of "true fire" and the root of life in Chinese medicine.</term> and is transformed into essence to be discharged. 

Therefore, if one takes the essence discharged by a person, stores it in a vessel, mixes it with a little salt and wine, and leaves it exposed for one night, it will revert back into blood. The left kidney belongs to **Water**, while the right is the **Life Gate**, belonging to **Fire**. One is Water and one is Fire; they are like the **Tortoise and the Snake** <note>original: "Yi gui yi she" (一龜一蛇). This refers to the North Star deity Xuanwu (the Dark Warrior), symbolizing the union of Yin and Yang energies.</note>, acting as **bellows and pipes** <note>original: "Tuoyue" (橐籥). A metaphor from the Tao Te Ching for the rhythmic, empty-yet-exhaustless functioning of the universe or the breath.</note> for one another. 

The bladder is the associated organ of the left kidney. The **Triple Burner** <term>Sanjiao (三焦). A conceptual system in traditional medicine that coordinates the movement of fluids and energy between the upper, middle, and lower regions of the body.</term> has a fatty membrane about the size of a palm, positioned directly opposite the bladder. Two white vessels emerge from the center, flank the spine, and run upward to penetrate the brain. The **Upper Burner** is in the center of the chest and corresponds internally to the heart. The **Middle Burner** is at the pit of the stomach and corresponds to the spleen. The **Lower Burner** is below the navel; this is the "Moving Qi between the Kidneys." 

The blood of the human body is dispersed through the Triple Burner, circulating day and night according to a regular rhythm. Within the hundred bones and at the tip of every single hair, there is nowhere this blood does not penetrate. This blood *is* the essence. Upon reaching the Life Gate, it transforms into essence and is then transported away. When a person is in their prime, the blood overflows throughout the body; if they father a child, the child will perfectly resemble the father. If the blood is weak, there will be parts of the child's form that do not match the parent. If the blood is withered, one cannot reproduce at all.

**Primordial Essence** <term>Yuanjing (元精). The original, inherited essence one is born with, as opposed to the essence replenished by food and drink.</term> in the body is like resin in wood. The "Vital Breath" (Qi) relies on it like a fish relies on water, or like mist covering a deep pool. Consider an infant: even though they do not yet know of the union of male and female, their **genitals stir** <note>original: "Zui zuo" (朘作). A reference to the Tao Te Ching, describing the peak of vital essence in a child.</note>; this is because their essence is at its height. It is pure and complete, harmonizing with the Great Way; it is vast and clear, harmonizing with the Infinite. 

At sixteen, the True Essence is full and the five organs are robust; only then can one father a child. However, once this essence is leaked, the "True Body" is already diminished and the original form is compromised. From then on, one relies solely on food and drink to nourish and produce essence and blood. Most people do not know how to "maintain fullness" or how to be frugal with their resources. What one possesses is limited, but what one consumes is limitless. Before reaching middle age, the five functions begin to decline, and one sees all the "hundred vessels" withering away. Therefore, those who cultivate health must make it their duty to "solidify their essence." The key to solidifying essence is nothing better than sleeping alone for years at a time. If it is absolutely necessary to continue the family line, then the bedroom...

It emphasizes that health preservation depends on conserving this limited vital resource, which is at its peak in childhood but easily depleted in adulthood.</summary>

...the bedroom matters should be limited to once a month; that is perhaps acceptable.

The way of **Accumulating Essence** involves:
1. Lessening desires.
2. Moderating labor.
3. Calming anger.
4. Abstaining from alcohol.
5. Being prudent with flavors.

Today, those who discuss "nourishing life" often speak of "plucking Yin to supplement Yang" <note>original: "cai yin bu yang" (採陰補陽). A controversial Daoist sexual practice involving the belief that a man can increase his vitality by absorbing the energy of a female partner.</note> or of engaging in "long battles without ejaculation." This is a great error. The kidneys are the storehouse of essence. In any sexual union, the kidneys are inevitably disturbed. When the kidneys are moved, essence and blood follow and flow. Even if one does not ejaculate externally, the essence has already "left its palace" <note>This means the vital fluid has been displaced from its biological storage and is essentially lost to the body's internal circulation, even if it stays inside.</note>. Even for those who can endure with great discipline, there will inevitably be several drops of **True Essence** that seep out as the organ becomes flaccid. This is the proof. It is like fire producing smoke; how can the smoke ever return to the wood?

Therefore, one must **lessen desires**. Essence is formed from blood. It is not only sexual intercourse that damages one's essence; every daily activity that drains the blood must be strictly guarded against. For instance, if the eyes are exhausted by looking, then blood is consumed through sight. If the ears are exhausted by hearing, then blood is consumed through hearing. If the mind is exhausted by thinking, then blood is consumed through thought. If I moderate myself in all matters, the blood receives its proper nourishment and accumulates day by day.

Therefore, one must **moderate labor**. That which governs "closing and storing" is the kidney. That which governs "draining and discharging" is the liver. Both of these organs possess **Ministerial Fire** <term>Xianghuo (相火). In traditional medicine, this is a physiological heat that drives the functions of the internal organs, but can become "pathological" and drain the body if overstimulated by emotion or desire.</term>, and their pathways are connected upward to the heart. The heart holds the **Sovereign Fire** <term>Junhuo (君火). The primary governing energy of the spirit and consciousness.</term>. Anger damages the liver and causes the Ministerial Fire to stir. Once stirred, the "draining" function takes over, and the "closing and storing" function can no longer do its job. Even if there is no sexual union, the essence will still flow secretly and be depleted in silence.

Therefore, one must **calm anger**. The blood of the human body normally remains condensed when it returns to its proper "dwellings." Alcohol, however, can agitate the blood. When a person drinks, their face and limbs turn red; this is because the blood has been disturbed and is racing about. For a person whose vital energy is already declining, even if they abstain from sex for months, their essence will become thick. However, if they get heavily drunk one night, that essence will immediately become thin. 

Therefore, one should **abstain from alcohol**. The *Internal Classic* <note>original: "Neijing" (内經). Referring to the *Huangdi Neijing*, the foundational medical text of ancient China.</note> says: "For those with insufficient essence, supplement it with flavors." However, rich and heavy flavors cannot generate essence. Only **simple and bland flavors** <note>original: "tiandan zhi wei" (恬淡之味). Referring to a diet of unrefined grains and vegetables.</note> can supplement it. Every living thing has its own flavor, but when seasoning is excessive, the "true flavor" is lost. Regardless of whether food is meat or vegetarian, if it is boiled simply and properly, it possesses a harmonious and tranquil Qi that benefits the stomach and intestines. The *Great Plan* <note>original: "Hong Fan" (洪範). A chapter of the *Classic of History* (Shujing).</note>, in discussing flavors, says that "sowing and reaping produces sweetness." Among all things in the world, only the **Five Grains** <term>Wugu (五穀). Rice, broomcorn millet, proso millet, wheat, and beans; considered the staple foundation of human health.</term> possess the most balanced flavor. Being able to eat the simple flavor of grains is the best way to nourish essence. Furthermore, when cooking porridge or rice, the thick juice that gathers in a mass in the center is the "essence-fluid" of the grain. Eating this is most effective at generating essence; it has been tested and proven.

There is a secret to **Refining Essence**, and it begins entirely with the kidneys. The opening of the internal kidneys is called the **Original Pass** <term>Yuanguan (元關).</term>, and the opening of the external genitals is called the **Female Gate** <term>Pinhu (牝戶). A term used here to describe the urogenital opening in both a physiological and alchemical sense.</term>. When the True Essence has not yet been leaked and the **Pristine Body** <term>Qianti (乾體). Literally "Qian Body," referring to the unbroken, pure state of a youth before sexual maturity or loss of essence.</term> has not been compromised, the "Yang Qi" of the external genitals rises at the **Zishi** <term>Zishi (子時). The midnight hour (11 PM – 1 AM), when Yin is at its peak and Yang begins to stir.</term>. The Qi of the human body and the Qi of Heaven and Earth coincide with one another. Once the essence is compromised, the time when the "Yang" stirs in my body becomes gradually later. For some, it arises at the *Chou* hour <note>1 AM – 3 AM</note>, and for others at the *Yin* hour <note>3 AM – 5 AM</note>...

<summary>Yuan Huang outlines five lifestyle practices to conserve blood and essence, warning that even mental strain or anger causes "silent leakage." He critiques popular sexual energy practices as damaging and advocates for a bland, grain-based diet as the best medicine for replenishing vitality.</summary>

...for those whose vitality is further diminished, it arises at the *Mao* hour <note>5 AM – 7 AM</note>. For some, it never arises at all; in such cases, the individual is no longer in harmony with the cycles of Heaven and Earth. 

The secret to **Refining Essence** is this: at the midnight hour <note>original: "Zishi" (子時); 11 PM – 1 AM.</note>, one must put on a robe and sit up. Rub the hands together until they are extremely hot. With one hand, cup the "external kidneys" <note>A traditional euphemism for the testicles.</note> and with the other hand cover the navel, while concentrating the spirit on the internal kidneys. If practiced for a long time, the essence and spirit will become flourishing.

## 2. Nourishing Qi

Humans receive the Qi of Heaven and Earth to be born. There must be a portion of **Original Vitality** <term>Yuanqi (元氣). The fundamental life force inherited from one's parents.</term> endowed before the fetus is even formed. This is what the Daoists call **Innate Ancestral Qi** <note>original: "Xiantian Zuqi" (先天祖氣).</note>. There is also **Acquired Qi** <note>original: "Houtian zhi Qi" (後天之氣).</note>, which is the breath that flows in and out, circulating and filling the body. These two share the same source but have different names. The Innate is a "generative mist" <note>original: "Yinyun" (絪縕). An ancient term for the productive mingling of Yin and Yang.</note> born from the formless, while the Acquired has form and can be seen. The Innate is flickering and vague, hidden in the imageless, while the Acquired has a visible image and can be sought. In truth, they are the same thing. 

Therefore, the study of **Nourishing Qi** must be discussed. One should carefully contemplate the teachings of Mencius <note>A famous Confucian philosopher (4th century BCE) who taught that one's "flood-like Qi" must be nourished by upright conduct.</note> regarding how "stumbling and hurried movements agitate the heart-mind." To nourish Qi: when walking, be slow and steady; when standing, be firm and respectful; when sitting, be upright and straight; when speaking, be low and harmonious. In every action, one must be deliberate, calm, and composed. One should practice "preservation" in the midst of movement and "stillness" in the midst of activity. This allows the body to remain constantly within the **Great Harmony of Original Qi** <term>Taihe Yuanqi (太和元氣). A state of perfect internal balance mirroring the harmony of the universe.</term>. If practiced for a long time, one will naturally take on the bearing of the sages and elders of the past.

When you wave a fan, a breeze is created; this is because the space between Heaven and Earth is entirely filled with Qi. Mencius said, "It fills the space between Heaven and Earth." How true this is! Humans exist within Qi just as fish exist within water. Qi nourishes the human form, yet humans are unaware of it; water nourishes the fish's form, yet the fish does not feel it. 

To nourish Qi, one must start with **Regulating the Breath** <term>Tiaoxi (調息).</term>. The Zen school <note>original: "Chanjia" (禪家).</note> teaches that there are four kinds of breathing:
1. When the breath through the nose makes an audible sound, this is "Wind," not "Breath." Focusing on Wind causes the energy to scatter.
2. When there is no sound but the breath is hesitant or blocked, this is "Panting," not "Breath." Focusing on Panting causes the energy to knot.
3. When there is no sound and no blockage, but the movement of the breath is still perceptible, this is "Qi," not "Breath." Focusing on this Qi causes fatigue.
4. That which is called **True Breath** <note>original: "Xi" (息).</note> carries the meaning of "neither exiting nor entering" <note>This refers to breath so subtle it seems to stop, often called "embryonic breathing."</note>. 

Master Zhu's <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian scholar, who also wrote on meditation.</note> *Maxims on Regulating the Breath* says: "When stillness reaches its limit, one exhales, like a fish in a spring pond. When movement reaches its limit, one inhales, like a hundred hibernating insects." A fish in spring moves with the Qi, and its movement is incredibly subtle. A hibernating insect contains its Qi and hides, and its dormancy leaves no trace. Regulating the breath must be like this: continuous and fine, deep and microscopic. When exhaling, the "ten thousand pores" of the body's frame release Qi along with the breath. When inhaling, the "ten thousand pores" take Qi in. If regulated without ceasing, the **True Qi** will be born from within. This is truly an essential secret.

The Qi of the human body has its specific regions. Within the body, there is: Circulating Qi, Horizontal-rising Qi, Joint Qi, Meridian Qi, Sinew Qi, Strength Qi, Bone-gap Qi, Waist Qi, Spinal Qi, Upper Qi, Lower Qi...

<summary>Yuan Huang explains the relationship between innate and acquired vitality, offering practical advice on physical posture and "True Breath"—a meditative state of breathing so subtle it mimics hibernation.</summary>

These various types of Qi <note>The different biological and energetic functions mentioned at the end of page 49.</note> each have their fixed positions. They must not be thrown into disorder. If they are disordered, they become "thieves" <note>An internal drain on one's vitality.</note>. In major cases, this leads to madness, collapse, or exhaustion; in minor cases, it creates an imbalance of **Deficiency and Excess** <term>Xu-Shi (虛實). A fundamental concept in traditional medicine where health is a balance between "fullness" (excess) and "emptiness" (deficiency).</term>. Where there is deficiency, there is itching; where there is excess, there is pain. The birth of all illness arises from this. 

The physician Han Feixia <note>A Ming-dynasty scholar and medical expert known for his work on "Returning to the Source."</note> once met an extraordinary man at the Yellow Crane Tower. This man granted him a single medicine to treat ten thousand diseases, which showed immediate results. It used **Nutgrass** <note>original: "Xiangfuzi" (香附子).</note> as the **Sovereign** <term>Jun (君). The primary active ingredient in a traditional formula.</term> and was assisted only by **Coptis** <note>original: "Huanglian" (黃連); a bitter herb used to clear heat.</note>. Since the Qi of a person causes illness when it loses its balance, Nutgrass is used to regulate the Qi. Because the "Fire" of the body was dominant at that time, Coptis was used to assist it. Is this not a profound understanding of the inner workings of creation?

One who nourishes life should never allow the Qi within the body to conflict or struggle. For instance, if you have been walking for a long time and wish to sit, this is a transition from movement into stillness. Before sitting, first walk slowly for several paces to slightly expand the Qi. Gradually relax the body so that the "still Qi" arrives and the "moving Qi" departs. If you sit after this, your essence will remain refined. Likewise, if you have sat for a long time and wish to walk—moving from stillness into activity—you must first move the body slightly or stretch the limbs as if performing a massage. Only then should you walk. If you do not, the "fine Qi" within the body will clash with the "coarse Qi" of movement. All other activities should be conducted according to this principle.

Practicing the retention of breath and swallowing it is called **Embryonic Breathing** <term>Taixi (胎息).</term>. Rinsing the mouth with the "spring" beneath the tongue <note>A poetic term for saliva.</note> and swallowing it is called **Embryonic Feeding**. To "eat the morning rosy clouds" in spring is to take in the red Qi of the rising sun. To "eat the sinking mists" in autumn is to take in the yellow-red Qi after sunset. To "eat the midnight moisture" in winter is to take in the Qi of the north at midnight. To "eat the three Yangs" in summer is to take in the Qi of the south at high noon. If practiced diligently, one can achieve **Refraining from Grains** <term>Bigu (辟穀). A Daoist practice of living on Qi and medicinal waters rather than solid food.</term>. I have tested this myself with great success.

While a person is in the womb, they do not breathe through the mouth or nose. Rather, the umbilical cord is connected to the mother's **Conception Vessel** <term>Renmai (任脈). An energetic meridian running down the front of the body.</term>. The Conception Vessel connects to the lungs, and the lungs connect to the nose. Therefore, when the mother exhales, the fetus exhales; when the mother inhales, the fetus inhales. The Qi moves back and forth through the navel. The Tiantai school <note>A major branch of Buddhism that emphasizes meditation and "stopping and seeing."</note> teaches that when the "conscious spirit" first takes birth and joins with the essence and blood, its root is in the navel. This is why, when a person is born, they are only connected by the navel. 

Beginners of **Regulating the Breath** must imagine the Qi emerging from the navel. Exhaling and inhaling both occur from the navel. Regulate it until it is extremely fine, and then stop using the mouth and nose entirely, breathing only with the navel as if in the womb. This is why it is called "Embryonic Breathing." First, hold a single breath and breathe with the navel, counting to eighty-one or one hundred and twenty. Only then exhale through the mouth. The exhalation must be extremely fine; the standard is to place a swan's down feather over the mouth and nose and have it remain unmoved as you exhale. Gradually increase the count over time until you reach one thousand. Then, the old will become young again, and day by day, one returns to vitality. Whenever it was the height of summer, the Immortal Ge <note>Ge Hong (283–343 CE), a famous Daoist alchemist and author of the *Baopuzi*.</note> would enter the bottom of a deep pool and stay there for an entire day before emerging. This was only possible because he could close his breath and perform Embryonic Breathing. If one only knows how to hold the breath but does not understand Embryonic Breathing, it is of no benefit.

The Qi of a person is cool when blown out <note>original: "Chui" (吹).</note> and warm when huffed out <note>original: "He" (呵).</note>. Temperature changes between the "blowing" and the "huffing." Therefore, in summer, one can make oneself cold, and in winter, one can make oneself hot. Those who circulate Qi can enter pestilential areas...

...one can repel plagues, forbid snakes and tigers from approaching, stay underwater, or walk upon its surface. One can even huff at the water and cause it to flow backward for a thousand miles. The transformations of Qi are infinite; they all stem simply from nourishing it according to the proper Way.

Qi desires to be soft, not strong. It desires to be smooth, not rebellious. It desires to be stable, not chaotic. It desires to be gathered, not scattered. Therefore, the Daoist schools most strictly forbid anger. Once a heart of anger arises, the Qi becomes strong rather than soft, rebellious rather than smooth, chaotic rather than stable, and scattered rather than gathered. If one tries to force the breath closed while in this state, it will cause a person to develop a cough. Therefore, a practitioner of the Way must be like "a gentle breeze and the clear moon after rain" or like "auspicious stars and celebratory clouds" <note>These poetic metaphors describe a state of perfect inner clarity, serenity, and benevolence.</note>. Only when there is not a single hair’s breadth of perverse or irritable Qi can one perform the exercises. Furthermore, eating raw vegetables or fatty, rich foods also makes one's Qi strong and difficult to regulate. Eating at improper times or consuming "Qi-moving" foods <note>Foods believed to over-stimulate or disrupt the body's internal rhythm.</note> also causes the Qi to become rebellious. Additionally, excessive thinking throws the Qi into chaos, and excessive talking causes the Qi to scatter. All of these must be deeply cautioned against.

### 3. Preserving the Spirit

The gathering of Essence depends on nourishing the Qi; the nourishing of Qi depends on **Preserving the Spirit** <note>Spirit (Shen) refers to the highest form of consciousness or divine spark within a person.</note>. The relationship of the Spirit to the Qi is like that of a mother to her child. Therefore, when the Spirit condenses, the Qi gathers; when the Spirit scatters, the Qi vanishes. If one treasures and protects their Essence and Qi but does not know how to preserve the Spirit, it is like **eating the flowers** <term>Ruqi hua (茹其華). A metaphor for focusing on the superficial beauty or "blossoms" of a practice while neglecting the "root" or source.</term> while forgetting the root. 

Yet, how can the Spirit have a physical form that one can seek? **Mencius** <term>Mengzi (孟子). A famous philosopher of the 4th century BCE whose work became a cornerstone of Chinese thought.</term> said: "To be a sage and yet be unknowable is called Spirit." It is that which cannot be reached through analytical thought and cannot be explained in words. For example, in writing an essay, one cannot abandon thought; however, the most marvelous and extraordinary parts of a text are often captured in a state of "non-thinking." This is the inspiration of the Spirit. When masters of talismans and incantations take up their brush, the very first dot must be made before a single thought has arisen; this is called **opening the foundation of chaos** <term>Hundun kaiji (混沌開基). A state of primordial unity before the mind begins to make distinctions.</term>. This is the movement of the Spirit. 

When one moves others with a "calculating heart," the effect is usually shallow; but when one moves others with "no-heart" <note>A state of spontaneity and sincerity free from ego.</note>, the effect is usually deep. This is the Spirit hitting its mark. This is why the heart of an old person is often less "efficacious," while the heart of an infant is constantly "efficacious." The schemes made while wide awake are often not efficacious, while the dreams had during the dimness of sleep are often efficacious. These are all the workings of the Spirit. The **Book of Changes** <term>Yi (易/I Ching). An ancient manual of divination and philosophy centered on the concept of constant change.</term> says: "In the world, what is there to think about, what is there to worry about?" This is the true realm of the Spirit. The Sage does not deliberate and does not force; this is the reality of the Spirit. Unless one reaches this stage, one can never truly alter their Heaven-sent destiny. Let the discerning practitioner be cautious of this.

In the **Daoist Tradition** <term>Daozong (道宗).</term>, the practices of "Observing the Mystery" or "Observing the Apertures" are merely methods for concentrating one's thoughts. They are not the ultimate Way of preserving the Spirit. However, since our habit of grasping at external things is so ingrained and our wandering thoughts are so hard to forget, we have no choice but to begin our work here and gradually enter the "exquisite realm." There is a method of preserving...
