...its soil, one must purify the heart. If the heart is clear and pure, the cycle of reincarnation will cease of its own accord.

The Master had a natural fondness for sipping congee; at noon, he would eat a single bowl. When finished, he would discuss the Way with others, tirelessly instructing and guiding younger students. The Master was of a compassionate nature, a gentleman of universal kindness. While in **Laiyang** <note>a city in Shandong province</note>, he composed lyrics, including the line: "Once the single bowl of congee is finished, one must apply ten-fold effort to the work." Students should reflect on this: for those who merely eat and drink or sit idly without making the Way their primary business, the burden of their transgressions can well be imagined.

***

**The Master said:**
"Those who study the Way need not read scriptures and books extensively. It disturbs the human mind and hinders one’s spiritual work. While it does no harm to occasionally look at Heshang Gong's commentary on the *Dao De Jing* or Jinling Zi's commentary on the *Scripture of the Hidden Tally* <note>original: *Yinfu Jing*, an important Daoist alchemical text</note>, even that is not as good as reading nothing at all. To dwell in the 'Purple Void' and nourish the **Energy** <term>Qi</term> is the most superior strategy."

***

**The Master said:**
"A person of the Way, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, must not let their heart be away from the Way for even a brief moment. When walking, place your feet on the level path; when standing, focus your feelings on the **Great Void** <term>Taixu: the boundless, primordial state of the universe</term>; when sitting, even out the breath at the tip of the nose; when sleeping, embrace the 'pearl' below the navel <note>referring to the lower Dantian, the center of energy in the body</note>. If you regulate the breath for a long time without interruption, appearing foolish all day long, only then is it genuine work. This is not a matter of artificial effort or outward ritual."

***

**The Master said:**
"For all who begin to study the Way, cut yourself off from this day forward; do not let past worldly affairs weigh on your heart. If even a tiny thread remains unsevered, the Way will not be firm. Do not think of past events, do not dwell on future matters; simply rely on what is before your eyes right now. Then, you will be a person who is 'free of affairs.'"

***

**The Master said:**
"A person of the Way does not loathe poverty. Poverty is the very root of nourishing life. When hungry, eat a bowl of congee; when tired, spread out a bundle of straw. Continuing in this way to pass the mornings and evenings—this is precisely the livelihood of a person of the Way. Therefore, know that the state of **Clarity and Stillness** <term>Qingjing</term> is something the wealthy and noble cannot obtain."

***

The Master passed through **Qingshe** <note>modern-day Qingzhou in Shandong</note>, and someone invited him to a vegetarian meal. Among those seated were several monks. One monk among them showed off his vast eloquence, posing difficult questions and challenging the Master incessantly. The Master replied slowly: "Aside from this single body of mine, I know nothing of other matters." The monk blushed and lost his composure, unable to find another word to say.

***

**The Master said:**
"To be a person of the Way, one must be a person of resolute character. By no means should you be indecisive or full of doubt. Simply keep in mind that the matter of **Inner Nature and Life** <term>Xingming: the spiritual and physical aspects of cultivation</term> is of the greatest importance. Practice with vigor and do not retreat, expecting certain success. If one has too much affection for family and too little 'ambition for the mist and clouds' <note>a poetic term for the desire to live as a hermit or immortal</note>, then they are not what is called a student of the Way."

**The Master said:**
"Regarding the inner nature of a person of the Way: one must absolutely not follow or pursue the affairs of the dusty, secular world. As for going from door to door to beg for food, being pushed away here or grabbed there—that is precisely the daily tradition and 'family style' of a person of the Way."

If you do not succeed in the Way in the future, you will never be finished with the matter—you will instead be required to go back and pay your debts <note>referring to the karmic debt of consuming resources without spiritual progress</note>."

***

**The Master stated:**

If one eats meat and drinks wine and yet still becomes a **Divine Immortal** <term>Shenxian</term>, the process is merely a bit slower. However, if the heart does not hold the Way, and yet one craves wine and food, then one's mouth is merely full of the stench of meat. The retribution for such a belly's crimes is hard to escape; in the end, such a person will surely fall among the lower class of ghosts."

**The Master stated:**

When he saw things plainly, he still held onto his 'treasures' <note>likely referring to internal spiritual realizations</note> and did not dare move or let them go. **Uncle-Master Liu** <note>Liu Chuxuan</note> also once spoke of this."

**The Master stated:**

The community heard of this, and the next day they made melon buns and brought them into the enclosure. I ate three of them, and for that, I was punished for two days by not being allowed to eat any food."

->The Master told the assembly: "The Dao has no form or name; it is the ancestor of **Spirit and Vital Breath** <term>Shen-Qi</term>. When the **Original Breath** <term>Yuan-Qi: the primordial energy one is born with</term> descends and transforms, the spiritual light is naturally born. Refining the spirit to unite with the Dao—this is the cultivation of reality. Other names and appearances are numerous and confusing, making them difficult to rely upon. After a long time of refined focus, the spirit will congeal and the breath will soar. If there is no leakage for six years, the **Middle Elixir** <term>Zhong-Dan: the energy center in the chest</term> will form. After nine [years]...<-

The shame of rich delicacies is not equal to the sweetness of <term>wild herbs and pulse</term> <note>original: 藜藿 (li-huo) — common, coarse food of the poor, often used to symbolize a life of virtuous poverty</note>. # Essential Instructions from the Records of the Immortals

## The Meaning of the Origin of the Dao
### Narrated by Pei Ao, Master of the Valley Spirit <note>original: 谷神子 (Gushenzi) — a title referencing the "Valley Spirit" from the Daodejing, representing the receptive, eternal power of the Dao</note>

In the West Mountains of Zhongling Prefecture stands the Altar of the Great Cliff. Beside this altar lived the Master of Dwelling in Truth, Mr. Yang. Knowing that I possessed the secrets of the Dao, he came to me and requested that I describe the essential purpose of how the Dao gives life. I said to him: "Have you not heard what is said in the <term>Scripture of Western Ascension</term> <note>original: 西昇經 (Xisheng Jing) — a Daoist text emphasizing internal cultivation and the return to the source</note>? It says: 'People only know the ten thousand things of Heaven and Earth, but they do not know the source from which life springs.' It also says: 'I and the Heaven and Earth share one breath in governance; I guard my own root and origin, rather than following the common crowd.' Thus we know that if a practitioner of the Dao does not know the source of life and the root of the Dao, they will be lost in a vast wilderness, unable to fathom where the Dao comes from. If you wish to seek long life, you must first cultivate the root of that which produced you. Can you understand this?"

Mr. Yang said: "I do not yet understand." I told him: "If you wish to understand, you must quickly prepare your formal oaths and precepts." Mr. Yang bowed twice and offered these words: "My talent and capacity are trivial and minute; my conduct and abilities are obscure and dim. I have used the blood of animals for my nourishment and found joy in a dull, worldly appearance. My roots of sin are deep, and my spirit’s luster is increasingly clouded. I have allowed my <term>Three Souls</term> <note>Sanhun: the three spiritual energies of a human being in Daoist psychology</note> to lead me into frivolity and have been besieged by the <term>Five Thieves</term> <note>Wuzei: the five senses or emotions that "steal" one's vital energy and distract from the Dao</note>. I have sought contentment in blurred visions, pushing joy and pleasure to their limits. Then, suddenly grieving over loss or moved by external things, I encounter extreme sorrow. This agitates my <term>Gate of Life</term> <note>Mingmen: an energy center in the body, often associated with the kidneys, vital for health</note> and causes my <term>Primordial Qi</term> <note>Yuanqi: the fundamental life energy one is born with</note> to collapse. Emptiness and frailty gradually press in upon me; how am I different from a living corpse? Decay is about to arrive, and soon I will be nothing but a standing skeleton. Like salt or plum blossoms dissolving and withering, I am scorched by the heat and frozen by the cold. Since I do not possess a body of gold or stone, I am battered by the winds and frosts of time. Great illness is about to arise; how can this tiny frame find peace? I am truly like the deaf and the blind, unable to perceive the principles of the Dark Mystery. Step by step I approach death, yet I remain stubbornly ignorant.

In the world of men, there are those whose Dao is as high as the <term>Master on the River</term> <note>original: 河上 (Heshang) — Heshang Gong, a legendary commentator on the Daodejing</note>, or whose arts allow them to enter the <term>Master of the Gourd's</term> <note>original: 壺中 (Huzhong) — a reference to the 'Gourd Heaven,' a pocket dimension or paradise found within a gourd</note> vessel. Clad in rainbow garments and feathered robes, they can shrink the veins of the earth with a single journey. Carrying pearl banners and jade staffs, they ascend the gates of heaven in a single bound. They transform rubble into the <term>Golden Elixir</term> <note>Jindan: the alchemical goal of eternal life</note> and change their appearance with the <term>Jade Elixir</term> <note>Yuye: a liquid form of the elixir or a metaphor for refined internal energy</note>. Creation and transformation originate from themselves; cultivation lies in the heart. Like a fish released into the vast waves, though their bones were dry, they grow flesh once more. I, your humble servant, with the life of an ant and a body like a tiny mustard seed, am dim-witted and ignorant. My ruin and death are scheduled. Suddenly, a divine light has inspected the openings of my soul, and Heaven has opened my heart. I wish to reach the <term>Mysterious Pass</term> <note>Xuanguan: the hidden gateway to spiritual realization</note> and seek the essentials of the Dao. I admire the true Immortals with an urgency like hunger or thirst. In my inner heart, I find this drifting world to be loathsome and stagnant, like smoke and dust filling the eyes. I hope to achieve the quality of the <term>Subtle and Invisible</term> <note>original: 希夷 (Xiyi) — terms from the Daodejing describing the Dao as that which cannot be seen or heard</note>, and to remain forever within the space of the <term>Bellows</term> <note>original: 橐籥 (Tuoyue) — a metaphor for the void between Heaven and Earth that acts like a bellows for the breath of life</note>. I shall stir away the machinery of the dusty world and search in the darkness for the True Simplicity. I track the Formless through the blurred state and see the "Thing" as it begins to sprout. At this moment, though the ten thousand images of the world shake in the void, my small sincerity shall not be deterred. I dare to crawl forward and earnestly request instruction, vowing to observe the deep precepts and climb to the Pure Altar of the Most High, to increase..."

<summary>This page introduces the disciple Yang Jun, who formally petitions Master Pei Ao for alchemical secrets. It contains a vivid confession of human frailty and a poetic aspiration to transcend mortality through the Daoist arts of transformation.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the dialogue between Master Pei Ao and the seeker Yang Jun. Following Yang’s formal plea for instruction, the Master begins the technical transmission of internal alchemy, explaining the embryological and elemental formation of the human body, focusing on the relationship between Qi (energy) and Shen (spirit), and the microcosm of the eyes.</meta>

<page-num>164</page-num>

I imagine the precious throne of the **Sovereign of Emptiness** <note>original: 虚皇 (Xuhuang) — a high-ranking celestial deity in the Daoist pantheon, representing the primordial void</note>. Immortal youths hold the ritual tallies and maidens burn incense. Now that I have received proof of these matters, how could my heart harbor any further hesitation? My frozen fears have melted like ice; the first signs of the treasure begin to flow. I bear the weight of your great virtue, which towers like a mountain, and I feel a deep gratitude that is already engraved upon my heart and liver. 

If this is recklessly leaked to the unworthy, or if one finds the right person but fails to transmit it, then one will encounter sin and calamity in every scene and suffer misfortune with every step. I point toward the bright sun and swear a covenant with sincere devotion; my startled soul and weeping blood reach the utmost limit of earnestness.

I <note>the Master, Pei Ao</note> then told him: "Since you are so sincere and earnest, I shall tell you the source of the cycle of life. Regarding the root of a human: once the male essence and female blood have congealed, the Dao follows nature to produce life. It begins as a single drop of water. The water currently in the **Bladder** is what remains of this original state. Within this water, Qi is contained, though it is dense and has not yet been released. It desires to be stimulated by the <term>Pure Yang True Essence</term> of Heaven and Earth, entering the Qi to rely upon it. The Qi then nourishes it, and this is what we call the **Spirit** <note>Shen: the spark of consciousness or divinity within</note>."

The Spirit is extremely subtle. Although it receives the nourishment and irrigation of the Water-Qi, it fears that the Qi might be too strong and overwhelm it. It is like the irrigation of water for a sprouting seed; one cannot simply submerge it. If it is submerged, the sprout will immediately die. Therefore, from the "Pure Yang True Essence" within the water, the **Two Kidneys** are produced. These two kidneys correspond to the numbers of Yin and Yang. Separated by the water, they hold up the Spirit. Only then can the Spirit and Qi be steamed and transformed into the numinous power of the Kidney-Spirit.

In this process, we say that **Qi is the Mother** and **Spirit is the Son**. Once the trunk of the Dao has been nourished, the ten thousand things take form. Once the "Mother" and "Son" have grown, they cannot remain in the same place. It is necessary to allow the "Son" to create and transform, establishing its own dwelling place so that the "Mother" may also find peace.

The Spirit requires external objects to lead it away from its Mother. Thus, it borrows two points of Qi from the Water, matching the number of the kidneys. The Spirit uses its "mountain-cave light" <note>a metaphor for internal vision</note> to guard and congeal this. However, there is a concern that the Water might be too abundant and the <term>Five Elements</term> <note>Wuxing: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water</note> insufficient to complete the formation of a being. 

Therefore:
*   **Earth** is borrowed to overcome the Water.
*   Fearing the Earth might overcome the Water entirely, **Wood** is borrowed to overcome the Earth.
*   Fearing the Wood might overcome the Earth entirely, **Metal** is borrowed to overcome the Wood.
*   Fearing the Metal might overcome the Wood entirely, **Fire** is borrowed to overcome the Metal.
*   If the Fire were to overcome the Metal entirely, then **Water** is used internally to save it.

This is called "revolving generation and revolving restraint" to form a being. This process results in the **Human Eye**. The eyes are in a state of union with the body of Heaven and Earth; the Five Elements are complete within them. Therefore, the center of the eye is **Black (Water)**; next is **Yellow (Earth)**; next is **Green (Wood)**; next is **White (Metal)**; and next is **Red (Fire)**. Their colors are bright and clear. Once the five colors are established, the **Yang Spirit** lodges its light within them. This is called the "Spirit Light," and it serves as the station for the eyes.

This is linked to the **Liver** because the light is as bright as the sun. The sun rises in the East, and the Liver resides in the East, belonging to the element of Wood. Thus, the Liver-Storehouse manages and controls it. As the <term>Yellow Court Scripture</term> says: *"The Liver-Spirit is the Dragon-Smoke, whose style-name is 'Containing Brightness'."* The commentary explains: "The sun rises in the East, therefore it 'contains brightness'." 

The Spirit is Pure Yang; its nature is to fly and move, rotating like the Sun and Moon in the Heavens. As the eyes gradually ascend and develop, they must illuminate the exterior. They become the **Pivotal Mechanism** of the Spirit. The Spirit then resides within, acting as the master of the center. The Spirit focuses its gaze through the eyes, and gradually, without realizing it, it has departed from its Mother <note>Qi</note>.

<summary>Master Pei Ao explains the alchemical embryology of the human body, describing how Spirit (Shen) emerges from Qi (Mother) and how the Five Elements interact to form the eyes as the "Spirit Light" and primary interface with the world.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the technical explanation of alchemical embryology. <page-num>165</page-num>

Regarding the **Eyes**: they only serve to lead the **Spirit** away from its **Mother** <note>Qi</note>. Residing on the exterior, they correspond with the Spirit. However, the Spirit must not be permanently attached to the eyes, or the process of <term>Creation and Transformation</term> <note>original: 造化 (zaohua) — the natural creative forces of the universe</note> will not be completed as it was before. 

Although the Qi-Mother is separated from her Son, she must ultimately nourish him until he is grown and stable. If the process stops midway, then neither will find peace. Thus, one must borrow **Wood** to generate **Fire**, which becomes the **Heart**. The Heart is made to hold the Spirit. Within the Heart is an empty space of one square inch; it receives the Spirit, and the Spirit residing there is called "Numinous." Therefore, the Heart is called the **Numinous Pedestal** <note>original: 靈臺 (Lingtai) — a common Daoist term for the mind or heart as a sacred, internal site</note>. 

The Spirit is **Yang**, and the Heart is **Fire**. Thus, the Spirit finds a place to reside within it. This follows the principle that "water flows toward what is damp, and fire moves toward what is dry." The Daoist scriptures say: *"The Heart is the capital of the Spirit."* The reason the Heart is more "numinous" than the other internal organs is solely because of the Spirit’s presence; it is not that the Heart is inherently numinous on its own. 

If the Spirit were not within, how would the Heart differ from the other organs? But because the Heart belongs to the element of Yang, its nature is to flutter and move, and thus it cannot remain still. However, if the eyes remain fixed and steady to settle the Spirit, then the Heart will also become unmoving. 

One must practice the Dao until proficient; otherwise, it is extremely difficult to keep the Heart from wavering. Next, the **Liver, Lungs, and Spleen**, the **Six Fu-Organs**, the **Five Limbs**, the **Nine Orifices**, and even the hair are all "created and transformed" by the Spirit. This follows the rule of the eyes; for the eyes are the "sprouts" of the five internal organs. 

After two hundred and seventy days <note>nine months of thirty days each</note>, the "Number of Yang" is fulfilled, and the human body is complete in every detail. Yet, once the Spirit has left its Mother, it never returns to the place where they first congealed. 

This is because humans are gradually weighed down by the **Five Flavors** <note>sensory desires and physical sustenance</note> and lose their clarity and coolness. Although Spirit and Qi function together and travel together, they no longer know how to nourish and complete one another; instead, they act in opposition. 

The reason the Mother and Son were originally separated was that there was no "Numinous Dwelling" <note>a stable physical body</note> and the various parts of the body were still missing. Therefore, they had to separate so that each could carry out its own creative work. Once they were both stable, they no longer looked after one another. 

How could the separation of Mother and Son be considered the proper order? We say today that the **"Heart is the horse of Qi."** Wherever the Intention arrives, the Qi arrives. People today may occasionally send their Qi to various places, but they do not know how to return it to the root—the place where they originally merged. 

Practitioners of the Dao must pay attention to this! The Spleen is near the Kidneys, just as the black and red parts of the eye are far apart; this is enough to clarify the principle. Although the Spirit has its capital in the Heart, it also resides within the **Essence** <note>Jing: the refined physical energy</note>. It nourishes the body, moistens the nature, and protects the bone marrow to make it strong. When the person is at peace, the Spirit can also remain at peace within the human body for a long time. 

Whenever a person faces danger and their hair stands on end, it is because the Spirit fears damage to its "dry dwelling" <note>the Heart-Fire</note>. If a person dies a violent or unnatural death, their **Original Qi** is still strong and has not yet weakened. They cannot return to the source or go back to the root; thus, they may become ghosts that haunt or possess others. This happens because the Original Spirit was not diseased and the physical vessel was not worn out. As the **Spring and Autumn Annals** says: *"When common men or women die a violent death, their <term>Hunyuan and Po souls</term> cling to others."* In such violent deaths, the Spirit might not be fully exhausted, but is instead carried away by the forceful Qi...

...clearly remembering the events of a previous life. This is like the stories of **Bao Jing** <note>original: 鮑靚 — a famous Jin dynasty official and Daoist master who claimed to remember a well from a past life</note> remembering the well, or **Yang Hu** <note>original: 羊祜 — a 3rd-century general said to have recognized a jade ring belonging to him in a previous incarnation</note> recognizing the ring. Generally, those who remember their past lives are children who died a violent or sudden death; because their **Essence-Qi** <note>the fundamental vitality</note> had not yet dissipated, it allows this memory to persist.

What we call **Essence** <note>term: Jing — the refined physical substance or "seed" of life</note> is formed by the accumulation of fluids and Qi. If it is agitated and released, the Spirit becomes uneasy; this leads to a slippery "leaking" or "discharge," which exhausts the utility of the Spirit. Once the Essence is depleted, the Spirit is also consumed, eventually becoming faint and returning to a state similar to when it first arrived. 

However, when the Heart-Qi is robust and the Water-Qi is abundant, the human body is firm and strong. If the **Five Flavors** <note>sensory overindulgence</note> are kept thin and sharp, but the Qi and Spirit are not properly balanced, one will eventually find it impossible to remain in this world and will suddenly depart. Returning to the Void, the Spirit becomes the "Essence-Flower" of the former true vitality and attaches itself to Heaven. As the saying goes, "the nature that is shed does not perish." Thus, the **Book of Rites** <note>original: 禮記 (Liji) — one of the Five Classics of the Confucian canon</note> says: *"The bones and flesh turn into earth, but the Soul-Qi returns to Heaven."*

The **Original Spirit** <note>term: Yuan Shen — the primordial, immortal consciousness</note> is like a Sovereign, while the **Governing Spirits** <note>the spirits of the various organs</note> are like ministers. Once the Original Spirit has departed, the Governing Spirits are left without a ruler; the "Kingdom" of the body is merely empty. This is why the Heart is called the **Emperor**. Once the Water-Qi is gone, the Yang-Qi takes over and soon dissipates as well. When these two substances have left, the human body collapses; this is called "Death," a state in which there is no longer any awareness.

Everyone in the world claims to love the **Dao** and to practice the **Dao**, yet they do not know what kind of "thing" the Dao actually is that they are practicing. When a person loves wine, they must know it is made of yeast and rice. When a person loves beauty, they must know of **Xi Shi** or the **Goddess of the Luo River** <note>legendary Chinese icons of female beauty</note>. When a person loves wealth, they must know of gold, jade, and precious goods. 

Consider how rhymes begin with the character *Dong* (East) and end with the character *Ma*. Tens of thousands of words have been categorized by their pronunciations, and people can identify all of them. Yet, when it comes to the single word "Dao," they are moved to tears of confusion and do not understand. Some say it is "dwelling in nothingness" or "spontaneously cultivating the heart and doing good," but they never truly grasp its core principle. If you do not know what it is, through which gate can you possibly practice?

They simply do not realize that the **Dao** is **Water**; in the human body, it is called **Qi**. This is why it is said, "The Dao produced the One" <note>a reference to the Dao De Jing</note>—for Water is "One." It is also said, "One Yin and one Yang are called the Dao"—for these are Water and Fire. Once the "One Yang" has departed, the "One Yin" also dissipates; this means the Dao is no longer complete, and the person must die. 

The Heavens and the Earth were born from the Dao, but this world is merely a floating surface. It is said that when the Dao leaves, the person dies, just as when the water dries up, the fish perish. Therefore, that which is called the **Yin-Qi Mother** is the root of the **Internal Yin**; it is not some external, heterodox Yin energy. What is called the **Yang Spirit** is the quintessential essence of Pure Yang—it is the **Original Spirit**. It is not the secondary spirits of the five internal organs or the various parts of the body. The Original Spirit is what gives birth to the **Three Hun and Seven Po souls** <note>the celestial and terrestrial components of the human soul</note> and the spirits of the various limbs. 

The **Yellow Court Classic** <note>original: 黃庭經 (Huangting Jing) — a primary text of internal alchemy</note> says: *"The Kidney deity is Xuanming, styled Nurturing the Infant."* 
<gloss>The commentary says: The Kidney-Essence is the 'Son,' therefore it is called 'Nurturing the Infant.'</gloss> 

Between the two kidneys, in men, there is the **Gate of Essence**, and in women, there is the **Womb**. Once the Gate of Essence is opened, the Kidney-Qi leaks out. Not only does the Internal Yang dissipate, but the Internal Yin is also exhausted. Therefore, the Kidneys are the "Capital of Yin," and the Heart is the "Capital of Yang." All creation and transformation first enter through the Yin; Yang represents the fact that the "ten thousand things" are born from the union of desires. Thus, Essence emerges from the Kidneys, and the "Son" (the new life or the internal elixir) is formed within the Kidneys; it never leaves the Kidney organ. Generally, the Original Spirit of the Heart relies entirely on...

He emphasizes the Kidneys as the "Capital of Yin" where the Essence is stored and where life begins.</summary>

<page-num>167</page-num>

...the physical body and govern it together. The **Three Hun** <note>original: 三魂 — the ethereal or celestial souls</note> also assist in this completion. However, those who specifically cause harm are the **Seven Po** <note>original: 七魄 — the corporeal or terrestrial souls associated with the physical body's desires</note> and the **Three Corpses** <note>term: San Shi — three parasitic spirits believed to live in the body and hasten death</note>. These are external, heterodox Yin energies that rob the body of life; often, when the Spirit-Qi cannot withstand them, the person dies. When a person dies, the Three Corpses and Seven Po flourish. 

The **Original Spirit** <note>term: Yuan Shen</note> is the Sovereign, while the Corpses and the Po are merely ministers. They are like treacherous and cunning ministers who bring chaos to the kingdom and coerce their ruler. If one practices the cultivation of Qi until it is robust, the Spirit will remain strong; then the Seven Po and Three Corpses can never triumph, and longevity will naturally result in "long life." 

Regarding those who do not suffer from illness but die suddenly, it is because the pulse has accidentally "tripped" or become obstructed, failing to reach even one internal organ. Once that organ becomes weak, the **Five Elements** <note>the elemental phases of wood, fire, earth, metal, and water</note> begin to overcome one another in a destructive cycle. When the "Fire" is exhausted and the Yang pulse is severed, the Spirit departs, and the person naturally dies. This is because the pulse, which should flow like an open sea, is blocked by an obstruction; this is also caused by internal injuries that assist this collapse.

In the past, the physician **Bian Que** <note>original: 扁鵲 — a legendary physician of the Warring States period</note>, when treating the illness of the Prince of Guo, described it as **Corpse-Syncope** <note>term: Shijue — a state of apparent death where the body is cold but the person is still alive</note>. Because the Yang pulse has plummeted and the Yin pulse is struggling to rise, the Qi becomes closed off and cannot circulate. Above, the pulse is exhausted and dried up; below, the meridians are broken and overwhelmed by Yin. The complexion reflects this severed Yang-Qi. Because the Qi is governed by the pulse, the physical form appears murky and dark, looking exactly like a corpse.

When the Yang enters the "branched vessels," the internal organs survive. When the Yin enters the "branched vessels," the internal organs die. These several phenomena occur from time to time within the **Five Organs** <note>Heart, Liver, Spleen, Lungs, and Kidneys</note>. A skilled physician can recognize this and act, while an unskilled one will remain in doubt and peril; this is truly a fact. 

Alas! Daily we manage ten thousand phenomena, yet the Heart remains empty and the "Sovereign" is sidelined. The Spirit is driven and pulled about, and the body has no one to manage or control it. Thus, it is only natural that the "house" has no master and the "kingdom" falls into ruin. If the master does not repair the dwelling and instead spends his time managing affairs outside, the dwelling will fall into danger and decay day by day. If a person knows what the Spirit governs and understands the "Mother and Child" cycle of energy, the gate to self-cultivation and realization will become visible. 

If there is no "master" in control, one simply leaves everything to the breathing in the throat, which merely handles the basic logic of the internal organs and the digestion of food. This is ultimately unable to "return the Yin to Yang" or "replenish the blood and the brain." Furthermore, the breathing of ordinary people is entirely different from the breathing of a **Realized Man** <note>term: Zhenren — a perfected Daoist master</note>. 

The **Southern Flower Scripture** <note>original: 南華眞經 — The Book of Chuang Tzu (Zhuangzi)</note> says: *"Ordinary people breathe with their throats; the Realized Man breathes with his heels."*
<gloss>The commentary says: This means the breath comes from the very root of one's being.</gloss>
It also says: *"Their breathing is deep and profound."* This is the meaning of the passage. How could this be achieved easily? If one simply trusts in their natural, involuntary breathing, they have not yet attained the Dao. 

If a single inhalation and exhalation are not governed by the Spirit, then the breathing is incomplete. A Realized Man said: *"If the Spirit can drive the Qi, then the nose will not lose the breath."* These words are supreme. If one can also swallow their saliva and use the **Intent** <note>directed consciousness</note> to send it down into the **Sea of Qi** <note>term: Qi Hai — an energy center located in the lower abdomen</note>, it will directly irrigate the **Spiritual Root**. 

Alas! People today do not understand the "right and wrong" relationship between the Spirit and the physical body. A person can calculate the value of ten thousand things, but they cannot calculate the nature of their own Spirit and body, or how the two are moved to complete one another. They only remember things that happened after they were three years old, yet they are completely ignorant and blind to everything before that age. If one can reach the point where their calculations return to the very end—the source—then they will naturally see the root of how the Spirit, the Body, and the **Original Qi** are combined. Then it becomes clear that they are not two separate things. Knowing that the Spirit and the True Qi are of the same substance, names are merely a temporary way to preserve the thought and return to the Truth...

...indeed. This is what is called "deep roots and firm foundations." As for the "Return of Qi," it means returning to the place of one's original birth. As the **Book of Changes** <note>original: 周易 — Zhouyi or I Ching</note> says regarding the hexagram **Return** <note>original: 復卦 — Fu; a hexagram symbolizing the return of light and life</note>: *"A single Yang line is born beneath five Yin lines."* This explains the true meaning of the **Returned Elixir** <note>term: Huandan — a state in internal alchemy where the refined energy returns to its original, pure state</note>; it is not a matter of physical suppression or the ingestion of substances. Its meaning is clear.

Heaven is the origin from which we receive Qi, and Qi is the root of the physical form. If Qi has no form to inhabit, it has no ground to stand upon; if the form has no Qi, it has no means of completion. These two elements nourish one another and can thus be blended and harmonized. The Sages knew that external pursuits were useless; therefore, they "returned the essence and reverted to the root." By practicing **Firm Grasping** <note>a meditative hand gesture (mudra) intended to keep energy from escaping</note> and **Fetal Breathing** <note>term: Taixi — a deep, subtle meditative breathing likened to an infant in the womb</note>, they attained profound clarity within and regulated their internal state. In this way, they united with the "Great Simplicity" of original harmony—the blessed courtyard of immortality.

When the Spirit is harmonious, it can shine through and illuminate the **Five Organs**. When the Qi is harmonious, it can be put to use by the four limbs. The **Scripture of the Dao** says: *"Practice internal vision for three months, focusing the heart on Oneness."* 
<gloss>The commentary says: Focus the heart and guard the One.</gloss>
Then, the "Spiritual Light" is born, entwining itself around the Five Organs. Ordinary people exhaust their Spirit through constant toil; not a single breath remains still within the body, yet they hope for long life. Is that not far-fetched? 

If one can complete the path of Fetal Breathing so that Essence and Qi have a "master" to govern them, then men will remain free of blockages in their vitality, and women will not suffer from obstructions in the womb. In the functioning of the ten thousand transformations of the universe, nothing comes before Qi. In the functioning of the **Perfected Man**, nothing is more subtle or wondrous than the Spirit. Within the "Great Void," there is a substance called Spirit. Within the "Great Obscurity," there is an essence called Qi. 

Alas! Spirit and Qi! Their arrival is indistinct and blurred, and their departure leaves no trace. Their coming is difficult, but their departure is very easy. Therefore, the Sages mourned and cherished them. Oh! How casually people of the world drive away their Qi! One who does not understand the physical body cannot speak of Qi. One who does not understand Qi cannot speak of the Spirit. One who understands the Spirit is truly nourishing the Dao. 

The **Book of Changes** says: *"Essence and Qi make up things; the wandering soul makes up change."* If these changes are not regulated, a person cannot live long. This is why the **Queen Mother** <note>original: 西王母 — Xiwangmu, the Queen Mother of the West, a powerful Daoist goddess of immortality</note> possesses the "Way of the Golden Brain and Jade Pendants," and **Xuan Yuan** <note>the Yellow Emperor</note> practiced the art of internal vision and returning to the root. One must believe in these things. 

Alas! All things have an end, yet Heaven and Earth endure. People die, but true longevity is found in the interlocking Qi of Yin and Yang. If a person can guard their Yin and Yang, then Yin and Yang can guard the person. Heaven and Earth do not die, yet humans die of their own accord, rotting away in between. 

A collapsed wall or a ruined battlement can be mended with earth. An old tree or failing fruit can be rejuvenated by grafting on new branches. A broken cart or a leaking boat can be repaired with wood. A broken tripod or a pierced cauldron can be made firm again with iron. When a person encounters the decline of old age, they can be revived by **Returning the Spirit**. These are the teachings of the Great Immortals regarding success and failure; one must not be ignorant of them. 

The **Yang Elixir** allows one to ascend to the heavens; the **Yin Elixir** allows one to rise lightly. The Yang Elixir is the "Great Returned Elixir," while the Yin Elixir is the principle of internal cultivation and returning to the root. The Yellow Emperor once asked about the Dao from **Guangchengzi** <note>a legendary Daoist immortal</note>. Guangchengzi replied: *"Do not toil your body, do not agitate your essence. Have few thoughts and few desires, and you can attain long life."* 

The most essential part of the Dao is taking **Essence** <note>term: Jing</note> as the root and **Qi** as the stem. The scripture says: *"If one deeply nourishes the spiritual root, why would it wither?"* The "Way of Embracing the Truth" and the "Art of Self-Preservation" are matters passed down through oral instruction; they are not recorded on paper or ink. As long as one can be silent and unmoving, and keep desires...

...and by remotely extinguishing the ten thousand worries, practicing until one is familiar with the art of "using darkness to bring forth light" <note>original: 用晦而明 — a concept from the Book of Changes suggesting that by concealing one's brilliance and looking inward, true spiritual clarity is achieved</note>, one will surely attain the Dao.

## Formula for Resolving Doubts on Nourishing Life

The **One Qi** <note>the primordial energy from which all life originates</note> has no fixed direction; it ebbs and flows with the passage of time. The life and death of the ten thousand things depend entirely on the flourishing or decline of this Qi. All things exist within the space of nature, yet none understand the reasons why they are as they are. That which they receive and practice occurs beneath the covering of Heaven and upon the support of Earth. 

Those who possess physical form must first understand their root. If the root is known, then the "branches"—the final results—will naturally be understood. Practitioners of the Dao must first rectify their source. If the source is rectified, then the "stream"—the flow of life—will respond accordingly. If one abandons the root to seek answers externally, or turns their back on the source to follow a crooked path, then even if they read the books of a hundred schools and exhaust the studies of every philosopher, they will merely gain the merit of empty discourse. In the end, they will see no practical effect in **Nourishing Life** <note>term: Yangsheng — the ancient Chinese practice of longevity and health through physical and spiritual cultivation</note>. Those who truly attain the path and observe it for themselves will realize this truth intuitively.

Today, if we look at the crowds of people in the world who claim to love the Dao, they are beyond counting. Though they know how to guard themselves through "tranquility and detachment," they do not understand that within that very tranquility lies a **Subtle Function**. Though they know that "Emptiness and Non-existence" are the guiding principles, they do not understand that within that Emptiness, "nothing is left undone." 

If one does not understand the principle of the subtle function within tranquility and emptiness, and merely commits their will to silence or acts wildly outside the harmony of form and spirit, this is what is called "useless use." It is not the "Great Progress" <note>original: 鴻漸 — a reference to the gradual, steady progress symbolized by the flight of a wild swan in the Book of Changes</note> of preserving life. Furthermore, the Spirit dwells because of the physical form, and the form remains because the Spirit stays within it. If the Spirit is allowed to wander outside, the form cannot be preserved. 

Moreover, some people ingest herbal medicines, minerals, or metals to try and strengthen their physical forms. However, they do not understand the true nature of these substances, nor do they investigate the cycles of the four seasons or the proper balance of energy. If they ingest these things for a long time, they actually end up harming their **Harmonious Qi**. Before they even reach middle age, diseases and ailments arise together. This causes frivolous people to believe that the Dao is like "chasing the wind and catching shadows"—impossible to achieve. They then look upon students of the Dao as unworthy, and regard true recluses as followers of a "deceptive path." Is this not tragic?

Someone once mocked me regarding these matters, saying: "I have heard that learning the Dao can lead to long life. From my childhood until my old age, I have seen thousands of people who claim to study the Dao. There are those who **Abstain from Grain** <note>original: 絕粒 — the practice of Bigu, or 'avoiding grains,' believed to purify the body</note> and ingest Qi, those who perform exorcisms and summon spirits, those who remain pure and without desire, and those who refine themselves to become immortals. Among all these types of people, I have never heard of one who did not eventually die. Their bodies end up in the dark earth, and their followers merely use the term **Corpse Deliverance** <note>term: Shijie — a belief that a high-level immortal only appears to die, leaving a 'fake' corpse or object in the coffin while their true self ascends</note> as a hollow excuse. Judging from this, success must depend on possessing **Spiritual Bones** <note>original: 靈骨 — the idea that one must be born with a specific skeletal or spiritual constitution to become an immortal</note> from birth; it is not something that can be learned."

When I heard these words, I felt a pang of sorrow within and a sense of distraction without. After a long moment of silent reflection, I sighed and replied: "Looking at what you have said, it is truly vulgar and deeply deluded. In this world, even when people learn ordinary, mundane skills, there are those who succeed and those who fail. How much more so with the 'Subtle Root' and the 'Dark Mystery'? How could one possibly attain such things through haste or superficial effort? The Great Dao is impartial, yet it responds to those who resonate with it. To suggest it is only for those born with 'spiritual bones'—is that not a major error? Now, regarding the practices of ingesting Qi and abstaining from grain..."

<summary>This page critiques superficial Daoist practices, such as the blind ingestion of minerals or mere silence, arguing that true immortality requires understanding the "subtle function" within emptiness. It also records a skeptic's argument that since all "immortals" seem to die, the Dao must be a myth or reserved only for those born with special "spiritual bones."</summary>

...these are what the Daoist school honors. If a person attains them, they all experience the effects of not eating and feeling light enough to lift off the ground. They then claim for themselves that their "intestines and stomach are free of dregs," that they can "instantly reach the clouds and mist," that their "physical forms have attained lightness," and they can "sit astride phoenixes and cranes." Those who seek such things use the "Hairy Woman" <note>original: 毛女 — a legendary Qin dynasty palace maid who fled to the mountains, ate pine needles, and grew green feathers/hair, becoming an immortal</note> as their proof; those who practice breathing techniques cite the "Spirit Tortoise" <note>original: 靈龜 — a symbol of longevity known for its ability to hold its breath for long periods</note> as evidence. Yet, none of them realize that their **True Qi** <term>Zhenqi — the refined, functional energy of the body</term> is being secretly extinguished and their **Embryonic Essence** <term>Taijing — the primordial vitality one is born with</term> is withering away within. They remain stubbornly attached to the principles found in "pine and bamboo" <note>referring to external longevity symbols or perhaps herbal ingredients</note> and cling to their delusions within "ink and paper." This is truly worth a long sigh! Is it not strange? As for those who practice exorcisms and the summoning of spirits, these are merely the ritual matters of the Dao. > The Scripture says: It was born before the existence of Heaven and Earth; this is the **Original Qi** <term>Yuanqi — the fundamental energy of the universe</term>.

That which this body possesses comes from the union of father and mother, who bestowed their **Original Qi**. This **Original Qi** is the **True Essence** <note>original: 真精 — the most refined substance of the body, often associated with reproductive vitality but used here as a spiritual fuel</note>. How can we understand this? When essence remains in the body, the body lives. When essence is bestowed upon another, a person is born. By moving this **Essence and Qi** <note>original: 精氣</note> to form the **Original Qi** of another, once the other's form is completed, one's own self suffers a loss.

> The Classic of the Internal Landscape says: Regarding long life, be most cautious and urgent concerning the "chamber." This refers simply to the way of "Subtle Function." <note>This is a veiled reference to sexual discipline or internalizing reproductive energy rather than depleting it.</note>

**Original Qi** congeals to become Essence. The Essence within the body is the root of **Original Qi**. If one can cause the Qi to consistently replenish the Essence, and move it between the **Upper Field** <term>Shangyuan — the 'Upper Cinnabar Field' located in the head/brain</term> and the **Lower Field** <term>Xiayuan — the 'Lower Cinnabar Field' located in the abdomen</term>, while also drawing in "New Qi," then within ten days it returns to being Essence. It is like a cauldron heating its contents: if you remove what is inside and add new material, cycling back and forth without end, then even Heaven and Earth are not long-lived enough to compare to you. When the **Upper Field** is filled, the hundred joints of the body naturally become solid. The old return to their prime, and those in their prime return to the state of an infant. Having attained the **Upper Field** and **Lower Field**, I can cause the meridians to connect and cross. Using "firmness and gentleness" as the rule, I carefully cultivate my palace. Immortality must be attained; but if one does not cultivate my palace, death will certainly prevail. A person exists within Qi like a fish exists in water. Whether sinking or floating, moving east or west, it is all up to the individual. When cultivation has proceeded for a time, the hundred joints will be completely free-flowing. Calamities will vanish like the arrival of spring; after a long time, one will know this for oneself. If there is a blockage or a place of disease, focus the mind on the **Middle Field** <note>original: 中元 — the Middle Cinnabar Field, located at the heart</note> and ignite a fire to burn through it; it will then open of its own accord. Once open, the illness is healed. The heart is the **Crimson Palace** <term>Jiang Gong — a Daoist name for the heart center</term>. The **Crimson Palace** is red in color, like fire. By maintaining the mind and igniting this fire until it pervades the entire body, one not only causes the Qi pathways to flow but also dissolves all "evil influences" <note>referring to pathogenic energies or negative thoughts</note>. Generally, before one wishes to **Circulate Qi** <term>Xingqi — the practice of moving breath/energy through the body using intention</term>, one should ignite it once.

> The Scripture says: Master Guangcheng accumulated fire to burn the five poisons. <note>Guangchengzi was the legendary immortal teacher of the Yellow Emperor.</note>

The "five poisons" are the "five flavors" <note>the heavy tastes of worldly food</note>. If the five grains and five flavors are not "burned" away, they will surely obstruct the Qi pathways. If the burning lasts too long, it may cause a person to feel irritable and hot. As soon as you feel the blockage is clear, you must immediately **Circulate Qi**. The method for **Circulating Qi** is simply to vanish all worries and let the spirit be at ease; the subtle **Original Qi** will then naturally pervade the body. As for Qi, the hundred joints and every pore all possess it naturally. Being able to move it with the intention is like a virtuous minister transforming the common people. How can we understand this "steaming" effect within the body? Take a ten-foot piece of bamboo and clear out its nodes. Block one end and blow into the middle; the air suddenly reaches the end of the tube, as the **Original Qi** pushes itself through. The human body is just like this tube.

## Song of the Lower Field

The Way of **Tallying with the Truth** <note>original: 契眞 — the process of aligning one's internal state with the ultimate reality of the Dao</note> is drifting and easily moved; yet within that movement, there is a stillness, as if something is "lodged" there. How can one know if it is present or absent? To be able to transcend and suddenly go or stay according to the **Profound Mechanism** <note>original: 玄機 — the subtle, hidden workings of the universe or the internal energy system</note>—this is its true meaning.

This chapter explains the secret of harmonizing the **Lower Field** <term>Xiayuan — the Lower Cinnabar Field in the abdomen</term>. The essence of Tallying with the Truth is not actually difficult; it is people who perversely make it hard for themselves. "Drifting" simply refers to a state of leisure and ease. If one can bring ease to the body, clear the heart, and sever all thoughts so that the **Three Fields** <note>the Upper, Middle, and Lower Cinnabar Fields/energy centers</note> are all flowing and connected, then immortality is close at hand.

That which "moves yet does not move" is the **Mysterious Pearl** <term>Xuanzhu — a symbolic concentration of refined internal energy and spirit</term>. This involves visualizing a pearl within the **Lower Field**; it should be about the size of a bullet, shining brightly as if it were vibrating or moving, yet it remains perfectly still. 

To be "lodged in the midst of movement" means to focus the attention on the center of the **Lower Cinnabar Field**, where the **Sea of Qi** <term>Qihai — an acupuncture point and energy reservoir below the navel</term> is located. One must make the breath very fine, allowing the Qi to circle the "pearl" from all four sides within that "sea." When the Qi reaches the feet, the pearl is truly "lodged" within the movement. When the energy of the **Middle Field** <gloss>the heart center</gloss> is poured down into the pearl of the **Lower Field**, the **Original Qi** then becomes settled. 

Once settled, external Qi does not enter and internal Qi does not leak out; one suddenly achieves a state of "Original Harmony" with Heaven and Earth. One's lifespan then becomes limitless. Even if Heaven and Earth were to collapse, my own nature would endure. 

The **Yellow Emperor** sought the **Mysterious Pearl** at the **Red River** <note>A reference to a famous parable in the *Zhuangzi*. In this context, the "Red River" symbolizes the blood or the heart's energy.</note>. The "Red River" refers to the red blood. Since the **Mysterious Pearl** exists within the Qi, if you seek this pearl and obtain it, you will certainly attain life. Thus, the Emperor employed **Imageless** <note>original: 象罔 (Xiangwang) — a character in the *Zhuangzi* whose name implies "seeming like nothingness." He was the only one who could find the lost pearl after Knowledge, Sight, and Speech failed.</note>, which signifies a state of no thoughts and no worries. After entering a state of darkness and stillness, one naturally obtains this pearl. 

If you wish to know the way of "transcending and flying upward," it begins with discarding the **Mechanism** <note>original: 機 (ji) — refers to the clever, calculating, or scheming mind that creates internal friction</note>. If the mechanism is discarded, the body remains; if the mechanism stays, the body dies. When there is no mechanism, the chest is pure white and empty. This is the secret of how to position oneself regarding gain and loss; this is the true meaning.

# Postscript

**Master Chonghezi** <note>literally "Master of Blended Harmony"</note> says: In my youth, I studied the **Way** <term>Dao — the ultimate reality and path of nature</term>, and as I grew older, my devotion only increased. There was not a famous mountain under heaven that I did not seek out and visit. I climbed dangerous heights and trod through perilous places, never daring to fear hardship or toil. My mind was set on witnessing extraordinary sights, and I did not consider a thousand miles too far to travel. 

In the year of *Yiwei* <note>a year in the sixty-year sexagenary cycle</note>, I walked through **Swallow Valley** at **Mount Qingcheng** <note>a major center of Daoism in Sichuan province</note>. The valley was deep and secluded for a hundred miles, with pines and vines obscuring the sky above. By chance, I followed a woodcutter into a stone grotto. Inside the cave was a **Realized Person** <term>Zhenren — a perfected spiritual being</term> who said his surname was Li. I did not know where he was from. His hair hung down past his waist, and his complexion was as pure as ice and snow. I bowed to him twice, and he appeared joyful and serene. 

After a long while, he asked where I had come from. I then described my sincere intentions and my wish to remain by his side to serve him. By heavenly luck, I was accepted. Forty-three years passed in a flash, and he suddenly bestowed upon me the **Technique of the Three Primes** <note>original: 三元之術 (Sanyuan zhi shu) — likely referring to the Three Cinnabar Fields or the three primordial energies of the universe</note>. I practiced according to the oral instructions, turning day into night. After twelve years, I found myself frequently able to fly. I refined my practice further and further; though it is difficult to master in just a few years, those who receive it may pass it on after thirty-one years of practice. If it is passed to the wrong person, divine punishment will surely follow. 

Those who practice this Way should reduce their intake of the **Five Pungent Spices** <note>traditionally: garlic, leeks, onions, scallions, and chives</note> and anything stale or foul-smelling. This reduction should be gradual rather than sudden. After one year, the **Qi** <term>vital energy</term> pathways will be full and solid, and one will naturally cease to need food. 

The great secret lies in **Eliminating the Mechanism** <note>original: 泯機 (minji) — as noted on the previous page, this refers to silencing the clever, calculating, or scheming mind</note>. When the mechanism is severed, the **Qi** arrives without being summoned and the work is completed without plotting. I have practiced this myself, and every single step has shown divine efficacy. I have now provided these annotations so that future seekers will not be lost. You noble followers of the Way: please keep these secrets with the utmost reverence.

<meta>This page transitions from the personal postscript of Chonghezi to the primary text of the manuscript: the "Discourse on Sitting in Forgetfulness" by the Tang dynasty Daoist master Sima Chengzhen. This work is a foundational guide to Daoist meditation and mental cultivation.</meta>

# Discourse on Sitting in Forgetfulness, with Preface, in Seven Chapters

->Written by Sima Chengzhen<- <note>Sima Chengzhen (647–735 CE) was a prominent high priest of the Shangqing school of Daoism during the Tang Dynasty</note>

What humanity values most is life. And what life values most is the **Way** <term>Dao — the fundamental principle of the universe</term>. For a person to possess the Way is like a fish possessing water. A fish in a dry rut still hopes for a splash of water, yet people caught in the customs of a decaying world have no heart for seeking the Way. They loathe the suffering of birth and death, yet they love the very karmic deeds that cause birth and death. They value the reputation of **Dao and Virtue** <note>original: 道德 (Daode)</note>, but they make light of the actual practice of Dao and Virtue. They delight in physical beauty and rich flavors, considering these to be "attaining their goals," while they despise tranquility and simplicity, viewing them as states of exhaustion and poverty. They use rare goods to "buy" blessings for a future life, yet they indulge in easily-tainted emotions and lose the Way in their current life. They call themselves clever and skillful, yet they are as if in a dream or a stupor. Coming into life and departing in death, they cycle through ten thousand eons. If we examine this "upside-down" state of being, what could be more extreme? 

Therefore, the **Scripture of Wondrous Truth** <note>original: 妙真經 (Miaozhen Jing)</note> says: "People constantly lose the Way; it is not the Way that loses people. People constantly depart from life; it is not life that departs from the Way." Thus, those who nourish life must be careful not to lose the Way. Those who practice the Way must be careful not to lose their life. Let the Way and life guard one another, and let life and the Way preserve one another. When the two do not depart from each other, only then can one achieve "long-enduring." To speak of "long-enduring" is to speak of the very essence of attaining the Way. The scripture says: "Life is the great virtue of Heaven. It is the great joy of the Earth. It is the great blessing of humanity." A practitioner of the Way achieves this through practice, not through mere fate or luck. 

Furthermore, the **Scripture of Western Ascension** <note>original: 西昇經 (Xisheng Jing)</note> says: "My destiny lies within me; it does not belong to Heaven." Based on this, whether one's life is long or short depends on oneself. Attainment is not a gift from Heaven, and loss is not something taken by others. I press my hand to my heart and lament that it is late; time does not tarry even for a moment. I regret that my years are like those of the **morning fungus** <note>a metaphor from the philosopher Zhuangzi referring to a creature that lives only a few hours, symbolizing the brevity of life</note> and have already passed the age of **knowing one's destiny** <note>traditionally age fifty</note>. As an "infant" returning to the Way, I am not yet proficient. Because I cherish every inch of shadow—which vanishes as quickly as a flickering candle—I have exerted myself to seek the meaning of the scriptures. The matters are prepared and the principles are direct; the tasks are easy to perform. For those suffering from "illnesses of the heart-mind," I have restricted myself to writing down the method of **Sitting in Forgetfulness** <term>Zuowang — a state of deep meditative absorption where one leaves behind the body and intellect</term> to put the mind at ease. I have summarized the essentials into seven chapters, arranged in the stages of practicing the Way.

---

## Faith and Respect

Faith is the root of the Way. Respect is the stem of Virtue. When the root is deep, the Way can endure. When the stem is firm, Virtue can flourish. However, even when the radiance of a jade jewel was enough to buy a city, **Bian He** suffered punishment. Even when words had the power to preserve a kingdom, **Wu Zixu** met with execution. <note>Bian He was a commoner who was mutilated for presenting a raw jade stone that kings thought was a fake; Wu Zixu was a loyal advisor who was forced to commit suicide by the king he served. Both represent how truth and value are often rejected by the ignorant.</note> This is because when physical forms and external vessels are prominent, the threads of the mind become confused; when the beginnings of truth and principle sprout, the thoughts of the emotions overlook them. How much more so when the Ultimate Way transcends color and taste, and the True Nature is separated from us by the objects of desire? And yet, to be able to...

<summary>This page introduces Sima Chengzhen’s classic manual on Daoist meditation, arguing that while humans value life, they mistakenly pursue worldly desires instead of the Way. He outlines a seven-stage process for "Sitting in Forgetfulness" to reclaim one's true nature, beginning with the foundations of Faith and Respect.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the first chapter, "Faith and Respect," quoting the philosopher Zhuangzi to define the practice of "Sitting in Forgetfulness." It then transitions into the second and third chapters, which deal with practical steps: "Severing Ties" with the mundane world and "Collecting the Mind" to achieve internal stillness.</meta>

<page-num>174</page-num>

...how can one hear the "infinitesimal" <note>original: 希微 (xiwei) — a reference to the Daodejing describing the Way as something that cannot be seen or heard</note> and maintain faith, or listen to the "image-less" <note>original: 罔象 (wangxiang) — a metaphor for the formless state of the Way</note> without becoming confused? If a person hears the method of **Sitting in Forgetfulness** <term>Zuowang — meditative absorption</term>, believes it is the essential for practicing the Way, respects and honors it without doubt, and adds to this diligent practice, they will surely attain the Way. 

Therefore, **Zhuang Zhou** <note>The philosopher Zhuangzi (c. 4th century BCE)</note> said: "Slough off the limbs and trunk, dismiss hearing and sight, depart from the physical form and cast off wisdom, and become identical with the **Great Pervasion** <term>Datong — the state of being one with the universal Way</term>. This is called Sitting in Forgetfulness." 

Regarding this Sitting in Forgetfulness: what is there that is *not* forgotten? Internally, one is unaware of one’s own body; externally, one is unaware of the entire universe. One becomes obscurely one with the Way, and the ten thousand worries are all left behind. Therefore, Zhuangzi said: "Become identical with the Great Pervasion." These words are shallow in appearance but deep in meaning. The confused hear them but do not believe; they are like people who "hold a treasure yet go seeking a treasure." What else can be done for them? 

As the scripture <note>the Daodejing</note> says: "Where faith is insufficient, there will be no faith." This means that if the heart-mind’s faith in the Way is insufficient, the disaster of "not believing" will fall upon them. In such a state, what hope is there for the Way?

### Severing Ties

"Severing ties" means cutting off the connections to "intentional" worldly affairs. When one abandons these affairs, the physical form is not labored; when one practices **non-action** <term>Wuwei — acting without artificial striving or ego</term>, the heart-mind is naturally at peace. Tranquility is approached day by day, and the burdens of the "dusty world" thin out day by day. As one's footsteps grow more distant from society, the heart-mind grows closer to the Way. The Way is most divine and most sacred; who has ever reached it without following this path? 

Thus the scripture says: "Block the openings, close the gates, and to the end of life you will not labor." Some people show off their virtue or display their abilities to attract others and protect themselves. Some exchange social visits and ceremonies out of obligation. Some pretend to be hermits while secretly hoping for a promotion. Some use invitations to food and wine to hope for future favors. These are all instances of "cunning in the heart-mind" used to chase worldly profit. Since these are not in harmony with the Way, they deeply hinder one's true work. All such things should be cut off. 

The scripture says: "Open the openings, increase the affairs, and to the end of life you will not be saved." If I do not initiate the "song," the other side will not harmonize with it. Even if they sing, I do not respond. Let old ties gradually be severed, and let no new ties be formed. When the physical and social pressures are managed this way, a state of daily detachment is naturally reached. Only when one is free of affairs and at leisure can one practice the Way. 

Zhuangzi said: "Do not escort [what goes] and do not welcome [what comes]." This is because one should not have the emotions of worldly social exchange. He also said: "Do not be a 'corpse' for fame; do not be a 'mansion' of schemes; do not be a 'bearer' of affairs; do not be a 'master' of knowledge." If there are affairs that truly cannot be discarded, one performs them only because there is no other choice; one must not allow them to produce attachment or bind the heart-mind as one's primary "work."

### Collecting the Mind

The heart-mind is the master of the entire body and the teacher of the hundred spirits. When it is still, it produces wisdom; when it moves, it creates confusion. People delight in being lost within "illusory realms," claiming that these are "real." They enjoy feasting within the world of "intentionality," yet who among them realizes its emptiness?

<summary>This page explains the philosophical basis of "Sitting in Forgetfulness" through the teachings of Zhuangzi and outlines "Severing Ties" as a prerequisite for meditation. It emphasizes that one must simplify worldly obligations and social performances to achieve the mental stillness required to practice the Way.</summary>

<keywords>Sitting in Forgetfulness (Zuowang), Zhuangzi, Great Pervasion (Datong), Severing Ties, Non-action (Wuwei), Heart-mind, Daodejing, Social Obligations</keywords>

--- Page 237 ---
<meta>This page continues the third chapter, "Collecting the Mind," which offers practical guidance on meditation. It transitions from the philosophical justifications of the previous page to specific instructions on how to handle the mind during "Sitting in Forgetfulness," warning against common pitfalls like "blind stillness" or "clinging to emptiness."</meta>

<page-num>175</page-num>

It is not that consciousness itself acts as an obvious obstacle; rather, it is because of the "ground" upon which the mind rests. If even when choosing a neighborhood to live in, one might change their habits to match, or when choosing friends to associate with, one seeks those who provide benefit—how much more so should the body leave the realm of **birth and death** <note>The cycle of suffering and reincarnation</note> and the heart-mind dwell within the **Ultimate Way**? How could one not abandon the former to gain the latter?

Therefore, at the beginning of learning the Way, one must sit peacefully, collect the mind, and move away from external environments. Dwell in the state of "having nothing," do not cling to a single object, and naturally enter the **Void** <term>Xuwu — the state of primordial potential and emptiness</term>. Then the heart-mind will merge with the Way. 

As the scripture <note>likely the *Daodejing* or a related commentary</note> says: "Within the Ultimate Way, all is silent and without existence; its spiritual function is limitless." The substance of the heart-mind is the same. The origin of the heart-mind's substance takes the Way as its root. However, because the heart-mind's spirit has been stained, and the shroud of ignorance has gradually deepened, it has drifted for a long time and thus become separated from the Way. Now, if one can cleanse the "grime" of the heart-mind and reveal the original spiritual root, it is called **Cultivating the Way** <term>Xiudao</term>. To stop drifting and merge obscurely with the Way, dwelling safely within it, is called **Returning to the Root** <term>Guigen</term>. To guard this root without leaving it is called **Stillness and Stability** <term>Jingding — a state of meditative equanimity</term>. 

When Stillness and Stability are maintained for a long time, ailments vanish and one's life-force is restored. When this restoration is continuous, one naturally comes to **Know the Eternal** <term>Zhichang — understanding the unchanging laws of the universe</term>. To know the eternal is to have nothing that is not illuminated. The eternal is forever without change or extinction. Escaping the cycle of birth and death truly stems from this. 

Therefore, in the Method of the Way, the most important thing in settling the heart-mind is to avoid "clinging." The scripture <note>Daodejing, Chapter 16</note> says: "All things flourish, and each returns to its root. Returning to the root is called stillness; stillness is called restoring the life-force; restoring the life-force is called the eternal. Knowing the eternal is called illumination." 

If you force the heart-mind to dwell in "emptiness," you are still "holding onto something" <note>original: 有所 (yousuo)</note>. This cannot be called "having no attachments." Whenever the mind dwells on something, it naturally causes the heart-mind to labor and the **vital breath** <term>Qi — the energy or life-force of the body</term> to be disturbed. Not only is this out of harmony with the natural order, but it actually causes illness. Simply let the heart-mind not cling to objects, and yet remain unmoved; this is the true foundation of **Correct Stability** <term>Zhengding</term>. Using this for meditation, the heart-mind and the *qi* will be in harmony. Over time, you will feel increasingly light and refreshed. Use this as a test to distinguish the false from the correct path. 

If every thought that arises is immediately extinguished without distinguishing right from wrong, and if you permanently cut off all awareness, you have entered **Blind Stability** <term>Mangding — a state of dullness or 'stone-like' meditation</term>. Conversely, if you let the heart-mind follow whatever arises without any restraint, you are no different from an ordinary person. 

Furthermore, if you only cut off the concepts of "good and evil" but the heart-mind has no direction to return to, and you let it drift aimlessly while waiting for it to settle itself—you are merely deceiving yourself. Finally, if you involve yourself in all sorts of worldly affairs while claiming "the heart-mind is unstained," your words may be beautiful, but your conduct is wrong. Those who truly study the Way must especially be wary of this. 

Now, the practice is this: stop the chaos without extinguishing the **inner illumination** <note>The natural awareness or 'light' of the mind</note>; guard the stillness without clinging to the void. Practice this consistently, and you will naturally attain **True Insight** <term>Zhenjian</term>. 

If there are occasional practical matters or essential doubts regarding the teachings, let yourself contemplate them so the matter can be settled or the doubt resolved. This is also a root for producing wisdom. Once the matter is finished, then stop. Do not overthink. Overthinking uses "knowledge" to harm "serenity," which wounds your own foundation. Though you might show off a moment of cleverness, you ultimately damage the work of ten thousand generations. 

If distracting or unwholesome thoughts arise, remove them as soon as you become aware of them. If you hear of fame, praise, or blame, or encounter good or evil events, cast them away immediately. Do not allow the heart-mind to receive them. If the heart-mind receives them, it becomes "full." When it is full, the Way has no place to dwell. Treat everything seen or heard as if it were not seen or heard; this means good and evil do not enter the heart-mind. When the heart-mind does not receive external things, it is called **Empty** <term>Xu</term>. When it does not chase external things, it is called **Peaceful** <term>An</term>. When the heart-mind is peaceful and empty, the Way will naturally come to rest there. 

As the scripture says: "If a person can empty the heart-mind and practice non-action, they do not even need to desire the Way, for the Way will naturally return to them."

It emphasizes that "True Stability" involves an empty, non-clinging heart-mind that remains aware without being "filled" by external praise or worldly affairs.</summary>
