Once the heart-mind has no attachments, external actions also have no purposeful striving. It is neither pure nor defiled; thus, praise and blame have no way to arise. It is neither wise nor foolish; thus, profit and harm have no means to reach it. In reality, following the "Middle Way" is the constant. Flexibility allows one to wax and wane with the times. If one can avoid all entanglements, that is true wisdom.

If it is not the right time or the right matter, yet one labors their thoughts and forces action while claiming "non-attachment," this is ultimately not true awakening. Why is this? The "law of the heart-mind" is like an eye. Even a tiny hair entering the eye makes it uncomfortable. When small matters concern the heart-mind, it will surely be disturbed. Once there is the "ailment of movement," it is difficult to enter the **Gate of Stability** <term>Dingmen — the entry point to deep meditative concentration</term>. 

Therefore, the essential point of cultivating the Way is the urgent need to remove this "ailment." If it is not removed, one will never attain stability. It is also like a fertile field where the **thorns** <term>Jingji — symbolic of mental distractions and worldly attachments</term> have not been uprooted. Though seeds are sown, the good sprouts will not grow. Attachments, biased views, and overthinking are the "thorns" of the heart-mind. If they are not pruned away, **Stability and Wisdom** <term>Dinghui — the twin goals of meditation</term> will not arise.

Some may live in wealth and honor, or be learned in the classics and histories. Their words may be compassionate and frugal, yet their actions are greedy and cruel. Their eloquence is enough to gloss over their faults, and their power enough to intimidate others. When they succeed, they take the credit; when they fail, they inevitably blame others. This "ailment" is the deepest; though such people study, there is no benefit. This is so because of their self-righteousness. 

However, this heart-mind has always relied on external environments; it is not used to standing alone. When it suddenly has nothing to lean on, it is difficult for it to be at peace. Even if it gains temporary peace, it returns to a state of scattered confusion. As thoughts arise, restrain them immediately, making it a priority to keep the mind unmoved. After a long time of such **taming and ripening** <term>Tiaoshu — the process of training the mind like an animal</term>, you will naturally attain a state of peaceful leisure.

Regardless of day or night, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, or even when responding to affairs, you must always intentionally settle the mind. If the heart-mind attains stability, you must simply nourish it and not allow any irritation or contact to disturb it. 

Once you have attained even a small measure of stability, you can enjoy it yourself. As the mind becomes gradually **tamed and familiar** <term>Xunxia</term>, you will only feel a sense of clarity and distance. The things you valued throughout your life will already seem worn out and turbid. How much more so when stability gives birth to wisdom, allowing you to deeply penetrate what is true and what is false?

Oxen and horses are domestic animals; yet if they are let loose and not gathered in, they become stubborn and refuse to be driven. Fawns and wild birds are wild; yet if they are bound by humans and kept in hand all day, they naturally become tamed. How much more is this true for the heart-mind’s indulgence? If it is let loose and not gathered, it only becomes coarser and more careless. How could it then contemplate the **Subtle Mystery**? 

Thus the scripture <note>Daodejing, Chapter 62</note> says: "Though one might have a **great jade disc** <term>Gongbi</term> followed by a team of four horses, it is not as good as sitting and advancing in this Way."

The wonder of the Method lies in the ability to practice it, not in the ability to talk about it. If practiced, then these words are appropriate; if not practiced, these words are false. Furthermore, what people of today learn is to value the difficult and despise the easy. When discussing the Method in the style of the **Liang dynasty** <note>Referring to the overly metaphysical and intellectual debates popular among the elite in the 6th century</note>, if one only speaks grandly of "void" and "non-existence"—things beyond the reach of thought and lacking any steps for practical use—then people sigh in admiration at the "inconceivable" and pay their utmost respects. 

But if the truthful words are not beautiful, pointing directly to matters and explaining the actual situation—words that, once heard, the heart-mind understands, and once spoken, can be acted upon—*this* is what is truly inconceivable. Yet people do not believe it. Thus the scripture <note>Daodejing, Chapter 70</note> says: "My words are very easy to understand and very easy to practice. But no one in the world can understand them, and no one can practice them. It is because they do not understand the principle that they do not understand me."

There are those who say, "Fire is not hot," or "A lamp does not illuminate the darkness," and call this a "subtle meaning." Now, fire is used for cooking, and a lamp's function is to illuminate. Today, people loudly proclaim that "fire is not hot," yet they never for a moment stop using fire. They speak empty words about how a "lamp does not illuminate the darkness," yet they must keep a lamp burning all night. When words and actions contradict each other, the principle has no real substance. These are merely words meant to **shatter appearances** <term>Poxiang — a concept of negating dualistic views to reach the truth</term>, yet people conversely...

...taking these paradoxes as the subtle mysteries of the deep origin. Even the grand eloquence of **Huizi** <note>Hui Shi, a famous philosopher known for his logical paradoxes and friendship with Zhuangzi</note>, **Zhuangzi** <note>The seminal Daoist philosopher</note> found unbearable. As for the common crowd, who among them can distinguish the truth? Those who truly study the Way should not let such things trouble their hearts. 

Someone might say: "For those who follow the Great Way, the mind remains unstained while among things, and the spirit remains undisturbed while in motion. There is nothing they do not do, yet no time they are not silent. Now, you still avoid affairs to seek stillness and leave motion to go toward stability; you labor at controlling the mind. This creates two minds—one of motion and one of stillness—and causes you to get stuck in 'holding on' to one state. This results in the dual sicknesses of 'grasping' and 'rejecting.' To not realize what you are clinging to, yet call it the essential ladder to the Way—how mistaken is that!"

I respond: Generally speaking, your description of the Great Way—that it is in all things yet unstained, and handles affairs without confusion—is indeed great and truly subtle. However, your insight, my friend, is not yet clear. Why? You only see the brilliant radiance of the **patterned brocade** <note>A metaphor for a finished, beautiful result or a realized sage</note>, but do not understand that it began with raw silk. You have only heard the **calling crane** <note>A symbol of a high-achieving person or a sage</note> soaring to the heavens, but do not recognize that it first required grain for nourishment. A tree that blocks the sun grew from a tiny sprout. A sage with a focused spirit achieved it through the accumulation of practice. Today, people merely learn to speak of the sage’s virtue without knowing *how* the sage became virtuous. This can be called "seeing an egg and demanding it crow at dawn," or "seeing a crossbow bolt and demanding a roast owl." How hasty! Thus the scripture <note>A variation of the Daodejing, Chapter 65</note> says: "Establishing virtue is deep and far; it goes against the nature of common things, and only then reaches Great Accord."

->## Simplifying Affairs<-

---

Human life must involve managing affairs. There are ten thousand types of affairs, and they cannot be handled by one person alone. A bird nesting in the forest uses only a single branch; it ignores the rest of the flowering thicket. A beast drinking from the river fills only its belly; it is not overwhelmed by the great waves. Externally, one should seek things only as needed; internally, one should be clear about oneself. Know that life has its allotted portion, and do not strive for what is outside that portion. Recognize that affairs have a natural order, and do not take on extraordinary tasks. If an affair is extraordinary, it harms one’s wisdom and strength. If one strives beyond their portion, they become an enemy to their own **form and spirit** <term>Xingshen — the physical body and the animating consciousness</term>. If the body is not at peace, how can the heart reach the Way?

Therefore, the cultivator of the Way must cut away and simplify affairs. Know what is leisurely and what is essential; weigh the light against the heavy; recognize what to discard and what to take. Anything that is neither essential nor heavy should be cut off. It is like people having wine and meat for food, or silk and gauze for clothes, or fame and rank for their person, or gold and jade for wealth. These are all the excess of passion and desire; they are "pleasures" but are not good medicine for benefiting life. The masses all pursue them and bring themselves to ruin. When you think of this in stillness, how can the delusion be so deep? 

Thus **Zhuangzi** said: "One who understands the reality of life does not strive for what is unnecessary for life." <gloss>That which is unnecessary for life refers to things outside of one’s allotted portion.</gloss> Simple vegetables and coarse clothes are enough to prolong one’s natural life. Why wait for fine wine, food, and silk to consider it "living"? Therefore, anything that is not essentially useful for life must be discarded. Even things that are useful but are in excess should be abandoned. Wealth has a "harmful energy"; when it accumulates, it harms people. Even a little is a burden—how much more so a lot? Today, if one used the **Pearl of Marquis Sui** <note>A legendary, priceless gem; the metaphor implies wasting something of infinite value on something trivial</note> to shoot at a bird a thousand cubits high, people...

<summary>The author argues that true sagehood is built on gradual practice rather than just talking about high-level "non-attachment." He introduces the principle of "Simplifying Affairs," advising the reader to reduce worldly desires and focus only on the essentials to protect their physical and mental energy.</summary>

...people would still laugh at such a person <note>referring to the metaphor on the previous page about wasting a priceless gem to shoot a bird</note>. How much more so for those who abandon **the Way and Virtue** <note>original: *Daode*</note>, ignore their own **inner nature and life-force** <note>original: *Xingming* — the core of one's being</note>, and pursue non-essential things to the point of hacking away at their own lives? 

If you compare fame and rank to the Way and Virtue, then fame and rank are false and lowly, while the Way and Virtue are true and noble. One who can distinguish the noble from the lowly must know what to choose and what to discard. Do not let fame harm your body; do not trade the Way for rank. 

Thus **Zhuangzi** said: "One who pursues fame and loses their true self is no scholar." The **Scripture of Western Ascension** <note>An early Daoist text attributed to Laozi as he traveled west</note> says: "Embrace the Primal and guard the One, and you will reach the state of a Divine Immortal. But you are unable to guard it; you merely sit in your glorious office." 

If you do not choose carefully and instead try to handle every single matter that comes your way, your body will become exhausted and your wisdom will be clouded; your practice of the Way will surely be neglected. Those who can handle affairs with ease and remain unburdened by things are those who have already achieved realization. If you have not yet achieved it, but claim to be "unburdened," you are merely deceiving yourself.

---

->## True Contemplation<-

---

Contemplation is the foresight of the wise and the sentinel of the capable. It investigates the fortune and misfortune that come by chance and examines the luck or calamity within movement and stillness. By seeing the hidden springs of action before they manifest, one can adapt accordingly. Through deep prayer and the protection of one's stability, the work of "preserving life" is completed. From beginning to end, one’s conduct leaves no lingering burdens, and one's logic never deviates from this. Therefore, it is called **True Contemplation** <term>Zhenguan — a clear, meditative insight that sees things as they truly are</term>. 

Even a single meal or a single sleep is a source of gain or loss for the self. A single word or a single action can become the root of fortune or misfortune. Although one might skillfully manage the "branches" <note>the outcomes</note>, it is better to clumsily guard the "root" <note>the source of thought and action</note>. To observe the root is to know the branches. Furthermore, this is not done with a restless or competitive spirit. This is why one must withdraw the mind and simplify affairs, daily reducing **purposeful action** <note>original: *youwei* — the opposite of the Daoist ideal of effortless action, *wuwei*</note>. Only when the body is still and the heart is at leisure can one truly behold the Truth.

Thus the Scripture <note>the Daodejing, Chapter 1</note> says: "Always be without desire, so as to contemplate the mystery." However, the person practicing the Way still requires clothing and food. There are affairs that cannot be abandoned, and things that cannot be discarded. In such cases, one should receive them with an open heart and face them with clear eyes. Do not view them as obstacles or let the heart become irritable. If you see a task and immediately feel annoyed by it, the "sickness of the heart" has already stirred. How can that be called "settling the mind"?

Human affairs like food and clothing are like my **boat or vessel**. I wish to cross the sea, and for that, I rely on the boat. Once the crossing is finished, the logic is that I do not stay on the boat. But why would I want to discard the boat before I have even crossed? 

Clothing and food are **illusory** <term>Xuhuan — temporary and lacking inherent substance</term>; they are not truly worth struggling for. Yet, because we wish to transcend this illusion, we must seek food and clothing to sustain ourselves. Though you may be engaged in seeking these things, do not let the heart be consumed by thoughts of "gain and loss." Then, whether there are affairs to handle or not, the heart remains in a state of great peace. You seek things alongside others, but you do not share their greed. You obtain things alongside others, but you do not share their hoarding. By not being greedy, you have no worry. By not hoarding, you have no loss. In your tracks, you appear the same as common people; in your heart, you are always different from the world. This is the core of actual practice, and you must apply your strength to it. 

Even if you have simplified affairs as described before, some "sicknesses" of the mind are difficult to remove. In such cases, contemplate according to the law. If the "sickness of beauty" <note>sensual or sexual desire</note> is heavy, you should contemplate that **beauty** <term>Se — form, color, or physical attraction</term> originates entirely from **perception** <note>original: *Xiang* — the mental labeling of an object</note>. If the perception does not arise, there is ultimately no issue of beauty. If you realize that the perception of beauty is externally empty and the heart that desires beauty is internally false—if the false heart contemplates empty perceptions—then who is the master of this beauty? The scripture says: "Beauty is entirely a matter of perception. Since all perception is empty, how can 'beauty' exist?" Furthermore, consider the repulsion and attraction...

<summary>Sima Chengzhen introduces "True Contemplation," explaining that a practitioner must use foresight to simplify their life. He uses the famous "boat" metaphor to explain that while worldly needs like food are illusory, they must be maintained as tools for spiritual transcendence without becoming a source of greed.</summary>

<keywords>True Contemplation (Zhenguan), Sima Chengzhen, Boat Metaphor, Daodejing, Zhuangzi, Form and Perception (Se/Xiang), Sitting in Forgetfulness (Zuowang), Non-attachment</keywords>

--- Page 241 ---
<meta>This page continues Sima Chengzhen’s discourse on "True Contemplation." Having established the need for foresight and the "boat" metaphor for worldly needs, he now provides specific meditative remedies for common mental "sicknesses": lust, resentment, and the suffering caused by poverty and illness.</meta>

<page-num>179</page-num>

**Sensual beauty** <term>Meise — refers to physical attraction or lust</term> is more dangerous than **fox-spirits** <note>original: *Humei* — shape-shifting fox spirits in Chinese folklore known for bewitching people</note>. A fox-spirit bewitches a person, causing them to become weary and ill. Even if it leads to death, one does not necessarily fall into the "evil realms" of rebirth. Because one feels weary of the affliction, one can eternally distance themselves from such wicked lewdness. 

But seductive beauty bewitches a person by making them feel love and attachment. Even unto death, the lingering obsession runs deep. Because of these **wicked thoughts** <note>original: *Xienian*</note>, upon death one falls into hell and eternally loses the **human path** <note>the opportunity to be reborn as a human being</note>. The road to fortune is forever abandoned. 

Thus a Scripture says: "Those who in this life vow to be husband and wife will not be reborn together in the human path after death." Why is this? It is because of their wicked thoughts of attachment. 

Furthermore, contemplate beauty: if it were truly "beautiful," why would **fish dive deep** and **birds fly high** upon seeing it? <note>A reference to *Zhuangzi*, Chapter 2, arguing that human standards of beauty are subjective and not recognized by nature</note> Immortals regard it as filth and turbidity; wise men compare it to knives and axes. 

To sustain a single life, if one does not eat for seven days, one dies. Yet if one goes a hundred years without "beauty," one remains free from heavenly harm. Thus we know that beauty is not an essential requirement for the body or mind. It is merely a "foe and thief" to one's **inner nature and life-force**. Why then remain attached to it and bring about your own destruction?

If you see others doing evil and your heart gives rise to resentment or loathing, it is just like seeing someone commit suicide and then stretching out your own neck to catch their blade, thereby harming your own life. Others commit evil for themselves; they cannot pass the consequences to you. Why then do you take up their evil and make it your own "sickness"? 

Furthermore, if those who do evil are to be loathed, then those who do good must also be loathed. Why? Because both [attachments] equally **obstruct the Way**. 

If you suffer from **poverty**, you should examine it closely: who gave this poverty to me? Heaven and Earth are equal; they cover and support all without bias. My current suffering from poverty is not caused by Heaven and Earth. Parents give birth to children wishing them to be rich and noble. My current poverty and low status are not caused by my parents. Humans, ghosts, and gods are all busy saving themselves; how could they have the power to take poverty and give it to me? 

Searching back and forth, you find it comes from nowhere. Then you realize it is my own **Karma** <term>Ye — the results of one's own past actions</term>; it is the **Mandate of Heaven** <term>Tianming — the natural lot or destiny one is born with</term>. Karma is created by me; the Mandate is bestowed by Heaven. The existence of Karma and the Mandate is like a shadow following a form or an echo following a sound. One can neither escape them nor resent them. Only the wise person can adapt and find the good within them. By **rejoicing in Heaven and knowing the Mandate** <note>a classic Confucian and Daoist ideal of being content with one's lot</note>, one no longer feels that poverty is bitter. 

Thus **Zhuangzi** said: "When Karma arrives, it cannot be discarded, for it is one's own doing." When poverty and illness arrive, they cannot be simply pushed away. The Scripture says: "Heaven and Earth cannot change one's integrity; the forces of Yin and Yang cannot reverse one's Karma." Based on this, we know that one's true destiny is not dependent on external things. What is there to resent?

Consider a brave warrior who encounters bandits. He has no fear. He swings his sword before him, and the crowd of outlaws scatters. Once his merit is established, he enjoys honor and rewards for the rest of his life. 

Now, poverty and illness which distress me are the **bandits**. My **upright heart** is the **brave warrior**. Using wisdom to observe them is the **swinging of the sword**. The elimination of distress and burden is the **victory**. Remaining serene and eternally joyful is the **honor and reward**. 

Whenever suffering presses in, if my heart does not maintain this contemplation and instead produces worry and distress, it is like a person who encounters bandits but fails to establish merit—instead throwing away their armor, turning their back on the army, and suffering the crime of being a deserter. Leaving joy and heading toward suffering—how can such a person be pitied?

If you are **ill**, you should contemplate this illness: "Inside there is my body. If I had no body, the affliction would have nowhere to rest." Thus the Scripture <note>the *Daodejing*, Chapter 13</note> says: "The reason I have great trouble is that I have a body. When I have no body, what trouble do I have?" 

Next, contemplate the **mind**: it also has no **True Master** <term>Zhenzai — a permanent, independent ego or soul</term>. Seeking inside and out, there is no one capable of receiving the suffering. All that we calculate...

<summary>Sima Chengzhen provides specific meditative strategies to overcome lust, resentment of others' evil, and the hardships of poverty and illness. He argues that suffering arises from attachment and "wicked thoughts," rather than external circumstances, and encourages a "warrior-like" application of wisdom to achieve serenity.</summary>

<keywords>Lust (Meise), Fox-spirits (Humei), Resentment, Karma (Ye), Mandate of Heaven (Tianming), Zhuangzi, Daodejing, Body and Mind, Poverty and Illness, Non-attachment</keywords>

--- Page 242 ---
<meta>This page concludes the section on mental remedies, specifically addressing the fear of death and the nature of delusion, before transitioning into "Great Settling" (Taiding), the final stage of meditative stillness described by Sima Chengzhen.</meta>

<page-num>180</page-num>

Thoughts arise from the **deluded mind** <note>original: *Wangxin* — the distracted, grasping mind as opposed to the "True Mind"</note>. If one makes the **body like withered wood and the mind like cold ashes** <note>A classic Daoist metaphor from the *Zhuangzi* describing a state of profound meditative stillness where external stimuli no longer provoke a reaction</note>, then the "myriad illnesses" of the mind will all vanish.

If you are one who fears death, you should contemplate that my body is merely the **dwelling of the spirit**. Now that the body is old or ill and my strength is fading, it is like a house that is decaying and broken, no longer fit to live in. It is only natural to leave it and seek a peaceful residence elsewhere. The death of the body and the departure of the spirit are exactly like this. 

If one clings to life and loathes death, resisting the natural course of **transformation** <note>original: *Bianhua* — the Daoist concept that life and death are simply different phases of a single process</note>, then the **spirit-consciousness** <term>Shenshi — the individual’s mental and spiritual awareness</term> becomes confused and disordered. One then loses their **correct karma** <note>original: *Zhengye* — here referring to the positive spiritual momentum built through practice</note>. At the moment of taking on a new life and receiving vital energy, if the spirit is confused, it will not be attracted to what is pure and elegant, but will instead encounter much that is turbid and disgraceful. The reason some are born into the lowest states of ignorance and greed is rooted in this confusion at death. 

Therefore, there are two reasons why one should not be joyful about birth nor fearful of death:
1. Because the principles of life and death are essentially equal.
2. To ensure the success of one's "karmic work" in the next life.

If you harbor greed or love for the "myriad environments" of the world, every attachment becomes a sickness. If even a single limb is diseased, the entire body is uncomfortable; how much more so if the single mind is afflicted by "ten thousand sicknesses"? If the mind is so burdened, how could one ever hope to attain **long life**?

All feelings of love or loathing are born of delusion. If these accumulated delusions are not removed, how can one see the Way? Therefore, the mind must discard all desires and dwell in "non-existence." One must eliminate worldly emotions and establish "Correct Faith." Only then, when you look back at your old foolish attachments, will you naturally feel a sense of weary detachment. 

If you observe a situation while your heart is still entangled with it, you will never realize its faults as long as you live. Only by observing a situation with a heart that has already detached from it can you clearly see the truth of the matter. 

This is like a sober person who can recognize the "evil" of a drunkard; if he were drunk himself, he would not perceive the other’s faults. Thus the Scripture says: "I originally abandoned the mundane and grew weary of the world of men." It also says: "The sounds and colors of the ears and eyes are a lingering offense to me; the fragrances and flavors enjoyed by the nose and mouth are my enemies." <note>These are attributed sayings of Laozi</note>. If **Lord Lao** <term>Laojun — the deified Laozi</term>, who abandoned the world, still viewed sensory pleasures as "enemies," how can those who are currently drowning in their desires ever know that the **dried fish market** <note>An allusion to the saying that if you stay in a dried fish market long enough, you cease to smell the stench—meaning one becomes desensitized to vice</note> is stinking?

## Great Settling <term>Taiding — a state of profound, unshakable meditative absorption</term>

"Settling" is the ultimate destination of leaving the mundane, the initial foundation for attaining the Way, the successful result of practicing stillness, and the final goal of maintaining peace. 

The form becomes like withered wood; the mind becomes like cold ashes. There is no stimulus and no seeking; it is the pinnacle of silent serenity. When one has "no mind" directed toward settling, yet there is nothing that is *not* settled—this is called **Great Settling**. 

**Zhuangzi** said: "For those who have Great Settling in their inner precinct, a **Heavenly Light** issues forth." <note>From *Zhuangzi*, Chapter 23</note>. The "precinct" is the mind. The "Heavenly Light" is **Wisdom** <term>Hui — spiritual insight or prajna</term>. The mind is the vessel of the Way. When the "precinct" of the mind is empty and still to the ultimate degree, the Way dwells there and Wisdom is born. This Wisdom issues from one's original nature; it is not something newly acquired. Thus it is called "Heavenly Light." 

It is only because of greed, attachment, and turbid disorder that we have become dim and confused. By "washing the mind with snow" <note>An idiom for internal purification</note> and becoming gentle and upright, we return to the pure, still, and original Truth. The spirit-consciousness gradually brightens of its own accord. It is not that a "different" kind of wisdom is born at this time. 

Once Wisdom has been born, treasure it and keep it within your heart. Do not use "much knowledge" to harm your state of Settling. The difficulty is not in giving birth to Wisdom, but in **having Wisdom and yet not using it**. Since ancient times, many have been able to "forget the body" <note>transcend physical needs</note>, but few have been able to "forget fame." To have Wisdom and not use it for worldly gain is to "forget fame." There are few in the world who can reach this, which is why it is considered difficult. 

He who is noble can remain humble; he who is rich can remain modest. Because they have no "mundane faults," they can long maintain their wealth and status. To be settled and remain unmoved, to have Wisdom and not use it, to have Virtue and not rely upon it—these are "faultless" states in the Way. Thus one can deeply realize the **Eternal**.

<summary>Sima Chengzhen explains that fearing death and clinging to life are delusions that lead to poor rebirth. He defines "Great Settling" (Taiding) as a state of ultimate stillness where innate "Heavenly Light" (Wisdom) emerges, emphasizing that the greatest spiritual challenge is possessing this wisdom without using it for worldly recognition.</summary>

<keywords>Great Settling (Taiding), Heavenly Light (Tianguang), Wisdom (Hui), Spirit-consciousness (Shenshi), Death and Transformation, Lord Lao (Laojun), Zhuangzi, Non-attachment, Internal Purification</keywords>

--- Page 243 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion on "Great Settling" (Taiding), emphasizing the relationship between wisdom and tranquility, before moving into the final stage of the manual: "Attaining the Way" (Dedao).</meta>

<page-num>181</page-num>

Regarding the Way, **Zhuangzi** said: "Knowing the Way is easy; not speaking of it is difficult. To know and not speak is the way of Heaven; to know and speak of it is the way of Men." The ancients followed the Heavenly and not the Human. To have **Wisdom** <term>Hui — spiritual insight</term> allows one to know the Way, but this is not yet the same as **Attaining the Way** <note>original: *Dedao* — the ultimate realization and embodiment of the Dao</note>. 

People understand the benefits of gaining Wisdom, but they do not yet understand the true profit of Attaining the Way. They use Wisdom to clarify ultimate principles or use eloquence to influence others' emotions. They allow their hearts to follow worldly affairs, and their reactions grow in complexity. They might claim, "I am in the midst of action, yet my mind is always silent," but how can they know what true silence is? True silence is a stillness that waits for things to be balanced. Both these actions and these words are far from "Great Settling." Though such a person’s intelligence may surpass the crowd, they are not close to the Way. This is like a hunter chasing a deer who returns home merely having escaped a trap; what he has gained is tiny, for his perspective was narrow.

Therefore, **Zhuangzi** said: "The ancient cultivators of the Way used tranquility to nourish wisdom. Once wisdom was born, they did not use it for action." This is called "using wisdom to nourish tranquility." When wisdom and tranquility nourish each other, harmony and order emerge from one's original nature. Tranquility and wisdom are **Settling and Insight** <term>Ding-Hui — the dual practice of meditative stillness and spiritual clarity</term>. Harmony and order are **Virtue and the Way**. By having wisdom but not using it, one secures their tranquility. If this is nourished for a long time, the Way and Virtue will naturally be perfected.

However, this state of Settling can be achieved through different means. Some achieve it by observing the benefit of practice and the harm of distraction; some by fearing misfortune and thus quieting the heart; and some through a process of "letting go" and internal cleansing until the habit of stillness becomes mature. All these paths return to a Settling that feels entirely natural. In such a state, a sudden **clap of thunder might shatter a mountain**, yet the practitioner is not startled; **white blades of unsheathed swords** might cross before them, yet they feel no fear. They view fame and profit as a fleeting glimpse through a crack in a wall, and see life and death as the bursting of a sore. Thus it is said: when the will is undivided, the spirit is condensed.

The emptiness and mystery of the mind are beyond comprehension! As a "thing," the mind’s essence is not "being," yet its functions are not "non-being." It travels without racing and arrives without being summoned. When it is angry, an arrow can pierce a stone; when it harbors resentment, frost can fall in the height of summer. If one indulges in evil, the **Nine Hells** <term>Jiuyou — the dark, subterranean realms of suffering</term> are not far off; if one accumulates goodness, the **Three Purities** <term>Sanqing — the highest celestial realms of the Daoist heavens</term> are close at hand. The mind comes and goes in a flash; neither "movement" nor "stillness" can fully name it. Sometimes it affirms, sometimes it denies; neither the divining stalks nor the tortoise shell can predict it. In terms of taming and guiding it, could the difficulty of a deer or a horse even compare?

**Lord Lao** <term>Laojun — the deified Laozi</term>, moving with eternal goodness to save humanity, ascended the **Spirit Terrace** <note>original: *Lingtai* — a metaphor for the mind, but also a celestial location</note> to expound these mysteries. He looked past the "cause and effect" of the **Two Vehicles** <term>Er-cheng — a Buddhist term for those seeking personal liberation, here used to contrast with the broader Daoist path</term> to broaden the natural state of all existence. He taught that one should diminish worldly attachments day by day, eventually "losing" the habit of study until one reaches a state of non-action. He used metaphors like "stringing a bow" or "carving out doors and windows." His methods involve "blunting the sharp edges" and "untying the tangles" of the mind.

There is a path to this cultivation, and through practice, it becomes one's nature. One must **cast off cleverness and discard the body** <note>original: *Chucong duoti* — a famous phrase from the *Zhuangzi* describing the state of "Sitting in Forgetfulness"</note>, sitting in "forgetfulness" like a slumped, lifeless branch. Remaining unmoved in silence, the slightest spark of insight enters one's awareness. For those who wander down diverging paths, the ultimate meaning is never found. For those who follow this Way, the observation of the Mystery can be expected. With little effort, the merit is great. It is essential; it is wondrous!

## Attaining the Way

The Way is a thing of divine wonder. It is spiritual and has its own nature; it is empty and has no form. You cannot see it coming or follow it as it leaves; its influence cannot be sought. One does not know *why* it is as it is, yet it is so. It permeates all life without being exhausted; this is called the Way. The Great Sages attained it, and from ancient times this marvelous method has been passed down to the present. If one follows the names to investigate the principles, it is entirely real. A seeker of the highest caliber has pure faith; they restrain themselves and practice diligently. By emptying the mind and becoming like the **Spirit of the Valley** <note>A reference to the *Tao Te Ching*, symbolizing an infinite, receptive, and creative void</note>, the Way alone will gather there. 

<summary>Sima Chengzhen explains the synergy between tranquility and wisdom, teaching that true "Settling" makes the practitioner unshakable by external events. He describes the mind's immense power to affect reality and introduces the final stage of "Attaining the Way" through the practice of "Sitting in Forgetfulness."</summary>

<keywords>Zhuangzi, Wisdom (Hui), Settling and Insight (Ding-Hui), Sitting in Forgetfulness (Zuowang), Lord Lao, Three Purities, Spirit Terrace, Attaining the Way (Dedao)</keywords>

--- Page 244 ---
<meta>This page concludes the final stage of "Attaining the Way" (Dedao), describing the total transformation of both the mind and the physical body into a divine state, and provides a closing summary of the path's superiority over other traditions.</meta>

<page-num>182</page-num>

With supreme power, one transforms both the physical form and the spirit. When the form follows the flow of the Way and becomes one with the spirit, this union of form and spirit identifies one as a **Divine Person** <term>Shenren — a perfected being who has transcended mortal limitations</term>. The nature of the spirit is empty and harmonious; its essence neither changes nor perishes. When the physical form becomes like the spirit, there is no more life and death. When hidden, the form is as subtle as the spirit; when manifest, the spirit is as visible as the form. Therefore, such a person can walk through water or fire without harm and stand before the sun or moon without casting a shadow. Existence and disappearance are within their own power; they move in and out of reality without obstruction.

Even the physical body, though made of murky matter, becomes supremely empty and wondrous through this process. How much more so for the spiritual intelligence, which grows ever deeper and more far-reaching? Thus, the **Scripture of Numinous Treasure** <note>original: *Lingbao Jing* — a foundational collection of Daoist texts</note> says: "When the body and spirit are one, it is the True Body." The **Scripture of Western Ascension** <note>original: *Xisheng Jing* — a text focusing on the refinement of the spirit and the transition to immortality</note> also says: "Because form and spirit are united, one can endure forever."

However, the path of the "empty mind" has degrees of depth. The deep path transforms the physical form as well; the shallow path reaches only the mind. Those who transform the form are Divine Persons. Those who only reach the mind obtain **Wisdom-Awareness** <gloss>spiritual insight</gloss>, but nothing more. Their bodies cannot avoid decay. Why? Because wisdom is the *use* of the mind; overusing it exhausts the *essence*. When a practitioner first gains a small amount of wisdom, they often feel delighted and become talkative. Their spiritual energy leaks away, failing to nourish the body, leading to an early death. Thus, the Way is difficult to perfect.

The scriptures call this **Deliverance from the Corpse** <term>Shijie — a "lower" form of immortality where the practitioner appears to die but the spirit departs the body to a celestial realm</term>. Therefore, the Great Person conceals their light and hides their brilliance to ensure total perfection. By condensing the spirit and treasuring the breath, and learning the Way with a "no-mind" state, the spirit merges with the Way. This is called **Attaining the Way**.

Thus the scripture says: "He who is one with the Way, the Way also attains him." It also says: "Why did the ancients value this Way? Did they not say, 'Seek and you shall find; have sins and you shall be forgiven'?" If a mountain has jade and precious herbs, the trees upon it do not wither. If a person harbors the Way, their physical body becomes eternally firm. Through long nourishment, the material quality changes to match the spirit. By refining the spirit into the subtle mystery, one merges into oneness with the Way.

One can then scatter the single self into ten thousand phenomena or blend ten thousand phenomena into a single self. Wisdom shines boundlessly; the form transcends all limits. One utilizes both emptiness and form, aligning with the forces of creation. Truth responds without a fixed direction; trust lies only in the Way and Virtue. The *Scripture of Western Ascension* says: "Having the same mind as Heaven, one is without knowledge; having the same body as the Way, one is without form." Only then is the Great Way flourishing. To say it "flourishes" means one has realized the ultimate limit.

It also says: "The spirit does not leave the body, enduring as long as the Way." If the body is one with the Way, it exists eternally. If the mind is one with the Way, it penetrates all principles. The ears become the "Ears of the Way," hearing every sound. The eyes become the "Eyes of the Way," seeing every color. The six senses reach total clarity because of this.

Regarding the establishment of these teachings, their benefits are deep and wide. Following the texts to investigate their principles, I will attempt to summarize: The secrets of **Supreme Purity** <term>Shangqing — a Daoist tradition emphasizing visualization and internal refinement</term> focus on refined resonance, using "divine elixirs" to refine the physical body until worldly knowledge is forgotten. The school of **The Way and Virtue** <note>The tradition of Laozi</note> opens its doors with diligent faith, harboring an empty mind to wash away burdens until the body casts no shadow. Though the "skilful means" differ, they both meet at the source of the Way.

The mind and body support each other, a relationship like the wheels and the carriage. Whether starting from the outside or the inside, different tracks return to the same destination. This encompasses all profound mysteries, where both discussion and silence fail to reach the truth. The wonder of these two paths is something that **Confucius or the Buddha** <note>original: *Kong-Shi* — referring to the founders of Confucianism and Buddhism</note> cannot approach. As for those who remain ignorant of this, that is simply the way of the common world.

(The End)

<summary>This final section describes the "Divine Person" who has achieved the union of form and spirit, rendering the body immortal and the mind omniscient. Sima Chengzhen concludes by asserting that the Daoist path of internal refinement surpasses the teachings of both Buddhism and Confucianism.</summary>

<meta>This page begins a new section containing a commentary by the famous Song Dynasty scholar Su Shi on the "Zhuangzi," a foundational Daoist text. It moves from the general theory of "Attaining the Way" discussed on the previous page to a specific historical-mythological dialogue between the Yellow Emperor and the immortal Guangchengzi.</meta>

# Explanation of Guangchengzi

### Compiled by Su Shi of the Song Dynasty

Su Shi, whose courtesy name was **Zizhan** <note>A traditional secondary name given at adulthood</note>, was a native of Meishan. In the second year of the **Jiayou** era <note>1057 CE</note>, he passed the second level of the imperial examinations. After responding to the palace policy exams, he was ranked in the third grade. He served in various high offices, including Drafter in the Secretariat, Scholar of the Hanlin Academy, and Minister of Rites. At the beginning of the **Shaosheng** era <note>1094 CE</note>, he was exiled to Huizhou and later moved to Changhua. He passed away in Changzhou during the first year of the **Jianzhong Jingguo** era <note>1101 CE</note>. He was posthumously granted the title of Grand Preceptor and the posthumous name **Wenzhong** <term>Wenzhong — "Cultured and Loyal," a high honorific for scholars</term>. His works include the *Collected Works of Dongpo*, the *He Tao Collection*, and the *Response to Imperial Edicts*.

---

**The Yellow Emperor had been established as the Son of Heaven for nineteen years, and his orders were carried out throughout the world. Hearing that Guangchengzi was residing atop Mount Kongtong, he went to visit him. The Emperor said: "I have heard, sir, that you have attained the Great Way. I dare to ask: what is the essence of the Great Way? I wish to take the essence of Heaven and Earth to assist the growth of the five grains and to nourish the people. I also wish to direct the Yin and Yang to benefit all living creatures. How should I go about this?"**
<gloss>The Way certainly possesses these powers. However, if one attempts to perform these actions through "doing" or intentionality, it becomes dangerous.</gloss>

**Guangchengzi replied: "What you seek to ask about is the mere substance of things; what you seek to direct is but the residue of things."**
<gloss>Those who possess the Way do not ask questions. Those who ask about the Way have not yet attained it. In the state of attaining the Way, there is neither "thing" nor "self." One who has not yet attained it will naturally prioritize the "self" and treat "things" as secondary. If one truly attains the Way, the self is naturally sufficient and things settle themselves—why would one need to prioritize them? Now, you set aside your "self" to ask about "things"; Guangchengzi dislikes the lack of genuine intent in this. Thus, he says: "What you ask about is the substance of things, and what you want to direct is the residue." This suggests that the Emperor’s true desire is for his own long life, while he outwardly claims to want to nourish the people and benefit living creatures. Is not eternal life the true "treasure" of things? And are not "nourishing the people" and "benefiting creatures" merely the "residue" <note>original: *can* — remnants or byproducts</note> of the Way?</gloss>

**"Since you have governed the world, the clouds..."**

<summary>This page introduces Su Shi’s commentary on the Zhuangzi, beginning with a biographical sketch of Su Shi and the opening of the dialogue where the Yellow Emperor asks the immortal Guangchengzi for practical administrative and agricultural secrets of the Dao.</summary>

<keywords>Su Shi (Su Dongpo), Yellow Emperor (Huangdi), Guangchengzi, Mount Kongtong, Great Dao (Zhi Dao), Yin and Yang, Governance, Substance and Residue</keywords>

--- Page 246 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Yellow Emperor and the immortal Guangchengzi from page 183. After Guangchengzi rebuked the Emperor for his superficial and "doing"-based approach to governance and nature, the Emperor undergoes a period of ascetic retreat to change his internal state.</meta>

<page-num>184</page-num>

...the clouds rain before they have even clustered; the plants and trees shed their leaves before they have turned yellow; and the light of the sun and moon increasingly fades into wasteland.
<gloss>Heaven produces timely rain, and the mountains and rivers release clouds. When clouds move and rain falls, the mountains and rivers do not treat this as a display of power or status, because the rain occurs only when it is inevitable; it is not "intended" by them. In spring and summer things grow, and in autumn and winter they turn yellow and fall, yet the plants and trees do not treat this as a sickness, because the falling occurs only when it is inevitable; it is not "intended" by them. Now, in your time, the clouds rain without waiting to cluster, and the plants fall without waiting to turn yellow. Even the essence of Heaven and Earth cannot supply the needs of such a "calculating mind" <note>The "calculating mind" refers to the Emperor's desire to intentionally control and "benefit" nature, which actually exhausts it</note>. Therefore, the signs of ruin and desolation appear first in the sun and moon. If one observes this within a single human body, the ears and eyes will be the first parts to fall ill.</gloss>

And you, a flatterer with a heart that is **shallow and narrow** <note>original: *jianjian* — describes a petty, fluttering, or superficial state of mind</note>, how could you be fit to speak of the Ultimate Way?
<gloss>The difference between a **True Person** <term>Zhenren — an idealized Daoist sage who lives in perfect harmony with the Way</term> and a flatterer is like the difference between grain and weeds. If what you plant is grain, then even with poor soil and a lazy farmer, weeds will not grow. But if what you plant are weeds, then even with beautiful fields and diligent plowing, grain will not grow. Now, you wish to learn the Way, but the "seeds" you bring—your questions—are already full of laziness, flattery, and falsehood. From where could the Way possibly grow?</gloss>

The Yellow Emperor retreated. He gave up his empire, built a special hut, laid out a mat of white reeds, and lived in solitude for three months. Then, he went back to visit the immortal again. Guangchengzi was lying down with his head to the south. The Yellow Emperor approached from the "downwind" side <note>A gesture of extreme humility, suggesting the Emperor did not want his own presence or "scent" to disturb the sage</note>, moving forward on his knees. He bowed twice, touching his head to the ground, and asked: "I have heard, sir, that you have reached the Ultimate Way. I dare to ask: how does one govern the self so that it may endure long?"
<gloss>By abandoning the world and living in solitude, the Emperor’s former mindset of "prioritizing external things over the internal self" had no further place to manifest. This is why his question changed to this new focus on self-cultivation.</gloss>

Guangchengzi rose up abruptly and said: "A good question indeed! Come, I shall tell you of the Ultimate Way."
<gloss>Did Guangchengzi only begin to speak of the Way to the Yellow Emperor at this specific moment? I say: No. For a man like the Yellow Emperor, the earlier rebuke—that he was "unfit to speak of the Way"—was itself a complete and profound teaching. It was because of that rebuke that he lived in solitude for three months and then returned; he had been shaken into a transformation. How could his reception of the Way only be starting now? It began with the rebuke.</gloss>

"The essence of the Ultimate Way is **deep and obscure**; the limit of the Ultimate Way is **dark and silent**."
<gloss>"Deep and obscure" describes a state like climbing to a great height to gaze into the distance, perceiving the tiniest tip of a hair a thousand miles away; or like standing over a deep abyss and looking down into the gloom to observe treasures hidden ten thousand fathoms deep. "Dark and silent" describes a state like withered wood or cold ashes, where there is no longer a path for things to grow or catch fire <note>This refers to the "fasting of the heart," where one becomes still and unresponsive to external provocations</note>. One might ask: "Does the Way stop at this stillness?" I say: This is the nature of the deep, obscure, dark, and silent...</gloss>

<summary>In this passage, Guangchengzi continues his critique of the Yellow Emperor's meddling nature, leading the Emperor to abandon his throne for three months of meditation. Upon his humble return, Guangchengzi begins to reveal the nature of the Ultimate Way as a state of profound, silent stillness.</summary>

<keywords>Zhuangzi, Zai You (Letting Be), Yellow Emperor, Guangchengzi, Ultimate Way (Zhi Dao), Self-Cultivation, Meditation, True Person (Zhenren), Deep and Obscure, Dark and Silent</keywords>

--- Page 247 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue from page 184. The immortal Guangchengzi is now delivering the core instructions of the "Ultimate Way" to the Yellow Emperor, who has returned from a three-month ascetic retreat. Having rebuked the Emperor's earlier meddling, the sage now describes a path of radical internal stillness and the unification of spirit and form.</meta>

<page-num>185</page-num>

...this is the state and the method of attaining the Way. If one merely "points" at the Way as if it were an object, could the state of being **deep, obscure, dark, and silent** truly be called the Way? If a person can abandon the world and live in solitude, reaching that state of deep obscurity and dark silence to enter the abyss of the ultimate essence, there is no one who will not obtain the Way. The student of the Way fears only distraction and duality. Therefore, the "deep, obscure, dark, and silent" are the means by which one attains **Oneness**.

### Be confused and silent! See nothing, hear nothing. Embrace the spirit with stillness, and the form will correct itself. You must be still, you must be pure. Do not labor your form,
<gloss>These are the means by which one preserves the **Authentic Self** <term>Zhen — the original, uncorrupted nature of a human being before it is shaped by social conventions</term>.</gloss>

## Do not agitate your essence, for only then can you live long. When the eyes see nothing, the ears hear nothing, and the mind knows nothing, your spirit will guard the form, and the form will endure. Be cautious of what is within you; close off what is outside you. Much knowledge is ruin.

<gloss>From this point upward, these are all "Words of Truth." Guangchengzi is "pulling the ear" <note>An idiom for giving direct, urgent instruction</note> to teach the Emperor. "No seeing and no hearing, embracing the spirit with stillness" is the practice of **Non-Action** <term>Wuwei — acting in alignment with the natural flow without forced effort</term>. "The mind knowing nothing" is the state of **No-Thought**. "Do not labor your form, do not agitate your essence" is the state of **No-Desire**. When these three—Non-Action, No-Thought, and No-Desire—are present, the form and the spirit become one. When form and spirit are one, there is long life. If the interior is not guarded and the exterior is not closed, the form and spirit will separate. Some might ask: "Is Guangchengzi not being overly repetitive and fussy about the Way?" I say: To ensure grain does not become weeds depends on a single seed at the time of planting. Where is the fussiness in that? However, the effort of diligent plowing and weeding can never be abandoned.</gloss>

## I will lead you to the heights of the Great Brilliance, to the very source of the Supreme Yang. I will lead you through the gates of the Deep Obscurity, to the very source of the Supreme Yin.

<gloss>Deep obscurity and dark silence are the roots of long life. Once this root is established, there must be a "congealing" or solidifying of the internal state. The two sources <note>Supreme Yang and Supreme Yin</note> act like the functions of the sun, moon, water, and fire; they are the tools for internal cultivation and transformation.</gloss>

## Heaven and Earth have their offices; Yin and Yang have their storehouses.

<gloss>This refers to the strengthening of the **Vital Breath** <term>Qi — the life force or energy that flows through all things</term> and the solidifying of the physical being. Cultivation must have a method. If one does not reach the "extreme" or the source, transformation will not occur. Guangchengzi uses silence to establish the root and uses the absence of thought, action, and desire to remove what harms long life. If a person uses the Supreme Yin and Supreme Yang to solidify themselves, my work here is done. Heaven and Earth have their own roles and will govern for me; Yin and Yang have their own stores and will accumulate for me. The "doing" is within me, but the "completion" belongs to the natural order.</gloss>

## Carefully guard your body, and all things will naturally flourish.

<gloss>This means that long life is a certainty. Is there any living thing that starts young and does not grow strong if properly nurtured?</gloss>

## I guard the Oneness, and thus I dwell in harmony. Therefore...

<summary>Guangchengzi provides the Yellow Emperor with practical instructions for longevity and spiritual alignment, emphasizing "Non-Action," the closing of the senses, and the unification of form and spirit through the balance of Yin and Yang.</summary>

<keywords>Zhuangzi, Yellow Emperor, Guangchengzi, Oneness, Non-Action (Wuwei), Yin and Yang, Vital Breath (Qi), Authentic Self (Zhen), Longevity, Stillness</keywords>

--- Page 248 ---
<meta>This page concludes the dialogue between the immortal Guangchengzi and the Yellow Emperor. Having provided the theoretical foundation for the "Ultimate Way" on page 185, the sage now offers himself as living proof of these teachings, revealing his age and his impending departure into the infinite. The page ends with a scholarly postscript by the Ming dynasty bibliophile Fan Qin.</meta>

<page-num>186</page-num>

## I have cultivated my person for one thousand two hundred years, and yet my physical form has never withered.

The Yellow Emperor bowed twice, his forehead touching the ground, and said: "Guangchengzi is truly the definition of greatness!"

Guangchengzi said: "Come! I will tell you more. That Way is infinite, yet men all think it has an end; that thing is unfathomable, yet men all think it has a limit.
<gloss>All things fundamentally have no end or limit. Their 'division' is their 'completion'; their 'completion' is their 'destruction.' <note>This refers to the cyclical nature of Taoist alchemy where the breaking down of one thing is the birth of another.</note> Matter itself never truly dies. Therefore, long life is the natural state of all things; it is not a power that I alone possess. Because I can guard the **Oneness** and dwell in harmony, I simply do not perceive the distinctions between division, completion, and destruction.</gloss>

## Those who set their will upon my Way: above, they become Sovereigns; below, they become Kings.
<gloss>The 'Sovereign' represents the refined essence of power, while the 'King' represents its coarser, earthly application.</gloss>

## Those who lose my Way: above, they see only the light; below, they become the dust.
<gloss>The living belong to the realm of brightness, and the dead to the realm of obscurity. Those in the dark do not know the light, and those in the light do not know the dark.</gloss>

## Now, the hundred varieties of flourishing life all spring from the earth and return to the earth. Therefore, I shall leave you to enter the gate of the Infinite and roam the boundless wilds.
<gloss>This suggests that the sage is about to manifest his transformation and depart from the world, releasing his physical form to return to the earth.</gloss>

## I shall blend my light with the sun and moon; I shall share the permanence of Heaven and Earth. When they merge with me, I am indistinguishable! When they move away from me, I am obscured! While all men must die, I alone shall endure."

<gloss>Nanrong Zhu <note>A character from another chapter of the *Zhuangzi*</note> once brought three men to see Laozi. Laozi scolded him, and he was so startled that he lost his sense of self. To bring others along on the path is a mistake, but to lose both 'self' and 'other' entirely is also a mistake. Among those who study the Way, those who can let the 'social person' die so that the 'True Self' alone remains are few indeed. Everything that can be seen, spoken of, grasped, or discarded belongs to the 'social person'—it is not the 'Me.' That which cannot be seen, spoken of, grasped, or discarded is the **Authentic Self** <term>Zhenwo — the eternal core of being that exists beyond social roles</term>. To be near this is wisdom; to be far from it is folly. To obtain this is to obtain the Way. This is what is meant by 'While all men die, I alone remain.' Ancient and modern languages differ; I do not know the exact ancient meaning of the word 'merged' <note>original: 緡 (min)</note>, but judging by the context, it likely means something like 'clarity' or 'becoming one with the light.'</gloss>

***

According to the *Classic of Mountains*, Guangchengzi governed the two hexagrams of *Tun* <note>Sprouting/Difficulty at the Beginning</note> and *Meng* <note>Youthful Ignorance</note> from the *Book of Changes*, and he regulated the movements of the sun and moon. He was a **True Human** <term>Zhenren — a perfected Taoist master who has transcended mortal limitations</term> of antiquity and the teacher of the Yellow Emperor. 
Postscript by Fan Qin.

The text concludes with a historical note identifying the sage as a master of the I Ching.</summary>

# Original Preface to the Record of Seeking Correction <note>The "Record of Seeking Correction" (*Jiuzheng Lu*) is a collection associated with Yuan Huang (1533–1606), a Ming dynasty figure famous for his work *Liao-fan’s Four Lessons*. The title refers to the practice of seeking the "correct" path through self-reflection and the guidance of others.</note>

Mr. Yuan Wuruo <note>Wuruo was the courtesy name of Yuan Huang, also known as Yuan Liao-fan.</note> of Daming <note>A prefecture in modern-day Hebei Province known for producing elite scholars.</note> is a heroic gentleman of great renown. In the third month of this spring, he came to travel through the district of Tangyi <note>An area in modern Jiangsu Province.</note>. He took up residence at the **Cundi Silent Retreat** <note>A Buddhist hermitage dedicated to the bodhisattva Cundi.</note>.

My friend, Mr. Li Shujing, became acquainted with him. Their friendship gradually grew deep. One day, Li said to me: "There is a Mr. Yuan, a fine scholar from the North. Why don't you go to meet him?"

I then inquired about his character. Shujing said: "The man is humble and harmonious, yet frank and resolute. Moreover, he constantly makes it his goal **not to let his own heart-mind be obscured**." <note>This refers to the practice of "lucidity" or "mindfulness," ensuring that one's innate moral conscience is not clouded by selfish desires.</note>

I replied enthusiastically: "This is a man of true learning!" <note>Literally "a man within the study," meaning one who truly embodies the philosophical life rather than just reading books.</note> Thereupon, I went with Shujing to meet him.

Furthermore, I used my own lifelong humble views to **seek his correction** <note>The phrase "seek correction" (*jiuzheng*) gives the book its title; it is a polite way of asking a master to point out one's faults.</note>. He graciously granted me his time. Every evening, I went to his residence to converse with him.

Mr. Yuan said: "When a great man lives in this world for a single lifetime, he must possess this **Great Learning** <term>Daxuewen — a reference to the Confucian ideal of self-cultivation and world-ordering found in the 'Classic of Great Learning'</term>. It is a pity that I am currently preoccupied with trivial matters and cannot fully ask for your guidance. What is to be done?"

I therefore, in return... <note>The text breaks off here at the end of the page.</note>

I, Lu, requested his instruction. Master Yuan was very pleased and said, "Wait until I return and find a moment's peace; I will then attend to these matters."

For more than ten days since then, I returned to the mountains for the **Dragon Boat Festival** <note>The "Wujie" or Double Fifth festival, a major holiday for family gatherings and ritual.</note>. Meanwhile, Master Yuan was also occupied with the burdens of his travels and had no spare time. Consequently, we were kept apart.

Just as I was feeling a deep longing to see him again, Master Yuan suddenly came to bid me farewell, as he was to return to his hometown the following day. I paced about for a long time, filled with lingering thoughts. I felt ashamed that I had nothing to give him as a parting gift. Furthermore, I regretted that our shared spiritual goals had not been fully expressed, and our plans for **cultivating nature and life** <term>Xingming — a fundamental concept in Chinese philosophy referring to the dual cultivation of one's inner spiritual essence (nature) and outward physical vitality or destiny (life)</term> had not been fully clarified.

Fearing that I might fail the spirit of being "of one mind across a thousand miles," I have ventured to take my usual views and draft them here. I do so in order to **seek correction** from one who possesses the Way.

<page-num>一八九</page-num>

# Foreword

I and the Master were both students of the venerable Master Qianju Jian. At first, our interactions were limited to literature and the arts, and I did not yet recognize the Master’s **true character** <note>Literally "true face," referring to his spiritual depth and realization.</note>. The Master did not cast me aside, but urged me toward moral discipline. At first, I could not understand him. The Master would lecture and discuss these matters so intensely that he forgot to sleep or eat. Later, I gained some realization and privately tested his teachings against the recorded sayings of the ancient sages. They did not differ by even a hair’s breadth. Therefore, I became even more delighted to hear his words. The Master once said:

> "The origin of human life is simply this and nothing more. **Lianxi** <note>The courtesy name of Zhou Dunyi (1017–1073), a pioneering Neo-Confucian philosopher.</note> told people to seek the **joy of Confucius and Yan Hui** <note>A classic Confucian ideal of finding spiritual happiness and contentment regardless of material circumstances.</note>; this is exactly what he meant."

After that, the number of those following him grew daily. The Master laid bare the very core of his teachings, providing guidance day and night on the methods of self-cultivation and governing others, the wonders of **substance and function, stillness and response** <term>Ti-yong and Ji-gan — philosophical pairs describing the fundamental nature of reality (substance/stillness) versus its active manifestation and interaction with the world (function/response).</term>, and the principles of the eternal and infinite. He grandly proclaimed these hidden depths. Together with like-minded friends, through flowery mornings and moonlit evenings, in wind, rain, darkness, or light, we spent several decades without interruption. I felt privately fortunate that this "secret learning" <note>Knowledge not widely transmitted or easily understood by the public.</note> was able to be preserved without falling into ruin.

Alas, many of our friends scattered in all directions. After several years, the Master finally left our circle and passed away. Among his writings are *The Source and Course of Sage Learning*, *Instruction for Youths*, *Observations of the Vast Universe*, *Record of Sayings*, and the eight-volume *Inquiries into Doubts*. These works clarify the profound mysteries of the sages and worthies; they are truly a rarity since the time of the **Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min** <note>Shorthand for the four great schools of Song Dynasty Neo-Confucianism, named after the home regions of their founders: Zhou Dunyi, the Cheng brothers, Zhang Zai, and Zhu Xi.</note> masters.

When my friend Mr. Huang Zuochen saw these works, he was delighted and wished to spread them widely. But as the volumes were so numerous, they could not all be sent to the **engraver's knife** <note>A poetic term for the woodblock printing process.</note> at once. The works Mr. Huang most admired were the *Record of Corrective Inquiries* and *Handwritten Letters from Forest Dwelling*; these two volumes were then sent for printing. Thus, I take up my brush to write this preface.

Throughout his life, the Master’s learning was extremely vast. When speaking with others, he would continue through day and night with great enthusiasm and never tire. Naturally, his knowledge is not something that these two books alone can fully contain. However, the Master often said:

> "Human life and the universe do not go beyond three words: **Form, Qi, and Spirit** <term>Xing, Qi, Ling — representing the physical body (Form), the vital energy (Qi), and the conscious soul or spiritual intelligence (Spirit).</term>. But Form is a thing that must eventually decay. When the form ends, the vital energy (Qi) is extinguished. What is called the 'True Self' relies solely on the Spirit. Spirit is the **Great Void** <term>Taixu — a concept referring to the boundless, formless source of all existence.</term>. The Great Void has no form; it uses things to give it form. It permeates the **Three Realms** <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.</note> and encompasses all ten thousand things. It passes through past and present, and spans across the entire universe."

With the Master’s virtue, literary talent, and **statesmanship** <term>Jingji — in this historical context, this refers to the ability to manage the world and provide for the people, not modern economics.</term>, had he achieved his ambitions and held high office, he surely would have been able to...

<summary>Lu Shichen provides a foreword explaining his long history as a student of the Master, the Master's tireless teaching style, and his core philosophy of the "True Self" as Spirit. Following the Master's death, Lu and his friend Huang Zuochen have arranged to print two of his most important works to preserve his legacy.</summary>

<keywords>Foreword, Neo-Confucianism, Zhou Dunyi, Confucius and Yan Hui, Substance and Function, Form Qi and Spirit, Great Void, Huang Zuochen, Printing, Statesmanship</keywords>

<meta>This page concludes the "Foreword" begun on the previous page. <page-num>一九〇</page-num>

...establish himself among the ranks of high officials. He surely would have been able to illuminate his principles. But alas, his fate was at odds with the times, and he remained a **humble scholar** <note>Literally "wearing the blue collar" (qingjin), a term for a student or candidate for the civil service who has not yet attained a high official post.</note> until the end of his days. Furthermore, he was only fifty-two years of age. If he is only remembered as a role model for our group through his spoken words, how could that possibly represent the full measure of the Master?

However, that which is immortal does not depend on whether one meets with worldly success or failure, nor on the length of one's years. In this world, those with high status and great wealth who enjoy long lives are numerous indeed. Yet, though they are illustrious for a time, before their bones are even cold, their names have already vanished. A thousand years from now, who will still know of this "high-ranking official" or that "long-lived man"? Worldly circumstances are never constant, and the lifespan granted by Heaven is unpredictable; these things truly cannot be used to weigh the Master's importance.

Whether one is wealthy or noble, poor or lowly, long-lived or dying young—everyone possesses **this** <note>Referring back to the "Spirit" or "True Self" discussed on the previous page as the only part of a human that does not decay.</note>. Those who can remain awake and aware in this regard are **complete persons** <term>Wanren — a philosophical ideal of a person who has fully realized their innate moral and spiritual nature.</term>. Those who cannot are, frankly, not truly human. The sages, worthies, and heroes of ancient and modern times were simply those who succeeded in being a "complete person," and nothing more. It is not that they possessed something extra that others do not. This is the central theme of the Master’s writings; even if he had written ten million words, they would be nothing more than the elaboration of this single principle. Those who read these two books well can grasp the general essence of the Master.

The Master’s taboo name was Shichen, his courtesy name was Kuixin, and his pseudonym was Yue’an. He was a scholar of the Liuhe County School and lived at **Dragon Mountain** <note>Longshan.</note> to the west of the city. For this reason, those who followed and studied under him called him **Master Longshan**.

# Record of Corrections

->Written by Lu Shichen of Yuexiang, Gutang<-

The way of learning is nothing other than this: to **seek the lost heart-mind** <note>A famous teaching from the philosopher Mencius. It suggests that humans are born with a good heart, but lose it through neglect; education is simply the process of finding it again.</note> and nothing more. These two sentences are the secret to the learning of a thousand sages pointed out by Master Meng <note>Mencius (c. 372–289 BCE).</note>. In our efforts, we do not need to seek far away. One only needs to find the starting point right here, and then success is attained. 

If one cannot perform the inner work upon the heart-mind, but instead merely searches among external objects and affairs, props oneself up with sheer willpower, or relies on cleverness and knowledge, in the end, no true seed of wisdom will be formed. Therefore, Mencius returns solely to the interior of the heart-mind. He speaks of "preserving the heart-mind" and "seeking the lost heart-mind." To preserve it is the means by which it is not lost. 

Returning to the heart-mind does not mean that one should abandon the affairs of the world. The work of preserving the heart-mind is actually performed within worldly affairs. To abandon worldly affairs is to follow **heterodox teachings** <note>Refers to paths outside of orthodox Confucianism, such as certain forms of Buddhism or Daoism that were seen as escapist or socially irresponsible by Confucian scholars.</note>. Not only is such a path untrustworthy, but people would rightly rise up together to attack it. How could we, in our pursuit of learning, be willing to be like that? 

What is called "returning to the heart-mind" is to treat the heart-mind as the master. In every affair and every object, in every action and every rest, this heart-mind must always be preserved. It is like a string threading coins; the whole cord is held in one’s hand. Thus it is said: "**One thread runs through it all**" <note>A famous phrase used by Confucius to describe the underlying unity and consistency of his teachings.</note>. 

Ever since the "learning of the sages" ceased to be discussed and the Great Way became obscured, people have mistaken external affairs for the heart-mind itself. As for those of lower character, they are not even worth mentioning. But even those of higher character are often constrained by rigid forms and conventions. Often, they perform one or two good deeds or virtuous acts and believe they have reached the ultimate state. They do not realize that while good deeds and virtuous acts are indeed the work of sages, the reason *why* they are good and *where* that goodness resides must be traced back to one’s own heart-mind through repeated reflection. Observe from where a thought arises and from where it emerges; then you will know where the **original heart-mind** <term>Benxin — the innate, pure moral consciousness that exists in every person before it is clouded by selfish desires.</term> resides. 

In the past, Master Xiangshan <note>Lu Jiuyuan (1139–1192), a major philosopher who argued that the universe and the mind are one.</note> discussed the "original heart-mind" with Yang Cihu <note>Yang Jian (1141–1226), a prominent disciple of Lu Jiuyuan.</note>, but Cihu did not understand it. One day, because Cihu was presiding over a legal dispute involving a broken fan, the Master said to him: "In observing this lawsuit over a broken fan just now, that which knows what is right is right, and that which knows what is wrong is wrong—that is your own original heart-mind, Jingzhong <note>Yang Jian's courtesy name.</note>." Upon hearing these words, Cihu attained a great awakening. 

Thus we see that if one pursues learning without recognizing the original heart-mind, it is ultimately not true learning. This is what is called "**acting without understanding and practicing without discernment**" <note>A quote from Mencius describing those who follow social customs or moral rules blindly without understanding their internal source.</note>. The flaw...

<summary>Lu Shichen opens his text by arguing that true Confucian learning is entirely a matter of cultivating the "heart-mind" (xin) rather than performing empty rituals. He uses the famous anecdote of Lu Jiuyuan and Yang Jian to illustrate that moral intuition is the "original heart-mind" in action.</summary>
