Those with the Vision of Appearances constantly observe only empty traces, and thus remain stuck in affliction. If a person can know that the nature of afflictions is empty and that they have never truly existed as independent laws—observing the Root from within the "traces"—this is called attaining the Vision of the Law.

# Treatise on Yin, Yang, and the Five Elements

**Yin** <term>The passive, cool, receptive, and feminine principle of the universe.</term> is hidden within **Yang** <term>The active, warm, creative, and masculine principle of the universe.</term>, and Yang is submerged within Yin. Because Yin is "steamed" by Yang, it is able to rise upward. Because Yang is restrained by Yin, it is able to descend. Yang steams Yin to produce **Breath** <term>Qi — The vital energy or life-force that flows through all things.</term>. Yin congeals Yang to clarify **Essence** <term>Jing — The refined, foundational substance of life.</term>. As the sun and moon rise and fall, and the forces of **Heaven and Earth** <note>original: "Qian" and "Kun," the first two hexagrams of the I Ching representing the pure creative and receptive forces.</note> interact in harmony, the ten thousand transformations of the world are completed. 

As Yin and Yang progress from their "young" to "old" stages, they divide into the **Five Elements** <term>Wuxing — The five phases of Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water that describe the cycle of change.</term>:
*   **Lesser Yang** <note>The beginning of the active cycle.</note> becomes **Wood**.
*   **Greater Yang** <note>The peak of activity.</note> becomes **Fire**.
*   **Lesser Yin** <note>The beginning of the passive cycle.</note> becomes **Metal**.
*   **Greater Yin** <note>The peak of passivity.</note> becomes **Water**.

These elements join and harmonize, becoming like husbands and wives. The nature of Fire is to flame and steam; the nature of Wood is to be strong and straight; the nature of Metal is to be firm and hard; the nature of Water is to be moist and nourishing; the nature of **Earth** is to be harmonious and soft. 
Therefore, Wood initiates growth, Fire transforms, Water nourishes, Earth harmonizes, and Metal provides strength. In this way, all varieties of things are brought to completion. The "Five Conquests" <note>The cycle of overcoming where elements control one another.</note> function such that "that which gives birth to me" is a benefit, and "that which I overcome" is for my use. This utility and overcoming multiply one another, resulting in success or failure. The Scripture says: *Through the mutual overcoming of the Five Elements, the ten thousand things can all be made whole.*

Movement and stillness are the Way of the end and the beginning. Gathering and dispersing are the gates of transformation and birth. Is not Yang movement? Is not Yin stillness? Through movement, things are born; through stillness, they find rest. Pure Yang alone cannot give birth, and pure Yin alone cannot form anything. Yin and Yang take turns in their use, and day and night support one another. During the day, Yang is in motion; at night, the moon carries out the work of Yin. Yang is nourished by Yin, and Yin is activated by Yang; thus, clarity and light are born. 

The **Harmonious Breath** <note>Heqi — The balanced state of energy.</note> of Yang manifests in the Spring, rules in the Summer, is harvested in the Autumn, and is stored in the Winter. Beneath the "Nine Depths of Earth," there is actually Yang; above the "Nine Heavens," there is actually Yin. This is why the **Divinatory Text** <note>The I Ching or Book of Changes.</note> for the eleventh month says: *"In the Return, does one not see the Mind of Heaven?"* <note>Referring to the hexagram "Fu" (Return), where the first line of Yang returns at the winter solstice.</note> This is because Yang is at the bottom. When Yang is submerged within the earth, in its hidden and silent state, that is the "Mind of Heaven."

In the human body, the kidneys house Yang, while the brain is submerged in Yin. When a person grows old and their "Harmonious Breath" is insufficient, the Yin and Yang begin to scatter: the Yang rises upward while the Yin sinks downward. Consequently, the brain becomes hot while the kidneys become cold. When the kidneys lack Yang energy, the legs lose their strength. When the brain lacks Yin energy, the eyes cannot see clearly. 

Therefore, if Yin and Yang do not interact, the ten thousand things cannot be formed. When pure Yang reaches a violent extreme, the sun and moon lose their light, and the grasses and trees are scorched and withered. When pure Yin is stagnant and pent up, there is relentless, drenching rain, and the land is flooded and washed away. 

Thus, as Yin and Yang rub against each other and Heaven and Earth shake one another:
*   When they tremble, it becomes **thunder**.
*   When they strike, it becomes **lightning**.
*   When they are drummed, it becomes **wind**.
*   When they congeal, it becomes **hail**.
*   When they steam, they become **clouds**.
*   When they liquefy into mist, they become **rain**.
*   When the dew freezes, it becomes **frost and snow**.

The "Harmonious Breath" becomes human beings; "Biased Breath" becomes birds and beasts; "Mixed Breath" becomes plants and trees; "Agitated Breath" becomes insects and fish.

# The Lord of Nourishing Life <term>Yangsheng Zhu — "Yangsheng" means to cultivate or nourish the vital principle of life; "Zhu" refers to the master or the essential theme of this practice.</term>

## Written by Zhuang Zhou <note>Better known as Zhuangzi (c. 369–286 BCE), one of the most significant figures in Daoist philosophy.</note>

Our lives have a limit, but knowledge is limitless. To pursue the limitless with the limited is perilous! To go further and act as if one possesses such knowledge is more perilous still. In doing good, do not seek fame; in doing evil, do not seek punishment. Follow the central meridian as your constant path <gloss>(Note: "Du" refers to the center.)</gloss> <term>Du — Often associated with the central energy channel of the spine, here it represents the "Middle Way" that avoids extremes.</term>. By doing so, you can protect your body, fulfill your life, nourish your parents, and complete your natural years.

Cook Ding was butchering an ox for Lord Wenhui. Where his hand touched, his shoulder leaned, his foot trod, and his knee pressed—there was a rhythmic *whisking* and *cracking* sound. The stroke of his blade was in perfect harmony, matching the rhythm of the "Mulberry Forest" dance <note>A famous, elaborate ritual dance from the ancient Shang dynasty.</note> and the movements of the "Jingshou" suite <note>A classical music arrangement from the time of the legendary Emperor Yao.</note>. Lord Wenhui exclaimed:
> "Ah! Wonderful! How can skill reach such heights?"

Cook Ding put down his blade and replied:
> "What I love is the **Dao** <term>The Way — The fundamental, underlying principle of the universe that transcends technical skill.</term>, which goes beyond mere skill. When I first began butchering oxen, I saw nothing but the whole ox. After three years, I no longer saw the whole ox. Now, I encounter it with my spirit rather than looking with my eyes. My senses stop, and my spirit acts as it will. I follow the natural structure <note>original: "Tianli" — literally 'Heavenly Principles' or the natural grain of things.</note>, striking the large gaps and sliding through the great openings. I follow what is inherently there. I never even touch the ligaments or tendons—where the grain of the meat and bone meet—let alone the great bones! A good cook changes his blade once a year because he cuts; an average cook changes his blade once a month because he hacks. I have used this blade for nineteen years, and it has butchered thousands of oxen, yet the edge is as sharp as if it were fresh from the whetstone. The joints have spaces, and the edge of the blade has no thickness. By inserting that which has no thickness into those spaces, there is plenty of room to move the blade <term>Youren youyu — A famous idiom meaning to handle a difficult task with ease and "room to spare."</term>. This is why, after nineteen years, my blade is still like new. However, whenever I come to a difficult part, I see the challenge. I proceed with caution, my gaze fixed, my movements slow. With a tiny movement of the blade, the ox falls apart like a clod of earth hitting the ground. I stand there holding the blade, looking all around, feeling completely satisfied <note>original: "chouzhu manzhi" — a sense of deep, quiet pride in a task perfectly performed.</note>. Then I wipe the blade and put it away."

Lord Wenhui said:
> "Wonderful! Hearing the words of Cook Ding, I have learned how to nourish life!"

Gongwen Xuan saw the Commander of the Right <term>Youshi — A high-ranking military or administrative official whose title implies he may have been a person of great influence.</term> and was startled, saying: 
"Who is this man? How did he come to have only one foot? Was it the work of Heaven <note>In this context, "Heaven" refers to nature or the innate Way, rather than a deity.</note>, or was it the work of man?"

The reply came:
"It was Heaven, not man. When Heaven gave him life, it intended for him to be unique <note>The text suggests his physical state—having only one foot—was a natural destiny rather than a punishment or an accident.</note>. A person’s appearance is granted to them; thus, we know it was Heaven and not man."

The pheasant of the marshes must walk ten steps for a single peck of food and a hundred steps for a single drink. Yet, it does not pray to be kept in a cage. Although its spirit might be treated like a king's within those bars, it would not be happy.

When Lao Dan <note>Lao Dan is the name used for Laozi, the legendary founder of Daoism and supposed elder contemporary of Confucius.</note> died, his friend Qin Shi went to mourn him. He let out three wails and then left the room. A disciple asked him:
"Were you not a friend of the Master?"
"I was," Qin Shi replied.
"Then is it acceptable to mourn him in such a way?"

Qin Shi said:
"It is. At first, I thought those inside were his true followers, but now I see they are not. When I went in to mourn, I saw old men weeping for him as if they were weeping for a son, and young men weeping as if for a mother. To gather together like this, there must have been words they felt compelled to say without wanting to, and tears they felt compelled to shed without wanting to. This is to **evade Heaven and turn one's back on natural feeling** <term>Duntian beiqing — A core Daoist critique of excessive emotion, which is seen as a violation of the natural order.</term>, forgetting what we have been granted. The ancients called this the 'punishment of evading Heaven.' 

When the Master came into the world, it was his time. When he left it, he was simply following the flow. If one is content with the time and dwells in the flow, neither sorrow nor joy can enter. The ancients called this **the release from the hanging bonds of the Divine** <note>original: "Di zhi xuanjie" — This refers to being freed from the 'dangling' state of worldly attachments and the fear of death.</note>."

The fingers may run out of fuel to add to the fire, but the **fire is transmitted** <gloss>(The flame moves on.)</gloss>, and we do not know when it will ever end.

# Treatise on Nourishing Life
## Written by Ge Hong, the Master Who Embraces Simplicity <term>Baopuzi — The pen name of Ge Hong, reflecting his philosophy of returning to a state of natural, uncarved simplicity.</term>

The Master Who Embraces Simplicity says: 
"The body of a single person is like the image of a single state. The arrangement of the chest and abdomen is like the palaces and chambers. The placement of the limbs is like the outlying borders. The divisions of the bones and joints are like the various government officials. The spaces within the skin's texture <term>Couli — In traditional Chinese medicine, this refers to the layers of the skin and the interstitial spaces where energy and fluids flow.</term> are like the four-way crossroads. The spirit is like the ruler, the blood like the ministers, and the breath <note>original: "Qi" — The vital life force or energy that animates the body.</note> like the common people. 

Therefore, a person of the highest attainment can govern their body just as a wise ruler can govern their state. By loving the people, one secures the state; by loving the breath and circulating it, one preserves the body. When the people are exhausted, the state perishes; when the breath is depleted, the body passes away. 

For this reason, the person of highest attainment and the superior scholar apply medicine before an illness occurs; they do not seek to repair the damage after the body has already failed. One must know that the spirit is difficult to preserve but easy to scatter, and the breath is difficult to purify but easy to cloud. If one can carefully examine the mechanisms of self-control, one can restrain desires and protect life. 

Furthermore, those who are skilled at nourishing life must first remove the **Six Harms**; only then can they extend their years to a full century. What are these? 
1. The pursuit of fame and profit. 
2. The indulgence in seductive sounds and sights <gloss>(sensuality)</gloss>. 
3. Greed for wealth and goods. 
4. The excess of rich flavors in food. 
5. Flattery and falsehood. 
6. Jealousy and resentment. 

If these six are not removed, the way of cultivation is established in vain. Because the person has not seen the benefit of removing them, even if their heart hopes for the 'Mysterious Way,' their mouth recites 'True Scriptures,' they chew on 'floral essence,' and they practice 'breathing the vital images' <note>These terms refer to specific Daoist meditative and alchemical practices intended to achieve longevity.</note>, they cannot compensate for the shortness of their life. This is truly choosing the branch while forgetting the root—it should be a profound warning! 

To preserve harmony and keep the True self whole, one should have: **less thinking, less worrying, less laughing, less speaking, less joy, less anger, less pleasure, less sorrow, less liking, less hating, less busywork, and less scheming.** 

For too much thinking scatters the spirit; too much worrying exhausts the heart; too much laughing causes the internal organs to heave; too much speaking leads to the depletion of the 'Sea of Breath' <note>original: "Qihai" — An energy center located below the navel, considered the reservoir of vital energy.</note>; too much joy lets 'guest winds' <gloss>(External pathogens or harmful environmental influences)</gloss> enter the bladder; too much anger causes blood to rush through the skin; too much pleasure makes the heart-spirit drift toward evil; too much sorrow makes the hair wither and the appearance fade; too much liking causes the will and breath to overflow; too much hating causes the essence-breath to surge uncontrollably; too much busywork makes the tendons and veins dry and tense; too much scheming leads to confusion in wisdom and thought. 

These excesses strike at a person’s life more sharply than an axe, and damage a person's fate more fiercely than wolves or tigers. 

Do not sit for too long, do not walk for too long, do not look for too long, and do not listen for too long. If you are not hungry, do not force yourself to eat; if you are not thirsty, do not force yourself to drink. Forcing food when not hungry tires the spleen; if you are not... <note>The text ends mid-sentence at the bottom of the page.</note>"

# Essential Points and Instructions for the <term>Mysterious Gate — A poetic name for the Daoist tradition, derived from the "Gate of All Wonders" in the Dao De Jing.</term> Taiji Longevity Exercises

->By Xiao Tianshi, the Hermit of Wenshan<-

1. The "Mysterious Gate Taiji Longevity Exercises" are also referred to simply as "Mysterious Exercises" (Xuan Gong). This is a high-level method belonging to the Daoist tradition of <term>Dual Cultivation of Movement and Stillness — A practice philosophy that balances active physical exercise with internal meditative quietude.</term> Its primary goals are to dispel illness, strengthen the body, and extend one’s lifespan, serving as the fundamental basis for transcending the mundane and entering the realm of the sacred—the first step toward becoming an immortal or a lineage master. Its contents encompass <term>Qigong — Breath-work and energy cultivation.</term>, rubbing techniques, stillness practices, <term>Daoyin — Ancient Chinese stretching and guiding exercises, a precursor to modern Qigong.</term>, massage, Tui-na (acupressure), percussion, kneading, and rhythmic tapping. It also includes the secret methods for refining and replenishing the "Three Treasures": <term>Essence, Qi, and Spirit — The three fundamental energies in Daoist internal alchemy; Essence (Jing) relates to physical vitality, Qi to breath/energy, and Spirit (Shen) to consciousness.</term> The effects of transforming the physical form and renewing the spirit are truly immediate. Not only does one benefit from the mutual nourishment of movement and stillness, but one can also achieve the combined results of both the Northern and Southern Daoist lineages. It can truly be described as a practice that is at once simple and profound, ordinary yet miraculous.

2. This system is also known as the "Qingcheng Sect Taiji Mysterious Exercises." Among the practitioners of <term>Internal Alchemy — A Daoist meditative practice that uses the body's internal energies to achieve health and spiritual liberation.</term> in the Qingcheng lineage, there are none who do not use this as the primary foundation for entering the path of truth. It is similar to how the Great Master <note>Bodhidharma (Da Mo) is the legendary 5th/6th-century monk credited with bringing Chan (Zen) Buddhism to China and developing the martial arts foundations at the Shaolin Temple.</note> Bodhidharma secretly transmitted the *Classic of Muscle Tendon Change* and the *Classic of Marrow Washing* as the foundational works for attaining the Dao. The complete system consists of four parts: the Divine Primordial (Shenyuan), the Upper Primordial (Shangyuan), the Middle Primordial (Zhongyuan), and the Lower Primordial (Xiayuan). If one masters all the secret keys and integrates them with alchemical practice, transforming the self and entering the "Sacred City" becomes as easy as turning over one's hand. Legend has it that the final section, the Divine Primordial practice, has been lost to time since the Song Dynasty. When we call these "Health Exercises," we are speaking of their simpler, more accessible effects. When we call them "Longevity Exercises," it is to encourage people of the world to cultivate their virtue and practice. However, the true aim is to lead the practitioner into the realm of <term>Pure Emptiness — A state of profound spiritual clarity and non-attachment in Daoism.</term>; one must not view them merely as a way to cure sickness or add years to one's life.

3. Those who practice this system will find that it cures them if they are ill and strengthens them if they are well; furthermore, it can ensure a life free from the suffering of disease. The final stage of the Divine Primordial practice even allows one to reach a state where they may "depart or remain as they wish." <term>Sitting off or standing to die — A high-level spiritual feat in Daoist and Buddhist traditions where a master consciously chooses the moment of their passing, often while in a meditative posture.</term> is considered a relatively easy matter within the Daoist and Buddhist gates; however, if...

Strengthening the form nourishes the Spirit; refining the Spirit completes the inner Nature. Preserving the Essence nourishes the Qi; refining the Qi completes the Mandate of Life. When both internal and external are attained, form and spirit become perfectly aligned. Essence, Qi, and Spirit are the "Three Treasures" of a person; the Five Viscera and Six Bowels are what life relies upon. The tendons, bones, and skin are the three pillars of the physical form; the limbs and skeleton are where life resides. Only then can one pass the final gate, complete the Great Dao, and enter the realm of the sacred and the true. Internal cultivation focuses on the formless; external cultivation focuses on the formed. Internal cultivation refines spirit and energy, while external cultivation refines the physical frame. These two interact as cause and effect, benefiting each other. Thus, the primary objective of this practice is first to move from the external to the internal—from the formed to the formless—and then to allow the internal fullness to permeate the external health, using the formless to solidify the formed. To exclusively cultivate the formless while abandoning the formed is certainly wrong; however, to exclusively refine the formed while ignoring the formless is even worse.

Even when compared to modern science and medicine, its principles are found to be in perfect agreement. When young people practice it, they easily see divine results. For the middle-aged and elderly, it is especially suitable, as it offers a hundred benefits without a single drawback—meaning it has no adverse reactions or side effects. If one practices without grasping the secret keys, the worst that can happen is that the results will be slow or too subtle to notice immediately; there is absolutely no such thing as it being ineffective.

The cultivation of this school’s arts is divided into three parts: standing, sitting, and lying. The "Lying Practice" can also be performed in a sitting or standing posture. For all three styles, one must first sit quietly for half an hour to clear the heart and quiet the thoughts, focusing the spirit and unifying the will. The complete practice is divided into four stages, called: **Spirit-Origin Practice**, **Upper-Origin Practice**, **Middle-Origin Practice**, and **Lower-Origin Practice**.

Generally, those seeking the "Method of Health, Longevity, and Peace" only need to practice the Upper-Origin and Middle-Origin sections to be successful. To begin, one first practices the Middle-Origin, which consists of the **First Nine Segments**. Next, one practices the Upper-Origin, the **Middle Nine Segments**. This is followed by the Lower-Origin, the **Latter Nine Segments**. Finally, one practices the Spirit-Origin, which comprises the **Final Nine Segments**.

When practicing the First Nine Segments, after completing the period of quiet meditation, adopt a reclining posture (use a hard wooden bed with a thick mattress or padding). The whole body should be straight, with both legs extended and slightly apart, at shoulder-width. The arms are straight at the sides, fingers extended, palms down, and pressed flat against the bed. The eyes are slightly closed, focusing the mind on the <term>Lower Dantian — The "Elixir Field," a center of energy located about two inches below the navel.</term> The breath should be continuous and soft, so quiet it cannot be heard. The mouth is closed, the teeth slightly touching, and the tongue is pressed against the upper palate. Keep the intent in the Dantian; if saliva fills the mouth, perform the **Saliva Swallowing Method** <note>original: "Tunjin fa"; a traditional practice where saliva is swallowed to nourish internal energy</note>. Relax the muscles and nerves of the whole body, allowing the blood and <term>Qi — Vital life force or energy.</term> to flow smoothly and comfortably, nourishing the entire body inside and out. Gradually reach a state where you forget both yourself and the external world, a realm where body and mind both vanish; this achieves the effect of "Great Rest." This concludes the preliminary work, and one may then begin the Middle-Origin Practice.

## 2. Middle-Origin Practice

The Middle-Origin Practice is divided into nine forms, hence it is also called the **First Nine Segments**. The movements of each form are simple and easy to perform, primarily focusing on tempering the <term>Zangfu — The internal organs, including the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, and kidneys.</term> At first glance, it appears to be purely a practice for training the physical form; in reality, it contains the work of training the Spirit. Furthermore, it encompasses the cultivation of both Essence and Energy <note>The "Three Treasures" of Daoist practice: Jing (Essence), Qi (Energy), and Shen (Spirit)</note>. If this practice is followed throughout one’s life, it can prevent all manner of diseases from arising in the internal organs. This is the effect of "training the internal from the external," resulting in an outer strength and an inner solidness. The details are described as follows:

**1. The First Segment:** The left hand cradles the <term>External Kidneys — A traditional euphemism for the testicles.</term> while the right hand is placed below the navel. (The waistband should be loosened and the upper garment lifted so that the chest and abdomen are entirely bare...)

Gaze steadily at the bridge of the nose for a moment, leading the Spirit to flow down into the center of the palm and penetrate straight through to the <term>Lower Dantian — The "Elixir Field," an energy center located below the navel.</term> The right hand moves from bottom to top, and from right to left, using the navel as the center. Massage in a circle around the navel, silently counting "one." Where the hand moves, the Spirit moves; where the hand stops, the Spirit stops. Where the Spirit moves, the <term>Qi — Vital life force or energy.</term> moves; where the Spirit stops, the Qi stops. Massage slowly; do not go too fast. <gloss>This instruction applies to all sections below.</gloss> Use a combination of pressing, rubbing, and kneading, ensuring the stomach and intestines all receive the benefit of the massage. Perform this thirty-six times as the standard.

### 2. The Second Segment:
Swap the positions of the hands: the right hand now cradles the <term>Kidney Sac — A traditional term for the scrotum.</term> while the left hand is placed below the navel, using the same posture as above. During the practice, the left hand moves from bottom to top and from left to right, massaging in a circle around the navel; silently count "one." The formula and method are the same as the previous segment. Perform this thirty-six times as the standard. The practice of the first and second segments resembles the <term>Taiji Diagram — The "Yin-Yang" symbol representing the balance of opposites.</term>; it is also called "Rubbing the Taiji," or the "Method of Rubbing the Microcosmic Orbit" <note>original: "Xiao Zhoutian Gong"; a foundational Daoist practice of circulating energy through the body's central vessels</note>.

### 3. The Third Segment:
Swap hands again: the left hand cradles the Kidney Sac, and the right hand is placed below the navel. From the center, push and massage straight up from the bottom, then return straight down from the top; silently count "one." When moving from bottom to top, stop at the <term>Solar Plexus — The "Heart Pit," located at the base of the breastbone.</term> between the two breasts. Then push downward until reaching the pubic hair line at the base of the kidneys. The secret of this method is that the upward push sends the "Kidney Qi" to the Heart, while the downward push sends the "Heart Qi" into the Kidneys, allowing the energies of the Heart and Kidneys to circulate and nourish each other. Perform this thirty-six times as the standard.

### 4. The Fourth Segment:
The hands do not need to swap. However, when the right palm pushes and massages, it should follow the line of the ribs on the left side. Push upward from the bottom until reaching the left lung area, then push downward from the top until reaching the pubic hair line. The secret of this method lies in allowing the energies of the Lungs and Kidneys to flow and communicate with each other. Perform this thirty-six times as the standard.

### 5. The Fifth Segment:
Swap hands: use the right hand to cradle the <term>External Kidneys — A traditional euphemism for the testicles.</term> and place the left hand below the navel. Follow the line of the ribs on the right side, pushing upward from the bottom until reaching the right lung area. Then push downward from the top, returning to the pubic hair line. Perform this thirty-six times. The function of this segment is the same as the one above.

### 6. The Sixth Segment:
Swap hands again: the left hand cradles the External Kidneys, and the right palm is placed flat below the navel. Follow the path described in the fourth segment, moving from the bottom upward to...

## 7. The Seventh Segment

Swap hands: your right hand cradles the <term>External Kidneys — A traditional euphemism for the testicles.</term>, and your left palm is placed flat below the navel. Follow the path described in the fifth segment, moving from the bottom upward. After reaching the area above the right breast, rub horizontally to the left across to the area above the left breast. Turn downward while pressing and kneading until you return to the starting point to complete one cycle. Silently count "one," continuing until you reach thirty-six repetitions. These two segments—the sixth and the seventh—are also known as the **Method of Rubbing the Macrocosmic Orbit** <note>original: "Da Zhoutian Fa"; a practice in Daoist alchemy involving the circulation of energy through a wider network of the body's meridians</note>.

## 8. The Eighth Segment

Swap hands: your left hand cradles the External Kidneys. Move your right palm as far to the right as possible, placing it horizontally against the right side of the abdomen. Using the back half of the palm to apply pressure, push from the right toward the left until you reach the left side of the abdomen. Then, use the front half of the palm and the four fingers to apply pressure and pull back toward the right. The strength should be concentrated entirely on the abdomen during this pushing and pulling motion. One full back-and-forth movement counts as "one." Silently count until you reach thirty-six repetitions.

## 9. The Ninth Segment

Swap hands: your right hand cradles the External Kidneys, and place your left palm on the left side of the stomach area. The method is the same as described above: use the palm to push with pressure from left to right, then use pressure to pull back. The strength should be concentrated entirely on the stomach area. One full back-and-forth movement counts as "one." Silently count until you reach thirty-six repetitions. This marks the completion of the **Initial Nine Segments of the Middle-Origin Practice**.

It is highly beneficial for the heart, liver, spleen, lungs, kidneys, stomach, and intestines. This is entirely an exercise for **Internal Health and Internal Strength**, focusing on internal solidity and stabilization. The movements are extremely simple and grounded, with nothing mysterious about them, yet when the practice is mastered, it often produces unexpectedly miraculous results.

## 3. The Upper-Origin Practice

The **Upper-Origin Practice** <term>Shangyuan Gong — The third stage of this system, focusing on the upper body and head.</term> is divided into nine forms, and is thus also called the **Middle Nine Segments** <term>Zhong Jiu Duan</term>. Once the Middle-Origin Practice has been mastered (requiring approximately one hundred and twenty days) and you feel your body and mind benefiting, you may begin practicing this Upper-Origin Practice. The ancient realized masters said: "If you wish to escape death, cultivate the **Kunlun** <note>original: "Kunlun"; in Daoist internal alchemy, this refers to the head or the brain, named after the sacred mountain range.</note>." This is precisely the method of "cultivating the Kunlun" found within the **Mysterious Gate** <term>Xuanmen — A traditional name for the school of Daoism.</term>. Its movements are also extremely simple, accessible, and grounded, yet their efficacy is infinite; the most important factor is consistency in practice. Like the initial nine segments, these are daily exercises for nourishing life.

The previously described Middle-Origin Practice primarily utilizes a reclining (lying down) posture; the Upper-Origin Practice described in this chapter primarily utilizes a seated posture. Those who are not familiar with the **Full Lotus Position** <term>Jiafuzuo — A cross-legged sitting posture where both feet rest on opposite thighs.</term> may use a "convenient seat" (sitting on a chair) instead. However, you must use a hard stool, and its height should be such that the thighs above the knees are level with the knees themselves. Ultimately, the lotus position is superior. You should practice it daily, gradually increasing the duration, moving from the **Half-Lotus Position** <term>Ban Jiafuzuo — Sitting with only one foot placed on the opposite thigh.</term> (single wrap) until you can comfortably achieve the full lotus (double wrap). The lotus position can also be practiced on a bed.

After completing the Middle-Origin Practice, rest for a short while to calm the heart, steady the spirit, and nourish the vital breath and true nature. During this time, you must not give in to the desire for sleep. Because one is prone to drowsiness at this stage, many people unconsciously fall into a deep slumber. Daoist cultivation of "stability" includes specific formulas for "refining the sleep demon" <note>a metaphor for overcoming the urge to sleep during meditation</note> and strictly warns against laziness and abandoning the practice for sleep. If you practice the work of **Silent Stability** <term>Jingding — A state of meditative stillness.</term> while waiting for the mind to be free of thoughts, it is easy to drift off. If you feel sleepy, you should immediately sit up and perform the exercises rather than resting for too long. This practice focuses primarily on the Kunlun (the head) and the back. Regarding the seated posture, please refer to the chapter in this book titled "Introductory Methods for Quiet Sitting." The segments are described as follows:

1. **The First Segment:** Sit cross-legged for a short while. When the heart is settled and the spirit is pleased, rub your two hands together until they are extremely hot. Then, use both palms to rub the left and right **Yaoshu Points** <term>Yaoshu — An acupuncture point located at the base of the spine/sacrum, believed to govern the lower back.</term>.

The secret formula for this is: "The spirit should follow the hands, and the heart must not wander outward." This principle applies to all the segments described below.

## 2. The Second Segment

Rub your two hands together until they are extremely hot, then simultaneously rub the <term>Weilü Point — Located at the tip of the tailbone or coccyx.</term> in an upward and downward motion. Moving downward, use your fingers to rub until you reach the tailbone; moving upward, use your palms to rub until you reach the <term>Jiaji Pass — The "Spine-Squeezing" Pass, located on the spine between the shoulder blades.</term>. When moving upward, the hands should separate; when moving downward toward the <term>Weilü Point</term>, the hands join together again. Each time you rub your hands until hot, perform about ten friction strokes, with nine to twenty-four repetitions in total. This is the **Method for Simultaneously Rubbing the Tailbone and Spine**. These first two segments of work can strengthen the internal kidneys, dispel back ailments, solidify the marrow and replenish the spirit, and assist in generating Yang energy and "Essence" <note>Jing, or vital essence</note>. It is also a method for the external cultivation of the <term>Du Channel — The "Governing Vessel," the primary energetic pathway running up the spine.</term>.

## 3. The Third Segment

Form the <term>Samadhi Mudra — A meditative hand gesture where hands are folded in the lap, palms up, with thumb tips touching.</term> with both hands. Keep the spine perfectly upright and perform the method of rotating the <term>Jade Neck — A poetic and anatomical term for the neck in Daoist cultivation.</term>. The technique is: first bow the head forward and down, then rotate from left to right twelve times; next, rotate from right to left twelve times; then, tilt forward and backward twelve times; and finally, bend to the left and right twelve times. Afterward, use the ten fingers of both hands to pinch and knead the entire **Jade Neck**. (This method exercises the cervical nerve plexus and the <term>Thyroid Gland</term>, and helps prevent esophageal cancer and <term>Goiter — A swelling of the neck resulting from an enlarged thyroid gland.</term>, among other illnesses.)

## 4. The Fourth Segment

Cup the head with both hands, fingers spread wide. Place the thumbs on the back of the head and the other four fingers on the frontal area (the cerebrum). Apply slight pressure with the fingertips and pinch and knead the entire <term>Kunlun Jade Peak — A reference to the crown of the head.</term>. Start from the hairline above the forehead and finish near the base of the neck at the back of the head, kneading and pressing evenly. Pressing from front to back counts as about ten finger-movements; continue until the four fingers of both hands meet the thumbs at the back of the head. (Note: The thumbs must also perform the pressing and kneading work, rather than remaining fixed in one spot.) This constitutes one cycle. Return to the starting position and repeat for nine to twenty-four cycles.

## 5. The Fifth Segment
The posture remains as described above, but the technique changes from kneading and pressing to methods of flicking, patting, and tapping. Each time, the movements should be of moderate intensity—neither too light nor too heavy—and should cover the entire <term>Jade Peak — A poetic term for the top of the head/crown.</term>. Between nine and twenty-four repetitions constitute a full segment. The specific methods are: use the fingers for flicking, the full palm for patting, the fingertips for tapping, and the "corners" (knuckles) of the fist for striking. It is of the utmost importance to avoid using brute force or tension during this practice. Lightness results in successful "work" (Kung), while heaviness results in injury. Striking a balance between light and heavy is the proper measure.

---

## 6. The Sixth Segment
Rub your two hands together until they are extremely hot, then cup them to warm the face. With the ten fingers pointing upward and the fingertips roughly level with the forehead, join the palms at the nose and rub outward toward the left and right, stopping behind the ears. Perform about five to ten strokes per heat, repeating the process for a total of nine cycles. Then, using the same method, rub upward from the bottom of the face; when the palms reach the forehead, separate them and rub toward the left and right, with the same number of repetitions as before. You must ensure the entire face is rubbed and massaged evenly. During this, you may also choose to add some kneading and pinching movements as appropriate.

---

## 7. The Seventh Segment
Rub the two hands together until extremely hot and use them to warm both eyes (the eyes should be closed). Move the hands outward to the left and right, massaging until you reach the ears. Repeat this twelve times to complete one cycle; perform nine cycles in total. Next, with the eyes still closed, perform the **Method for Transporting the Pupils**: slowly rotate the eyes up, down, left, and right, repeating the rotation twelve times in each direction. Finally, perform the <term>Beating the Heavenly Drum — A technique where the ears are covered with the palms and the fingers flick against the back of the head, creating a resonant thumping sound in the skull.</term> twenty-four times.

---

## 8. The Eighth Segment
Form the **Samadhi Mudra** <note>a meditative hand gesture with hands folded in the lap</note> with both hands. Settle the heart and sit in silence, focusing the spirit on the <term>Niwan — The "Mud Pill" Palace, the Daoist term for the Upper Dantian or the center of the brain.</term>. The method for this segment is: first shrug the right shoulder once, then shrug the left shoulder once, then shrug both shoulders together once. This constitutes one cycle. When both shoulders are shrugged together, you must ensure that the central nervous system feels a slight vibration that reaches the cerebral cortex. Perform between nine and thirty-six cycles in total. This method benefits the shoulders, the upper back, and the spinal cord.

---

## 9. The Ninth Segment
Sit in silence and settle the heart, condensing the spirit to shine serenely upon the <term>Qixue — The "Qi Cave," a focal point for internal energy, often located in the lower abdomen.</term>. After a short while, you will feel the **Qi** <note>Vital life force or energy</note> penetrate the <term>Weilü — The tailbone or coccyx.</term>, rise through the <term>Jiaji — The "Spine-Squeezing" pass between the shoulder blades.</term>, follow the <term>Yuzhen — The "Jade Pillow" pass at the base of the skull.</term>, and reach the **Niwan**. Keep the spirit focused in the **Niwan**, allowing the **Primordial Qi** <note>original: "Yuan Qi"</note> to swirl like a thick mist, filling the crown and the face. Gradually, this energy will merge into one with the energy of the <term>Marrow Sea — A Daoist term for the brain as the reservoir of essence and spirit.</term>. Continue by circulating...

## 4. Lower-Origin Practice

Regarding the **Lower-Origin Practice** <note>original: "Xiayuan Gong"</note>, the original manuscript was somewhat damaged and incomplete due to insect-eating. When I previously stayed at the <term>Tianshi Cave — The "Celestial Master’s Cave," a famous Daoist site on Mount Qingcheng associated with Zhang Daoling.</term>, I did not have time to transcribe it, and now I no longer remember it fully. 

Broadly speaking, the practice consists of nothing more than the four paths: <term>Internal Refining — Cultivating energy within the body through meditation and breath.</term>, <term>External Refining — Physical exercises or using external substances for health.</term>, <term>Self-Nourishing — Independent practice to sustain one's health.</term>, and <term>Nourishing via the Other — Practices involving an external partner or catalyst, often more controversial in Daoist history.</term>. 

For the most part, it does not differ greatly from the techniques of the <term>Southern Sect — A tradition of Daoist internal alchemy focused on the cultivation of nature and life.</term> or the <term>Eastern Sect — Another major lineage of internal alchemy.</term>. Regarding the "Forging of the Sword" <note>a metaphor for refining vital essence or "Jing"</note>, although there is a method for "Simmering the Furnace" <note>the process of maintaining steady internal heat during meditation</note>, it is not the primary focus here. The subtlety of this practice lies in prioritizing self-nourishing over nourishing via others, and internal refining over external refining. It belongs entirely to the orthodox tradition, ensuring the noble style of the Immortals does not fall into decline.

---

## 5. Spirit-Origin Practice

As for the **Spirit-Origin Practice** <note>original: "Shenyuan Gong"</note>, the original manuscript only preserved the title, with the rest of the text entirely lost or missing. This likely corresponds to the final two stages of the alchemical process: <term>Refining Spirit to Return to Emptiness — A high-level stage where individual consciousness merges with the void.</term> and <term>Refining Emptiness to Accord with the Tao — The final stage of becoming one with the ultimate, nameless reality.</term>. However, at that time, <term>Daoist Li — A reference to a teacher or monk mentioned earlier in the transcription.</term> did not discuss it, and I do not dare to speculate on the similarities or differences of its techniques.

---

## 6. Concluding Remarks

Finally, the original manuscript was very simple and did not contain many of the phrases used in the segments described above. I have chosen not to mind the complexity and have provided detailed descriptions here, replacing the esoteric codes and metaphorical terms with modern terminology. This is to help readers interested in these simple health-preserving exercises find them easier to practice after reading. 

As for the secrets of <term>Circulating Qi — The practice of moving vital energy through the body's channels.</term> and <term>Absorbing Qi — Drawing in energy from the environment.</term>, the methods for applying strength and spirit, and the keys to <term>Pressing and Kneading Acupoints — Manipulating specific energetic points on the body for health.</term>, some aspects still remain unsaid. Once the practice becomes skillful and complete, you will naturally come to realize them yourself. When trying to put these things into words, one often feels there is no way to start or describe the subtle sensations—a feeling for which I am deeply apologetic!

<note>Note: Upon completing the Spirit-Origin Practice, there are also concluding exercises to be done before getting up from the seated position.</note>

# CHAPTER I.
->Concerning Purgatory.<-

<margin>Matthew 5. 1 Corinthians 3. Philippians 2. Revelation 21.</margin>
Thus far we have spoken of the <term>Church Militant <note>original: "Ecclesia Militante," referring to the body of Christians currently living on earth who struggle against sin and the world.</note></term>: now follows the <term>Church Suffering <note>original: "Ecclesia Patiens," referring to the souls of the faithful departed who are being purified before entering heaven.</note></term>, which is called **Purgatory**. Now, <term>Purgatory</term> is a place in which the souls of the deceased—who departed in the grace of God, but have not yet fully satisfied for their sins through worthy penance—are punished by fire and purified, so that, once purified, they may then be received into heaven. Moreover, that <term>Purgatory</term> exists is proven by a two-fold argument.

### I. THE ARGUMENT from Authority.

<margin>2 Maccabees 12:43–46.</margin>
1. *By the Authority of Scripture*. In the Old Testament, it is read that <term>Judas Maccabeus <note>A Jewish leader of the 2nd century BCE who led a revolt against the Seleucid Empire.</note></term> sent twelve thousand silver drachmas to <term>Jerusalem</term> so that a sacrifice might be offered for the sins of the dead, thinking well and religiously concerning the resurrection. *It is therefore a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the deceased, that they may be loosed from their sins.* For if there were no Purgatory, it would be in vain to pray for them: since in Hell there is no redemption, and in Heaven there is no need.

<margin>Matthew 12:32.</margin>
In the New Testament, <term>Christ</term> says: *Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit, it will not be forgiven him, neither in this age, nor in the age to come.* From these words, St. <term>Augustine</term> (Book 21 of *The City of God*, chapter 24) and St. <term>Gregory</term> (Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 39) conclude that certain sins are forgiven in the age to come, specifically in Purgatory.

<margin>1 Corinthians 3:12–15.</margin>
Likewise St. <term>Paul</term>: *If anyone builds upon this foundation with gold, silver, precious stones, wood, hay, or stubble, each one's work will become manifest: for the Day of the Lord will declare it, because it will be revealed in fire; and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done. If anyone’s work which he has built survives, he will receive a reward; if anyone’s work is burned up, he will suffer loss; but he himself will be saved, yet so as through fire.* By *wood, hay, and stubble*, venial sins <note>Lesser sins that do not break a person's relationship with God but still require purification.</note> are understood, which are purified in the fire of Purgatory.

<margin>Matthew 5:25–26.</margin>
Likewise: *Be at agreement with your adversary quickly, while you are on the way with him; lest perhaps the adversary deliver you to the judge, and the judge deliver you to the officer, and you be cast into prison. Amen I say to you, you shall not go out from there until you have paid the last penny.* St. <term>Cyprian</term> (Letter 52) and St. <term>Ambrose</term> (commenting on this passage) understand this *prison* to mean Purgatory.

<margin>Philippians 2:10. Revelation 5:3, 13.</margin>
Likewise, it is said that *at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, those on earth, and those under the earth*: and that *no one, neither in heaven, nor on earth, nor under the earth, was able to open the book*. By those *under the earth* and those in the lower regions are understood the souls who are in Purgatory; for the damned do not bow the knee to <term>Christ</term> out of devotion.

2. *By the Authority of the Councils and the Fathers*. The Council of <term>Florence</term> and the Council of <term>Trent</term> (session 25) defined that <term>Purgatory</term> exists. All the <term>Fathers <note>Ancient and influential Christian theologians and writers.</note></term> teach the same. <term>Dionysius the Areopagite</term> (chapter 7 of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*), <term>Tertullian</term> (*Concerning the Soldier's Crown*), <term>Cyprian</term> (Book 4, Letter 2), <term>Chrysostom</term> (Homily 3 on the Letter to the Philippians), and <term>Augustine</term> (Book 9 of the *Confessions*, chapter 13; and in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 110; and on Psalm 37), where he says: *Lord, rebuke me not in your fury, nor chastise me in your anger. Purify me in this age, and make me such a person who no longer has need of the amending fire.* Also <term>Gregory</term> (Book 4 of the *Dialogues*, chapter 39) and others.

### II. THE ARGUMENT from Reason.

It is proven by Reason that <term>Purgatory</term> exists: because it can happen that someone departs this life with a venial sin, or has not fully satisfied the temporal punishment <note>The remaining penalty for sin after the guilt has been forgiven.</note> owed for mortal sins. Such a person cannot immediately enter Heaven: because *nothing defiled shall enter it* (Revelation 21). Nor should they be sent to Hell: because they departed in the grace of God. Therefore, it is necessary that a third place be given, in which such a person is purified and makes satisfaction. This is the common [belief] of all <term>Christians</term> universal- <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword "vniuersa-", likely continuing as "universally held."</note>

<summary>This page defines Purgatory as a place of temporary purification by fire for souls who die in God's grace but with remaining debt for sin. It defends the doctrine using Old and New Testament passages, the consensus of early Church Fathers, and the logical necessity of a "third place" between Heaven and Hell.</summary>
<keywords>Purgatory, Church Suffering, Church Militant, Church Fathers, Council of Trent, venial sin, temporal punishment, satisfaction, afterlife, Catholic theology</keywords>

# ESSENCE OF THE TAOIST CANON, SERIES 1, VOLUME 2

## The Rectified Meaning of the Kinship of the Three in the Book of Changes

->The Rectified Meaning of the Kinship of the Three in the Book of Changes .................. 1<-
->Page Number<-

Written by <term>Wei Boyang <note>A legendary semi-historical figure of the Eastern Han Dynasty, often called the "Ancestor of Alchemy" and credited with writing the Cantong Qi.</note></term> of the Han Dynasty. This work is recorded in the "Bibliographic Treatise" of the *Supplement to the Book of the Later Han*, the *Old Book of Tang*, and the *History of Song*. The preface by Xu Lichun of the Qing Dynasty states: "Among the ten thousand volumes of alchemical books, the <term>Kinship of the Three <note>original: "Cantong Qi," the earliest book on alchemy in China, which uses the symbolism of the I Ching (Book of Changes) to describe alchemical processes.</note></term> is foremost." Alchemists of later generations all look to this work as their ancestor. Its language is ancient and its prose is obscure, yet its principles are profound and its scope is vast, leaving nothing out, whether great or small. 

Regarding the *Book of Changes*, it describes the transformation of <term>Yin and Yang <note>The complementary forces of the universe.</note></term> and the cultivation of Heaven and Earth. Regarding <term>Alchemy <note>original: "Dan," referring to the "elixir" or the process of spiritual/physical transformation.</note></term>, it clarifies both the <term>Fire Phases <note>original: "Huohou," the timing and intensity of the meditative or chemical heat in alchemy.</note></term> and the medicinal ingredients, both internal and external. It is truly a supreme text where Confucianism and Taoism run parallel, and a righteous principle that does not contradict the teachings of the Immortals or the Buddha. Whether used to govern a nation and manage administration, to nourish one’s nature and cultivate reality, or to understand the mind and see one's true nature, it never fails. It truly rivals the various Classics and Philosophers in beauty and remains immortal through the ages. 

The world often fails to examine it closely, frequently neglecting its relationship to the principles of the *Changes* and labeling it purely as a book of alchemy; this is a great error. The great <term>Song Dynasty scholar Zhu Xi <note>One of the most influential Confucian philosophers in Chinese history.</note></term> spent years exhausting his efforts on this text, providing critical annotations and calling it the "Pre-heaven learning" <note>Knowledge concerning the primordial state of the universe before the physical world was formed.</note> within the *Changes*. He once said: "Master Shao <note>Shao Yong, a famous cosmologist.</note> received his knowledge from <term>Xiyi <note>The Daoist master Chen Tuan.</note></term>, and Xiyi’s lineage originates from the *Kinship of the Three*." He also remarked: "My eyes see it clearly as such, yet I have no place to set my hand to the work." Later, he spent sleepless nights discussing and correcting it with Mr. Cai of Xishan. From this, its high value can be known. 

There have been over a hundred commentators throughout history, but the versions by Yu Yan, Zhu Yunyang, and <term>Master Yuanzhen of Sifengshan <note>A noted commentator who organized the text into a logical "Rectified Meaning."</note></term> are the most refined. Master Yuanzhen’s edition provides detailed explanations chapter by chapter and is titled the "Rectified Meaning." It ensures that the three elements—the Great *Changes*, internal cultivation, and the "furnace and fire" <note>The practical application of alchemical theory.</note>—are all explored deeply and reach far, uniting them at their source. The true mechanism is revealed, shining as brightly as the sun and stars. The Way is clarified and the meaning is rectified. If the reader is not deterred by the difficulty and persists in refined study, then once a sudden understanding is reached, they may "enter the hall and the inner room," <note>An idiom meaning to master a subject or reach a high level of proficiency.</note> transcend the mundane to become a sage, and reach the subtle heights of the mysterious.

->Elucidations on the Kinship of the Three in the Book of Changes .................. 133<-

This book is based on the edition from the private collection of Bao Shigong of Zhejiang. It was written by <term>Yu Yan <note>Also known as Yuyangzi, a famous Song/Yuan scholar who interpreted alchemy through the lens of natural philosophy.</note></term> and is recorded in the *Complete Library of the Four Treasuries*. It uses the <term>Water and Fire <note>In alchemy, these represent the kidneys/heart or essence/spirit.</note></term> and the Yin and Yang of the individual body to explain alchemical principles through broad associations. The material gathered is very extensive. In elucidating the subtle meanings of the *Kinship of the Three*, it is entirely based on the "Pre-heaven" principles of the *Changes*, discussing Confucianism and Taoism together. Every word remains faithful to the original intent of Lord Wei [Boyang]. Within the book, one frequently sees former...

[He reveals] what people have not yet seen and brings to light what predecessors have not yet expressed; he is not to be compared with those who merely perform the task of <term>philological commentary <note>original: "xun-gu," the traditional scholarly practice of explaining the literal meaning and pronunciation of ancient words.</note></term>. Moreover, each volume includes appended diagrams to clarify the principles, making this Way even more manifest. 

Even small matters, such as the subtle details of the <term>alchemical oral secrets <note>original: "koujue," specific, often cryptic instructions passed down verbally from master to student to ensure the practice is performed correctly.</note></term>, are not omitted. Thus, Ruan Dengbing said that Yu Yan must have received instruction from a miraculous master, and this is truly no empty boast.

# Resolving Doubts on the Kinship of the Three in the Book of Changes

Written by Yu Yan (literary name Yuwu) of the Song Dynasty, in three sections. The *Kinship of the Three* is a book where the Way is extremely high and profound, and its principles are extremely mysterious and remote. Despite the vast knowledge of <term>Master Zhu Xi <note>The preeminent Confucian scholar of the Song Dynasty, who despite his brilliance, found this text difficult.</note></term>, he ultimately could not help but say: "Only now have I found the threads of it, but I have not yet grasped its specific ingredients and key openings." 

Because its secrets are hidden and difficult to penetrate, later generations frequently changed the text recklessly; their division into chapters and explanations of meaning were often riddled with errors. This book is more accurate and appropriate than the edited versions by Master Peng Zhenyi, Master Chen Baoyi, and Master Zheng Xuyi, as well as the "Critical Examination of Differences" by Master Zhu of Chaiyang. This is because Yu Yan both received instruction from an enlightened teacher and was able to cross-reference and <term>collate <note>original: "chou-jiao," the scholarly process of comparing different versions of a text to identify and correct errors.</note></term> the various regional editions from Shu (Sichuan), Yue (Zhejiang), and Ji (Jiangxi), along with the various versions from the Qiantang schools.

<summary>This page concludes the praise for Yu Yan’s scholarship, noting his inclusion of diagrams and oral traditions. It introduces his work "Resolving Doubts," positioning it as a superior, highly accurate edition of the "Kinship of the Three" based on rigorous comparison of multiple regional manuscripts.</summary>

# Preface to the <term>Rectified Meaning <note>original: "Zhengyi," a scholarly commentary intended to establish the "correct" or orthodox interpretation of a classic text.</note></term> of the <term>Kinship of the Three <note>original: "Cantong Qi," the foundational text of Taoist alchemy which uses the "Book of Changes" to explain spiritual and physical transformation.</note></term> according to the <term>Book of Changes <note>original: "Zhouyi," commonly known as the I Ching.</note></term>

Among the ten thousand volumes of <term>alchemical books <note>original: "danshu," literally "books of the elixir," referring to texts on the pursuit of immortality.</note></term>, the *Kinship of the Three* is foremost. Its language is ancient, its explanations are profound, and its underlying principles are deep and vast. When it speaks of the *Book of Changes*, it describes the transformation of Yin and Yang and the union of Heaven and Humanity. When it speaks of the <term>Elixir <note>original: "dan," the substance or state of immortality.</note></term>, it clarifies both the <term>fire phases <note>original: "huohou," the timing and intensity of the meditative or laboratory heat.</note></term> and the <term>medicinal ingredients <note>original: "yaowu," the substances or internal energies being refined.</note></term>, making both the internal and external aspects clear. Truly, it is a supreme work where <term>Confucianism and Taoism <note>original: "Ru Dao."</note></term> walk hand in hand. It is indeed a masterpiece that stands alongside the Classics and Histories, remaining immortal throughout the ages.

How regrettable it is, then, that narrow-minded men and those of shallow learning cannot refine their study of its meaning or fully grasp its mysteries! They all point to it merely as a book for refining elixirs, while neglecting its Confucian purpose. This causes the Great Way to sink into obscurity and these most perfect words to become clouded. This is deeply pitiable. Occasionally, one or two scholars may wish to expound upon its Way and support this book, but they have not met a true teacher nor received the oral instructions. Relying only on their own <term>subjective guesswork <note>original: "yidu."</note></term>, how can they explore the <term>hidden clockwork <note>original: "yuanji," the subtle, divine mechanics of the universe.</note></term> of <term>Lord Wei <note>original: "Wei Gong," referring to Wei Boyang, the legendary 2nd-century author of the text.</note></term>? Consequently, their works are confused and numerous, and their errors are many indeed. Alas! Even if such commentaries were to "sweat the oxen and fill the house to the rafters" <note>A traditional idiom for an overwhelming number of books.</note>, what benefit would they bring to this text? And if there is no benefit, does it not actually cause harm? This is the reason why this Way is so often not practiced.

I have long admired the <term>mysterious cultivation <note>original: "xuanxiu."</note></term> and have applied myself to this Way for many years. However, I have been hindered by the <term>toil of the "trap and the snare" <note>original: "quantishi," a philosophical metaphor from the Zhuangzi meaning being stuck on the tools or words rather than the actual truth.</note></term> and the entanglements of worldly affairs. I have not yet been able to devote my full will to practice or enter the "inner chambers" of this knowledge to correct the errors in this book; for this, I am quite ashamed.

Now, Master <term>Yuanzhen <note>literally "Original Truth."</note></term> of Mount Sifeng treats profit and fame like <term>worn-out sandals <note>original: "bixi," a metaphor for something utterly worthless.</note></term> and views his own life and the world as mere floating foam. He has received the essential instructions of a <term>Perfected Person <note>original: "zhiren," a high-level Taoist adept.</note></term> and attained the subtle mysteries of the Great Way. Unwilling to let this true scripture fall into oblivion, he has created detailed explanations for each chapter and meticulous analyses of every sentence. He has washed away the crude habits of various other schools to create a fresh perspective. He ensures that the three paths—the Great *Changes*, <term>internal cultivation <note>original: "neiyang."</note></term>, and <term>laboratory alchemy <note>original: "luhuo," literally "stove and fire."</note></term>—are all explored to their furthest depths and traced back to a single source. The true mechanics of the universe are revealed here, shining as brightly as the sun and stars. This is what is meant by "the Way being clarified and the meaning being rectified." His service to the masters of the past and his kindness to the students of the future are truly significant.

In the future, when the Master’s work is complete and he ascends to meet the various Immortals in the <term>Jasper Orchards of the Fairy Isles <note>original: "Penghu," "Qiongyuan," mythical abodes of the immortals.</note></term>, Lord Wei will surely say to him: "You have truly been able to participate in my mystery, unify with my essence, and harmonize with my book." In that moment, how joyful he will be!

Those of outstanding talent who possess ancient <term>spiritual roots <note>original: "linggen," an innate predisposition for spiritual practice.</note></term> and are able to view this book are experiencing the great fortune of three lifetimes. You must apply your mind with single-pointed focus and study it with diligence over a long period. In this way, your studies may return to the Correct Way without being confused by many branching paths, allowing you to enter the inner chambers and wonderfully ascend to the Mystery. This is my great hope for all you gentlemen.

Respectfully prefaced on the full moon of the first month of spring in the <term>fifty-fourth year of the Qianlong reign <note>February 1789 AD.</note></term>.

<summary>This preface by an admirer of Master Yuanzhen argues that the "Kinship of the Three" is a masterwork uniting Confucianism and Taoism, which has been misunderstood by many as a simple chemistry manual. It introduces Yuanzhen's commentary as the definitive guide that reveals the "Rectified Meaning" through secret oral traditions.</summary>

It focuses on the historical relationship between the "Three Teachings" (Confucianism, Taoism, and Buddhism) and argues that the path of the Taoist immortal is fundamentally compatible with the social virtues of the Confucian scholar.</meta>

# Self-Preface to the <term>Rectified Meaning <note>original: "Zhengyi."</note></term> of the <term>Kinship of the Three <note>original: "Cantong Qi."</note></term> according to the <term>Book of Changes</term>
## Written by Xu Lichun, the <term>Wayfarer of Pingyang <note>original: "Pingyang Daoren," a Taoist sobriquet.</note></term> and junior scholar of Yu, at the Kuocang Mountain Studio.

The ancient sages’ choice to enter or leave public life followed two paths: <term>official service and reclusion <note>original: "shi yin," the tension between serving the government and living as a hermit.</note></term>. Those who were hermits first and later became officials were men like <term>Yi Yin and Tai Gong <note>Yi Yin was a sage-minister of the Shang Dynasty; Tai Gong (Jiang Ziya) was the strategist who helped found the Zhou Dynasty.</note></term>. Those who served as officials first and later became hermits were men like <term>Weizi and Jizi <note>Princes of the falling Shang Dynasty who withdrew from society to maintain their integrity.</note></term>. There were those who served entirely as officials, such as <term>Gao, Kui, Zhou, and Zhao <note>Famous ministers of the legendary sage-kings and the early Zhou Dynasty.</note></term>. There were those who remained entirely in reclusion, such as <term>Chao, Xu, Bo Yi, and Shu Qi <note>Chao Fu and Xu You were legendary hermits who refused the throne; Bo Yi and Shu Qi died of hunger rather than serve a new dynasty.</note></term>. There was also <term>Confucius</term>, who moved between service and reclusion, serving when it was appropriate and stopping when it was necessary. Furthermore, there was <term>Laozi</term>, whose service and reclusion were never fixed and whose presence and absence were unpredictable. These were all sages and worthies of old. Though their choices to serve or hide differed, they were united in <term>Virtue and the Way <note>original: "Daode."</note></term>. Thus, whether they served or withdrew, they moved in harmony with the times. When successful, they shared their goodness with the whole world; when in poverty, they cultivated their own goodness in solitude. The sages never had a rigid or fixed mind regarding their actions; they simply listened to Heaven and followed their <term>destiny <note>original: "ming."</note></term>.

Now, as for the <term>study of the immortals <note>original: "shenxian zhi xue," referring to Taoist practices for longevity and spiritual transcendence.</note></term>, is it not primarily a matter for those in reclusion? They follow the examples of Chao and Xu by escaping the world and avoiding people; they imitate Bo Yi and Shu Qi by gathering herbs and eating simple vegetables. They practice the <term>social ethics <note>original: "lunchang," the Five Relationships of Confucianism.</note></term> to honor sacred learning, and they cultivate their <term>nature and life-destiny <note>original: "xingming," a central concept in Taoist alchemy referring to both spiritual essence and physical vitality.</note></term> to reach the True Source. They accumulate <term>essence <note>original: "jing."</note></term>, build up <term>energy <note>original: "qi."</note></term>, nourish their will, and preserve their <term>spirit <note>original: "shen."</note></term>. When their path is complete and their virtue established, they apply their merits to the world. Although this may not reach the vast scale of the <term>Confucian teachings <note>original: "shengjiao," literally "the Sage's teachings."</note></term>, they nonetheless provide aid according to the times and extend their blessings to the people. Regarding the Way of Governance, how could this be considered a small contribution? This is why, when <term>Confucius and Laozi discussed ritual</term>, there were no words of disagreement between them. And when <term>Mencius</term> rejected the schools of Yang Zhu and Mozi, he was never heard to speak a word against Laozi. This clearly shows that their Way is the same and their Virtue is in harmony. Otherwise, would Mencius have remained silent and failed to speak out against it?

Thus, from the time of the <term>Three Dynasties <note>The Xia, Shang, and Zhou (approx. 2070–256 BC).</note></term> down through the Qin and Han, there was no distinction between "us" and "them." It was not until the Tang and Song dynasties that Confucian scholars began to group Buddhism and Taoism together. From that point on, a Confucian was a Confucian, and a Taoist was a Taoist; they could no longer be unified or return to the same source. What was the reason for this? It was because at that time, <term>Buddhism flourished greatly</term> in the world, and those who studied immortality often used Buddhist concepts for evidence and comparison. Occasionally, they even criticized Confucian scholars. Furthermore, their residences, temples, and their ways of coming and going all resembled those of the Buddhists. The only difference was that they did not shave their heads and retained their family names. This caused Confucian scholars to view them as a "heterodox study." All of this is the fault of later generations who did not properly uphold the Way. Could it be that things were originally like this in the past? That the Way is not understood and the Way is not practiced is precisely due to this. Yet, the Way itself...

<summary>In this preface, Xu Lichun argues that Taoism and Confucianism were originally a single, harmonious path. He blames the later division between the "Three Teachings" on the influence of Buddhism and the poor conduct of later practitioners who lost sight of the original unity of the ancient sages.</summary>

<keywords>Xu Lichun, Three Teachings, Confucianism, Taoism, Buddhism, Official Service and Reclusion, Sage Kings, Xingming, Internal Alchemy, Historical Philosophy, Tang and Song Dynasties</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Self-Preface" by Xu Lichun. While the previous page established the theoretical harmony between Confucian service and Taoist reclusion, this page traces the specific lineage of masters who embodied this unity and introduces the "Kinship of the Three" (Cantong Qi) as the definitive text that synthesizes the Book of Changes with the art of alchemy.</meta>

# Self-Preface to the <term>Rectified Meaning</term> of the <term>Kinship of the Three</term> (Continued)

The origins of how this knowledge was transmitted from the high antiquity are difficult to know in full detail. However, from the time <term>Laozi</term> passed it to <term>Guan Yinzi <note>Also known as Yin Xi, the gatekeeper who traditionally requested Laozi to write the Tao Te Ching.</note></term>, every generation has produced its masters, too numerous to count. In the Han dynasty, there were Lord <term>Wei Boyang</term>, Lord <term>Dong Feng</term> of Luyang, and Lord <term>Yang Qingxia</term>. There was also Lord <term>Zhongli Quan <note>A legendary immortal often depicted with a fan, said to be the teacher of Lü Dongbin.</note></term>. In the Tang dynasty, there was Lord <term>Lü Dongbin <note>One of the most famous of the Eight Immortals.</note></term>, who then transmitted the Way to <term>Liu Haichan</term> of Liao. Liu, in turn, passed it to <term>Zhang Boduan <note>Author of the "Understanding Reality" (Wuzhen pian), a foundational text of Internal Alchemy.</note></term> in the Song dynasty. Zhang transmitted it to <term>Shi Xinglin</term>, who passed it to <term>Xue Zixian</term>, who passed it to <term>Chen Niwan</term>, who finally passed it to <term>Bai Ziqing <note>This identifies the "Southern Lineage" of Taoist Internal Alchemy.</note></term>.

These ten or so masters were all able to <term>unify the Confucian and Taoist paths <note>original: "Ru Dao heyii."</note></term> into a single source. Thus, their names are recorded in the <term>blue annals <note>original: "qingbian," a poetic term for history books.</note></term>, and their persons have ascended to the <term>cerulean heights <note>original: "biluo," the Taoist heavens.</note></term>. Their names are praised by everyone; even women and children know their surnames, their life stories, and their origins. They are truly the most illustrious among the immortals. There were also the two masters <term>Tao Hongjing</term> and <term>Chen Tuan</term>. They were <term>True Confucians</term> and <term>True Immortals</term> simultaneously, proving that these paths can run parallel without contradicting one another. These men are the outstanding paragons of the unified teachings of Confucianism and Taoism.

Regarding the emergence of Taoist books: after the *Tao Te Ching* and the *Book of Guan Yinzi*, although every generation produced new works, they ultimately failed to fully express the profound mysteries. It was not until Lord <term>Wei Boyang</term> that the study of the <term>Pre-heaven <note>original: "Xiantian," referring to the primordial state before the physical universe manifested.</note></term> principles of the *Book of Changes* was brought to light. He clarified the meaning of the sun and moon forming the character for "Change" <note>The Chinese character for "Change" (易) is traditionally explained as a composite of "Sun" (日) and "Moon" (月).</note>. He used the four hexagrams—<term>Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li <note>The hexagrams representing Heaven, Earth, Water, and Fire.</note></term>—as the "substance and function" of Yin and Yang, serving as the primary framework for all other hexagrams. The remaining sixty hexagrams all emerge from the transformations of these four, reaching into the principles of good and ill fortune, and the cycles of growth and decay. This covers the calculations of the seasons and the solar terms, elucidating the way the Great Changes govern both politics and the calendar.

Furthermore, he used the principles of the <term>intercourse of Yin and Yang</term> and the mechanics of the sun and moon's cycles. He used <term>Qian and Kun</term> as the Cauldron and Furnace, and <term>Kan and Li</term> as the Medicinal Ingredients. He used the various hexagrams as the "Fire Tallies" <note>Timing instructions for the alchemical heat.</note>, employing the interaction of the firm and the yielding to clarify the <term>Alchemical Way <note>original: "Dandao."</note></term> of cultivation associated with the Yellow Emperor and Laozi. This is truly a book where Confucianism and Taoism run side-by-side; it is a work that succeeds and continues the *Book of Changes*. Therefore, the fact that it is titled *The Kinship of the Three according to the Book of Changes* is truly meaningful!

However, among the dozens of later commentators who have explained this book—setting aside the false and heterodox theories which I will not discuss—some point to it only as a study of <term>Internal Alchemy <note>original: "Neidan," spiritual cultivation within the body.</note></term>, while others point to it only as the art of the <term>Furnace and Fire <note>original: "Luhuo," meaning External Alchemy or laboratory chemistry.</note></term>. Consequently, they fail to deeply investigate the "Way of Changes" that is the very root and source of the text. They also fail to understand the hidden mechanics and profound meanings of the alchemical methods. Some even claim that the discussion of hexagrams and the imagery of the *Changes* are merely borrowed metaphors used to express the Alchemical Way.

Alas! This is why the *Kinship of the Three*, though seeking to be clear, has actually become obscured. These people fail to consider that this book actually contains all three subjects: the Great Changes, Internal Cultivation, and the Alchemical Furnace. Therefore, Chapter Six of the final volume says:

->The three paths stem from one,<-
->All emerging from the same track.<-

And Chapter Seven says:

->They emerge together but have different names,<-
->All originating from a single gate.<-

These two chapters list the effects and functions of the "Three Paths" in order to summarize the Great Purpose of the three volumes. What Confucius called "returning to the same point by different routes" and "reaching a single result through a hundred thoughts" is exactly what the *Kinship of the Three* describes. 

Now, I, with my lazy and humble character from the mountains...

<summary>Xu Lichun traces the lineage of Taoist masters from Laozi to the Song dynasty, arguing that the "Kinship of the Three" is a perfect synthesis of I Ching philosophy and alchemical practice that later commentators have narrowly misinterpreted.</summary>
