<meta>This page concludes the preface by Dong Dening (writing under the pseudonym Yuanzhenzi). While the previous context established the lineage of the "Kinship of the Three," this concluding passage explains the author's personal journey, his struggle to find a true teacher, and his eventual decision to publish this commentary to guide others away from "crooked paths." Note that while previous pages may have mentioned Xu Lichun, Dong Dening is the primary commentator of the "Rectified Meaning" (Zhengyi) edition.</meta>

I am a man of simple character, lacking in literary refinement. However, my family's heritage was rooted in the books of the <term>Sages <note>Refers to the Confucian classics.</note></term>. Although I cannot claim to have mastered their inner depths, I have at least stepped within their gates. Furthermore, since my youth, I have admired the <term>Way of Cultivating Nature and Life <note>original: "Xingming zhi dao," the dual cultivation of internal spirit and physical vitality.</note></term>, yet for a long time I did not encounter its <term>True Transmission</term>. Over twenty years passed by in this way.

Then, in the <term>Renyin year</term> of the <term>Qianlong reign <note>1772 CE.</note></term>, relying on the protection of Heaven, I finally obtained the <term>True Explanation</term>. For over ten years, I have spent my mornings and evenings elucidating and practicing it. Although the "fluttering wings of <term>ascension</term>" <note>A poetic reference to becoming a Taoist immortal and flying to heaven.</note> are still something I must wait for, I have already grasped the <term>Primal Mechanism</term> of internal cultivation. How could I keep this knowledge hidden and silent? To do so would be to betray the intent of Heaven.

Thus, not minding my own lack of skill, I annotated this book. The first draft was completed in the early summer of the <term>Jiachen year <note>1784 CE.</note></term>. Five years have passed since then, and the manuscript has undergone ten complete revisions. Originally, I intended to keep it secret within the mountains, having no desire to present it to the world. However, I was once again instructed by my <term>True Teacher</term> to circulate it widely. Therefore, I have committed it to the <term>printing blocks <note>original: "li zao," literally "pear and jujube," the wood commonly used for carving book-printing blocks.</note></term>.

I have titled it the <term>Rectified Meaning</term>. This title is drawn from the words of <term>Master Dong <note>Dong Zhongshu (c. 179–104 BCE), a famous Han dynasty scholar.</note></term>: "Rectify the meaning and do not plot for profit." Furthermore, "Meaning" <note>The word "Yi" (義) can mean "meaning," "righteousness," or "correct principle."</note> is the correct path for humanity. My humble desire is to lead future scholars back to the <term>Righteous Way</term>, ensuring they do not wander into crooked paths or <term>heterodox sects <note>original: "pangmen," literally "side doors," referring to incorrect, marginal, or dangerous spiritual practices.</note></term>. This is the extent of my simple intention. I add these few words as a preface to the head of these volumes, so that those who truly possess the Way may examine and correct them.

->Written on the first day of the second month of the <term>Wushen year</term> of the <term>Qianlong reign <note>1788 CE.</note></term><-

->By the junior scholar of <term>Kuaiji</term>, **Dong Dening** (also known as **Yuanzhenzi**), at the <term>Jiyang Pavilion</term> of the <term>Four Peaks Mountain Residence</term>.<-

He spent the following sixteen years refining this commentary, which he titled "Rectified Meaning" to guide students toward the authentic Taoist path and away from heterodox practices.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from Dong Dening's personal preface to the "General Principles" (Fanli) of the manuscript. # Rectified Meaning of the Kinship of the Three: General Principles

First, the <term>Kinship of the Three <note>original: "Cantong Qi." A foundational text of internal alchemy, traditionally attributed to Wei Boyang of the Han Dynasty.</note></term> was originally a book intended for the use of the <term>Taoist community <note>original: "Daozhong," referring to those practicing spiritual cultivation.</note></term>. If a <term>Confucian scholar <note>original: "Ruzhe."</note></term> employs it, they can govern the state and manage the administration. If a <term>Taoist practitioner <note>original: "Daojia."</note></term> follows it, they can nourish their nature and cultivate their physical life. Unfortunately, the various commentaries on this book all designate it solely as the <term>Way of the Elixir <note>original: "Dandao," or internal alchemy.</note></term> and neglect its <term>Principles of the Changes <note>original: "Yili," the philosophical and cosmological principles found in the I Ching (Book of Changes).</note></term>. For this reason, Confucian scholars have set it aside and do not examine it. Only <term>Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200 CE), the preeminent philosopher of Neo-Confucianism.</note></term> understood its fundamental source. Furthermore, he stated that the <term>Pre-celestial Study <note>original: "Xiantian zhi xue," referring to the cosmic order before the physical world manifested.</note></term> within the *Book of Changes* was lost to later generations until <term>Master Shao <note>Shao Yong (1011–1077 CE), a Song dynasty philosopher famous for his cosmological and mathematical studies of the I Ching.</note></term> first began to elucidate it. This Master Shao obtained his knowledge from <term>Chen Xiyi <note>Chen Tuan (c. 871–989 CE), a semi-legendary Taoist figure credited with transmitting diagrams that became central to Neo-Confucian cosmology.</note></term>, and the lineage of Xiyi’s source was actually rooted in the *Kinship of the Three*. Thus, Master Zhu once engaged in repeated debates and discussions with <term>Cai Xishan <note>Cai Yuanding (1135–1198 CE), a close associate of Zhu Xi and an expert in the mathematical principles of the I Ching.</note></term> regarding the purpose of the *Kinship*. He even went as far as to produce a <term>Critical Collation and Explanation <note>Refers to the "Zhouyi Cantong Qi Kaoyi," a commentary attributed to Zhu Xi (written under the pseudonym Zhou Yi).</note></term> of it. Today, the writings of these two worthies are preserved within the <term>Confucian forest <note>A metaphor for the community of Confucian scholars and their published works.</note></term>, and they serve as clear, verifiable evidence that this is not a false claim.

First, the book of the *Kinship of the Three* uses the language of the <term>Han Dynasty</term>. Its prose and vocabulary are ancient and obscure. Added to this are the profound and subtle principles of the *Changes*, and the mysterious, wondrous nature of the *Way of the Elixir*. Therefore, among all books, this one is particularly difficult to understand. Later people who read this book are not only unable to reach its mysterious logic, but even the literal meaning of the text is difficult to clarify. This leads to everyone having their own individual views, resulting in a confusing multitude of divergent paths. That this <term>Way</term> is not practiced is due to it not being understood. Therefore, those who annotate this work should detail and examine the literal meaning of the text, deeply investigate the principles of the *Changes*, and only then research the depths of alchemical study. In this way, perhaps the internal and external may be fused together, the merit of the work will equal that of <term>creation and transformation <note>original: "zaohua," referring to the natural creative power of the universe.</note></term>, and the Way can be attained.

First, Master Zhu said that the literary style of the *Kinship of the Three* is exceptionally fine, and its use of characters is entirely based on ancient texts. He also said that it is crafted with extreme wonder and precision. Therefore, regarding the classical allusions cited within this *Kinship*, I am but a <term>late-coming student</term>; how could I fully understand them all? Furthermore, I am limited by the <term>size of the pages <note>original: "chifu," literally "foot of cloth," referring to the physical space constraints of the manuscript or woodblocks.</note></term> and cannot include them all. I have only marked out those that originate from the *Changes* one by one, while also briefly explaining their meaning, to clarify that this *Kinship* was written as a successor to the *Book of Changes*.

First, those who have historically written commentaries on alchemical books have generally not provided the <term>fanqie <note>An ancient method of indicating the pronunciation of a Chinese character using two other characters.</note></term> pronunciation for characters, nor have they explained the definitions of the words. I do not know why this is the case. Now, the <term>Four Books and Six Classics <note>The foundational canon of Confucianism.</note></term> were certainly used by the Sages to <term>order the heavens <note>The text breaks off here at "jing tian" (经天).</note></term>...

<summary>Dong Dening argues that the Kinship of the Three is essential for both Confucians and Taoists, noting that the great Neo-Confucian Zhu Xi recognized its importance. He explains that his commentary focuses on clarifying the archaic language and the text's deep connection to the I Ching to prevent the misunderstandings common in other alchemical works.</summary>

<keywords>Kinship of the Three, Zhu Xi, Shao Yong, Chen Tuan, Cai Yuanding, I Ching principles, Internal Alchemy, Pre-celestial study, Han dynasty prose, fanqie, General Principles</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "General Principles" of Dong Dening’s commentary. It completes a sentence from the previous page regarding the "Four Books and Six Classics" used to "order the heavens and weave the earth," and proceeds to justify the author's pedagogical approach—focusing on literal meaning before profound mystery—and his selection of sources.</meta>

...and <term>weave the earth <note>original: "weidi." This completes the classical idiom "jingtian weidi," meaning to possess great administrative or creative talent that orders the world.</note></term>. Only those who are thoroughly conversant and widely learned can hope to glimpse its threshold. Even when the former sages annotated these works, they still feared they might not be understood, so they first detailed the pronunciations and definitions of the characters before explaining the principles of the commentary. This is true for all commentaries, even those for the <term>various philosophers and the hundred schools <note>original: "zhuzi baijia," referring to the diverse philosophical traditions of ancient China.</note></term>.

Regarding the <term>alchemical books <note>original: "danshu," texts concerning internal alchemy.</note></term> of today: not only is the <term>alchemical method <note>original: "danfa."</note></term> itself mysterious, profound, and difficult to grasp, but the pronunciations and definitions of the words and phrases are often not understood, yet no explanations are provided for them. Could it be that all those who study the <term>Way</term> are naturally fluent in literary meaning and already know every character's pronunciation? It is no wonder that those who read these books are few, and those who study them are even fewer. Therefore, in my commentary on this book, I would rather risk being seen as <term>lowly or unrefined <note>original: "bilou."</note></term>; I have provided the specific character pronunciations and explained the definitions of the words, and only then have I explained the mysterious principles in detail. In this way, perhaps the wise and the simple alike may follow this path together. Is this not also the <term>natural spontaneity <note>original: "ziran," a core Taoist concept referring to things as they are in themselves.</note></term> of the Way?

**First**, there are dozens of people who have annotated this book. However, the books in my collection are few, and I am of a <term>lazy disposition <note>original: "xinmu yonglan," literally "heart and eyes are lazy."</note></term> and lack the patience to hunt everything down. Consequently, I have seen only six or seven versions. Most of this commentary arises from my own humble ideas. This is truly the result of a solitary view and limited hearing, and omissions are unavoidable. However, I have not dared to engage in <term>baseless fabrication <note>original: "duzhuan."</note></term>; I have received a lineage for my views. I trust that those who are enlightened will recognize this.

**First**, regarding the words of predecessors: where they have failed to meet the requirements of proper <term>principles <note>original: "yili."</note></term>, I should technically argue against them point by point to return to the truth. However, the purpose of writing a book is to develop <term>virtue and the Way <note>original: "daode."</note></term>. If one simply indulges in a flurry of criticisms and pointing out errors, it becomes a **book of litigation** rather than a study for attaining the Way. Therefore, where there have been errors in the past, I have simply doubled my efforts to be detailed and clear in my own commentary. If the reader's heart and eyes are made clear, they will naturally not be swayed or misled by other theories.

**First**, the revolutions of <term>Heaven and Earth <note>original: "Tiandi."</note></term> and their creative power, and the rising and sinking, the darkness and brightness of the sun and moon, are the most vast and most enlightened expressions of <term>Yin and Yang <note>original: "Yinyang."</note></term>. Whether one is governing a state or cultivating the self, one must investigate these deeply. As it is said: "When <term>the Creative and the Receptive <note>original: "Qiankun," the first two hexagrams of the I Ching, representing Heaven and Earth.</note></term> operate and act, the world is then governed." It is also said that to study the Way, one must thoroughly understand Yin and Yang and reach the depths of <term>creation and transformation <note>original: "zaohua."</note></term>. Only then can one pursue the <term>two breaths <note>original: "er qi," Yin and Yang.</note></term> in the <term>Ecliptic <note>original: "huangdao," the sun's path.</note></term> and assemble the <term>three natures <note>original: "san xing," often referring to the original essence, breath, and spirit.</note></term> in the **Primordial Palace**. Therefore, this commentary is quite detailed regarding the way of the Heavens and the <term>Seven Regulators <note>original: "qizheng," the Sun, Moon, and the five visible planets.</note></term>, in order to verify the mechanism of the **synchronized activation of Heaven and Man**.

**First**, in this commentary, I have cited both <term>Confucian and Taoist <note>original: "Rudao."</note></term> books, selecting only those that are appropriate to verify the meaning. I have not dared to recklessly drag in the classics or mix in <term>heterodox and false <note>original: "xie wei" </note></term> theories, lest I offend Heaven and...

<summary>Dong Dening explains his pedagogical choice to define basic vocabulary and pronunciations to make the text accessible. He notes that while his sources are limited, his commentary focuses on clarifying principles and celestial movements (Yin/Yang) to show the harmony between humanity and the cosmos, rather than attacking other scholars.</summary>

...bring ridicule from the <term>truly learned <note>original: "daya," referring to people of high refinement or the "Great Odes" of the Classic of Poetry.</note></term>. If those who share these goals can cultivate their virtuous conduct, study with benevolent intensity, and thoroughly investigate until they achieve the wonders of <term>spiritual awakening <note>original: "xinling shenwu."</note></term>, they may then reach the <term>Great Way of True Mystery <note>original: "Zhenxuan zhi Dadao."</note></term>.

**First**, ever since I <term>bound my hair <note>original: "shufa," indicating the age of fifteen, the traditional start of adulthood and serious study.</note></term>, I have admired the study of <term>nurturing life <note>original: "yangsheng," practices for longevity and spiritual health.</note></term>. However, whenever I read <term>alchemical classics <note>original: "danjing."</note></term>, it was just like **chewing wax** <note>original: "jiao la," a common idiom for something completely flavorless, boring, or incomprehensible.</note>. Because of this, I once made a vow: if I were ever to attain clarity regarding this Way, I would inform other students without concealment to fulfill my long-held wish. Now, having received the protection of Heaven, I have obtained the <term>true explanation <note>original: "zhenquan."</note></term>. Therefore, although I do not dare to completely leak the **secrets of Heaven** in this commentary, when compared to previous books, its organization is more detailed and clear, and the <term>true mechanism <note>original: "zhenji," the hidden workings of the universe or the body.</note></term> is revealed. The difference between this and older works is <term>vast <note>original: "jingting," literally the distance between a courtyard and a gate.</note></term>. Those who have the will to seek the Way may follow the stream to reach the source.

**First**, the chapter divisions in this commentary are mostly similar to the old editions, though I have further edited and refined them to establish the main theme of each chapter. As for the structure of the individual sections, it is quite different from older interpretations. I have followed the method used by <term>former Confucian scholars <note>original: "xianru," referring to the rigorous philological and philosophical standards of Neo-Confucian commentators.</note></term> in their commentaries on the classics: I detail the principles and investigate the wording, dividing or combining sections where appropriate. Within the commentary, I have strived to ensure the logic remains connected and threaded together, not daring to recklessly fragment the text. Furthermore, at the end of each chapter, I have added a few words of summary to clarify the general meaning of that chapter. This is because of my own <term>simple-mindedness <note>original: "yulu," a humble way of saying he is not naturally clever and struggled to learn.</note></term>; I have often suffered from the difficulty of reading, and thus in commenting on this book, I did not mind being repetitive or wordy. Yet, I also hold a hope: I wish for everyone to know the Way and for everyone to be able to discuss the <term>mysterious <note>original: "xuan," the profound depths of Taoist philosophy.</note></term>, so that determined and benevolent people may reach the summit and enter the <term>sacred realm <note>original: "shengyu," the state of sagehood or ultimate achievement.</note></term> of <term>non-action <note>original: "wuwei," the Taoist ideal of acting in perfect harmony with the natural flow.</note></term>. This is indeed my deepest wish.

Regarding the three parts of the *Kinship of the Three* <note>original: "Cantong Qi"</note>: since ancient times, it has been attributed to the work of Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the legendary 2nd-century alchemist.</note>. Peng Zhenyi <note>A famous Daoist commentator.</note> also once stated this. Others claim it was written by Lord Wei together with the Attendant Xu and Chunyu Shutong, suggesting that each of the three men described one part. However, as many years have passed and the era is remote, errors have inevitably crept in. It is ultimately difficult to investigate the original source, so one should not rashly make changes. 

Unfortunately, later generations have treated the first part as the main text while treating the middle and lower parts as mere commentaries. Others have taken the four-word verses, five-word verses, and prose sections and grouped them into chapters, claiming they were original "scripture" and "commentary." This has led to much confusion and many actual errors. They fail to consider that within the book, the four-word, five-word, and prose sections are often inseparable; such instances are found everywhere and are too numerous to list. Furthermore, the three parts—Upper, Middle, and Lower—each have their own unique logic and meaning. How could they be split into "scripture" and "commentary"? A person with a clear eye <note>meaning a discerning scholar</note> will naturally recognize this, so I will not elaborate further.

In the composition of these three parts, the author provides a general overview of the *Great Changes* <note>The I Ching</note> and the three paths of <term>Internal Cultivation</term> and <term>Laboratory Alchemy</term> <note>original: "Luhuo," literally "Furnace and Fire," referring to external chemical alchemy.</note>. 
*   In the **Upper Part**, the "Way of the *Changes*" is discussed most frequently, followed by internal cultivation, with laboratory alchemy mentioned only occasionally. 
*   In the **Middle Part**, "Internal Cultivation" is the primary focus, followed by the Way of the *Changes*, and then laboratory alchemy. 
*   In the **Lower Part**, "Laboratory Alchemy" is discussed most frequently, followed by internal cultivation, with the Way of the *Changes* being mentioned least. 

Because the level of detail regarding these three paths differs across the three parts, Lord Wei created three sections to mirror the forms of the <term>Three Primal Powers</term> <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity.</note>. Now, in my commentary, I have divided the Upper Part into sixteen chapters to mirror the balance of the "Two Eights" <note>A reference to the sixteen ounces in a traditional pound, used as a metaphor for the perfect measure of Yin and Yang.</note>. The Middle Part consists of twelve chapters to mirror the cycle of the months and the year. The Lower Part consists of eight chapters to mirror the application of the Eight Trigrams. In total, there are thirty-six chapters, mirroring the number of <term>Old Yang</term> <note>The number 36 is associated with the "Old Yang" or "Great Yang" in I Ching numerology.</note>. Taken together, they form the *Kinship of the Three*, mirroring the ultimate principle of the "Great Ultimate containing the Three." This is what is meant by the "Way of the Correct Meaning."

# The Correct Meaning of the Kinship of the Three of the Zhou Changes, Volume One

### Commentated by Dong Dening, the Master of Primal Truth, a junior scholar from Huiji

## Part One

**The hexagrams Qian and Kun are the gateway to the *Changes*. They are the parents of all the hexagrams. Kan and Li are the outer walls; they drive the hub and steady the axle.** <gloss>The word "hub" is pronounced *gu*. The word "axle" is pronounced *zhou*.</gloss> <note>These glosses in the original text clarify the pronunciation of the specific Chinese characters for 'hub' and 'axle' for the reader.</note>

〇 The *Book of Changes* <note>original: "Yi"</note> says: "Are not Qian and Kun the gate of the *Changes*?" It also says: "Closing the door is called <term>Kun</term> <note>The hexagram representing the Receptive, the Earth, and pure Yin.</note>; opening the door is called <term>Qian</term> <note>The hexagram representing the Creative, Heaven, and pure Yang.</note>. One closing and one opening is called 'transformation.' The unending coming and going is called 'penetration.'" It further says: "Are not Qian and Kun the inner essence of the *Changes*?" Therefore, the transformations and penetrations of Qian and Kun involve all the other hexagrams and contain all the individual lines <note>The "yao" or six horizontal lines that make up a hexagram.</note>. It is like how people and objects are housed, stored, enter, and exit through a gateway.

Furthermore, the second chapter of this book states that the *Changes* are composed of the hexagrams <term>Kan</term> <note>The hexagram representing Water and the Moon.</note> and <term>Li</term> <note>The hexagram representing Fire and the Sun.</note>, and that the Sun and Moon constitute the *Changes*. Since Qian and Kun are Heaven and Earth—fixed in their positions above and below—while the Sun and Moon travel between the East and West, entering and exiting the space of Heaven and Earth, then surely Qian and Kun are the gateway for the Sun and Moon. Thus it is said: "Qian and Kun are the gateway to the *Changes*."

By taking Qian as the father and Kun as the mother, Qian and Kun transform and give birth to the "six children." The hexagram *Zhen* <note>Thunder</note> obtains the first line of Qian and is called the eldest son. *Kan* <note>Water</note> obtains the middle line of Qian and is called the middle son. *Gen* <note>Mountain</note> obtains the top line of Qian and is called the youngest son. *Xun* <note>Wind</note> obtains the first line of Kun and is called the eldest daughter. *Li* <note>Fire</note> obtains the middle line of Kun and is called the middle daughter. *Dui* <note>Lake</note> obtains the top line of Kun and is called the youngest daughter. In this way, Qian and Kun seek each other out and interact to give birth to the six children, forming the <term>Eight Trigrams</term>. These eight trigrams overlap and combine to transform into the sixty-four hexagrams. Therefore, Qian and Kun are considered the parents of all hexagrams.

Regarding <term>Kan and Li</term>: the *Changes* considers Kan to be the Moon and Li to be the Sun. The word "outer" <note>original: "kuang"</note> means "to correct" or "to rectify." In ancient times, there was also a city named Kuang. The term used here, "outer walls" <note>original: "kuangguo"</note>, refers to the defensive walls of a city. This is a metaphor for the visible disks of the Sun and Moon. As the scholar Xu Tianchi once said, it is like the common saying for a "frame" or "casing." 

The "hub" <note>original: "gu"</note> is the center of a wagon wheel which receives the axle. The "axle" <note>original: "zhou"</note> refers to the spokes and the shaft of the wheel that meet at the hub. If the walls are straight, the city is secure; if the axle is straight, the wheel turns. The forms of the Sun and Moon are like the outer walls, and the movement of the Sun and Moon is like the hub and the axle. 

Furthermore, Kan and Li represent the two "functions" of Qian and Kun. The "outer walls" are like a boundary. These two functions transform the many hexagrams and circulate through the "six voids" <note>The six positions within a hexagram, representing the totality of space/time.</note>, just as city walls encompass the people and their goods, or as the hub and axle rotate the carriage. Therefore, they are called the "outer walls" that "drive the hub and steady the axle." Since Qian and Kun are the "substance" of Yin and Yang, while Kan and Li are the "function" of Yin and Yang, all thousands of changes and ten thousand transformations emerge from them. Therefore, Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang</note> first...

# The four female and male hexagrams act as the bellows and the covering.

# The Way of Yin and Yang is like a craftsman or a charioteer: following the plumb line and ink, holding the bit and reins, straightening the compass and square, and following the wheel ruts.
<gloss>The word for bit is pronounced *xian*. 〇 Female refers to a mother animal; male refers to a father animal. These are metaphors for <term>Yin and Yang</term> <note>The fundamental dual forces of the universe—receptive/dark and active/bright.</note>. The scholar Chen Baoyi said: "Qian is the male/female of pure Yang. Kun is the female hexagram of pure Yin. Kan is Yang within Yin. Li is Yin within Yang. These are the hexagrams where male and female intersect. Therefore, they are called the 'four female and male hexagrams.'" 

The "bellows" <note>original: "tuoyue"</note> are empty vessels. The *tuo* is the bag, and the *yue* is the pipe. These are the tools used by blacksmiths to blow air into a forge. The *Dao De Jing* <note>The foundational text of Taoism</note> says: "The space between Heaven and Earth, is it not like a bellows?" This is because Heaven and Earth cover and support from the outside, while a single breath moves back and forth within, just like a bellows. 

Thus, Qian and Kun are the "substance" of the bellows, while Kan and Li are the "function" of the bellows. Every instance of the waxing and waning of Yin and Yang, and every change in the interacting symbols, occurs within the "covering" of these four hexagrams. They create the seasonal nodes and serve as the guiding thread for all the other hexagrams. The *Book of Changes* says: "The *Changes* opens up things and completes tasks, covering the Way of the world." This is exactly what is meant here. 

Furthermore, this Way is like a craftsman following his plumb line and ink—then the compass and square are accurate and without error. It is like a charioteer holding the bit and reins—then the wheel ruts are followed and not lost. This describes how Heaven, Earth, the Sun, and the Moon have fixed paths, and the cycles of energy and numbers are full or empty; it has been thus since antiquity, without the slightest error or deviation.</gloss>

# Governing from the center to control the outside; the numbers are recorded in the pitch-pipes and the calendar.
<gloss>"Governing" <note>original: "chu"</note> means to manage; "control" <note>original: "zhi"</note> means to direct. The "pitch-pipes" <note>original: "lü-lü"</note> refer to the twelve musical pipes that correspond to the months. There are twelve pipes, which are distributed evenly to mark the balance of a year. Qian and Kun control from the outside. The rising and falling of Yin and Yang, and the coming and going of the Sun and Moon between East and West, create dawn, dusk, day, night, heat, and cold. Thus, the numbers of the pitch-pipes and calendar can be recorded, and the work of the year is completed. Therefore it is said: "Governing from the center to control the outside; the numbers are recorded in the pitch-pipes and the calendar."</gloss>

# There are five or six markers in a node; the longitude and latitude serve the Sun’s command.
<gloss>Regarding the "five or six" markers in a monthly node: a month has thirty days. Five days constitute one "waiting period" <note>original: "hou"</note>, and six of these waiting periods constitute one monthly "node" <note>original: "jie"</note>. Regarding "longitude and latitude serving the Sun's command": vertical is called longitude, and horizontal is called latitude. Also, North-South is longitude, and East-West is latitude. If we take the year as the longitude, then the month is the latitude. If we take the month as the longitude, then the day is the latitude. "Command" <note>original: "shi"</note> means "order" or "master." When speaking of years and months, they all generally follow the Sun as the primary master. For...</gloss>

# Meng then takes its turn; there is one hexagram for day and one for night. They are used in sequence, until After Completion and Before Completion reach the dark and the dawn. When the end is reached, the cycle begins again.
<gloss>The word *Tun* is pronounced like *zhi* <note>meaning "to take charge."</note>. The word *Fu* is pronounced like *fu-hou*.</gloss>

〇 There are sixty-four hexagrams in the <term>Zhouyi</term> <note>The *Book of Changes*, the foundational Chinese divination manual used here as a cosmological map.</note>. Now, the text mentions only sixty because the four hexagrams <term>Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li</term> act as the "substance" and the "function." They are the guiding principles of all the hexagrams. The remaining sixty hexagrams all arise from the Yin and Yang interactions of these four, the circulation of the two functions through the "six voids" <note>the six positions of a hexagram</note>, the shifting of the lines, and the merging of their forms. Therefore, it is said that "combined they make sixty."

Generally, hexagrams belonging to Yang are "firm," such as those in the categories of Qian, Kan, Gen, and Xun. Those belonging to Yin are "yielding," such as those in the categories of Xun, Li, Kun, and Dui. Furthermore, there is the firmness or yielding of the individual lines: single lines <note>—</note> are firm, and broken lines <note>--</note> are yielding. Every doubled hexagram has six lines. The bottom three lines are the "inner hexagram," which is the interior. The top three lines are the "outer hexagram," which is the exterior. Therefore, it is said: "The firm and the yielding have an interior and exterior."

"On the new moon day, the hexagram Tun takes charge; until evening, Meng then takes its turn": The "new moon" <note>original: *shuo*</note> is the first day of the month. "Dawn" <note>original: *dan*</note> is early morning. As the previous text mentioned, the four female and male hexagrams cover and regulate the Way of Yin and Yang to establish the numbers of the seasons and nodes. Now, these combined sixty hexagrams are distributed throughout the month to establish the measures of the days, hours, day, and night. Thus, on the morning of the first day, the hexagram *Tun* <note>Hexagram 3, "Initial Difficulty"</note> is in charge. On the evening of the first day, the hexagram *Meng* <note>Hexagram 4, "Youthful Folly"</note> takes over the duties. This is what is meant by "one hexagram for day and one for night."

"Used in sequence" means following the order of the Upper and Lower Classics of the *Zhouyi*, but excluding the four hexagrams Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li; the rest are used in their established order. "Until After Completion and Before Completion reach the dark and the dawn": <term>After Completion</term> is the hexagram *Jiji*. <term>Before Completion</term> is the hexagram *Weiji*. "Dark" <note>original: *hui*</note> is the end of the month, or darkness. "Dawn" <note>original: *shuang*</note> is light. This means that at the dawn of the thirtieth day, *After Completion* is used; at the dark of the thirtieth day, *Before Completion* is used.

"When the end is reached, the cycle begins again" means that starting from *Tun* and *Meng* on the new moon and ending with *After Completion* and *Before Completion* on the final day, once the end is reached, it begins again, like a ring with no end. In the <term>Alchemical Method</term>, these sixty hexagrams are used for the <term>Fire Phasing</term> <note>original: *huohou*; the precise timing and intensity of the meditative or chemical heat</note>. Within the tripod and furnace, there are also phases of the new moon, full moon, and the quarters. The student should deeply investigate the substance and function of these hexagrams.

# The solar hours serve as the periodic measures; movement and stillness have their mornings and evenings. Spring and Summer rely on the internal substance, from the hour of the Rat to the hours of the Dragon and Snake. Autumn and Winter correspond to the external function, from the hour of the Horse until the hours of the Dog and Pig.
<gloss>The word *Qi* <note>meaning "to finish"</note> is pronounced *ji*.</gloss>

〇 A year has twelve months. A month has thirty days. The period of a single day is measured by the twelve double-hours <note>original: *chen*</note>. Sunrise is morning and corresponds to movement; sunset is evening and corresponds to stillness. Therefore, it is said: "The solar hours serve as the periodic measures; movement and stillness have their mornings and evenings."

In the Way of Heaven, Earth, Yin, and Yang: Yin is internal and serves as the "substance"; Yang is external and serves as the "function." Yin governs descending, while Yang governs ascending. Just as the Winter Solstice in the month of the Rat <note>the 11th lunar month</note> marks the ascent of Yang, it emerges from the internal substance to reach the external function. The Summer Solstice in the month of the Horse <note>the 5th lunar month</note> marks the descent of Yin; it then withdraws from the external function to be stored in the internal substance. Thus, the hour of the Rat <note>11 PM – 1 AM</note> marks the birth of Yang, continuing until the hour of the Snake <note>9 AM – 11 AM</note> where Yang reaches its peak. Then the hour of the Horse <note>11 AM – 1 PM</note> marks the [birth of] Yin...

# Rewards and punishments correspond to Spring and Autumn; dusk and dawn follow cold and heat. The line statements contain benevolence and righteousness; joy and anger are expressed according to the seasons. Thus, they correspond to the four seasons, and the five elements find their order.

<gloss>The word *Yao* <note>hexagram line</note> is pronounced like *yao* <note>original: 肴</note>.</gloss>
<gloss>○ "Correspond" <note>original: *ying*</note> means "to match" <note>original: *dang*</note>.</gloss>

The Yang energy matches Spring and brings about life; this giving of life is "reward." The Yin energy matches Autumn and brings about the "withering-kill" <note>the natural cessation of growth</note>; this killing is "punishment." Therefore, it is said: "Rewards and punishments correspond to Spring and Autumn."

Sunrise brings light and the air is warm; sunset brings dusk and the air is cool. To "follow" means to comply with. This means that the warmth and coolness of a single day’s dawn and dusk comply with the cold and heat of a full year’s Winter and Summer. Therefore, it is said: "Dusk and dawn follow cold and heat."

Regarding "the line statements contain benevolence and righteousness": The <term>lines</term> <note>original: *yao*</note> are the physical marks drawn in a hexagram. The <term>statements</term> <note>original: *ci*</note> are the words attached to them by the Duke of Zhou and the commentaries written by the Master <note>Confucius</note>; these are collectively called "line statements," and they are used to judge the good or bad fortune of each line. Just as lines can be "firm" or "yielding," the statements contain "benevolence" or "righteousness." Firmness is Yang and corresponds to benevolence; yielding is Yin and corresponds to righteousness. As the *Book of Changes* says: "Establishing the Way of Heaven, it is called Yin and Yang. Establishing the Way of Earth, it is called Yielding and Firm. Establishing the Way of Man, it is called Benevolence and Righteousness." This is the meaning.

Regarding "joy and anger are expressed according to the seasons": To "follow" means to comply with, and "seasons" refers to the four seasons. Spring and Summer govern growth and life; they are Yang and represent "joy." Autumn and Winter govern harvesting and storage; they are Yin and represent "anger." This means complying with the "commands" of the four seasons by contracting or expressing the Yin and Yang of joy and anger.

Regarding "thus they correspond to the four seasons, and the five elements find their order": The previous sections have listed the "substance and function" of the four primary "male and female" hexagrams. These are used to transform the sixty-four hexagrams and encompass the divine mechanism of Heaven, Earth, Yin, and Yang. By doing so, they establish the cosmic timing for years, months, days, and hours. Consequently, Spring is naturally warm, Summer is hot, Autumn is cool, and Winter is cold, with each of the four seasons matching its proper climate. Spring is Wood, Summer is Fire, Late Summer is Earth, Autumn is Metal, and Winter is Water; thus, the <term>Five Elements</term> <note>the fundamental phases of energy: Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, Water</note> find their correct sequence.

<meta>This page transitions from the conclusion of Chapter One into a deeper metaphysical analysis of the four core hexagrams. # Heaven and Earth set the positions, and the Changes operate within them.
<gloss>"Set" means to establish or place. The "Changes" <term>Yi</term> <note>original: *Yi* 易</note> refers to the principle of "life-begetting-life." This is because Yin and Yang produce one another endlessly. This includes things like the intersection of Yin. Therefore, Heaven and Earth set the positions above and below, and the transformations of Yin and Yang move between them. These two lines are the words of the Master <note>Confucius</note> from the *Great Commentary* of the *Book of Changes*. Now, Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the author of the *Seal of the Unity of the Three*</note> cites them to clarify that the "Changes" refers to the hexagrams Kan and Li, and that the Sun and Moon together constitute the meaning of "Changes." This is explained in detail in the text below.</gloss>

# Heaven and Earth are the images of Qian and Kun; "setting the positions" means arranging the positions where Yin and Yang match.
<gloss>The *Book of Changes* says: "Qian is Heaven." It also says: "Kun is Earth." Therefore, Heaven and Earth are used as the images for the hexagrams Qian and Kun. Heaven sets its position above, and Earth sets its position below; this is the arrangement of Yin and Yang. The *Book of Changes* says: "Heaven is noble and Earth is humble; thus Qian and Kun are determined." It also says: "In its breadth and greatness, it matches Heaven and Earth; in its transformations and continuity, it matches the four seasons. The meaning of Yin and Yang matches the Sun and Moon." Therefore, it is said: "Setting the positions" means arranging the positions where Yin and Yang match. This section is Lord Wei’s explanation of the phrase "Heaven and Earth set the positions."</gloss>

# The "Changes" refer to Kan and Li. Kan and Li are the "two functions" of Qian and Kun. These "two functions" have no fixed line positions; they circulate through the "six voids," coming and going without certainty, and their movement between top and bottom is never constant.
<gloss>Kan represents the Moon. Li represents the Sun. Together, the Sun and Moon form the character for "Changes" <note>The Chinese character for *Yi* (Changes) 易 is traditionally interpreted as being composed of the characters for Sun 日 and Moon 月</note>. Thus, Kan and Li are considered the two "functions" or "tools" of the primary forces, Qian and Kun. These "two functions" are what the *Book of Changes* calls the "Use of Nine" <note>the number representing a dynamic Yang line</note> and the "Use of Six" <note>the number representing a dynamic Yin line</note>. Generally, the single/odd lines of a hexagram are Yang and called "Nine," while the broken/even lines are Yin and called "Six." The *Original Meaning of the Changes* <note>a famous commentary by Zhu Xi</note> states: "The Yang number nine is 'old' [active], while seven is 'young' [stable]. The old changes while the young does not; therefore a Yang line is called a Nine." It also says: "The Yin number six is old, while eight is young. Therefore a Yin line is called a Six." However, these two functions of Nine and Six have no fixed line position; they circulate through the "six voids." The <term>six voids</term> <note>original: *liuxu*</note> are the six empty positions of any hexagram. "Coming and going" refers to what the *Changes* calls "the departing is a contraction, the coming is an expansion." This means the two functions are constantly expanding and contracting within all the various hexagrams without having a fixed physical form. "Top" refers to the outer (upper) trigram, and "bottom" refers to the inner (lower) trigram. This means the two functions ascend and descend through the internal and external parts of the hexagrams and have no permanent dwelling place. The *Book of Changes* says: "As a Way, it frequently shifts, changing and moving without staying still, circulating through the six voids, moving between top and bottom without constancy, firm and yielding transforming into one another." This is the meaning. Furthermore, Kan and Li are the Sun and Moon, and the Sun and Moon are the "Changes."</gloss>

# The guiding principle uses nothingness to control existence. The utility of a vessel lies in its emptiness. Therefore, by deducing the cycles of waxing and waning, Kan and Li disappear.
<gloss>The "two functions" <note>Kan and Li, representing the Sun and Moon</note> have no fixed line positions; they circulate through the "six voids." This is what is meant by "hidden, submerged, and concealed." However, the firm and yielding lines of these two functions exchange places, and the odd and even numbers give birth to one another, with the actual transformation occurring in the center of the six positions. "Things" are like "events." This says that the manifestation of the two functions within the various hexagrams encompasses the waxing and waning <term>xiaoxi</term> <note>original: *xiaoxi* 消息, referring to the growth and decay of Yin and Yang</note> of all things. It contains the good and bad fortune of all matters to determine the timing of progress, retreat, survival, or death. Is this not, then, the guiding thread of the Way of the Changes? The *Tao Te Ching* <note>The foundational text of Taoism by Laozi</note> says: "We knead clay to make a vessel, but it is on the space where there is nothing that the utility of the vessel depends." It also says: "Therefore, what has existence serves for profitable adaptation, and what has nothingness serves for utility." Generally, "kneading clay to make a vessel" means mixing earth to create a container. "The space where there is nothing" refers to the empty center. Because the vessel is empty in the middle, it is good at holding things. People only recognize the "existence" of the vessel holding things as beneficial, but how many recognize that the "nothingness" of its emptiness is what provides its utility? Now, Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang</note> says "using nothingness to control existence" and "the utility of a vessel lies in its emptiness" to employ this specific meaning. He considers the "two functions" to have no fixed line positions, yet they create the hexagram images that "exist"—just as the emptiness of a clay vessel provides its utility, allowing it to hold things for our benefit. Therefore, when we deduce the waxing and waning of the line positions, we only see the physical forms of the various hexagrams, while the two functions of Kan and Li seem to "disappear." This is because they are circulating through the six voids and are concealed within the three poles <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</note>. This section and the previous one are Lord Wei's explanation of the phrase "the Changes operate within them." In the "Alchemy of the Elixir" <term>danfa</term>, Qian and Kun are the "body" (the Cauldron and Furnace), while Kan and Li are the "function" (the Medicinal Ingredients). Their Yin and Yang functions also circulate through the six voids, coming and going within the cauldron and furnace, producing existence from nothingness to form the "Sacred Embryo."</gloss>

# The Changes consist of 384 lines. Based on these lines, one selects the "tallies"; "tallies" refers to the sixty-four hexagrams.

<gloss>"Based on" <note>original: *ju* 據</note> means to follow. "Select" <note>original: *zhai* 摘</note> means to take. Furthermore, according to antiquity, there were "Three Changes," belonging to the three dynasties: the *Mountain Connection* <note>original: *Lianshan* 連山</note> of the Xia; the *Return to Receptivity* <note>original: *Guizang* 歸藏</note> of the Shang; and the *Changes of the Zhou* <note>original: *Zhouyi* 周易</note>. There are also the three Changes of "Heaven," the "Sage," and the "Mind." The rising and falling of Yin and Yang and the coming and going of the Sun and Moon are the **Heavenly Changes**. The transformations of the firm and yielding lines and the principles of good and bad fortune, growth and decay, are the **Sage’s Changes**. The constant observation of good and evil and the unpredictability of movement and stillness are the **Mind Changes**. Yet, the "Sage’s Changes" actually encompass all three. 
> Therefore the Master <note>Confucius</note> said: "The Changes are on par with Heaven and Earth; thus they can encompass the Way of Heaven and Earth." He also said: "Extend it and stretch it; touch upon similar things and grow them, and the world's tasks are complete." 
Therefore, those who study the Way must understand the movement of the Heavenly Changes, the transformations of the Sage's Changes, and the stillness and movement of the Mind Changes. By doing so, they will have mastered more than half of the art of self-cultivation.</gloss>

### Chapter Three (to the right)

# The Sage is not born in vain. Looking up, he observes the visible tallies of Heaven. The tallies of Heaven have advance and retreat; contraction and expansion respond to the seasons.

There is the coming and going of cold and heat, and the rising and setting of the Sun and Moon. These are the "advances, retreats, contractions, and expansions" of the tallies of Heaven, each responding to its specific season. Therefore, the Sage is born in the midst of Heaven and Earth; he looks up to observe the celestial and looks down to examine the terrestrial in order to establish the "human ultimate" <note>the highest standard for human conduct</note> and provide a law for the world. How could he be born in vain? The *Book of Changes* says: "Observe the divine path of Heaven, and the four seasons do not err." The Sage establishes his teachings based on this divine path, and the world submits to them. This is what the text refers to.

The first sprout of the **Return** hexagram <term>Fu</term> is established at the Winter Solstice in the eleventh month. Thus, the Master <note>Confucius</note>, in praising the **Return** hexagram in the *Changes*, said: "In **Return**, do we not see the heart of Heaven and Earth?" 

The "Heart of Heaven" is the impulse of Heaven and Earth to bring forth life. Although this impulse is visible at all times, one must wait until the tenth month—the month of "Pure Earth" <note>the **Receptive** hexagram, Kun</note>—when the Yang breath has reached the extreme of its contraction. Then, at the Winter Solstice in the eleventh month, beneath the accumulated Yin, a single Yang is born again. This is the point where the life-will of the ten thousand things, though nearly extinguished, is renewed; therefore, it is called "**Return**." The philosopher Shao Yaofu <note>Shao Yong, a famous Song dynasty cosmologist</note> said: "At the midpoint of the Rat hour during the Winter Solstice, the Heart of Heaven does not shift. At the place where the first Yang begins to move, the ten thousand things are not yet born." This is the meaning here. 

In the **Return** hexagram, the inner trigram is **Thunder** <term>Zhen</term> and the outer trigram is **Earth** <term>Kun</term>. **Thunder** represents the eldest son, who succeeds to the body of the father, **Heaven** <term>Qian</term>, and takes charge of affairs. However, he actually relies on the body of the mother, **Earth**, to establish his foundation. This is because **Earth** first "sought" from **Heaven** and obtained a single Yang line to form **Thunder**. As for the waxing and waning of the Yin and Yang transformations, they correspond to the twelve seasonal markers of the pitch-pipes. The rising, falling, brightness, and darkness of the Sun and Moon are measured by the movement of the Dipper's pivot. 

Regarding the Winter Solstice: in the year, it is the eleventh month; in the lunar month, it is the interval between the dark moon and the new moon; in the day, it is the transition between the hours of the Pig and the Rat <note>around midnight</note>. However, within the human body of the practitioner of internal alchemy <term>danfa</term>, there is also a Winter Solstice. As the *Poem on Returning to Life* says: "To refine the elixir, one need not look for the external Winter Solstice; within the body, a single Yang naturally takes birth." This is something one must understand.

## On the third day [the moon] emerges as brightness; Thunder receives the position of Geng in the West on the eighth day.

<gloss>"Brightness" <note>original: *shuang* 爽</note> means clarity or light. "Receives" means to take in. This refers to the relationship between the Moon and the Sun.</gloss>

## Joy receives the position of Ding; the first quarter is level like a string. On the fifteenth day, the body of Heaven is complete, full at the position of Jia in the East.

<gloss>Between the dark moon and the new moon—the hours of the Pig and the Rat—after the Sun and Moon have "joined their jade disks" <note>conjunction</note>, they gradually separate. By the evening of the third day, the moon first emerges with a tiny light in the West at the position of *Geng* <note>the seventh Celestial Stem</note>. Its image is like the **Thunder** hexagram <term>Zhen</term>, and it corresponds to the alchemical principle of **Thunder** receiving *Geng*; this is the birth of the "first Yang." By the evening of the eighth day, the moon appears half-bright in the South at the position of *Ding* <note>the fourth Celestial Stem</note>. Its image is like the **Joy** hexagram <term>Dui</term>, and it corresponds to **Joy** receiving *Ding*; this is the birth of the "second Yang." This time is called the "upper string" <note>first quarter moon</note> because its shape is flat like a bowstring and straight like a plumb line. By the evening of the fifteenth day, the moon pours out its full light in the East at the position of *Jia* <note>the first Celestial Stem</note>. Its image is like the **Heaven** hexagram <term>Qian</term>, and it corresponds to **Heaven** receiving *Jia*; this is the "three Yang lines" being complete. At this time, the Moon and Sun are directly opposite one another; therefore, it is called the "Full Moon" <term>Wang</term>. Its body is grand and full, without the slightest deficiency.</gloss>

# The eight paths are completed; the cycle bends and descends.

<gloss>The word "Toad" is pronounced *chu*; "Bends" is pronounced *she*. The **Toad** <term>chanchu</term> is the essence of Metal; it constitutes the physical form and body of the Moon. The **Rabbit’s spirit** <term>tupo</term> is the breath of Wood; it constitutes the radiant light of the Moon. Essentially, the Moon has no light of its own; it receives the Yang breath of the Sun, and through their mutual influence, its brightness is born. Therefore, it is said that their "breaths shine together." Furthermore, on the evening of the full moon <term>wang</term>, the Sun is about to set in the West while the Moon has already emerged in the East. At the dawn of the full moon, the Moon is about to set in the West while the Sun has already emerged in the East. The folk saying "the moon and the ox, both ends red" also refers to this meaning of "shining together." "Toad" <note>original: *chan* 蟾</note> means "to observe" <note>original: *zhan* 瞻</note>; it means that the Moon’s physical body observes the hexagram images to determine the seasonal intervals. A single month has six intervals <term>hou</term>, and the hexagrams of these six intervals are the previously mentioned **Thunder**, **Joy**, and **Heaven**, and the following **Wind**, **Mountain**, and **Earth**. Their images contain the markers of the waxing and waning of Yin and Yang, just as the Moon has its phases of fullness and deficiency. "Rabbit" <note>original: *tu* 兔</note> means "to spit out" <note>original: *tu* 吐</note>; it means the Moon’s radiance spits out its essence-breath to produce brightness. Seven and eight make fifteen; this means that when the Moon reaches the fifteenth day, its abundance has reached the limit and its path is exhausted. It must inevitably bend and descend, gradually diminishing its light.</gloss>

# On the sixteenth, the cycle turns to receive the succession of Wind; at the position of Xin, it appears at the break of dawn. Mountain corresponds to the position of Bing in the South; on the twenty-third, the "lower string" appears. Earth is at the position of Yi on the thirtieth day; in the Northeast, it loses its light.

<gloss>The word "Appears" is pronounced *xian*; "Corresponds" means "to meet." "Loses" is in the falling tone. "Succession" <term>tong</term> refers to a lineage or thread. From the new moon to the full moon, Yang has reached its limit. When Yang reaches its extreme, it turns into Yin, and Yin receives the succession of the Yang line. Therefore, at the dawn of the sixteenth day, the moon appears at the position of *Xin* <note>the eighth Celestial Stem</note> in the West. Its brightness suddenly shows a deficiency. Its image is like the **Wind** hexagram <term>Xun</term>, and it corresponds to the alchemical principle of **Wind** receiving *Xin*; this is the birth of the "first Yin." By the morning of the twenty-third day, it meets the position of *Bing* <note>the third Celestial Stem</note> in the South. Its brightness is half-deficient. Its image is like the **Mountain** hexagram <term>Gen</term>, and it corresponds to **Mountain** receiving *Bing*; this is the birth of the "second Yin." This time is called the "lower string" <note>last quarter moon</note>. By the morning of the thirtieth day, it is at the position of *Yi* <note>the second Celestial Stem</note> in the East. Its light is entirely lost. Its image is like the **Earth** hexagram <term>Kun</term>, and it corresponds to **Earth** receiving *Yi*; this is the "three Yin lines" being complete. This time is called the "Dark Moon" <term>Hui</term>. "Northeast" refers to the direction of the *Gen* and *Yin* positions; it is the place where the Moon’s cycle begins. Now, on the dark day, it is here that the light is completely lost, so that on the day of the new moon, it may revive its spirit from this same place. Thus, the third chapter of the *Middle Volume* <note>of the *Cantong qi*</note> says: "It begins in the Northeast, the region of the Winnowing Basket and the Dipper; revolving to the right, it vomits the wheel and spits out the sprout." This is the meaning here.</gloss>

# They shine upon one another and succeed the body; the Dragon is born again. Ren and Gui match Jia and Yi; Heaven and Earth enclose the beginning and the end. Seven and eight sum to fifteen; nine and six also correspond. These four join to make thirty; the Yang breath is exhausted and hidden.

<gloss>"Shine" is in the falling tone. "Again" is pronounced *fu*. "Intervals" refers to the seasonal markers of the six hexagrams mentioned above. "Succeed" means to transmit. It means that once the intervals of the six hexagrams are finished, then—</gloss>

The dark moon and the new moon continue to succeed one another in this way. The Sun and the Moon meet in the front like a **Joined Jade** <note>a celestial omen where the sun and moon are perfectly aligned</note>. Then, **Earth** <term>Kun</term> and **Return** <term>Fu</term> transmit their energy to **Thunder** <term>Zhen</term>. Therefore, it is said: "The seasonal intervals reach their end and yield to one another." "The Body" refers to the body of **Heaven** <term>Qian</term>. "The Dragon" refers to the fact that **Thunder** <term>Zhen</term> acts as the Dragon. This means that when Thunder receives the single Yang line of Heaven, it is succeeding the body of its father, Heaven. The image of the **Thunder** hexagram shows a moving thing beneath double Yin; this is the image of a living dragon. This represents Yin once again giving birth to Yang. Therefore, it is said: "Succeeding the body, the Dragon is born again." Each of the eight hexagrams receives one Celestial Stem, but **Heaven** receives *Jia* and *Ren*, and **Earth** receives *Yi* and *Gui*; these two alone receive two stems. Therefore, it is said that *Ren* and *Gui* match *Jia* and *Yi*. The ten stems begin with *Jia* and *Yi* and end with *Ren* and *Gui*. Furthermore, the new moon and the sixteenth day are the beginnings of Yin and Yang; the full moon and the thirtieth day are the endings of Yin and Yang. Since **Heaven** and **Earth** encompass all ten stems, they govern the beginning and the end. Seven and eight sum to fifteen; nine and six also correspond to fifteen. When these four numbers are joined, they make thirty days. At this time, the Yang breath of the Moon loses its brightness; it becomes utterly extinguished and hidden, becoming the **Dark Moon** <term>Hui</term>. But why is it that when discussing the six hexagrams receiving the eight stems, the hexagrams **Water** <term>Kan</term> and **Fire** <term>Li</term> and the stems *Wu* and *Ji* are the only ones not included? It is because **Water** receives *Wu* and **Fire** receives *Ji*. **Water** and **Fire** act as the "function" of **Heaven** and **Earth**, moving back and forth through the six voids, while *Wu* and *Ji* represent the soil of the **Central Palace**; they are present everywhere. Furthermore, the directions of the Moon’s rising and setting and the dates of the quarter and full moons mentioned here are only general descriptions. They are meant to clarify how the waxing and waning of Yin and Yang in the six hexagrams relate to the positions of the eight stems in the *Najia* system <note>a system of matching the I Ching hexagrams to the calendar and directions</note>. One must not be overly rigid or literal. When examining the laws of the calendar, day and night have different lengths, the Moon rises and sets early or late, its position varies, months are "long" or "short," the new moon alignment may be fast or slow, and the quarter and full moons may occur earlier or later. Yu Quanyang <note>Yu Yan, a famous 13th-century Taoist commentator</note> once debated this. Therefore, students should not let the specific words obscure the underlying meaning.

## Mirroring the Mid-winter season, the plants and trees are all broken and harmed; assist the Yang, question the traveling merchants, and let the Ruler hide himself away.

# Following the timing and obeying the seasonal command, close the mouth and do not speak.

<gloss>
The word "Question" <note>original: *jie* 詰</note> is pronounced *qi*. Once the six intervals of a single month are finished, the Dark Moon and New Moon yield to one another. When the Sun and Moon reach their "Joined Jade" alignment here, the Yang breath is extinguished and hidden. Thus, the image is like that of the **Mid-winter season** <note>the 11th lunar month</note>, when the ten thousand things are hidden and destroyed, and the plants and trees are all broken and withered. At this time, one must assist the "faint Yang" <note>the first spark of returning energy</note>. One must remain still and quiet to solidify the root of its birth. Below, one must question and restrict the traveling merchants; above, the Ruler must remain deeply hidden. Neither should be allowed to move. The **Return** hexagram <term>Fu</term> in the *Book of Changes* says: "Thunder is in the middle of the Earth: The image of Return. The former kings, on the day of the solstice, closed the passes. Merchants and travelers did not travel, and the Ruler did not inspect the provinces." The "Ruler" is the sovereign. The former kings used the day of the Winter Solstice to close the roads and gates, ensuring that both the sovereign and the people were peaceful and still to nourish that faint Yang energy. Therefore, this is called obeying the command of the season. Not only should the body be still and not move, but the mouth should also be closed and not speak. In the alchemical method, there are also the four sequences of the dark, new, quarter, and full moons, and the six intervals of the Yin and Yang fire-tally. When the "First Yang" is initially born at the "Winter Solstice" of the internal cycle, one should also be quiet and motionless, allowing the Spirit to congeal and the Breath to gather, in order to transform and nourish the **Great Medicine** <term>dayao</term>.
</gloss>

# All is silent and cannot be observed. The framing enclosure has withered and vanished. Mistakes lead to a loss of the sequence of events; boastful words return to cause self-injury. I distinguish the sequence of the Four Images to enlighten the blindness of future generations.

<gloss>
The word "Blindness" <note>original: *mang* 盲</note> is pronounced *meng*. The **Framing Enclosure** refers to the physical shapes and images of the Sun and the Moon. The **Four Images** <term>sixiang</term> refer to the numbers mentioned previously: seven, eight, nine, and six. Seven is "Young Yang," eight is "Young Yin," nine is "Old Yang," and six is "Old Yin"; these are what we call the Four Images. 

This section explains that during the **Mid-winter season**, plants and trees are destroyed and withered, and the "ten thousand things" are closed away and hidden. Although the **Single Yang** has returned <note>referring to the *Fu* or Return hexagram</note>, the spark of life is still faint. The **Way of Heaven** is vastly great, high, and wide; the **Great Mystery** <term>Taixuan</term> is utterly profound and distant, possessing no physical form. In this state, one cannot see even the slightest hint of its beginning. Now, in the interval between the **Dark Moon** and the **New Moon**, the Sun and Moon hold one another in a state of **Primordial Chaos** <term>hundun</term>. The atmosphere is empty, deep, and silent—it cannot be observed. The physical images of the Sun and Moon have vanished and are hidden in extinction. This follows the same natural principle. 

If one makes a mistake and moves recklessly, they will lose the proper thread and sequence of the work. If one boastfully claims to have reached the "peak" <note>of cultivation</note> prematurely, they bring the blame of failure and injury upon themselves. Therefore, I distinguish between the brightness and the darkness and set the Four Images in their proper order to open the eyes of those future students who are currently "blind and deaf" to these truths. 

Note: Regarding the structure of the text, from the line "Mirroring the Mid-winter season" <note>on the previous page</note> to the line "enlighten the blindness of future generations" here: in older editions, this appeared before the phrase "a common man of Kuaiji" in the Lower Chapter. Chen Baoyi moved it to the Middle Chapter, above the phrase "the Son [of Heaven] should turn to the right." However, **Yu Quanyang** <note>the 13th-century commentator Yu Yan</note> argued that both were incorrect and moved it to its current position. Upon examining the meaning of the text and the rhyme scheme, this placement is the most logical, and thus I follow it here.
</gloss>

<meta>This page continues the astronomical and cosmological explanation of the "Chaotic Heaven" (Huntian) theory, which serves as a macrocosmic model for the internal alchemical process. It details the precise movements of the Sun and Moon, the degrees of the celestial sphere, and the necessity of the intercalary month to harmonize the solar and lunar cycles.</meta>

<page-num>25</page-num>

...egg. The Earth dwells in its center, just as the shell encloses the yolk. It is as round as a pellet. Therefore, it is called the **Chaotic Heaven** <term>Huntian</term> <note>original: *huntian* 渾天</note>, describing its form as vast, unified, and revolving. This system of measurement posits that half of the heavens cover the Earth from above, and half lie beneath the Earth. The portion of the heavens visible above the Earth measures 181 degrees, and the same is true for the portion below. The North Pole rises 36 degrees above the ground, and the South Pole enters 36 degrees below the ground. The North and South poles hold the two ends of the axis, while the heavens, along with the Sun, Moon, and stars, revolve around them at an angle. 

**Master Lu of Xiangshan** <note>Lu Jiuyuan, 1139–1193 AD, a famous philosopher of the "School of Mind"</note> said: "The commentaries state that the circumference of the heavens is 365 and 1/4 degrees. The celestial body is round like a pellet, high in the north and low in the south. The North Pole is 36 degrees above the ground, and the South Pole is 36 degrees below. The diameter from the South Pole to the North Pole is 182 degrees. The midpoint between these two poles is called the **Red Path** <term>Chidao</term> <note>the Celestial Equator</note>. At the Spring Equinox, the Sun travels along the Red Path; from there, it gradually moves north. At the Summer Solstice, it travels 24 degrees north of the Red Path. After the Summer Solstice, the Sun gradually moves south until the Autumn Equinox, when it returns to the Red Path, just as it did during the Spring Equinox. At the Winter Solstice, it travels 24 degrees south of the Red Path. After the Winter Solstice, the Sun again gradually moves north. The path where the Sun travels is called the **Yellow Path** <term>Huangdao</term> <note>the Ecliptic</note>. There is also a path for the Moon's travel, which is close to the Sun's path, crossing it as it passes. Half of it is inside the Sun's path, and half is outside. Where they cross, the two paths align. At their furthest point, the two paths are 6 degrees apart. This is a general summary of the paths of the Sun and Moon."

**Master Zhu** <note>the preeminent philosopher Zhu Xi</note> further stated: "The celestial body is perfectly round, with a circumference of 365 and 1/4 degrees. It rotates to the left around the Earth, completing one revolution every day and exceeding it by one degree. The Sun is attached to the heavens but moves slightly slower; thus, in one day, it also circles the Earth once, but in terms of its position in the heavens, it falls short by one degree. After 365 and a fraction days, it meets the heavens again at the starting point; this is the measurement of the Sun's travel for one year. The Moon is attached to the heavens but is even slower; in one day, it falls short of the heavens by 13 and a fraction degrees. After 29 and a fraction days, it meets the Sun. There are twelve such meetings in a year, totaling roughly 354 days; this is the measurement of the Moon's travel for one year. A year has twelve months, and a month has thirty days; thus, 360 days is the standard number for a year. Therefore, when the Sun meets the heavens, there are over five extra days, which is called the **Solar Excess** <term>Qiying</term> <note>original: *qiying* 氣盈</note>. When the Moon meets the Sun, it is short by over five days, which is called the **Lunar Deficiency** <term>Shuoxu</term> <note>original: *shuoxu* 朔虛</note>. Combining the solar excess and the lunar deficiency gives rise to the **Intercalary Month** <term>Run</term> <note>original: *run* 閏; an extra month added to the calendar to keep the lunar year aligned with the solar seasons</note>."

**Master Hu of Yuzhai** <note>the Yuan dynasty commentator Hu Fangping</note> said: "We must consider that both the Sun and Moon are attached to the heavens. The Sun's travel falls short of the heavens by only one degree, while the Moon's travel falls short by thirteen degrees—meaning it falls twelve degrees short of the Sun. Why is this? It is because Heaven partakes of Yang and dwells above; the Sun is the essence of Yang, and the Moon is the essence of Yin. Within the process of creation, Yang is great and Yin is small; Yang is abundant and Yin is deficient. Yang can encompass Yin, but Yin cannot encompass Yang. This is why the Sun's movement always exceeds the Moon's, and the Moon's movement always falls short. If the Sun's cycle is always in surplus and the Moon's cycle is always insufficient, and one does not establish an intercalary month to align them, then the initial loss of an intercalary month would cause the first month of Spring to slide into Summer, and the first month of the year <note>the Rat month</note> to slide into the second. After three such losses, the entire season of Spring would enter Summer; after twelve, the entire year of the Rat would enter the year of the Ox. How then could the work of nature's creation be completed?"

**Master Zhu** also said: "The Way of Heaven, the Sun, the Moon, and the five planets all rotate to the left. The Way of Heaven completes one circuit of the heavens daily, always exceeding it by one degree. The Sun also completes one circuit daily, beginning and ending at its proper point; thus, compared to the Way of Heaven..."

It highlights the importance of the intercalary month in balancing the "Solar Excess" and "Lunar Deficiency" to maintain the order of the seasons.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discourse on celestial mechanics from the previous page, specifically concluding Master Zhu Xi's argument regarding the relative speeds of the Sun and Moon. It then introduces the perspectives of Master Wu of Caolu on why astronomers use "rightward" motion for calculations, and provides the author’s own synthesis of cosmology using the "Great Qi" and the egg analogy.</meta>

<page-num>26</page-num>

...is always short of the heavens by one degree. The Moon’s movement falls short of the heavens by thirteen and a fraction degrees. People today say the Moon moves fast and the Sun moves slow; this is an erroneous statement. It is only because calendar makers use the theory of **Rightward Rotation** <term>Youxuan</term> <note>the apparent motion of the planets from west to east against the background of the stars</note> to make it easier to observe the degrees of the Sun and Moon.

**Master Wu of Caolu** <note>Wu Cheng, 1249–1333 AD, a prominent Yuan dynasty scholar</note> said: "The astronomers of old were certainly not unaware that the **Seven Luminaries** <term>Qizheng</term> <note>original: *qizheng* 七政; the Sun, Moon, and the five visible planets: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note> also move to the left. However, forward motion is impossible to calculate, so they had to calculate using their retrograde retreat, matching them against the degrees of the heavens. Because of this, later generations eventually said the Sun, Moon, and Five Planets move in reverse. However, the heavens and the Seven Luminaries—all eight of these—are in motion. If we rank them by the speed of their travel, Heaven is first, **Saturn** <note>the "Filling Star" or Earth star</note> is second, **Jupiter** <note>the "Year Star" or Wood star</note> is third, **Mars** <note>the "Sparkling Deluder" or Fire star</note> is fourth, the **Sun** <note>the Great Yang</note> is fifth, **Venus** <note>the "Great White" or Metal star</note> is sixth, **Mercury** <note>the "Hour Star" or Water star</note> is seventh, and the **Moon** <note>the Great Yin</note> is eighth. Generally, the heavens, Saturn, Jupiter, and Mars move faster than the Sun, while Venus, Mercury, and the Moon move slower than the Sun. This is the general rule."

While the discussions by the various scholars mentioned above are indeed detailed and thorough, I have also heard from a **Perfected Person** <note>a Daoist term for an enlightened being or sage</note> who said: Since the **Great Ultimate** <term>Taiji</term> <note>the supreme source of all things</note> combined and formed, and **Yin and Yang** began, the Way of Heaven and Earth is nothing other than a single Qi. That Qi which flows and circulates up, down, and in the four directions without ceasing is Heaven. That which condenses into physical form and substance in the center and does not move is Earth. However, physical form has boundaries, while Qi is boundless. The Earth has its limits, but Heaven is inexhaustible. Therefore, the **Six Harmonies** <note>the four cardinal directions plus up and down; the universe</note> are all Heaven, and the Earth dwells in their center. This is what the *Classic of Internal Medicine* <note>original: *Suwen* 素問</note> means by "The Great Qi holds it up."

The ancients compared the heavens to a bird's egg and the Earth to the yolk inside the egg; this is the most accurate comparison. The center of the Earth is the hardest and most solid part; it carries the **Great Peaks** <note>original: *Huayue* 華嶽; the sacred mountains of China</note> and stabilizes the rivers and seas. People dwell upon it, and the ten thousand things are born there. Near the edges of the Earth, it gradually becomes softer and more void until there are no people or things, and the **Three Lights** <note>the Sun, Moon, and stars</note> become dim. At the furthest limit, it blends with the heavens and becomes one. It is just like the center of an egg yolk being the most solid, while the part near the egg white is slightly softer, and the yolk and white stick together, blending without a clear divide. It is only because Heaven and Earth are so vast and wide that people do not perceive this.

As for the Sun, Moon, and stars, they are the condensed essence of the Two Qi <note>Yin and Yang</note> and the Five Elements, manifesting as phenomena in the heavens. Since the Way of Heaven revolves to the left in a forward direction, the Sun, Moon, and stars naturally follow it, turning to the right <note>relative to the stars</note> and moving forward. Regarding the degrees of their travel: the Sun is the Great Yang and the Moon is the Great Yin. In the Way of Creation, Yang is active and Yin is still; Yang is firm and Yin is soft. Thus, it naturally follows that the Sun is fast and the Moon is slow. This is an unchanging principle, and the arguments of the various scholars are correct.

To summarize: the degree of the Sun's travel is such that it moves from the Midnight position <note>the Rat/North direction</note> to the Noon position <note>the Horse/South direction</note>, completing one full circuit of the heavens in a single day and returning to its original starting degree; therefore, it is called a **Day** <note>the character for Day and Sun is the same: *Ri* 日</note>. The degree of the Moon's travel is such that it aligns with the Earth at the New Moon and crosses the heavens at the Full Moon; it completes one full circuit of the heavens in one month and returns to its original starting degree; therefore, it is called a **Month** <note>the character for Month and Moon is the same: *Yue* 月</note>. The degree of Heaven's travel is the most vigorous; in one day, it travels the full count of degrees in the celestial sphere and exceeds it by one degree. Over the course of a year, these exceedances total one full circuit of the heavens, returning to the original starting degree; this is called "one full cycle of the Way of Heaven."

This is merely my **limited view** <term>Guanjian</term> <note>original: *guanjian* 管見; literally "viewing through a tube," a humble expression for one's own narrow perspective</note>. I do not know if it is correct or not, and I hope those of high intelligence will instruct me.

# The Original Essence is subtle and hard to observe; calculations of degrees validate the signs. When dwelling, observe its images.

The author uses the egg analogy to explain the relationship between the solid Earth and the boundless Qi of Heaven, defining the "Day" and "Month" through these celestial cycles.</summary>
