# Imitate its forms; establish the gnomon as a standard; observe the omens to determine fortune.

<gloss>The character for "subtle" (miao 眇) is pronounced like *miao* 藐. The character for "measure" (duo 度) is pronounced like *duo* 鐸.</gloss> 

The **Original Essence** <term>Yuanjing</term> <note>the fundamental, purest form of vital energy</note> is the Original Qi of Heaven and Earth; it is the **Original Yang** <term>Yuanyang</term>. This is what the *Record of the Stone Casket* <note>original: *Shihan ji* 石函記</note> means when it says the Original Yang is the Original Essence. "Subtle" means small. A **Gnomon** <term>Biao</term> <note>a vertical pole used to measure the sun's shadow</note> is used by astronomers to measure shadows and calculate the seasons. A "Standard" <term>Fan</term> is a template or model. 

The Original Yang Qi of Heaven and Earth travels within the **Six Harmonies** <note>the universe; the four directions plus up and down</note> and flows within the **Three Powers** <term>Sancai</term> <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</note>. There is no time it is not present, and no object that does not possess it. However, this Qi is extremely subtle and difficult to observe. Therefore, one must calculate the degrees of the movement of the **Seven Luminaries** <note>the Sun, Moon, and five planets</note> and examine the evidence of the "Heavenly Tallies" <note>celestial indicators</note> in their advancement and retreat. Only then can one silently recognize the clues of the universe. 

Internally, one observes the changes in the **Hexagram Images** <term>Guaixiang</term> to imitate the signs of their appearing forms. Externally, one establishes the gnomon as a model to observe the "Climate" <note>original: *qihou* 氣候</note> of the waning of Yin and the waxing of Yang. In this way, the good or bad fortune of all things can be determined in advance, and the favor or disaster of movement and stillness can be known beforehand. The *Book of Changes* says: "When the Superior Man dwells at home, he observes the images and contemplates the oracles; when he moves, he observes the changes and contemplates the divinations." It also says: "The Sages, seeing the complexities of the world, imitated them in forms and represented what was appropriate for each thing; therefore, these are called 'Images.'" This is the meaning here.

# Issue commands in accord with the seasons; do not miss the moment the lines move. Above, observe the patterns of the River Map. Below, order the flow of the Earth’s terrain. In the middle, examine the intentions of the human heart. Integrate and examine the Three Powers.

To "issue commands" refers to both words and actions. "Season" refers to the timing of the seasons, and "Order" refers to laws and regulations. The *Book of Changes* says: "Words and actions are the **Hinge and Spring** <term>Chuji</term> <note>original: *chuji* 樞機; the most critical mechanism of a device, like a door pivot or a crossbow trigger</note> of the Superior Man. The triggering of the hinge and spring is the master of honor or disgrace. Through words and actions, the Superior Man moves Heaven and Earth. Can he not be cautious?" Therefore, whether governing a country or cultivating one's own character, every word and action must be in accord with the seasons and follow the regulations. Thus it is said: "Issue commands in accord with the seasons." 

The *Book of Changes* says: "Good and bad fortune, regret and stinginess, are produced by movement." It also says: "The movement of the **Six Lines** <term>Yao</term> <note>the individual lines of a hexagram</note> is the Way of the Three Extremes." "Lines" means "to imitate." "Movement" means "change." Every hexagram has six lines: the top two represent Heaven, the middle two represent Humanity, and the bottom two represent Earth. The "Three Extremes" are the ultimate principles of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity, and each of these Three Powers is itself a **Great Ultimate** <term>Taiji</term>. Therefore, the movement and change of the lines are connected to the Way of the Great Ultimate of the Three Powers; this is where good and bad fortune arise. One must not miss the timing of these emerging signs. Thus it is said: "Do not miss the moment the lines move."

When speaking or acting, one must harmonize with the Way of the Three Powers. Therefore, above, one observes the patterns of the **River Map** <term>Hetu</term> <note>a mystical diagram of dots said to have been revealed on the back of a dragon-horse; it is a foundational map of Chinese cosmology</note> in the stars, such as the movements of the Seven Luminaries having their degrees, and the waxing and waning of Yin and Yang having their times. Below, one orders the flow of the geographic terrain, such as the great mountains standing tall without moving, and the rivers and seas circulating without drying up. In the middle, one examines the "Hinges of the Heart" <note>the inner intentions</note> in human movement and stillness, such as the firmness or softness of nature and temperament being fixed, and the changes of the will and Qi being inconstant. These three must be integrated and tested against one another. If the Way of the Three Powers is complete, then one's words and movements can be without fault. The *Book of Changes* says: "Looking up, we observe the images in [the heavens]..."

...of Heaven. Looking down, we observe the patterns on the Earth. We observe the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land. Near at hand, we find these principles in our own bodies; further away, we find them in all things. This is what is meant here.

## In movement, rely on the changes of the hexagrams; in stillness, follow the judgment of the words. The application of Qian and Kun is set in motion,
# and carried out across the world, after which order prevails.

<gloss>The character for "Judgment" (Tuan 彖) is pronounced like *tu-wan*. The character for "Order" (Zhi 治) is read in the departing tone.</gloss> "Rely" means to depend upon. **Hexagram changes** <term>Guaibian</term> refer to the transformations of the hexagram images, such as when a yielding "soft" line transforms into a firm "hard" line, or a hard line becomes soft, circulating throughout the six lines of every hexagram. "Follow" means to attend to or hold close. The **Judgment** <term>Tuan</term> is what the *Book of Changes* <note>the I Ching</note> refers to as the "material" or substance of the hexagram; it also means "to decide." The "Words" <term>Ci</term> refer to the statements attached to each hexagram by King Wen <note>the legendary founder of the Zhou Dynasty</note> to determine good or bad fortune, such as the phrases "Supreme success, furthered by perseverance" found in the hexagram for Heaven. There are also the "Image Commentaries," which are the words of the Master <note>Confucius</note> explaining the classic text, such as "Great indeed is the primal power of the Qian hexagram." Collectively, these are called the "Image Words." 

The *Book of Changes* says: "Therefore, when the Superior Man dwells at home, he observes the images and contemplates the words. When he moves, he observes the changes and contemplates the oracles. Thus, he receives help from Heaven; there is good fortune and nothing that is not beneficial." This means that when the Superior Man is at rest and has not yet performed a divination, he studies the hexagram images and the written judgments to understand the principles of when to advance, when to retreat, when to persist, and when to let go. When he is in motion and reaches the moment of performing a divination, he observes how the lines change to perceive the hidden mechanisms of growth and decay. 

The *Book of Changes* is a standard that is level with Heaven and Earth. If the Superior Man’s actions and stillness do not deviate from the laws of Heaven, then Heaven will assist him. Therefore, Lord Wei <note>likely referring to Wei Boyang, a famous Han dynasty alchemist</note> used this meaning to say: in times of movement, one relies on the manifest changes of the hexagram lines to divine fortune; in times of stillness, one follows the meaning of the Judgments and Images to clarify the underlying numerical principles. "Application" refers to the use of **Qian and Kun** <note>the pure Yang/Heaven and pure Yin/Earth hexagrams</note>, which are functionally expressed through **Kan and Li** <note>the hexagrams for Water and Fire</note>. When the energies of Water and Fire are applied to Heaven and Earth, the four seasons proceed and all things are born. When these energies circulate through the "Six Voids" <note>the empty spaces of the universe or the six positions of a hexagram</note>, the firm and the yielding are decided, and transformation appears. If this is so, how could the affairs of the world not be governed? The *Book of Changes* says: "They let their robes hang down and the world was governed," which means they followed the effortless principles of Heaven and Earth.

# Must one not be cautious? This is the priority of governing: keeping the mechanisms subtle and secret, opening and closing to distribute treasures. This is the Essential Way.
# The Dipper's handle governs transformation; the guiding rope and the knot.

<gloss>The character for "Closing" (He 闔) is pronounced like *kai*. The character for "Handle" (Biao 杓) is pronounced like *biao*.</gloss> "Must one not be cautious?" refers back to the "movement and stillness" mentioned previously, and the "governing" mentioned below—both require the utmost prudence. The *Book of Changes* says: "Words and actions are the means by which the Superior Man moves Heaven and Earth. Can he not be cautious?" This is the meaning. "The priority of governing" refers to the first concern of leadership. "Guan" <note>the "Pipe" or "Mechanism"</note> refers to a key or latch. "Subtle and secret" refers to things that are hidden. As the *Book of Changes* warns: "If a ruler is not secret, he loses his ministers; if a minister is not secret, he loses his life; if plans are not secret, the outcome is harmed." 

"Closing" also implies opening. "Distributing treasures" refers to spreading one's benevolence and virtue from the "Precious Position" <note>the throne or seat of power</note>. As the *Book of Changes* says: "The great virtue of Heaven and Earth is called life. The great treasure of the Sage is called the Position. How does one guard the position? Through benevolence." Planning an affair requires keeping the subtle mechanisms of the "latch" secret as the essential point, while issuing political orders requires the open distribution of virtue from the throne. Thus it is said: "Keep the mechanisms subtle and secret; open and close to distribute treasures." **The Dipper's Handle** <term>Kuibiao</term> refers to the seven stars of the **Big Dipper** <note>Beidou</note>. The *Suoyin* commentary on the *Records of the Grand Historian* says: "The *Spring and Autumn: Movement of the Dipper's Hinge* states: The Dipper is the first..."

<vocab>Hexagram changes (Guaibian), Judgment (Tuan), Words (Ci), Qian and Kun (Heaven and Earth), Kan and Li (Water and Fire), Governing (Yuzheng), Dipper's Handle (Kuibiao), Big Dipper (Beidou), Records of the Grand Historian (Shiji), Book of Changes (Yijing/I Ching)</vocab>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the principles of governance by drawing a direct parallel between the celestial order of the stars and the administrative order of a kingdom. It specifically details the stars of the Big Dipper and the "Wenchang" constellation as metaphors for the central authority and the watchful oversight of a ruler over his ministers.</meta>

<page-num>29</page-num>

The first star is called the **Celestial Pivot** <note>original: Tianshu</note>. The second is the **Jade Rotating Star** <note>original: Xuan</note>. The third is the **Pearl Star** <note>original: Ji</note>. The fourth is the **Balance Beam Star** <note>original: Quan</note>. The fifth is the **Level Star** <note>original: Heng</note>. The sixth is **Opening Heat** <note>original: Kaiyang</note>. The seventh is **Shimmering Light** <note>original: Yaoguang</note>. 

The first through the fourth stars form the **Body** <term>Kui</term> of the Dipper, while the fifth through the seventh form the **Handle** <term>Biao</term>. Together, they constitute the Dipper. It dwells in the Yin <note>the dark/hidden North</note> but distributes Yang <note>light and life</note>; therefore, it is called the **Northern Dipper** <note>the Big Dipper</note>. The "Treatise on Astronomy" in the *Book of Han* says: "The Dipper is the Emperor’s chariot. It revolves around the center, overseeing and controlling the four directions. It divides Yin and Yang, establishes the four seasons, balances the Five Elements, shifts the seasonal markers, and determines all chronological records—all of these are tied to the Dipper." The philosopher *He Guan Zi* says: "When the Dipper moves above, affairs are established below. When the Dipper points to a specific direction, the four seasons are completed accordingly." This is what is meant here. 

Therefore, it is said that the "Pivot" of the Way of Heaven lies in the Dipper's Handle, while the "Supreme Way" of governing lies in the human heart. Thus, it is said: "The Essential Way is found in the Body and Handle of the Dipper." The phrase "Governing the transformation and the guiding knot" means that the **Guiding Rope** <term>Gang</term> refers to a general summary, and the **Knot** <term>Niu</term> refers to the binding together of parts. This means that the Dipper’s Body and Handle summarize and tie together the creative transformations of both Heaven and humanity, just as a net has a main rope or a robe has a binding knot.

# Good and bad fortune arise from the internal movement of the hexagram lines.

This means that when the movements and transformations of the hexagram lines occur, they manifest within the hexagram being cast. The omens of good or bad fortune are then verified in the external world of people and objects. Therefore, it is said: "Internal" refers to the inside of the hexagram lines; "External" refers to the world of external things. This is what the *Book of Changes* means when it says: "The lines and images move within; good and bad fortune appear without." 

In the celestial patterns, those that are fixed are called the "Warp" <note>the fixed stars</note>, and those that move are called the "Woof" <note>the planets</note>. Therefore, stars are classified by this warp and woof. Today, the **Five Woofs** <term>Wuwei</term> refer to the Five Planets. They are the essential spirits of Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water, which congeal above to form images and serve as the leadership for the multitude of stars. Their movement follows the leftward rotation of the heavens, some moving quickly and others slowly. Together with the Sun and Moon, they are called the "Seven Regulators." "The seasons" refers to the four seasons. If the Five Planets follow their proper courses, the four seasons respond in harmony; if the Five Planets fall into disorder, the four seasons lose their sequence. This is all due to the resonance and movement between Heaven and humanity. Thus, it is said: "The Five Planets move in order or disorder, responding to the seasonal changes."

# Externally, the five planets move in order or disorder, responding to the times; the twenty-eight mansions fall into conflict, showing signs of separation between the heavens and the earth.

<gloss>The character for "Signs" (Zhen 診) is pronounced like *xiu*. "Internal" refers to the inside of the hexagram lines; "External" refers to the world of external things.</gloss> 

"Four-Sevens" refers to the **Twenty-Eight Mansions** <note>the 28 constellations of the Chinese zodiac</note>, as noted in the *Zuo Zhuan* commentary. "Signs" <term>Zhen</term> means to distinguish or diagnose. "Looking up and looking down" <note>Yangfu</note> is like saying "above and below." The Twenty-Eight Mansions are the "Warp" stars; above, they connect to the degrees of the celestial sphere, and below, they correspond to the different geographical regions of the Nine Provinces. If they fall into conflict and lose their proper measures, then the signs of separation are seen between the heavens above and the earth below. In summary, it means that cultivating oneself and governing a country both require caution and secrecy; one must not lose the "Pivot and Knot" of leadership, because good fortune, bad fortune, regret, and humiliation all arise from one’s actions.

# Wenchang oversees the records, questioning and censuring the high ministers and various officials, each presiding over their own department.

**Wenchang** refers to the "Wenchang Palace" mentioned in the "Book of Celestial Officials" in the *Records of the Grand Historian* <note>the Wenchang stars are associated with the celestial bureaucracy and literature</note>. "Overseeing the records" means that Wenchang is responsible for recording the duties of all various departments. "Questioning and censuring" <term>Jieze</term> means to hold accountable or interrogate. **High Ministers** <term>Taifu</term> refers to the stars described in the "Treatise on Astronomy" in the *Book of Han*: the six stars below the Dipper’s body, arranged in pairs, are called the **Three Terraces** <term>Santai</term>. The four stars surrounding the Celestial Pivot that assist the North Star are called the **Four Assistants** <term>Sifu</term>.

<meta>This page continues the analogy between celestial bodies and the imperial bureaucracy. It moves from the Northern Dipper and Wenchang to the "Three Terraces" (high ministers) and explains how the cycles of the sun and moon, as well as the alignment of stars like the "Law-Enforcer," reflect the moral state of the government and the balance of internal alchemy.</meta>

For the **Terrace-Assistants** <term>Taifu</term> serve above to aid the Emperor’s Throne, and below they lead the hundred officials. In human terms, they are the **Three Dukes** and **Prime Ministers** <note>the highest-ranking advisors to the Emperor</note>. Their responsibility to question and hold others accountable is the most vital of duties. Therefore, it is said: "They question and censure the Terrace-Assistants." Since the **Wenchang** stars govern the records from above, and the Terrace-Assistants hold those below accountable, the Yin and Yang will naturally be harmonized and the **Sacred Cauldrons** <note>original: dingnai; a metaphor for the state's welfare and governance</note> will be balanced. Then, the various officials and departments will faithfully guard their sectors and each fulfill the duties of their office.

# The Sun combines the essence of the Five Elements; the Moon receives the regulation of the Six Pitch-pipes. Five times six makes thirty degrees; when the degrees are completed, the cycle begins again.
<gloss>The word "combines" is written here as "contains." "Five Elements" refers to the **Five Movements** <term>Wuyun</term>. In sound, these are the **Five Tones**. The Five Elements are divided among the "days" of the ten **Heavenly Stems**, forming five Yang and five Yin pairs. "Essence" refers to the quintessence. The **Six Pitch-pipes** <term>Liulü</term> refer to the **Six Qi** <note>the seasonal environmental factors</note>. In the months, these form the six seasonal markers. The Six Pitch-pipes are distributed among the "months" of the twelve **Earthly Branches**, with six belonging to Yin and six to Yang. "Regulation" <term>Ji</term> means the guiding thread or discipline. "Completed" means to end. This means that the Sun contains the quintessence of the Five Phases, and the Moon receives the guiding discipline of the Six Qi. Furthermore, five days constitute one "marker," and six markers constitute one month. Therefore, combining the numbers five and six results in a cycle of thirty days. The Moon then meets the Sun. When the degrees of the cycle end, they start once more, like a ring without an end. This is also caused by the revolving movement of the Dipper’s Body and Handle.</gloss>

# Trace the origin and seek the end to see the threads of survival and ruin. Perhaps the Ruler is arrogant and overflowing, violating the Way; or perhaps the Minister is wicked and sycophantic, not following the proper tracks.
<gloss>The character for "Seek" <term>Yao</term> is read in the level tone. The character for "Arrogant" <term>Kang</term> is pronounced *kou-lang*. "Trace the origin" means to push back to the source. "Seek" means to search for. This means that by investigating the initial beginning and searching for the final end, one can know the omens of good fortune, bad fortune, survival, or ruin. Therefore, it is said: "Trace the origin and seek the end; these are the threads of survival and ruin." The *Book of Changes* says: "Trace the origin and seek the end to establish the substance." It also says: "Also seek the survival, ruin, good, and bad fortune, then the path to follow can be known." This is what is meant here. "Overflowing" means to be full. "Arrogant" means to exceed limits. This describes a ruler who might be arrogant and exceeds the proper measures of self-restraint, or whose pride violates the Way of governance. Or perhaps a minister is wicked and sycophantic rather than honest and good, acting outside the "tracks" of proper conduct. In such cases, the beginning and end can be investigated, and survival or ruin can be known in advance. In the **Methods of Alchemy** <term>Danfa</term>, the Spirit is the Ruler and the Breath (Qi) is the Minister; this passage carries that same meaning.</gloss>

# The phases of the moon wax and wane; deviation and change bring ill fortune. The Law-Enforcer pierces, mocks, and questions faults, passing them to the Master.
<gloss>"The phases of the moon wax and wane" refers to the first and last quarters and the full moon. "Waxing" is fullness; "Waning" is deficiency. "Deviation" means opposition; "Ill fortune" means error or calamity. This means the moon has its phases, becoming full or deficient based on how much sunlight it receives. Similarly, human affairs have ill fortune because of the wickedness in people's hearts, which creates deviation and change. Therefore, it is said: "The phases wax and wane; deviation and change bring ill fortune." The **Law-Enforcer** <term>Zhifa</term> is the name of a star in the **Supreme Tenuity Enclosure** <note>one of the three great star groupings representing the celestial government</note>. It is divided into left and right positions. In human terms, these are the offices of the **Ministers of Justice** and **Censors**. Their role is to point out and "pierce" evil and villainy. "Piercing and mocking" refers to satirical admonishment. "Questioning" means holding accountable. "Passing" means to hand over. It means that when the Ruler...</gloss>

By also investigating whether human affairs are appropriate or not, one clarifies the path of good and bad fortune, of progress and retreat, and of survival and ruin. Naturally, the state will be governed and the self will be cultivated, and the way to pray to Heaven for an everlasting mandate can be attained.

# Sinking into the Earth to Nurture the Pearl; Looked for but Not Seen, though Near and Easy to Seek

## Close off the Apertures; Build Firmly the Spiritual Stalk; The Three Lights

<gloss>The character "Easy" <note>易</note> is pronounced *yi*. The **Aperture** <term>Dui</term> refers to the *Dui* hexagram <note>from the I Ching, symbolized as a lake with an opening at the top</note>; it does not refer specifically to the mouth, but is a general term for the openings of the "Upper Source" <note>the sensory orifices of the head</note>. The **Spiritual Stalk** <term>Lingzhu</term> refers to the foundation of Water and Fire at the "Lower Source" <note>the pelvic/abdominal region</note>. This means that in cultivation, one must close off the gaps and openings of the upper gates while building and solidifying the root and stalk of the lower gates. Then, inside and outside will be without "leakage" <note>loss of vital energy</note>, and the **Spiritual Reishi** <term>Shenzhi</term> <note>a metaphor for the immortal elixir</note> can be obtained. The *Yellow Court Classic* <term>Huangting Jing</term> says: "Bind the pearl and solidify the essence to nurture the spiritual root; the jade tablets and golden chapters are always complete." Therefore, it is said: "Close off the apertures; build firmly the spiritual stalk." The **Three Lights** <term>Sanguang</term> are the Sun, Moon, and Stars of Heaven. A person's breathing—the coming and going—captures the movement and function of the Sun and Moon, called the "Internal Sun and Moon." This is what the *Yellow Court Classic* means by: "The Sun exits and the Moon enters as the breath is preserved; the Original Qi joins and the constellations are distributed." The movement of the stars depends on the **Dipper**, and the opening and closing of the orifices depends on the **Heart-Mind**. The *Yellow Court Classic* says: "Embrace the jade and hold the pearl to harmonize the child's chamber; if the child can guard the One, ten thousand matters are concluded." This is the meaning. However, although this Way is extremely simple and easy, it is "looked for but not seen, listened to but not heard." If one does not meet a True Master to point it out...</gloss>

# The Yellow Center Gradually Penetrates the Patterns; The Moistening Luster Reaches the Skin

# When the Beginning is Correct, the End is Cultivated; Once the Trunk is Established, the Branches Can Be Sustained

The *Commentary on the Words of the Text* in the *Book of Changes* <term>Yi Wenyan Zhuan</term> says: "The superior man is yellow in the center and penetrates the patterns; he occupies the correct position and dwells in his body." <note>original: "君子黃中通理。正位居體。"</note> This is Confucius explaining the phrase "The yellow lower garment brings supreme good fortune" from the fifth line of the **Receptive Hexagram** <term>Kun Gua</term> <note>symbolizing Earth and the feminine</note>. Generally, yellow is the color of the *Kun* Earth, and the "lower garment" refers to the clothing of the lower body. "Center" is the position of Earth; "Correctness" is the essence of *Kun*. "Patterns" <term>Li</term> refers to the inner elegance that is manifested on the outside. This describes how a superior man possesses central virtue: even when occupying a high position, he remains humble and modest toward those below him. This is like having inner beauty while wearing simple garments on the lower body. Thus, Confucius further praised this, saying: "Beauty is within, and it flows through the four limbs and manifests in one's deeds; this is the height of beauty." This is the sage’s explanation of the principles within the symbols of the *Book of Changes*.

Now, Lord Wei <note>referring to Wei Boyang, the legendary author of the "Cantong Qi"</note> uses this meaning when he says: "The yellow center gradually penetrates the patterns; the moistening luster reaches the skin." **Yellow** refers to the **Yellow Court** <term>Huangting</term> <note>a central energy center in the body</note>. **Patterns** <term>Li</term> refers to the *Shengli* <note>the textures and interstitial spaces of the skin and flesh</note>. This continues from the previous text’s method of internal nurturing: it means that when the "True Accumulation" of effort has lasted a long time, the **Original Harmonious Qi** <term>Yuanhe zhi Qi</term> within the Yellow Court gradually flows and penetrates through the skin's textures. Its moistening luster naturally reaches the limbs and the skin.

This is what is meant by: "Harmony and compliance accumulate within, and excellence blossoms without." "When the beginning is correct, the end is cultivated; once the trunk is established, the branches can be sustained" means that in studying the Way, holding to correctness is essential so that one does not enter "winding paths or side doors" <note>unorthodox or heterodox practices</note>. Making the will firm comes first, so that one does not start with diligence and end with laziness. This is what is meant by: "Once the heart is rectified, the self is cultivated; once the root is established, the Way is born."

However, if one wishes to practice this Way, one must receive the "Single Thread" heart-transmission <note>direct, secret teaching from master to disciple</note>, understand the origin of the **Great Ultimate** <term>Taiji</term>, and obtain the **Pre-celestial One Qi** <term>Xiantian Yiqi</term>. Only then can one succeed. But this so-called "One"—how could it be easy to know? As the *Book of Changes* says: "One Yin and one Yang is called the Dao." The *Dao De Jing* says: "The Dao produced the One; the One produced the Two; the Two produced the Three; the Three produced the ten thousand things." <note>original: "道生一。一生二。二生三。三生萬物。"</note> This "One" is exactly what is called the "Pre-celestial One Qi." It divides into two and transforms into three; once the **Three Powers** <term>Sancai</term> <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</note> are established, transformations become infinite. Therefore, this "One Qi" is so great that nothing is outside it, and so small that nothing is inside it. Every object possesses it, and it is so at all times. It is the root of Yin and Yang, the source of Water and Fire, the wellspring of Principle, and the beginning of Number. It is what we call the Dao, or the Great Ultimate. Therefore, practitioners use only this Pre-celestial One Qi to form the "Elixir Seed" and achieve the True Body. As it is said: "Obtain the One, and the ten thousand matters are concluded." Yet, unless one meets a perfected person to point it out, and unless one accumulates merit and practices long-term nurturing, this One Qi cannot be fathomed or known. Thus it is said: "The One is concealed; the people of the world cannot know it."

# The One is Concealed; The People of the World Cannot Know It

The *Yellow Court Classic* <term>Huangting Jing</term> says: "The Mysterious Original Supreme One refines the souls; the One as a thing cannot be seen suddenly." <note>original: "玄元上一魂魄煉。一之為物叵卒見。"</note> Is this not what is being discussed here?

# Highest Virtue is Non-Action; It is Not Observed

It interprets these philosophical concepts as metaphors for the relationship between the Spirit (Shen) and Vital Energy (Qi) within the practitioner's body during the alchemical process.</meta>

# Seeking Lower Virtue by Acting; Its Use is Without Ceasing

The *Book of the Way and Virtue* <term>Dao De Jing</term> says: "Highest virtue does nothing and has no intention to do; lower virtue acts and has an intention to do." <note>original: "上德無爲而無以為。下德爲之而有以爲。"</note> This text quotes those phrases to reveal the secret of both **Spirit** <term>Shen</term> and **Vital Energy** <term>Qi</term>. In the method of internal nurturing, the Spirit is the sovereign and the Qi is the minister. Therefore, the sovereign represents "Highest Virtue," while the minister represents "Lower Virtue." Furthermore, "virtue" means the "root" or "foundation." The root of the higher is in the Spirit; the root of the lower is in the Qi.

Because of this, the Spirit should be clear, quiet, and practice "non-action" <term>Wuwei</term>; it should not seek or observe with even a hair’s breadth of effort, which would burden the heart. Meanwhile, the Qi should be rotated and moved through "action"; it should be "continuous, as if it barely exists," and its use should never cease. When the Spirit is allowed to govern the Qi for a long time, the Qi will naturally return to its root. However, the meaning of these "upper and lower" or "being and non-being" concepts is simply the division of the "One" mentioned in the previous text into "Two." This is explained in further detail below.

# Closing the Upper, it is Called "Being"; Closing the Lower, it is Called "Non-being." This is to Serve the Upper, Where the Spiritual Virtue Resides. These Two Apertures and Methods, and the Metal-Qi, Also Depend on Each Other.

"Closing the upper" refers to what the previous text called "closing the mouth and senses" <note>literally "closing the Dui gate," Dui being the hexagram for the mouth</note>. "Closing the lower" refers to what the previous text called "fortifying the **Spiritual Root**" <term>Linggen</term> <note>the lower energy center or dantian</note>. 

"Being" refers to **Water**. The *Return to Life Chapters* <term>Fuming Pian</term> says: "In the Palace of the **Li Hexagram** <note>associated with Fire and the Heart</note>, there are images that conceal the **True Water**." <note>original: "離宮有象藏眞水。"</note> This is what is meant here. 
"Non-being" refers to **Fire**. The *Return to Life Chapters* also says: "At the Gate of the **Kan Hexagram** <note>associated with Water and the Kidneys</note>, the formless hides the **Crimson Dragon** <note>a metaphor for Fire/Spirit</note>." <note>original: "坎戶無形隱赤龍。"</note> 

Therefore, it is said: "Closing the upper is called Being; closing the lower is called Non-being." "To serve the upper" means the rising of the **Original Qi** <term>Yuanqi</term>. "Spiritual Virtue" refers to the inherent virtue of the **Original Spirit** <term>Yuanshen</term>. This means that the Original Qi is used as "Lower Virtue" to rise and serve the upper, while the Original Spirit resides as "Highest Virtue" to govern the lower. This is exactly what was meant by "Highest Virtue does nothing, Lower Virtue acts."

In general, the Kan and Li hexagrams represent the function of Yin and Yang, while Water and Fire are the sources of the upper and lower. **Yang Qi** <note>active, light energy</note> primarily rises. When the **Great Ultimate** <term>Taiji</term> produces Yin, it transforms into Water and becomes "Being." **Yin Qi** <note>passive, cool energy</note> primarily descends. When the Great Ultimate produces Yang, it transforms into Fire and becomes "Non-being." Thus, Water and Fire are each other's roots, and Yin and Yang depend on each other for their use. This is the Way of refining the **Elixir** <term>Dan</term> and governing the Qi. 

Today, the phrase "Non-being serves the upper, where the Spiritual Virtue resides" carries this meaning. The text omits mentioning "Original Qi" and its relationship to the "Being" and the "Lower" likely for the sake of brevity. "These Two Apertures" <term>Liangkong</term> refers to the fact that Spirit and Qi are the two essential keys to the upper and lower apertures of the body. The *Dao De Jing* says: "These two emerge from the same source but have different names" <note>original: "此兩者。同出而異名。"</note>; this follows the same logic. 

As for "Metal and Qi also depend on each other," this is because **Metal** <note>associated with the lungs and purity</note> can produce Water, and Qi can become Fire. Metal acts to transform the Qi, and Qi acts to melt the Metal. Thus, Metal and Qi depend on and support each other just as Being and Non-being do. Therefore, Metal and Qi are the pivotal mechanisms of the Alchemical Way.

It explains the alchemical circulation of Water and Fire between the heart and kidneys, emphasizing that these dualities must work in harmony to refine the internal elixir.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general cosmological principles discussed in the first five chapters to the specific practical methods of "Nourishing Life and Cultivating Nature." This chapter speaks of the Way of **internal nurturing** <term>Neiyang</term>. It describes how the body and mind should be unified in the center, and how **Spirit and Qi** <term>Shenqi</term> must rely on each other for their use. It clarifies the "One Qi" and reaches into its two sources, which constitutes the great beginning of the refinement practice. 

The previous five chapters spoke generally of the secret depths of the *Way of the Book of Changes* <note>The Zhouyi</note>, revealing the ultimate principles of the **Three Realms** <term>Sancai</term> <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</note>. These principles encompass everything from governing a nation to governing the body, and the methods of the Elixir are also contained within them. As the saying goes: "The spirit and its clarity depend on the individual." 

Arriving at this chapter, the text finally speaks of the study of **Nourishing Life and Cultivating Nature** <note>the practical aspects of Daoist longevity and spiritual development</note> to reveal its first clues. Thereafter, each chapter will provide a detailed, step-by-step analysis to clarify the mysteries of the **Great Elixir** <term>Dadan</term>, while still not abandoning the profound logic of the *Book of Changes*. Therefore, the book is titled *The Kinship of the Three According to the Book of Changes* <term>Zhouyi Cantong Qi</term> for a very good reason.

# Knowing the White, Guarding the Black, Spiritual Radiance Comes of Itself; White is the Essence of Metal, Black is the Foundation of Water.

The *Book of the Way and Virtue* <term>Dao De Jing</term> says: "Know the white, but keep to the black, and be a model for the world." <note>original: "知其白。守其黑。爲天下式。"</note> This generally means that by concealing one’s light and obscuring one’s traces—waiting for the right time to move—one can become a standard for the world. 

Today, the phrase "Knowing the white, guarding the black, spiritual radiance comes of itself" is quoted here to reveal the substance and function of **Metal and Water**. It suggests that the two colors, black and white, must rely on each other for their use. It is like wanting to know the white light of the moon; one must "guard" or focus on the moon’s black body. Or, if one wants to know the whiteness of silver, one must guard the black color of lead. Therefore, when the new moon begins to produce light, or when the refining of lead causes the silver to float to the top, this is what is called "Spiritual Radiance coming of itself." 

This is a metaphor for the idea that **Silver** <note>the refined essence</note> is hidden within **Lead** <note>the raw material</note>, and the silver emerges from the lead. The *Return to Life Chapters* <term>Fuming Pian</term> says: "If only one can guard the black, the white will appear of itself; black and white are originally not two different colors." The *Chapters on Understanding Reality* <term>Wuzhen Pian</term> says: "The white within the black is the Mother of the Elixir." These all carry the same meaning. 

In terms of the **Five Elements** <term>Wuxing</term>, the color white belongs to Metal and is the essence of silver. The color black belongs to Water and is the foundation or "base" of lead. Thus it is said: "White is the essence of Metal; Black is the foundation of Water." The text below explains this in further detail.

# Named "One," the Beginning of Yin and Yang's Establishment; Containing the "Yellow Sprout," the Sovereign of the Five Metals, the Northern "River Chariot."

<gloss>Water is the pivot of the Way; its number is called "One."</gloss>

Water is the source of "Heavenly One." Water is the beginning of the "Five Metals." Therefore it is said: "Water is the pivot of the Way; its number is called One." 

According to the **Numbers of Generation and Completion** <note>a numerological system where certain numbers 'generate' an element and others 'complete' it</note> of Heaven, Earth, and the Five Elements:
*   Heavenly **1** generates Water; Earthly **6** completes it.
*   Earthly **2** generates Fire; Heavenly **7** completes it.
*   Heavenly **3** generates Wood; Earthly **8** completes it.
*   Earthly **4** generates Metal; Heavenly **9** completes it.
*   Heavenly **5** generates Earth; Earthly **10** completes it.

This is the pairing of the "Odd" and the "Even." The odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) are **Yang**, and the even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8, 10) are **Yin**. There is also an interpretation where all "Generating" numbers are Yang and all "Completing" numbers are Yin. The *Book of Changes* says: "Heaven 1, Earth 2, Heaven 3, Earth 4, Heaven 5, Earth 6, Heaven 7, Earth 8, Heaven 9, Earth 10. The numbers of Heaven are five, and the numbers of Earth are five. The five positions correspond to each other..."

...and each has its match. Master Zhu’s <note>Zhu Xi, 1130–1200</note> *Inquiry into the Study of the Changes* says: "To gain each other is like brothers; to match each other is like husband and wife." 

In general, "gaining each other like brothers" refers to the odd numbers (1, 3, 5, 7, 9) and the even numbers (2, 4, 6, 8, 10). Here, Yin and Yang find their own kind; odd and even share the same substance, which is the meaning of "brothers." "Matching each other like husband and wife" refers to the pairings of 1 with 6, 2 with 7, 3 with 8, 4 with 9, and 5 with 10. Here, Yin and Yang find their partners; odd and even join together, which is the meaning of "husband and wife." 

Furthermore, the Way of the *Changes* uses 1 and 9 to represent **Great Yang**, 2 and 8 for **Lesser Yin**, 3 and 7 for **Lesser Yang**, and 4 and 6 for **Great Yin**. These are called the **Four Images** <term>Sixiang</term>. The numbers 5 and 10 represent **Earth**, which resides in the **Central Palace**. Between these Four Images, Earth is everywhere present. Therefore, every hexagram, image, line, and counting-rod calculation is produced by these "Numbers of Generation and Completion," crisscrossing and transforming to accomplish the great work of the Way of the *Changes*. 

Thus, the *Changes* also says: "The numbers of Heaven are twenty-five; the numbers of Earth are thirty. The total numbers of Heaven and Earth are fifty-five. This is what allows for transformation and the movement of the gods and spirits." This is the meaning here. Viewed from this perspective, the fact that Water constitutes the Way and its number is One—is this not the Primal Qi of Heaven and Earth and the pivot of the Five Elements? Thus it is called: "The beginning of Yin and Yang."

In the Way of the Elixir <term>Dandao</term>, "Heavenly One generates Water" corresponds to **Lead**. Today, the phrase "The Dark contains the Yellow Sprout" means that within Lead there is Silver. When it is cooked and refined by fire, its color becomes yellow and the silver "sprouts" forth. Furthermore, **Darkness** <note>associated with the sky/Heaven</note> and **Yellow** <note>associated with the earth</note> are the correct colors of Heaven and Earth. Now, with Black Lead on the outside and the Yellow Sprout contained within, it is like the image of Heaven enveloping the Earth. 

Moreover, Lead belongs to Water, and the "Generating Number" of Water is one. When it gains the "Generating Number" of Earth, which is five, they combine to form the "Completing Number" of Water, which is six. This is also the meaning of the Dark and Yellow containing one another. As for being the "Sovereign of the Five Metals," Lead is the Mother of the five metals and the beginning of the Five Elements. 

Regarding the **Northern River Chariot** <term>Heche</term>, because the substance of Lead is black, its position is in the North. The "Correct Qi" of the North is titled the "River Chariot." In the Way of the Elixir, this refers to that which is used to raise and lower Water and Fire. Generally, all "chariots" travel on land, but the "River Chariot" travels on water. This is a metaphorical term used in the methods of the Elixir. As the *Collection on Transmitting the Way* <term>Chuandao Ji</term> says: whether from above or below, front or back, traveling through the **Nine Provinces** <note>the whole body</note>, or patrolling the **Three Cinnabar Fields** <term>Dantian</term>, moving the True Fire or transporting the Jade Nectar—even unto the point of the spirit exiting or entering stillness—all are the functions of this Chariot. However, there are also the "Three Chariots" known as the Small, the Great, and the Purple River Chariots. The names are numerous and varied, but to sum them up in one word: they are nothing more than the **One Qi**. If the student reflects deeply on this, the meaning will be grasped naturally.

# Therefore, Lead is Black Outside but Embraces Gold Within; Like "Wearing Coarse Wool but Hiding Jade,"

**Coarse Wool** <term>He</term> refers to cloth made of hair; it is the clothing of the lowly. The *Book of the Way and Virtue* says: "Those who know me are few; those who follow me are noble. Therefore, the Sage wears coarse wool but hides jade." <note>original: "知我者希。則我者貴。是以聖人被褐懷玉。"</note> 

Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the purported author</note> quotes this to metaphorically describe how Lead contains Silver, just as a person wearing coarse wool might hide a precious jade. If one does not know the treasure contained within and judges only by the outward appearance, one would see only a lowly "madman." # Metal is the Mother of Water; the Mother is Hidden in the Child’s Womb. Water is the Child of Metal; the Child is Hidden in the Mother’s Enclosure.

Metal has the capacity to generate Water, and Water fundamentally takes its birth from Metal. Therefore it is said: "Metal is the mother of Water, and Water is the child of Metal." This is the "following" <note>the natural or productive cycle</note> of the Ordinary Way. However, the fact that "White is found within Black" and "Silver is embraced within Lead" is why we say the mother is hidden in the child’s womb and the child is stored in the mother’s enclosure. This represents the "reversing" <note>the counter-natural or internalizing process</note> of the **Way of the Elixir** <term>Dandao</term>. 

Although this is spoken of in terms of Lead and Silver, the same principle applies to **Mercury** <term>Gong</term> within **Cinnabar** <term>Zhu</term>, where "Green is hidden within Red." The *Folio on Understanding Reality* <term>Wuzhen pian</term> <note>a foundational 11th-century alchemical text</note> says: "The Dragon of the Zhen trigram—its Mercury leaves the Palace of Li; the Tiger of the Dui trigram—its Lead is born in the direction of Kan. These two substances are entirely due to the child producing the mother; the Five Elements are all married into the Central Palace." This is exactly what is meant here. 

However, what the alchemical methods call "Lead, Cinnabar, Silver, Mercury, and Earth" are **Outer Affairs** <note>physical substances</note>. What are called "Spirit, Soul, Intent, and Vitality" <note>Jing, Shen, Hun, Po, Yi</note> are **Inner Affairs** <note>internal psychological/spiritual states</note>. The inner is used to illustrate the outer, and the outer is used to symbolize the inner; the two are spoken of interchangeably to clarify the Way. Therefore, the metaphors and names established in alchemical books are beyond counting. If one grasps the essential point, the meaning of more than half of them will be understood.

# The Realized Man is Utterly Subtle; As If Existing, As If Not, a Faint Appearance.
## Within the Great Abyss, Suddenly Sinking, Suddenly Floating; Advancing, Retreating, and Distributed, Each Guarding Their Own Corner.

<gloss>The "Realized Man" <term>Zhenren</term> <note>a perfected Daoist being</note> is a metaphor for **True Lead**, which is the **Qi of True Unity**. For Qi is the person, and the person is the Qi. This is what Master Zhu meant by "Qi acts to complete the form." Between Heaven and Man, as Yin and Yang wax and wane to preserve and unite the inner nature and life-destiny, nothing is more numinous or subtle than Qi. 

Therefore, "as if existing, as if not" refers to its ethereal presence between Heaven and Earth. "A faint appearance within the Great Abyss" describes how the White is within the Black, and how Gold <note>Silver/Metal</note> is hidden within Water. "Suddenly sinking, suddenly floating" describes the swirling movement of the vapor between the upper and lower regions of the body. "Advancing, retreating, and distributed" refers to its movement: when it advances, it is Yang, rising from the East; when it retreats, it is Yin, descending from the West. "Each guarding their own corner" means they keep to the cardinal positions <note>represented by the zodiacal signs Zi, Wu, Mao, and You</note> to align with the four turning points of the year <note>the solstices and equinoxes</note>. 

However, this is the function of the True Lead; one must seek it within the **Furnace and Tripod** <term>Luding</term> and must not search for it in high or distant places. As for what is called the "Furnace and Tripod," in the "Outer Alchemy" of laboratory fires, one can perhaps understand its physical boundaries, so there is no need for many words. But the "Furnace and Tripod" of **Inner Alchemy** <term>Neidan</term> <note>cultivating the elixir within the body</note> is where students are most easily confused. Therefore, the student must seek it within their own body. Do not seek it externally or through other means, lest you allow heterodox theories to throw the Great Way into chaos. Take heed!</gloss>

# Square and Round, an Inch in Diameter; Blended and Constrained; Born Before Heaven and Earth, Towering and Grand.

"Square and round, an inch in diameter" refers to the symbolic form of the **Golden Elixir** <term>Jindan</term>, which aligns with the Way of the "Three Powers" <note>Heaven, Earth, and Humanity</note>. The *Yellow Court Classic* <term>Huangting jing</term> <note>a foundational Daoist text on internal visualization and meditation</note> says: "Sitting within the Nine-Fold Golden Curtain City; square and round, one inch wide, inside the Gate of Life." This is what it refers to. 

"Blended and constrained" describes how the "Metal-Water" (the symbolic White and Black substances) are subjected to the heat of the fire's refining. They merge and bind together to become the inch-wide Elixir. 

"Born before Heaven and Earth" means that the condensation of the **Embryo of the Elixir** <term>Dantai</term> is produced by the **True Unity Qi** <note>the primordial, undifferentiated breath of the universe</note> that existed before the physical world. It is not transformed from the physical, shaped substances of our material world. The *Classic of the Way and Virtue* <term>Daodejing</term> says: "There was a thing blended and formed, born before Heaven and Earth." This is the same meaning. 

"Towering and grand" refers to its exalted status. This says the Golden Elixir is born before the universe itself and is not comparable to ordinary things; is it not then the most supreme and magnificent of all?

# Exalted and High, Flanked by Walls and Watchtowers, Looking Like the Island-Mount of the Immortals.

"Flanked by walls and watchtowers": "Walls" refers to an enclosure; "watchtowers" refers to the gated entrances. This means that while the Golden Elixir resides within the **Tripod** <term>Ding</term>, it is sealed and solidified with "Earth" <note>symbolizing intent and stability</note> and warmed by the fire. The top, bottom, and four sides of the tripod are surrounded, protected, opened, and closed as if there were walls guarding the exterior and gates allowing access to the interior. 

"Looking like the Island-Mount" <note>original: "Penglai" or "Penghu"</note> refers to the mythical spirit-mountains in the sea where immortals dwell. Storing the Divine Elixir in the **Central Palace** <note>the middle of the torso or the central point of cultivation</note> is like an immortal dwelling on the spirit-mountains of Penglai or Fanghu. This is a very clever metaphor.

# Encircled and Closed, Connecting the Four Directions, Lingering in Place; Guarded Tightly to Exclude Wickedness; Winding Galleries Interconnected to Guard Against the Unexpected.

<gloss>The word "Encircled" means round and complete without any gaps. "Closed" means all-encompassing. This indicates the Elixir stays in the tripod, deeply sealed and hidden, and is complete in every direction. 

"Closed" also refers to the method of refining: one must ensure that internal states do not leak out and external distractions do not enter. This prevents any risk of the "Embryo of the Elixir" leaking away. 

"Connecting the four directions" refers to the Yin and Yang vapors within the tripod-furnace, which reach and circulate through the four cardinal positions <note>the directions of North, South, East, and West, represented by the zodiacal signs Zi, Wu, Mao, and You</note>. 

"Lingering" describes the appearance of moving without rushing forward. This refers to the operation of the **Yang Fire** and **Yin Tally**. The movement must be gentle and balanced, neither too fast nor too slow, using the "Literary" <note>soft</note> and "Military" <note>intense</note> fires appropriately. Upon reaching the four cardinal positions, one must pause and "bathe" <note>a technical term for a state of stillness where the fire is paused</note> to prevent the danger of the fire becoming too dry or the water overflowing. This allows Yin and Yang to wax and wane naturally to achieve harmony. 

"Guarded tightly" means that the physical form and the spirit rely on one another, with the spirit kept strictly within, never straying for a moment. This is what the fifth chapter of the next volume means when it says "guard closely against confusion." 

"To exclude wickedness": "Exclude" means to stop. "Wickedness" refers to internal or external demonic obstacles, as well as errors in the timing of the fire-intensities. One must guard against these and cut them off. The *Folio of Emerald Emptiness* says: "The spiritual flag sweeps, the night-fire mushroom glows; the addition and subtraction of the fire must be carefully guarded against danger." Master **Qiu Changchun** <note>a famous 13th-century Daoist master and founder of the Dragon Gate sect</note> said: "Even if your blessings are light and demonic obstacles are heavy, if you keep to the work, you will certainly reach perfection." These all mean the same thing.</gloss>

# He Who Can Keep and Guard It Will Thrive; He Who Loses It Will Perish. Movement and Stillness, Rest and Activity, These Always Accompany the Person.

# It Can Be Done Without Thought; It Is Difficult with Worry and Toil. When Spirit and Qi Fill the Room, Nothing Can Harm It.

If there is anxious thought, the Qi becomes knotted and the Essence is shaken. If there is sorrowful toil, the Spirit is injured and the Qi is depleted. This is mostly said for ordinary people. Now that the **Embryo of the Elixir** <term>Dantai</term> has already formed within, one must add even more protection and caution. Therefore, when entering the chamber for one year of seclusion, the myriad worries are all forgotten, and the hundred affairs are not undertaken. It is like a dragon nursing its pearl, or a hen brooding her egg, to warmly nourish the spiritual embryo. Thus it is said: "It can be done without thought; it is difficult with worry and toil." How profound the meaning!

<margin>Master **Tan Changzhen** <note>a famous 12th-century Daoist master of the Quanzhen school</note> said:</margin>
> Let not a single thread of thought hang upon the mind; when the spiritual embryo forms within, you are destined for immortality.

This is exactly it. And **Mencius** <note>a foundational Confucian philosopher</note> said: "Hold fast to the will, and do not do violence to the Qi." He also spoke of "preserving the heart, nourishing the nature, and cultivating the self to await destiny." This is how one "establishes life." It all shares this same meaning. 

"Spirit and Qi fill the room, and nothing can harm it" means the Elixir resides in the tripod. If the timing of the fire is without error, and true accumulation of effort is long-lasting, then the **Valley Spirit Will Not Die** <note>a famous phrase from the *Daodejing* meaning the inner spiritual capacity remains vital and receptive</note>. Great Harmony will overflow, and the transformation will naturally occur without being forced. This is what the fifth chapter of the middle volume refers to as: "Completing the ten months, it emerges from the womb." When Mencius said, "I am good at nourishing my **Great Flood-like Qi** <term>Haoran zhi qi</term>, which fills the space between Heaven and Earth," it follows the same principle. 

"He who guards it thrives; he who loses it perishes" means that although the Elixir Embryo has been released, one must still **Embrace the Origin and Guard the One** <note>a state of unified, meditative focus</note> to wait for it to reach maturity. If one considers only the act of "coming and going" <note>projecting the spirit out of the body</note> as mastery and lightly allows it to stray far away, encountering demonic obstacles will cause no small harm.

<margin>The *Chapter on Returning to the Sublime* says:</margin>
> Ascension requires a period of three years; cherish and nurture it with diligent affection.

This is what is meant here. Mencius recounted the words of Confucius:
> "Hold it and it survives; let it go and it perishes. Its coming and going have no fixed time; no one knows its home."

The meaning is the same. "Movement and stillness, rest and activity, these always accompany the person" means that during times of action or stopping, and in moments of peaceful rest, one always relies on the form and spirit being together, and the essence and Qi being guarded together. Nine years of "Embracing the One," ten years to complete the work—this is how one becomes a Spirit-Man or an Immortal.

...this is the case. The **Book of Changes** <term>Yijing</term> says: "That which is unfathomable in its Yin and Yang is called Spirit." It also says: "One who understands the path of transformation, does he not know the actions of the Spirit?" And it says: "Spirit is that which mysteriously empowers the myriad things." Therefore, the title of **Spirit-Immortal** <term>Shenxian</term> is likely derived from this meaning.

I have often examined the teachings of the Sages <note>referring to Confucius and his followers</note>. By using benevolence, righteousness, ritual, and music to cultivate the self, regulate the family, govern the state, and bring peace to the world, they have left instructions for ten thousand generations and blessed everyone with their virtue. This is the "Path of Action" for the accomplished scholar. 

On the other hand, the learning of the **Perfected Immortals** <term>Xianzhen</term> takes the ethical constants of daily life as its foundation and internal cultivation as its primary labor. Though they may seem to stand in humble retreat, they harbor great purpose, transcending the physical to enter the realm of the Spirit. This is the "Path of Non-Action" for the recluse. 

Therefore, while the classics of the Sages mostly focus on clarifying righteous principles and do not explicitly speak of the secrets of nourishing life, a careful examination reveals that their profound meanings contain these secrets within. These can be found in the *Four Books* and *Six Classics*, as well as in the histories and collections of early Confucian scholars, in numbers too great to count.

Now, although Master Wei’s **Token of the Three Accordant** <term>Cantong qi</term> <note>the fundamental text of internal alchemy</note> is considered the ancestor of all elixir scriptures, it is in fact a book where Confucianism and Daoism run parallel. It clarifies the "Pre-heaven" <note>primordial or original state</note> learning of the *Book of Changes* and the principle of the Sun and Moon forming the character for "Change" <note>the Chinese character for Change (易) is traditionally seen as a combination of the characters for Sun (日) and Moon (月)</note>. This is something no one had spoken of since ancient times. 

Furthermore, within this book, he speaks of the principles of Heaven and Earth and the way of governance; it is truly comprehensive. It is called the *Kinship of the Three in Accordance with the Book of Changes* for this very reason. Thus, Confucianism is rooted in the Dao, and the Dao is rooted in Confucianism. Outside of the Dao there is no Confucianism, and outside of Confucianism there is no Dao; they share the same source and their principle is one. 

Moreover, Master **Zhu Xi** once wrote a commentary on the *Cantong qi* and discussed its meaning repeatedly with **Cai Xishan** <note>Cai Yuanding, a famous mathematician and music theorist</note>. In his *Instruction for Beginners on the Study of Changes*, he also cited the Pre-heaven learning found in this text. This is enough to prove that Confucianism and Daoism share a single origin and that there is no fundamental difference between them. 

In summary: that which upholds the ethical constants is both Confucian and Daoist. That which lacks these constants is heterodox and evil. There is no need for further debate; those of high intelligence will know this instinctively.

It uses "Gold" and "Water" as the medicinal ingredients, which are gathered and refined to form the embryo, then sealed and guarded against danger and risk until the "emergence from the womb" and the "Embracing of the One" are achieved. At that point, the work of cultivation is complete.

Thus, one month counts for sixty hexagrams, cycling round and round like a ring without an end. However, in short, the use of hexagrams and lines in the Alchemical Path is merely a metaphor for the methods of cultivation and practice. # The moon mimics the cauldron and furnace; the White Tiger is the roasting pivot. Mercury is the Sun, the flowing pearl; the Azure Dragon accompanies it. Lifting the East to join the West, the souls bind one another.

<gloss>The word "mercury" <note>汞</note> is pronounced like "Gǒng."</gloss> 

"Recumbent" <note>偃, yan</note> means lying down or facing upward. This states that the cauldron and furnace, which can contain water and fire, are modeled on the imagery of the **recumbent moon** <note>the crescent moon appearing like a bowl</note>. The cauldron resembles the fullness of the moon at the middle of the month, capable of holding the medicinal ingredients, while the furnace resembles the waning crescent of the moon, capable of receiving the fire tallies. Thus, it is said that the recumbent moon provides the model for the cauldron and furnace. 

The ordinary use of the cauldron and furnace is to harmonize water and fire to transform matter, but their ultimate work is the "cooking and refining" of Lead and Mercury to form the Elixir. Lead is associated with **Metal**; Metal is located in the West, and its color is white. The **White Tiger** is also a creature of the West. Therefore, the cauldron and furnace are called the "roasting pivot" for refining the White Tiger. 

Mercury is quicksilver; because it flows like water and its form is silver, it is called "water-silver" <note>quicksilver</note>. This is distinct from the "True Lead" that is sometimes also called quicksilver. The nature of mercury is like flowing water, and its body is round like a pearl. Its form is bright and shining, and because it moves inconsistently, its image is like that of the Sun. Thus, it is said: "Mercury is the Sun, the flowing pearl." Furthermore, the nature of mercury belongs to **Wood**; Wood is located in the East, and its color is azure. The **Azure Dragon** is also a creature of the East. Therefore, the "flowing pearl" is said to accompany the Azure Dragon. 

There is another interpretation where the flowing pearl is the "palace," the place where the spirit is stored and water gathers—this is the "Mercury-Sun Cauldron." The "roasting pivot" is the "office," the place where the breath is received and the fire is ignited—this is the "Lead-Moon Furnace." This is another layer of meaning. Lead is called the "moon" because the body of lead is black, but the silver that comes out of it is white—much like the substance of the moon is inherently dark, yet the light it emits produces a white image. 

"Lifting the East to join the West" refers to taking the Wood of the Eastern Azure Dragon to join with the Metal of the Western White Tiger. This represents the union of Dragon and Tiger, and the merging of Metal and Wood.

> The *Fuming pian* <note>the "Chapter on Returning to Life," a classic alchemical text</note> says: "The master points to the Azure Dragon's mercury, matching it to the White Tiger's lead." This is exactly the meaning.

"The souls bind one another" refers to the *Hun* and the *Po*. The **Hun-soul** <note>the ethereal, heavenly soul</note> is the Yang-spirit, which is the spirit of the Sun. The **Po-soul** <note>the corporeal, earthly soul</note> is the Yin-spirit, which is the spirit of the Moon. The *Hun* belongs to Wood and governs human nature; the *Po* belongs to Metal and governs human emotion. The statement that the Dragon and Tiger of the East and West join together means that the *Hun* and *Po*, emotion and nature, are bound to one another.

> Chapter Five of the *Middle Volume* says: "The *Hun* and the *Po* serve as each other's dwellings." 
> The *Fuming pian* says: "The Dragon and Tiger are originally one body; the eastern neighbor is simply the western house." 

All these share this meaning. In short, it means that emotion is joined to nature, and the spirit drives the vital energy <term>qi</term>, while inhalation and exhalation nurture one another. However, regarding the meaning of the "recumbent moon," Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the legendary author of the "Cantong qi"</note> spoke of it in terms of both the cauldron and the furnace, whereas later people only...

# The first quarter is the number eight of Dui; the last quarter is also the eight of Gen. When the two quarters combine their essence, the body of Heaven and Earth is complete.

<gloss>The "number eight of **Dui** <note>Hexagram 58, "Joy," representing the waxing moon</note>" refers to the fourth chapter of this text, which states: "On the eighth day, Dui receives the solar pillar, and the first quarter is level as a rope." The "number eight of **Gen** <note>Hexagram 52, "Keeping Still," representing the waning moon</note>" also refers to the fourth chapter: "Gen stands straight at the southern solar pillar; the last quarter is on the twenty-third day." 

Essentially, the first quarter of the moon represents the expansion of **Yang** and the contraction of **Yin**—the growth of light and the fading of shadow. Here, the **Hun-soul** <note>ethereal/spiritual</note> advances while the **Po-soul** <note>corporeal/physical</note> retreats, as Yin transforms into Yang. The *Classic of the Dragon and Tiger* calls this "the first quarter's half-catty of Metal." 

By the time of the full moon (the 15th), the Yang energy is at its peak, forming the pure body of **Heaven** <term>Qian</term>. The last quarter of the moon represents the expansion of Yin and the contraction of Yang—the growth of shadow and the fading of light. Here, the *Po* advances and the *Hun* retreats, as Yang turns back into Yin. The *Classic of the Dragon and Tiger* calls this "the last quarter's half-catty of Water." 

By the final day of the lunar month, the Yin energy is at its peak, forming the pure body of **Earth** <term>Kun</term>. This waxing and waning of Yin and Yang, the coming and going of growth and decay, alternate their functions to complete the work of creation. Just as the two quarters combine the essential energy of "Metal" and "Water" to form the body of Heaven and Earth, the full and new moons represent the fundamental reality of Yin and Yang. Thus it is said: "When the two quarters combine their essence, the body of Heaven and Earth is complete." 

Furthermore, these first and last quarters correspond to the previous meaning of the Dragon ascending and the Tiger descending. The two quarters forming Heaven and Earth is the same concept as the souls of the East and West binding one another; these are complementary ways of explaining the same principle.</gloss>

## Two eights correspond to one catty.

# The Way of the Changes is upright and does not tilt. There are three hundred and eighty-four *zhu*, which also corresponds to the number of hexagram lines.

<gloss>The word *zhu* <note>the smallest unit of weight in ancient China</note> is pronounced like "Shū." 

The phrase "two eights correspond to one catty" <note>a catty or *jin* traditionally consisted of 16 ounces or *liang*</note> refers to the half-catty of Metal in the first quarter and the half-catty of Water in the last quarter. From the new moon to the eighth day (first quarter) is one "eight." From the new moon’s disappearance to the twenty-third day (last quarter) is another "eight." Together, these two eights make sixteen, fulfilling the count of one catty. 

Furthermore, whether looking at the cycle before or after the full and new moons, or reading the cycle forward or backward, they always form "two eights." 

Regarding "The Way of the Changes is upright and does not tilt": this refers to **Water** <term>Kan</term> and **Fire** <term>Li</term>. The Sun and Moon constitute the *I Ching* (the Book of Changes). The Sun contains the Yin energy of the Moon to radiate its brilliance, and the Moon receives the Yang energy of the Sun to produce its light. This is the interactive use of Yin and Yang, with the *Hun* and *Po* souls alternating as the driving force. This is why the Way of the Changes never collapses or tilts. 

One catty contains sixteen ounces <term>liang</term>, and twenty-four *zhu* make one ounce. Thus, sixteen ounces total three hundred and eighty-four *zhu*. In the *I Ching*, there are sixty-four hexagrams, and each hexagram has six lines <term>yao</term>. Sixty-four hexagrams total three hundred and eighty-four lines. Therefore, it is said: "There are three hundred and eighty-four *zhu*, which also corresponds to the number of hexagram lines." 

However, in the Alchemical Path <term>Dandao</term>, the mention of "catties" and "ounces" is merely to understand the proportions and balance; there is no literal "heavy" or "light" weight. When "inches" and "feet" are mentioned, it is to clarify the degree of progress, not literal length. One must not cling stubbornly to the literal text. As Lord Lü <note>Lü Dongbin, a famous Daoist immortal</note> said: "When Water and Fire are perfectly balanced, that is the medicine; any error in Yin and Yang, and the Elixir will not form." This is truly the speech of one who has mastered this Path.</gloss>

# Chapter Nine

<gloss>
This chapter discusses the method of "operating the fire" <note>the timing and intensity of meditative focus or breath</note> in the Alchemical Path. It derives its practical application from the symbols of the *I Ching* (Book of Changes). Therefore, the substances being refined within the cauldron are the Green Dragon and the White Tiger <note>metaphors for Wood/East and Metal/West, or the fluctuating energies within the body</note>, along with the souls of the waxing and waning lunar quarters. Together, they combine to form the body of **Heaven and Earth** <term>Qian and Kun</term>. The "one catty" dose of the Great Medicine also corresponds to the total number of hexagram lines; this entire process follows the Way of the Changes.
</gloss>

**When gold enters a fierce fire, its color is not robbed of its refined brilliance. Since the beginning of creation, the Sun and Moon have never lost their light. Gold does not lose its weight.**

**The forms of the Sun and Moon remain as they ever were.**

<gloss>
All things in the world eventually decay over time. If cast into fire, they are destroyed instantly. Only gold is indestructible through ten thousand eons. When placed in a fierce fire, its color is not stolen; though refined a hundred times, it becomes even more pure and brilliant. This is because gold is a substance that embodies the Metal element, yet its flexibility resembles Wood, and its color resembles Earth. When melted, it yields the properties of Water, and it is governed by the power of Fire. Thus, it is a treasure where the **Four Emblems** <note>the Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird, and Black Tortoise representing the cardinal directions and elements</note> constitute its nature and the **Five Elements** form its substance. 

Since the opening of Heaven and Earth, all things with physical form eventually perish. Only the Sun and the Moon, though they frequently undergo eclipses, never lose their fundamental light, because they are the two primordial breaths of Heaven and Earth and the spiritual essence of Yin and Yang. Thus, the nature of gold never rots or fails, nor does it lose its substantial weight; likewise, the forms of the Sun and Moon remain constant through the ages, never changing their luminous bodies. 

This is why the practice of nourishing life and cultivating the Way is called the **Golden Elixir** <term>Jindan</term>. "Gold" is chosen because its substance contains the Five Elements and its nature is firm and indestructible. "Elixir" <note>originally referring to cinnabar or a refined pill</note> is chosen because its color is endowed by the Sun and its shape is round and without flaw. 

Furthermore, if we examine the Way of the Sun and Moon: the Sun is the essence of the True Fire of Great Yang, and the Moon is the essence of the True Water of Great Yin. They are the condensed spiritual energy <term>qi</term> of the Yin and Yang of Heaven and Earth, which formed their physical shapes. Therefore, if Heaven and Earth were destroyed, the Sun and Moon would perish; but as long as Heaven and Earth are not destroyed, how could the Sun and Moon ever fail? 

The *I Ching* says: "Heaven and Earth are set in their ranks, and the Changes are established between them." If Heaven and Earth were destroyed, there would be no way to see the Changes; and if the Changes could not be seen, Heaven and Earth might as well cease to exist. Previous scholars have explained this scripture by saying that everything in the *I Ching* consists of Yin and Yang, and every line of a hexagram belongs to either Heaven <term>Qian</term> or Earth <term>Kun</term>. Once the lines are set, Heaven and Earth are ranked, and the body of the "Changes" is established. If Heaven and Earth were destroyed, the lines would not stand, and the "Changes" would cease. This is an explanation based on the symbols of the *I Ching*, and the logic is indeed sound. 

However, I also have a theory. When it is said that "Heaven and Earth are set in their ranks," it means Heaven and Earth constitute the world, and they are positioned above and below. When it says "the Changes are established between them," it means the Changes represent the Sun and Moon, and the Sun and Moon are established within the space of Heaven and Earth...
</gloss>

It explains that the alchemist seeks a state of being that, like gold in fire, becomes more refined rather than being destroyed by the "fires" of the world.</summary>
