...is the center. For **Heaven and Earth** <term>Qian and Kun</term> constitute the substance of Yin and Yang, while the Sun and Moon constitute the function of Yin and Yang. Substance and function rely on one another; Yin and Yang revolve in succession. From ancient times to the present, they remain constant and unchanging. This is the reason why Heaven and Earth endure and the Sun and Moon remain as they have always been. When the Sage said, "If Heaven and Earth were destroyed, there would be no way to see the Changes," and "If the Changes could not be seen, Heaven and Earth might as well cease to exist," these were words intended to provoke a reaction. He was actually clarifying the principle that Heaven and Earth are indestructible and the Sun and Moon are imperishable, thereby reaffirming that Heaven and Earth are ranked together and the logic of the **Changes** <term>Yi</term> is established between them.

Therefore, in the *Seal of the Unity of the Three* <note>original: "Wei Gong Qi," referring to the alchemical classic by Wei Boyang</note>, the "Changes" are associated with the hexagrams **Water and Fire** <term>Kan and Li</term>. The idea that the Sun and Moon form the literal written character for "Changes" <note>The character for Changes (易) is traditionally explained as being composed of the characters for Sun (日) above and Moon (月) below</note> is rooted in the meanings found within the Sage's classics. **Water and Fire** <term>Kan and Li</term> represent the elements, while the Sun and Moon are the refined essences of those elements. They emerge and enter within the space of Heaven and Earth to provide light in turns, traveling between East and West in a continuous cycle. This is precisely the path of "interchange" and "transformation"—the true meaning of why the Sun and Moon represent the "Changes." Furthermore, the Sage wrote that "Heaven and Earth set the stage, and the Changes operate within." This also carries the meaning of the Sun and Moon acting as the "Changes." This is my humble perspective; I do not know if more learned scholars would agree.

# Gold Fundamentally Arises from the Moon; On the New Moon, it Receives the Tally of the Sun

The previous text mentioned that gold does not lose its brilliance or weight; that referred to the gold of the world. Now, "Gold fundamentally arises from the Moon" refers to the "gold" within the Moon. The white light of the Moon is considered Gold, while the black body of the Moon is considered Water. The brilliance of this "White Gold" emerges from the silhouette of the "Black Water." If the Moon did not have its black body, where would the white light come from? Thus, it is said that the birth of Gold is rooted in the Moon. This is the same meaning as "Knowing the White, Guarding the Black," mentioned in Chapter Seven of this book. 

As for "receiving the tally of the Sun on the New Moon": the "New Moon" <term>Shuo</term> is the first day of the lunar month. It also signifies "revival." It means the body of the Moon completely exhausts its light on the final day of the previous month; its **spiritual soul** <term>hun</term> is extinguished and its **physical soul** <term>po</term> is hidden. When it reaches the morning of the New Moon, it receives the "tally" or matching essence of the Sun’s **Yang** energy. Only then does the physical soul revive and the spiritual soul begin to grow again.

I respectfully note that Master Shen <note>Shen Kuo (1031–1095), a famous Song dynasty scientist</note> said: "The Moon itself has no light; it is like a silver ball. It is the Sun shining on it that creates the light. When the light first appears, the Sun is to its side, so the light hits the edge, and we see only a crescent like a hook. As the Sun moves further away, it shines from an angle, and the light fills more of it. It is much like a bullet: if you paint half of it with white powder and look at it from the side, the white part looks like a hook; if you look at it head-on, it is a perfect circle." 

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the preeminent Neo-Confucian philosopher</note> said: "Shen Kuo’s explanation is correct. The body of the Moon is always round and its substance is fundamentally dark; it only appears bright because it receives the Sun's light. It does not actually wax or wane, but people see it that way. On the dark moon <term>hui</term>, the Moon and Sun are layered together, so there is no light. By the third day, they gradually move apart; people below see it from the side, so the light appears as a crescent. By the full moon <term>wang</term>, the Moon and Sun are directly opposite each other; people in the middle see it head-on, so the light is perfectly round." He also said: "The first quarter is when the Moon is half-full, like a bow with the string facing up. The last quarter is when the Moon has lost half its light, like a bow with the string facing down." 

The explanations above from previous scholars regarding the angles of the Sun's light and the principles of the lunar phases are most accurate; there is no need to add more. However, there is still something to be said about the way the lights of the Sun and Moon influence one another. Between Heaven and Earth, the most miraculous and inscrutable things are **Spirit** <term>shen</term> and **Vital Energy** <term>qi</term>. Spirit and energy can enter any hardness, penetrate any thickness, and reach any distance. They can even pierce through gold and stone, and they pass through Heaven and Earth...

# Gold Returns to its Mother; On the Dark Moon, they Embrace and Hide

## Its Outer Frame Sinks into the Cavernous Void; Gold Recovers its Original Nature; the Tripod’s Majestic Light then Blazes.

<gloss>
The character "sink" <note>lun</note> is pronounced like *lun*. The character "blaze" <note>xi</note> is pronounced like *xi*. <note>These are original phonetic annotations for the reader.</note> "Return" means to go back. It also implies darkness. This section explains that when the Moon reaches its dark phase <term>hui</term> and loses its light, the "Gold Energy" of the white light has returned to the "Earth Mother" <term>Kun</term>. "Mother" refers to the Earth element or the Kun hexagram. The "dark moon" is the end of the lunar month when it is dark and without light. Thus it is said: "Gold returns to its mother; on the dark moon they embrace." This is the same meaning as "The Sun and Moon wrestle and clasp each other" mentioned in Chapter Three of this book. 

"Outer frame" <term>kuanguo</term> refers to the physical forms of the Sun and Moon (as noted in the first chapter). "Sinking" means disappearing. This says that during the dark moon, the physical images of the Sun and Moon are hidden and cannot be seen, as if they have sunk into a void of emptiness. Thus it says: "Its outer frame sinks into the cavernous void." 

"Tripod" <term>ding</term> is a metaphor for the physical body of the Moon. "Blaze" <term>xi</term> means to be radiant or flourishing. This means that from the morning of the New Moon, when the Moon receives the "tally" of the Sun, until the third day of the month, the light is born again. The "White Gold" of its original nature is restored. Within the outer frame, a majestic light once again blazes forth. Thus it is said: "Gold recovers its original nature; the tripod's majestic light then blazes." This carries the same meaning as "When the cycle ends, they pass the power to one another; the successor body again gives birth to the Dragon," as found in Chapter Four. 

In the alchemical method of "operating the fire," "guarding the belly of the Mother" <term>Kun</term> corresponds to the dark moon, while "moving to the head of the Father" <term>Qian</term> corresponds to the brightness. Ultimately, this is all the work of spirit and energy; the principle is one and the same.
</gloss>

# The Numbers of Zi and Wu Combine to Three; Wu and Ji are Called Five. When Three and Five are Harmonized, the Eight Minerals Correct the Principles. Breathing Sustains and Nourishes One Another.

# Quiet Reflection Becomes Husband and Wife.

<gloss>
The character "Quiet" <term>zhu</term> is pronounced like *zhu*. <note>original: "佇音柱"</note>

**Zi** corresponds to Water; the generative number of Water is one. **Wu** corresponds to Fire; the generative number of Fire is two. <note>In ancient numerology, 1 + 2 = 3, hence "Zi and Wu make three."</note> **Wu** and **Ji** correspond to Earth; the generative number of Earth is five. Thus, the "three" and "five" are harmonized and joined. 

Regarding "the **Eight Minerals** <term>bashi</term> correct the principles": the Eight Minerals usually refer to external substances used in laboratory alchemy. By combining the "three" and the "five," the sum is eight. Using the "Eight Minerals" as a metaphor here is a way of comparing external alchemy to internal processes. Just as Heaven and Earth combine Water, Fire, and Earth to create endless transformation, the practitioner of the Elixir must cause Water and Fire to rise and fall, using Earth to harmonize them and form the "seed" of the Elixir. Thus, are these so-called "Eight Minerals" not the very principles that govern both Heaven and Man? 

Regarding "**Breathing**": "Exhaling" is the rising of energy; "Inhaling" is the descending of energy. Now, there is the breathing of Heaven and Earth, the breathing of the human body, and the breathing of the Alchemical Method. 

The "Breathing of Heaven and Earth" refers to the Winter Solstice when the **Yang energy** is born and the energy of the Earth rises—this is "Exhalation." At the Summer Solstice, the **Yin energy** is born and the energy of Heaven descends—this is "Inhalation." Furthermore, the growth of Spring and Summer is "Exhalation," while the harvest and storage of Autumn and Winter is "Inhalation." The philosopher Shao Yong <note>a famous Song Dynasty cosmologist</note> said: "After the Winter Solstice is the Exhalation; after the Summer Solstice is the Inhalation." This is the single yearly breath of Heaven and Earth; this is the meaning here.

As for the "Breathing of the Human Body," medical books state: "Sending energy out is called Exhalation; taking energy in is called Inhalation." One exhalation and one inhalation make one "breath." It is also said: "In the duration of two breaths, the energy travels six inches. In one full day and night, there are 13,500 breaths, and the energy completes fifty circuits around the body." This is the state of a healthy person. The *Classic of Difficult Issues* <term>Nan Jing</term> says: "Exhalation comes from the Heart and Lungs; Inhalation enters the Kidneys and Liver. Between exhalation and inhalation, the Spleen receives the energy of grain <note>nutrition</note>." Master Zhang Zai said: "The fact that humans have breath is an image of the Hard and Soft rubbing together, and the opening and closing of Heaven <term>Qian</term> and Earth <term>Kun</term>." This explains the principles of breathing in the human body.

But regarding the "Breathing of the Alchemical Method," the *Classic of the Way and Virtue* <term>Tao Te Ching</term> says: "Continuous, as if it exists; use it without effort." The master Bai Ziqing said: "When establishing the energy of the 'Mysterious Female' <note>the source of life</note>, let it enter its root. If you hold it too tightly, you err toward urgency; if you let it go completely, you err toward dissipation. One desires it to be continuous and unbroken." "As if it exists" means to let it exist according to its own nature. When the Spirit is long-held, it becomes peaceful; when the breath is long-held, it becomes stable. When one's inner nature enters the realm of the natural, it is a "wondrous use of non-doing," never reaching the point of toil or frantic effort. This is what is meant by "using it without effort." 

Xiao Zixu said: "Exhaling, one connects to the Root of Heaven; Inhaling, one connects to the Root of Earth. Exhaling, the Dragon moans and clouds rise; Inhaling, the Tiger roars and the wind is born." By breathing the wind and clouds, one condenses the **Golden Liquid** <term>jinye</term>. Thus, the breathing of the Alchemical Method arises from the spontaneity of the One Energy. It cannot be compared to ordinary breathing. It traces the very origin of the growth and shedding of Yin and Yang, imitating the cycles of the Sun and Moon...
</gloss>

## Yellow Earth is the Father of Gold; Liquid Pearl is the Son of Water. Water takes Earth as its Ghost; Earth suppresses Water so it does not rise.

The color of Earth is yellow. According to the Five Elements, Earth generates Gold. Therefore it is said: "Yellow Earth is the father of Gold." "Liquid Pearl" <term>liuzhu</term> refers to the Wood-Mercury <note>a symbolic term for the fluid, volatile aspect of the spirit</note>. Since Water generates Wood, and Wood is the "child" of Water, it is said: "Liquid Pearl is the son of Water." 

In the system of the Five Elements, the relationships of generation and overcoming are matched with the "Six Relations" <note>a system used in traditional divination to categorize relationships</note>: 
* That which generates me is my **Parent**.
* That which I generate is my **Child**.
* That which overcomes (restricts) me is my **Official Ghost** <term>guangui</term>. 
* That which I overcome is my **Wife/Wealth**. 
* That which is the same as me is my **Brother**.

Now it is said: "Water takes Earth as its Ghost" because Earth overcomes Water; thus, Earth is the "Official Ghost" of Water. "Earth suppresses Water so it does not rise": "Suppress" means to press down. This means that when Water is restricted by Earth, it is pressed down and cannot overflow or rise uncontrollably. This section discusses the mutual generation of Earth, Gold, Water, and Wood, while also mentioning the restriction between Water and Earth, to introduce the following discussion on how the "Three Natures" control and transform one another.

## The Vermilion Bird is the Essence of Fire, holding the balance to adjust victory and defeat. When Water is abundant, Fire is extinguished; both die and return to Thick Earth.

"The **Vermilion Bird** <term>zhuque</term> is the Essence of Fire" because the Vermilion Bird is the symbolic creature of the South and represents the essence of the **Li-Fire** trigram. "Holding the balance to adjust victory and defeat": "Balance" means equality or equilibrium. The previous text mentioned that Water is suppressed by Earth and cannot rise. Now, by employing the fire of the Vermilion Bird to hold the balance, the "victory" (overpowering nature) of Earth can be adjusted, and the "defeat" (restriction) of Water can be harmonized. 

"When Water is abundant, Fire is extinguished": Fire has the power to cook water and make it boil; through this, the water-energy rises, and thus Water becomes "abundant" and is no longer suppressed by Earth. However, if Water becomes too abundant, the Fire will instead be overcome and extinguished. 

"Both die and return to Thick Earth": This means that once the Fire is overcome by Water, and the Water is in turn restricted by Earth, both Water and Fire return to the "Thick Earth" <note>the central, stabilizing element</note>. Once the "Three Natures" (Water, Fire, and Earth) have converged, they each maintain their substance, but Water and Fire meet within the Earth. This is what is meant by "combining the Three Natures." 

"The Original Nature shares a common ancestor": Because Water and Fire are the "children" of Gold and Wood, and Gold and Wood are ultimately generated and nourished by Earth, the very substance and nature of all Five Elements are rooted in Earth as their ancestor. As Chapter 11 of the Middle Volume states: "The Yellow of the Spleen <note>associated with Earth</note> is the Ancestor." This carries the same meaning.

## Even the "Great Victory" can extend one's years; how much more so when the Returned Elixir enters the mouth? The nature of Gold does not decay or rot; therefore, it is the treasure of all things. The practitioner who ingests it will obtain longevity of life.

### Right, Chapter Eleven

Their mutual restraint and submission to one another to congeal the "Elixir Seed" is called "Harmony," "Nurturing," or "Union." # **Confucius** <gloss>The meaning and sound are rare</gloss> **was a hero among the ordinary Sages. The "Ten Wings"** <term>Shiyi</term> <note>The "Ten Wings" are the traditional commentaries on the *Book of Changes* attributed to Confucius.</note> **served to assist him. These three lords were raised up by Heaven** <gloss>pronounced *tu-ding*</gloss>**. They rose in succession to govern their times. Though their paces differed in excellence, their merit and virtue were no different.**

<gloss>The "Utmost Sage" represents the very peak of sageliness. **Fuxi** (also written as Baoxi) was the ruler among the Five Emperors. The *Book of Changes* says: "In ancient times, when Baoxi ruled the world, he looked up to observe the images in the sky and looked down to observe the patterns on the earth. He observed the markings of birds and beasts and the suitability of the land. Nearby, he took examples from his own body; far away, he took examples from things at large. Thus, he began to create the Eight Trigrams to communicate the virtue of the divine and clear light, and to categorize the essential nature of all things." Therefore, Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the purported author of this text</note> says that Fuxi first drew the Eight Trigrams to model himself after Heaven and Earth.

**King Wen** was the ancestor of all kings. His supreme virtue served as the master and model for ten thousand generations of emperors. Using Fuxi's "Earlier Heaven" trigram arrangements as a foundation, he bound them into the "Later Heaven" application. He deduced the strength and flexibility of the six lines of the hexagrams, the transformations of the two primary images, and created the "Judgment" or "Image Descriptions" <term>Xiangci</term> to determine the good or ill fortune of every hexagram and clarify the mathematical principles of the entire *Book of Changes*. Thus it is said: "King Wen was the ancestor of emperors; he structured the hexagrams and developed the line descriptions."

The *Doctrine of the Mean* says: "Therefore, one of great virtue must receive the Mandate." Now, although **Confucius** (Fuzi) possessed great virtue, he did not hold a high position of power. This is why he is called the "hero of the ordinary sages." The **"Ten Wings"** consist of: the first and second parts of the *Commentary on the Judgments* <term>Tuanzhuan</term>, the *Great Image* and *Small Image* commentaries, the *Words of the Text* <term>Wenyan</term>, the first and second parts of the *Appended Phrases* <term>Xici</term>, the *Explaining the Trigrams*, the *Order of the Hexagrams*, and the *Mixed Hexagrams*. These were created by Confucius to assist and support the *Changes of the Zhou* <term>Zhouyi</term> and to clarify the principles of good and bad fortune, and the waxing and waning of things. Thus it is said: "Confucius was a hero among the ordinary sages, and the Ten Wings served to assist him."

Even though these three sages existed, they were raised up by the power of Heaven and Earth. They rose in succession, one after another, to govern and guide their eras using the Way of the *Changes*. How could there be any distinction of "better or worse" in their steps? Their merit and virtue do not differ in height. This describes the profound intent of the Sages in creating the *Changes*—to open up the nature of things and complete the world's tasks, weaving together the Great Way of Heaven, Earth, and Humanity. 

<note>Translator's note: The commentator observes that the *Changes* is usually attributed to four sages (including the Duke of Zhou), but Lord Wei only mentions three. He suggests King Wen might be intended to represent the Duke of Zhou as well, or there may be another reason unknown to us.</note></gloss>

For the world, they established this book. I lacked any natural gift for foreknowledge, but through a teacher, I woke to the truth. It was as bright as drawing aside a curtain, or opening one's eyes wide upon climbing a high tower.**

Having established the lineage of the Three Sages (Fuxi, King Wen, and Confucius), Lord Wei (Wei Boyang) now justifies why he has committed these "hidden" alchemical secrets to writing, balancing the fear of revealing divine secrets against the sin of letting the Way be forgotten.</meta>

The phrase "the meaning of the sentence is the same" refers to why this specific character was used; we follow that convention here. 

**Lineage** <note>original: 踵 zhong</note> refers to the heel of the foot, or to follow in succession. **Drawing aside** <note>original: 褰 qian</note> means to lift up a garment or a curtain. **Opening eyes wide** <note>original: 瞋 zhen</note> refers to a wide-eyed stare, often associated with intense focus or clarity. 

Lord Wei says: "My book, *The Kinship of the Three* <term>Cantong Qi</term>, is not without a foundation. It follows in the footsteps of the Three Sages' *Book of Changes* to invent and reveal the divine mysteries of both the Way of the *Changes* and the Way of Alchemy <term>Dandao</term>." Therefore, he measured the waxing and waning of Yin and Yang without error and examined the precise weights <note>literally "grains and ounces"</note> of the refinement process without loss. 

Things that have a physical form are easy to calculate and measure. However, matters that have no outward sign or omen are difficult to plan for or deliberate upon. Therefore, the way of acting and establishing words must be done so that both the wise and the simple can use them as a model. He has now fixed this book, *The Kinship of the Three*, to serve as a standard for students of later generations. 

This also reflects Lord Wei’s humility. He speaks in a veiled way, appearing to simply praise the Three Sages for creating the *Changes*. However, if he were merely providing a commentary on the Sages' *Changes*, he would not use technical phrases like "examining the grains and ounces." It is clear he is describing his own work in composing this alchemical text. 

He then asks: "Among the clever people of the world, who is not my equal?" There is certainly no shortage of students who love to learn. He admits: "I possessed no innate, heaven-sent talent or gift of foreknowledge. My understanding came from the awakening granted by a teacher; only then did I realize the true mechanism of the Way." It was like pulling back a thick curtain to reveal a brilliant light, or like climbing a high tower and opening one's eyes wide—suddenly, nothing is too far to be seen. This is a teaching for later students: one must seek a true teacher to open one's ignorance so that one may truly enter the "inner chamber" of alchemy.

# **The Fire Records** <term>Huoji</term> <note>These are traditional manuals or sections of text describing the timing and intensity of the alchemical fire.</note> **consist of six hundred chapters. Their goal and direction are not different. Though the words are spoken with great gravity, the people of the world do not reflect on them deeply. Search out and measure their source and flow; the hidden and the manifest dwell together.**
<gloss>The word "measure" <note>original: 度 duo</note> is pronounced *duo*.</gloss>

> The **"Six Hundred Chapters of the Fire Records"** refers to the method of "operating the fire" in alchemical cultivation. This is based on a system where two hexagrams <term>Gua</term> govern the work of a single day. The cycle begins with the hexagrams *Difficulty at the Beginning* <term>Tun</term> and *Youthful Folly* <term>Meng</term>, and ends with *After Completion* <term>Jiji</term> and *Before Completion* <term>Weiji</term>. In one month, this totals sixty hexagrams. If one practices the "warm nourishment" of the elixir for ten months <note>the symbolic length of a pregnancy</note>, it results in six hundred hexagrams. 

> The phrase **"their goals are not different"** means that within a single month, every hexagram follows the same underlying principle, and across the ten months, every chapter remains consistent. Their essential purpose is identical. However, the writings concerning the **"fire timings"** <term>Huohou</term> must be expressed with great solemnity and care. Unfortunately, people of the world only understand the superficial language and do not think deeply about the refined, subtle meanings. If one can find the root of Yin and Yang and trace the source of Water and Fire, they will realize that the "hidden" metaphors of alchemy and the "manifest" logic of the *Changes* may seem like different paths, but they actually dwell together and return to the same truth.

# **I secretly speak for the sake of the worthy. How would I dare to write this book lightly? If I were to tie my tongue and remain silent, I would be cutting off the Way and would deserve the punishment of death. To express my inner feelings, I follow this single pattern.**

This "forging and smelting"** <note>The process of internal transformation</note> **possesses its own laws and measures. It cannot yet...**

# **I fully set forth and briefly describe the essential principles; its branches and leaves appear flourishing.**

<gloss>The character for **mute** <note>瘖 yin</note> is pronounced *yin*. **Leaking** <note>泄 xie</note> is pronounced *xie*. **Bowing** <note>俛 fǔ</note> is the same as the character for "looking down" <note>俯 fǔ</note>. **To weave together** <note>綴 zhui</note> is pronounced *zhui*. **Manifest** <note>現 xian</note> is pronounced *xian*. Regarding the meaning of the characters: the author says he "could not stop thinking," which exactly describes how he composed the book through much deliberation. Let this be recorded as a testament for those of high insight.</gloss>

**Hesitation** <note>original: 猶豫 youyu</note> is the name of a beast that is naturally suspicious and prone to doubt. **Bamboo and silk** <term>Zhubo</term> refer to the materials needed for writing. **Flourishing** <note>original: 扶疎 fushu</note> refers to the abundance of branches and leaves. 

Lord Wei says: "I have written this book originally for the sake of worthy and good people who love the Way. Therefore, I have discussed these matters repeatedly to enlighten them. How would I dare to write this book lightly and thus mislead later students? Yet, if I were to tie my tongue like a mute and say nothing, then the Way would be cut off by my own hand, and I would be guilty of a crime against Heaven. If I were to write everything down on bamboo and silk with total transparency, I would then be leaking the Heavenly secrets <note>literally "the Heavenly tally"</note> and would fear divine punishment." 

Therefore, he was caught in **hesitation**, and his sighs increased as he began his discourse. Looking up and down, he wove together many thoughts to complete this book. It is much like a potter or blacksmith who smelts and fires a vessel; there must be a law and a measure to serve as a standard. However, he does not dare to fully disclose every minute detail, but only briefly narrates the essential principles. This is like a tree: when one sees the branches and leaves flourishing and manifesting, one knows they originate from the root. 

As Mencius said: "The gentleman draws the bow but does not release the arrow; he leaps as if to shoot. He stands in the middle of the Way, and those who are able follow him." The *Book of Changes* says: "Making it spiritual and illuminating it depends on the person." These quotes refer to exactly this approach.

# Below there is the breath of the Great Sun, steaming and subduing; in a brief moment, it first becomes liquid and then solidifies, called the "Yellow Carriage." # **The blazing fire spreads below; day and night the sound is diligent. Start with the "Civil" fire so it may be cultivated; finish with the "Martial" fire as it is displayed.**

## **Watch the stages with added caution; examine and adjust the cold and warmth. Rotate through the twelve periods; when the periods end, one must attend to it again.**

<gloss>"The blazing fire spreads below" means that once the medicines are stored and sealed within the vessel, one must use the "Yang Fire" and "Yin Talisman" <note>the two phases of the heating cycle</note> to cook and refine them from above and below. This is the meaning. It says that day and night one must apply the energy of the fire-timing schedule <term>Huofu</term> without allowing any negligence or error.
> *The Chapter of Emerald Emptiness* says: "By day, move the spirit flag; by night, fire the numinous fungus. In the process of taking away and adding fire, one must strictly guard against danger."

This is the principle. In the method of the alchemical firing process <term>Huohou</term>, one must first use the "Civil" fire <note>a gentle, rising heat</note> to initiate growth, and afterward use the "Martial" fire <note>an intense, descending heat</note> to bring the Elixir to fruition. Yin and Yang alternate in their movement, and firmness and softness are applied to one another. Thus it is said: "Start with the Civil fire so it may be cultivated; finish with the Martial fire as it is displayed." However, there is also a secret to the Civil and Martial fire-timing for each specific hour. For instance, in the hours of the Ox, Dragon, Monkey, and Pig <note>Chou, Chen, Shen, and Hai</note>, the fire used is Civil. In the hours of the Tiger, Snake, Goat, and Dog <note>Yin, Si, Wei, and Xu</note>, the fire used is Martial.
> *The Chapter on Returning to Life* says: "Yin-Civil and Yang-Martial are added or subtracted accordingly."

This is exactly that principle. "Watch the stages with added caution" means that while conducting the fire, one must constantly check and be mindful at every moment.
> This is what *The Chapter of Emerald Emptiness* means by: "If there are no like-minded companions to observe and regulate, one fears the firing process in the furnace will go wrong."

"Examine and adjust the cold and warmth": If the fire is too strong, it results in dryness; if it is too weak, it results in coldness. Therefore, one must carefully adjust the temperature to find the middle ground, ensuring the speed and intensity are measured. "Rotate through the twelve periods": This means the Yang fire advances from the hour of the Rat <note>Zi, midnight</note> and reaches its peak at the hour of the Snake <note>Si, mid-morning</note>. The Yin talisman retreats from the hour of the Horse <note>Wu, noon</note> and ends at the hour of the Pig <note>Hai, late night</note>. These are the twelve periods <term>jie</term> that complete a full cycle. "When the periods end, one must attend to it again": This means that once the application of the fire schedule ends at the hour of the Pig, it begins again at the hour of the Rat, like a ring without an end. Furthermore, the method of "warm nourishment" must be maintained within a single day, throughout the twelve hours, without interruption, beginning again as soon as it finishes. In Chapter 4 of this book, the phrase "when the periods end, they pass the succession to one another, and the dragon is reborn in continuation" refers to this same logic. This section's meaning concerns the firing process for warm nourishment; being cautious is of the highest importance.
> Thus, *The Essay on Understanding Reality* says: "Even if you recognize Cinnabar and Black Lead, if you do not know the firing process, your efforts are in vain. It all depends on the power of the practice; a hair's breadth of error will not produce the Elixir."

This is what is meant.</gloss>

# **Deducing the numbers of the Five Elements is concise and not complicated.**

<gloss>The "Five Elements" <term>Wuxing</term> are Water, Fire, Wood, Metal, and Earth. The "Numbers" refer to one, two, three, four, and five, which are the "Generative Numbers" of the Five Elements; and six, seven, eight, nine, and ten, which are the "Completion Numbers" of the Five Elements. "Deducing" means to investigate the source and flow of these numbers. In the numbers of the *River Map* <note>original: *Hetu*; an ancient cosmological diagram used to explain the universe</note>, the numbers 1 and 6 reside in the North, 2 and 7 in the South, 3 and 8 in the East, 4 and 9 in the West, and 5 and 10 in the Center. If one deduces their meaning, the Generative Numbers 1, 2, 3, and 4 represent the Completion Number 10 of the central "Earth" element being dispersed into the four directions. Meanwhile, the Completion Numbers 6, 7, 8, and 9 represent the Generative Number 5 of the central Earth element being combined with the four directions. If one takes "one" from each of the four directions and merges them with the "one" of the center, they form the Generative Number 5. If all the Generative Numbers of the four directions return to the center, they form the Completion Number 10. 

The *Book of Changes* <note>I Ching</note> speaks of the "Number of Great Expansion" being fifty; this is also derived from the center of the *River Map*, where the "Heavenly 5" <note>Yang/Generative Earth</note> multiplies the "Earthly 10" <note>Yin/Completion Earth</note>. Therefore, among the Five Elements, nothing can be generated or completed without Earth, just as all things in the world are without a foundation if they lack Earth. As for the principles of how the Five Elements generate, overcome, restrain, and transform one another, these also arise from nature. The scholar Mr. Sizhai Weng said: "In the movements of creation, if there is generation without overcoming, then those things being generated would have no way to be pruned or regulated. If there is overcoming without generation, then the process of overcoming would eventually be interrupted." This speaks to the mystery of generation and overcoming—neither can be missing. Thus, it is said that deducing the numbers of the Five Elements is not a matter of forced calculation, but is actually "concise and not complicated." If one is willing to learn, anyone can understand and master it.</gloss>

# **Lifting water to stir the fire, it suddenly...**
# **...extinguishes the light. The Sun and Moon encroach upon and eclipse each other, usually between the last and first days of the lunar month. Water is abundant in the Kan trigram, invading the Yang; Fire declines in the Li trigram, and the day turns to darkness. Yin and Yang consume each other; this resonance is the natural Way.**

<gloss>The character *Yan* <note>suddenly/extinguished</note> is pronounced *Yuan-jian*. *Bo* <note>encroach/thin</note> is pronounced like *Bo*. *Shi* <note>eat/eclipse</note> is pronounced like *Shi*. 

If one extrapolates the principles of the Five Elements overcoming one another: if you lift up Water to toss against Fire, the Fire is suddenly extinguished and its light is hidden. "Encroaching" means to press in or invade. "Eclipsing" means to fail or be defeated. Generally, when the Moon covers the Sun, a solar eclipse occurs; when the Sun faces the Moon <note>is opposite to it</note>, a lunar eclipse occurs. Now, when the text says "The Sun and Moon encroach upon and eclipse each other, usually between the last and first days of the lunar month," it refers specifically to solar eclipses, while implying lunar eclipses as well. 

The reason for a solar eclipse is that the Water of the *Kan* <note>the trigram representing Water and the Moon</note> is abundant, and thus it invades and defeats the Yang light. This causes the Fire of the *Li* <note>the trigram representing Fire and the Sun</note> to decline, so that even in the middle of the day, it becomes dark. However, this encroaching and eclipsing of the Sun and Moon, where Yin and Yang hold each other in check, is like the concept of them "consuming" each other. This explains that the tossing of Water and Fire against one another is the natural Way of Heaven and Earth; it is not something forced or artificial. 

Regarding the principle of the Sun and Moon eclipsing each other, Master Shao <note>Shao Yong, a famous 11th-century philosopher</note> said: "When the Sun and Moon eat each other, it is the intersection of their numbers. When the Sun faces the Moon, it is a lunar eclipse; when the Moon covers the Sun, it is a solar eclipse. It is like the mutual overcoming of Water and Fire." Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi, the preeminent Confucian scholar</note> said: "Astronomers say that at the time of the full moon <note>the 15th</note>, the Sun's light is distant and 'robs' the Moon's light, hence the lunar eclipse. At the meeting of the Sun and Moon <note>the new moon</note>, the Sun is covered by the Moon, hence the solar eclipse. However, the Sages did not speak of the 'Moon being eaten,' but used the general term 'eclipse' in writing to acknowledge things they could not see." Master Zhu also said: "At the time of the new moon <note>the 1st day of the month</note>, the Sun and Moon..." <note>the text cuts off here</note></gloss>

It then uses solar and lunar eclipses as natural metaphors for the interaction and mutual "consumption" of Yin (Water/Moon) and Yang (Fire/Sun).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of celestial eclipses as a metaphor for the union of Yin and Yang, specifically focusing on the mechanics of solar and lunar eclipses. It then transitions to the internal alchemical application of these principles, moving from the macrocosm (Sun/Moon) to the microcosm (human Nature and Emotion), represented by the elements of Wood and Metal.</meta>

<page-num>63</page-num>

...between the east and west. Even if they are on the same degree of longitude, if the paths of the Moon to the north or south are significantly different from the Sun’s, an eclipse will not occur. Or, if their north-south positions are close, but the Sun is "inside" while the Moon is "outside," an eclipse also will not occur. 

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi</note> also said: "The reason the Sun is eclipsed during the new moon <note>the 1st day of the lunar month</note> is that the Moon is typically below and the Sun is above. When they meet, the Moon is positioned beneath the Sun and obscures it; thus, a solar eclipse occurs. At the full moon <note>the 15th day</note>, the Moon is eclipsed; this is certainly a case of Yin <note>the Moon</note> daring to oppose Yang <note>the Sun</note>. However, astronomers also call this the 'Dark Void' <note>original: *Anxu*; the shadow cast by the Earth</note>. Because the Sun is like a fire, its outer light casts a shadow, and the center of that shadow is actually dark. At the full moon, the Moon happens to enter that dark center, and thus a lunar eclipse occurs." 

Mr. Chen of Qianshi <note>Chen Xianwei, a Southern Song alchemical commentator</note> said: "When the Sun and Moon intersect and the Sun is covered by the Moon, it is a solar eclipse. When the Sun and Moon face each other and the Moon opposes the Sun, it is a lunar eclipse. This naturally occurs when their orbital paths cross at these specific points. Astronomers use calculations to determine the frequency of these events; they are not inherently meant to be seen as omens. However, when the heavens encounter such a moment, it represents a 'point of distress' for Yin and Yang. In human affairs, this inevitably brings disaster or blame. Therefore, the Sages feared these events and practiced self-cultivation <note>side-stepping or correcting their behavior</note>, hoping to mitigate the calamity."

The theories of the various scholars mentioned above regarding the principles of eclipses are most accurate. In general, the Sun is the symbol of the Ruler, and the Moon is the path of the Minister. During the daylight of the new moon, the Sun and Moon travel together through the heavens; the Sun resides above and the Moon below. If the Moon does not yield slightly but stands directly in line with the Sun, the Sun's brilliance is obscured by the Moon—this is a solar eclipse. This represents a Minister obscuring the Ruler’s wisdom, or the subordinate hiding the virtue of the superior. This is why the Sages feared it and offered warnings. 

As for the night of the full moon, the Moon is in the sky while the Sun is below the earth. If the Moon "stands tall" against the Sun and faces it directly, the Moon’s light is "snatched" from a distance by the Sun; thus, a lunar eclipse occurs. This represents a Minister daring to rival the Ruler, resulting in the Ruler stripping the Minister of his office. While a lunar eclipse is also considered "unbeautiful," it ultimately represents Yang <note>the Sun/Ruler</note> overcoming Yin <note>the Moon/Minister</note>. This is why the Sages placed great importance on solar eclipses but treated lunar eclipses more lightly. 

In Lord Wei’s *Tripartite Unity* <note>original: *Cantong qi*; the foundational text of internal alchemy</note>, it is said that solar eclipses represent the way Yin and Yang intersect. This is a metaphor for the "mechanism of the mutual use of Water and Fire" in creating the Elixir, and the principle of "Spirit and Qi" merging into one. Therefore, the emphasis is placed on the solar eclipse. This is why the "Way of the Elixir" <note>Alchemy</note>, the "Way of Heaven" <note>Astronomy</note>, and the "Way of the Sages" <note>Ethics/Philosophy</note> all coincide without exception. The *Classic of the Hidden Accord* <note>original: *Yinfu Jing*</note> says: "Observe the Way of Heaven and persist in the actions of Heaven; that is all." Truly, these are honest words.

# **Names are used to define the Emotions; Style Names are derived from Nature. When the Metal returns to the source of Nature...**
## **...only then can it be called the Returned Elixir.**

The fact that humans have Names and Style Names <note>original: *Ming* and *Zi*; a person's given name and the secondary name taken in adulthood</note> is the same principle as the body having "Emotion" and "Nature." A "Name" is determined by a person’s <term>Qing</term> <note>Emotion, Passions, or Reactive feelings</note>. A "Style Name" is spoken of in relation to a person’s <term>Xing</term> <note>Innate Nature, Essence, or True Self</note>. 

Emotion and Nature are the "functions" inside the body, while Name and Style Name are the "titles" outside the body. Within the Five Elements, Emotion belongs to "Metal" <note>representing the West and contraction</note>, while Nature belongs to "Wood" <note>representing the East and growth</note>. Thus, Metal and Wood are the "Name and Style Name" of Emotion and Nature. 

In the "Way of Cultivation," one uses "Metal" <note>Emotion/Will</note> to return to and merge with "Wood" <note>Nature</note>. When Nature goes forth to govern and gather the Emotions, returning to the original state of the Great Beginning and the source of the Pre-celestial realm, it is called the <term>Huandan</term> <note>Returned Elixir; "Huan" means to return, "Dan" means elixir</note>. 

The *Chapters on Understanding Reality* <note>original: *Wuzhen pian*; a famous alchemical text</note> says: "The Nature of Wood loves the righteousness of Metal; the Emotion of Metal yearns for the benevolence of Wood. They swallow each other and gulp each other down, yet they are intimate; only then do you realize the 'man' is pregnant." This is precisely the meaning. 

The previous section discussed Water and Fire agitating each other and Yin and Yang intersecting to form eclipses. This section discusses Metal and Wood restraining each other and Emotion and Nature needing each other for the "Returned Elixir" to be completed. Ultimately, these are all the effects of deducing the numbers of the generation and overcoming of the Five Elements.

It then introduces the internal alchemical concept of the "Returned Elixir," achieved by harmonizing the "Metal" of human emotion with the "Wood" of innate nature.</summary>

# **I do not dare to speak empty words; I follow the writings of the Sages. Ancient records mention the "Dragon and Tiger"; the Yellow Emperor praised the "Golden Flower." The King of Huainan refined "Autumn Stone"...**

# **...and Yuyang added "Yellow Sprout." The worthy are able to maintain the practice, but the unworthy are not permitted to join. From ancient times to the present, the Dao has remained one; I speak these plans to you now in conversation.** <gloss>The character *fang* (倣, to emulate) is pronounced like *fang* (紡). Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the legendary author of the text</note> is speaking about his own purpose in writing this book.</gloss>

# **Students must apply themselves with diligence, keeping this in mind and contemplating deeply. The most essential words are very exposed; they are clear and do not deceive.**

These are not hollow or baseless theories; they are modeled after the writings of the Sages. For instance, ancient records use titles like <term>Dragon and Tiger</term> <note>original: *Longhu*; metaphors for the volatile and stable elements within the body, often associated with Lead and Mercury</note>, and the Yellow Emperor has writings praising the <term>Golden Flower</term> <note>original: *Jinhua*; a symbol of the flourishing of internal light/energy</note>. The King of Huainan <note>Liu An, a famous patron of alchemy</note> practiced the elixir and named it <term>Autumn Stone</term> <note>original: *Qiushi*; historically a substance derived from urine, but here used as a metaphor for a refined essence</note>. Master Yuyang refined the medicine and called it <term>Yellow Sprout</term> <note>original: *Huangya*; the first sign of the "Golden Elixir" beginning to grow</note>. These are all cases of the ancients using "images" to convey "metaphors" and using "fables" to house "meaning."

However, only the worthy recognize that the Dao is honorable and Virtue is precious; they are able to hold fast to it and practice it. Those who are unworthy will inevitably be frivolous and lack proper conduct; how could they possibly receive the Great Dao? If one recklessly leaks or lightly transmits these secrets, both the giver and the receiver will incur punishment. One must be cautious. The Dao is simply One. From ancient times to the present, all follow this same path; how could there be another? Now, I engage in this discussion and reveal these strategies. Those who study the Dao must apply themselves with diligence, keep these thoughts in mind, and investigate them with precision. If you contemplate deeply and study thoroughly, the most essential words will be clearly revealed. They are bright and self-evident, and you will know that my words do not deceive. 

Ah! Lord Wei’s benevolence in bestowing these teachings upon later students is truly of the highest depth. Should those who aspire to the Dao not exert themselves to practice it?

***

According to Yu Quanyang <note>an alchemical commentator</note>: "In studying the Dao, do not say one must possess <term>Immortal Bones</term> <note>original: *Xiangu*; a pre-destined or innate spiritual aptitude</note> from birth before one can seek it. The main thing is to distinguish whether one has a 'willing heart'; if so, there is nothing that cannot be achieved. What kind of people were the Sages and Worthies? What kind of person am I? Anyone who acts can be like them. My only fear is that one might study but not meet a teacher, or meet a teacher but not receive the truth. Or perhaps one receives the True Secret but cannot keep it—acting in the morning but wanting results by evening, or sitting to practice and standing up expecting an effect. If that is the case, even if Guangcheng or Laozi were your teachers, or Liezi and Zhuangzi were your friends, there would be nothing they could do for you."

In general, the Way of Cultivation is extremely simple and easy. If one receives the true transmission, even a simple man or woman can know it and practice it. But if one lacks a teacher's instruction, or if one's will is not firm, then even a person of great talent and wisdom will find it difficult to comprehend or clarify. Therefore, regardless of whether a person is wise or simple, they should only seek the true explanation and receive the ultimate Dao. If they can then concentrate their mind and will, practicing with diligence and refinement over a long time, why worry that the Elixir will not form or the Dao will not be completed? One can achieve spiritual transcendence right before one's eyes; why wait for another life or a future world? 

Mencius said: "Every person can become a Yao or a Shun <note>legendary sage-kings</note>." The *Chapters on Understanding Reality* <note>original: *Wuzhen pian*</note> says: "Every person possesses the medicine of longevity." These all mean the same thing. Some say that studying the Dao requires "great potential" or "deep roots" from past lives, or talk about "immortal features and Daoist bones." If one examines the Confucian books and Daoist scriptures, these claims have no basis. They are merely the views of the common and vulgar—baseless words. One must absolutely not believe them.

It emphasizes that the Dao is accessible to all who are sincere and diligent, rejecting the idea that "immortal bones" or innate talent are required for success.</summary>

# **The above is Chapter Sixteen**

In this chapter, I have deduced the numerical principles of the <term>Five Elements</term> <note>original: *Wuxing*; the five phases of Wood, Fire, Earth, Metal, and Water that govern the transformation of the universe</note> and their cycles of generation and overcoming. Just as Water overcoming Fire results in a solar eclipse, the merging of Metal and Wood leads to the **completion of the Elixir**. This is the most authentic and essential Way. The various arguments presented throughout this <term>Agreement</term> <note>original: *Qi*; referring to the "Cantong qi," where "Qi" means a tally or agreement with the truth</note> are not baseless or empty words; since ancient times, the Sages and Worthies have practiced them with proven results. 

However, this Way is such that only the worthy may harmonize with it. How could those who are unworthy be fit for it? The Dao originates from the One and there is no second path. If those who are determined to study will investigate deeply and contemplate with precision, the essential meaning will naturally reveal itself—bright, clear, and without deception. It is as the saying goes: "Seek, and you shall find."

<term>Wang Yangming</term> <note>original: Wang Yangming (1472–1529); one of the most influential Neo-Confucian philosophers, known for his theory of the "unity of knowledge and action."</note> said: "Doing good is naturally the constant duty of a scholar. <header>The Correct Meaning of the Tripartite Unity of the Book of Changes, Volume Two</header>

# The Correct Meaning of the Tripartite Unity of the Book of Changes, Volume Two

->Annotated by Dong Dening, styled <term>Yuanzhenzi</term> <note>meaning: "Master of Primal Truth," a Daoist name</note>, a humble scholar from <term>Kuaiji</term> <note>A historical region in modern-day Zhejiang province, China</note><-

## Middle Chapter

**<term>Qian</term> <note>The hexagram representing Heaven and the Creative</note> is firm and <term>Kun</term> <note>The hexagram representing Earth and the Receptive</note> is yielding. They pair together and enfold one another. <term>Yang</term> <note>The active, masculine principle</note> endows and <term>Yin</term> <note>The passive, feminine principle</note> receives. Male and female depend on each other. Through this dependence, the <term>Great Transformation</term> <note>original: *zaohua*; refers to the creative processes of nature or the universe</note> occurs, and the essence and breath are released.**

<gloss>The phrase "<term>Qian</term> is firm and <term>Kun</term> is yielding" comes from the "Treatise on the Hexagrams" in the <term>Book of Changes</term> <note>original: *Yi Jing*</note>. <term>Qian</term> is pure <term>Yang</term> and supremely vigorous; its nature is therefore firm. <term>Kun</term> is pure <term>Yin</term> and supremely compliant; its nature is therefore yielding. Thus, the *Book of Changes* describes the virtue of <term>Qian</term> as "strong, persistent, central, and correct," while the virtue of <term>Kun</term> is "yielding, compliant, and focused on perseverance." "Pairing together and enfolding" means that <term>Qian</term> matches from above and <term>Kun</term> pairs from below. Heaven enfolds the outside of the Earth, and Earth resides in the center of Heaven. As the *Book of Changes* says: "Heaven is noble and Earth is humble; thus <term>Qian</term> and <term>Kun</term> are determined." This is the meaning here. Furthermore, it says: "<term>Qian</term> is a <term>Yang</term> thing; <term>Kun</term> is a <term>Yin</term> thing. When <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> combine their virtues, the firm and yielding take on a physical form." This explains the pairing and enfolding. The virtue of <term>Yang</term> is to lead through giving and endowing, while the virtue of <term>Yin</term> is to lead through containing and receiving. Thus, "the <term>Yang</term> endows and the <term>Yin</term> receives." "Male" refers to the father bird and "female" refers to the mother bird—metaphors for <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>. "Depend" means to rely upon or utilize. It means that these two, <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, constantly rely on each other to serve as both the substance and the function of the world. In the third chapter of the first volume, the text says: "Male <term>Yang</term> spreads and establishes its influence; female <term>Yin</term> transforms and enfolds the yellow <note>original: *huangbao*; likely referring to the "center" or the womb of the earth</note>." These share the same meaning. The phrase "Through this dependence, the Great Transformation occurs, and the essence and breath are released" means that the pairing of firm and yielding and the mutual reliance of male and female is the natural Way of creation. Only then can the essence and breath of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> expand and flow to fulfill their role in life and change. In the <term>Way of Internal Cultivation</term> <note>original: *neiyang zhi dao*; referring to internal alchemy or Neidan</note>, one uses the <term>Qian</term> and <term>Kun</term> of one's own body as the cauldron and furnace. The expansion and contraction of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> and the union of essence and breath to form the <term>Returned Elixir</term> <note>original: *huandan*; a goal of alchemical practice representing spiritual perfection</note> follow this same principle.</gloss>

**<term>Kan</term> <note>The hexagram representing Water and the Moon</note> and <term>Li</term> <note>The hexagram representing Fire and the Sun</note> crown the head. Their radiance shines down and spreads. They are established in the profound and are difficult to fathom; they cannot be captured in a diagram. The Sages deliberated upon them to organize the primal foundation.**

<gloss>The *Book of Changes* uses <term>Kan</term> to represent the Moon and <term>Li</term> to represent the Sun. It also uses <term>Qian</term> to represent the head and <term>Kun</term> to represent the belly. Now, when it says "<term>Kan</term> and <term>Li</term> crown the head," "crown" means to be the leader or the foremost of all things. This indicates that as the Sun and Moon move through the heavens, they are positioned as the "crown" atop the "head" of <term>Qian</term>.</gloss>

<summary>This page introduces the second volume of the commentary, explaining the fundamental relationship between the cosmic principles of Qian (Heaven) and Kun (Earth) and how their interaction drives all natural transformation and internal alchemical progress.</summary>

...this imagery. Furthermore, in the structure of the <term>Pre-heaven</term> <note>original: *xiantian*; refers to the primordial state of the universe before physical form</note>, <term>Qian</term> is in the South and <term>Kun</term> is in the North. However, in the application of the <term>Post-heaven</term> <note>original: *houtian*; refers to the manifested, physical world of change</note>, <term>Kan</term> is in the North and <term>Li</term> is in the South. This means that <term>Kan</term> and <term>Li</term> have attained their proper positions and are placed above all the other hexagrams; this is the meaning of them "crowning the head." Regarding "the radiance shines down and spreads," "spreads" means to distribute. It refers to the Sun and Moon moving through the heavens while their light is cast down and distributed upon the earth. <term>Xuanming</term> <note>literally "Dark Obscurity"</note> is the Water God of the North. Furthermore, the <term>Yellow Court Classic</term> <note>a foundational text of internal alchemy</note> says: "The spirit of the kidneys is <term>Xuanming</term>, whose style-name is 'Nurturing the Infant'." This indicates that the kidneys are the "water organ." Here, it means that during the interval between the end of one lunar month and the beginning of the next <note>the new moon</note>, the Sun and Moon enter the "northern realm of dark obscurity." At this moment, Heaven and Earth broadcast their essence, and the Sun and Moon wield their influence in this place; the essential breath of the <term>True One</term> <note>the primordial, unified state of energy</note> establishes its foundation here. Yet, at this time, the cycles of Heaven and Earth are present but not yet active; the Sun and Moon are hidden and difficult to fathom. How could one possibly draw a diagram of such an image? Therefore, the text says: "They are established in the profound and are difficult to fathom; they cannot be captured in a diagram." However, only the Sages can deliberate upon the mechanisms of the waxing and waning of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> and measure the principles of the Sun and Moon’s brightness and obscurity. Then, the foundation of the <term>Primal Breath</term> <note>original: *yuanqi*</note> can be organized and understood. Thus, it says: "The Sages deliberated upon them to organize the primal foundation." This is exactly what was meant in the fifth chapter of the first volume: "The primal essence is so subtle it is hard to see; by calculating and measuring, one confirms the signs." In the <term>Way of the Elixir</term> <note>Internal Alchemy</note>, the roles of <term>Kan</term>, <term>Li</term>, the Sun, and the Moon are exactly the same. One must seek them within one's own body, causing the "outer" Sun and Moon to reflect back upon the "inner," while the "inner" Sun and Moon circulate within. Inside and outside serve each other, and the body and mind merge in dark union without separation. If the <term>fire-phasing</term> <note>original: *huohou*; the timing and intensity of the alchemical heat/meditation</note> is without error, and the work is deep and long-lasting, the spirit will naturally congeal and the breath will gather. Thus, the great task of cultivating the Elixir is complete.

# These Four are in Primordial Chaos

<gloss>The "Four" refers to the previously mentioned hexagrams: <term>Qian</term>, <term>Kun</term>, <term>Kan</term>, and <term>Li</term>. <term>Primordial Chaos</term> <note>original: *hundun*</note> is the state where <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> are not yet divided; this is the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> <note>original: *Taiji*</note>. Since <term>Qian</term> and <term>Kun</term> are the "substance" of <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term>, and <term>Kan</term> and <term>Li</term> are their "function," substance and function now merge into one, and <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> are blended.</gloss>

# Moving straight into emptiness, the sixty hexagrams spread around like a chariot. The Dragon-Horse is harnessed, and the Wise Ruler governs the seasons.

<gloss>This is the natural state. "Straight" means direct. "Emptiness" refers to the <term>Non-Ultimate</term> <note>original: *Wuji*; the state of absolute nothingness preceding the Supreme Ultimate</note>. It means these four—substance and function—enter directly into the realm of the Non-Ultimate and the Supreme Ultimate to forge <term>Yin</term> and <term>Yang</term> and give birth to the Primal Breath. Therefore, it says: "These four are in primordial chaos, moving straight into emptiness." This describes the <term>Pre-heaven Way</term>. It is what the former scholars called: "Deep, silent, and without signs; the Supreme Ultimate is still and gives birth to <term>Yin</term>." There are sixty-four hexagrams in total. If we set aside <term>Qian</term>, <term>Kun</term>, <term>Kan</term>, and <term>Li</term>, these four remain silent and unmoving, returning to the Non-Ultimate to nourish the <term>True One</term> and foster the <term>Primal Yang</term>. When <term>Qian</term> and <term>Kun</term> open up the world and <term>Kan</term> and <term>Li</term> form their images, the remaining sixty hexagrams respond and penetrate all things, starting with <term>Tun</term> and <term>Meng</term> and ending with <term>Ji-ji</term> and <term>Wei-ji</term>, cycling round and round. They spread out like a chariot and rotate like the hub of a wheel. Thus, it says: "The sixty hexagrams spread around like a chariot." This describes the <term>Post-heaven Way</term>. It is what the former scholars called: "The transformation and nourishment flow; the Supreme Ultimate moves and gives birth to <term>Yang</term>." Regarding the "Dragon-Horse": in the "Summer Officials" section of the <term>Rites of Zhou</term>, a horse over eight feet tall is called a "Dragon." A <term>Dragon-Horse</term> <note>a mythical creature</note> carried the <term>River Map</term> <note>a mystical cosmological diagram</note> out of the river, and the sage <term>Fuxi</term> used it as a model to draw the hexagrams. Now, the spreading of the sixty hexagrams is like the rotation of a chariot wheel, just as the Dragon-Horse was harnessed to carry the map. The Sage Ruler relies on the hexagrams to govern the seasons and settle the affairs of the world.</gloss>

...to cut through the doubts of the world. Thus it says: "The Dragon-Horse is harnessed, and the Wise Ruler governs the seasons." This section summarizes the four hexagrams mentioned above to clarify the transformations of the entire system of the <term>Way of Changes</term> <note>the *I Ching* or *Book of Changes*</note>.

In the way of internal cultivation, when the body and mind merge in dark union and the spirit and breath return to their root, becoming dark and obscure—this is the <term>Primordial Chaos</term> <note>original: *hundun*; the state of undifferentiated unity</note> of <term>Qian</term> <note>Heaven</note> and <term>Kun</term> <note>Earth</note> within our own bodies. This is called the <term>Pre-heaven</term> state, and it is where the breath of the <term>True One</term> <note>primordial energy</note> is conceived and nurtured.

When the first <term>Yang</term> energy begins to move, and a warm breath surges and harmonizes in a state of blurring indistinctness—this corresponds to the operation of <term>Kan</term> <note>Water</note> and <term>Li</term> <note>Fire</note> within our own bodies. This is called the <term>Post-heaven</term> state. At this time, one must "pluck" the medicine of the <term>Primal Yang</term>.

Therefore, in the <term>Way of the Elixir</term> <note>Internal Alchemy</note>, "non-action" is considered the substance (the foundation), while "action" is considered the function (the application). The spirit is the horse, and the breath is the carriage. When substance and function merge as one, and spirit and breath rely on each other, the <term>Returned Elixir</term> <note>a state of spiritual perfection and physical longevity</note> can be completed. This is why the Way of the Elixir and the Way of Heaven are fundamentally no different from each other.

I respectfully note that in Shao Kangjie's <note>Shao Yong, 1011–1077, a famous philosopher and cosmologist</note> *Book of Supreme World Ordering*, the number representing the beginning and end of Heaven and Earth is 129,600 years; this is called one <term>Great Cycle</term> <note>original: *yuan*</note>. His son, Shao Bowen, said: "One Great Cycle governs 12 <term>Conjunctions</term> <note>original: *hui*</note>, 360 <term>Eras</term> <note>original: *yun*</note>, and 4,320 <term>Generations</term> <note>original: *shi*</note>." Since one generation is thirty years, 129,600 years make up the count of one Great Cycle. Within the context of the <term>Great Transformation</term> <note>the lifespan of the universe</note>, this is like a single year.

Scholar Cai of West Mountain <note>Cai Yuanding, 1135–1198, a mathematician and music theorist</note> said: "The number of a Great Cycle is the same as the number of a single year. A Great Cycle has 12 Conjunctions, 360 Eras, and 4,320 Generations, just as a year has 12 months, 360 days, and 4,320 double-hours."

The first six Conjunctions represent "growth" <note>the waxing of Yang energy</note>, and the last six Conjunctions represent "decline" <note>the waning of Yang energy</note>. This is exactly like a year where the period from the months of the <term>Rat to the Snake</term> <note>roughly December to May</note> is growth, and the period from the months of the <term>Horse to the Pig</term> <note>roughly June to November</note> is decline. The "opening" of things occurs in the month of the <term>Tiger</term> <note>early spring</note>, which is like the "Awakening of Insects" in the solar calendar. The "closing" of things occurs in the month of the <term>Dog</term> <note>late autumn</note>, which is like the "Beginning of Winter."

A Great Cycle has 129,600 years; a Conjunction has 129,600 months; an Era has 129,600 days; and a Generation has 129,600 double-hours. These are all natural numbers, not something forced together. This is how former scholars discussed the progression of Heaven and Earth from primordial chaos to its opening, and finally to its closing.

Now, when <term>Lord Wei</term> <note>Wei Boyang, the legendary author of the text being commented upon</note> speaks of "Primordial Chaos," does he really mean the massive, hazy beginning of Heaven, Earth, Sun, and Moon? He is simply using this as a metaphor for the "dark of the moon" at the very end of the lunar year. This is the end of the year and month; the Way of Heaven has completed one full circuit, and the Sun and Moon meet in total alignment. This is like the time of the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> <note>Taiji</note> and Primordial Chaos. When the first day of the new year arrives, the ten thousand things are renewed, and Heaven and Earth open up into prosperity; this is like the time when Heaven and Earth were first created. This is what Shao Bowen meant when he said that the count of one Great Cycle is like one year within the Great Transformation.

Lord Wei is revealing the transformations of the Way of Changes while also using them as metaphors for the methods of the Way of the Elixir. If we expand on this, the end of a Great Cycle is a "Great Chaos," and the end of a single year is a "Small Chaos." Scaling down even further, the interval between the end of one month and the start of the next, or the transition between the hours of the <term>Pig and the Rat</term> <note>midnight</note>, are all moments of the Supreme Ultimate and the hazy Primordial Chaos.

Even more, if we look for this within our own bodies, the space between one inhalation and one exhalation—reaching the miracle of "no-breath"—is also the Way of Primordial Chaos. Therefore, Master Shao's "Pre-heaven Chart" considers the space between the hexagrams <term>Kun</term> and <term>Fu</term> <note>the moment of deepest stillness before movement begins</note> as the <term>Non-Ultimate</term> <note>Wuji</note>. His theories regarding the "supreme miracle" existing in the space between movement and stillness all draw from this meaning.

Thus, former scholars said that Master Shao’s "Pre-heaven Learning" originated with Chen Xiyi <note>Chen Tuan, a famous 10th-century Daoist hermit</note>, and that the source of Chen Xiyi’s knowledge was actually based on the *Seal of the Unity of the Three* <note>original: *Cantong Qi*; the text this manuscript is commenting on</note>. These words are indeed true!

## The preceding is Chapter One

This chapter uses the four hexagrams **Qian**, **Kun**, **Kan**, and **Li** as the substance (the foundation) of the transformation and nourishment of Yin and Yang. ### When the superior person stays in their room and speaks, if the words are good, people from a thousand miles away will respond. This refers to the ruler of ten thousand chariots, dwelling in the ninefold chambers, issuing commands while following Yin and Yang and regulating the "stored vessels," waiting for the proper time without violating the hexagram-months.

The *I Ching* says: "When the superior person stays in their room and speaks, if the words are good, people from a thousand miles away will respond—how much more so for those close at hand? If they stay in their room and speak words that are not good, people from a thousand miles away will oppose them—how much more so for those close at hand? Words come from the self but affect the people; actions begin nearby but are seen from afar." This is the Master’s <note>Confucius</note> explanation of the meaning of the second line of the hexagram <term>Zhong Fu</term> <note>Inner Truth</note>.

It means that the words and actions of a superior person must be rooted in sincerity and trust. When one connects with others in this way, there is a resonance like this. Therefore, one must be extremely careful regarding the expression of words and deeds. Now, **Lord Wei** <note>Wei Boyang</note> cites this, using the ruler of <term>ten thousand chariots</term> <note>a standard term for the Emperor</note> who dwells in the <term>ninefold chambers</term> <note>the innermost, most secluded parts of the imperial palace</note> as a metaphor. In such seclusion, it is extremely difficult to achieve sincere communication, and the gap between the high and the low is easily blocked. 

Therefore, every issuance of government policy or decree must follow the seasonal cycles of Yin and Yang in Heaven and Earth. This is like the "Monthly Ordinances" <note>a classical ritual calendar found in the *Book of Rites*</note>, which says that in the first month of spring, the Son of Heaven orders his ministers to spread virtue and harmonize decrees; while in the first month of autumn, he orders the generals to select soldiers and sharpen weapons. This is the meaning. Chapter Five of the previous volume also says: "Issue commands according to the seasons; do not lose the timing of the moving lines." This is the same principle. The "vessels" refer to the tools for cultivating the self and governing the state...

Therefore, this is called "storing the tools and waiting for the right time." 

The **hexagram-months** refer to the hexagrams assigned to the twelve months of a single year, representing the seasonal cycles of Yin and Yang. 
* In the eleventh month (the Winter Solstice), we have the <term>Return</term> <note>original: *Fu* (復)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the first **Yang** energy. 
* In the twelfth month, we have the <term>Approach</term> <note>original: *Lin* (臨)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the second **Yang** energy. 
* In the first month, we have the <term>Pervasiveness</term> <note>original: *Tai* (泰)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the third **Yang** energy. 
* In the second month, we have the <term>Great Strength</term> <note>original: *Da Zhuang* (大壯)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the fourth **Yang** energy. 
* In the third month, we have the <term>Resoluteness</term> <note>original: *Guai* (夬)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the fifth **Yang** energy. 
* In the fourth month, we have the <term>Pure Force</term> <note>original: *Qian* (乾)</note> hexagram; here, all six lines are **Yang**. 

When **Yang** reaches its ultimate limit, it gives birth to **Yin**. This is what **Master Zhou Dunyi** <note>a foundational neo-Confucian philosopher, 1017–1073</note> meant when he said: "Through movement, Yang is produced; when movement reaches its limit, stillness follows." 

* Therefore, in the fifth month (the Summer Solstice), we have the <term>Coming to Meet</term> <note>original: *Gou* (姤)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the first **Yin** energy. 
* In the sixth month, we have the <term>Retreat</term> <note>original: *Dun* (遯)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the second **Yin** energy. 
* In the seventh month, we have the <term>Obstruction</term> <note>original: *Pi* (否)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the third **Yin** energy. 
* In the eighth month, we have the <term>Contemplation</term> <note>original: *Guan* (觀)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the fourth **Yin** energy. 
* In the ninth month, we have the <term>Stripping Away</term> <note>original: *Bo* (剝)</note> hexagram; this marks the birth of the fifth **Yin** energy. 
* In the tenth month, we have the <term>Pure Field</term> <note>original: *Kun* (坤)</note> hexagram; here, all six lines are **Yin**. 

When **Yin** reaches its ultimate limit, it gives birth to **Yang**. This is what Master Zhou meant by: "Through stillness, Yin is produced; when stillness reaches its limit, movement returns." Thus, the cycle begins again from **Return** and ends with **Pure Field**, revolving like a ring without an end. This is the principle of what **Master Cheng Yi** <note>a prominent Song dynasty philosopher</note> called "movement and stillness without end, Yin and Yang without beginning." 

However, regarding these twelve hexagrams of the months, they are contained within the *I Ching*, and the Sages have provided teachings for all of them; one should follow and uphold them. One should act in response to the mechanisms of the waxing and waning of Yin and Yang seasons. Therefore, the text says: "Do not violate the hexagram-months." This is **Lord Wei’s** <note>Wei Boyang</note> explanation of the Master's <note>Confucius's</note> words, used to illuminate the path of governing the state and cultivating the self. ## Using Difficulty [at the Earthly Branches] Zi and Shen, and Enlightenment at Yin and Xu; the remaining sixty hexagrams each have their own days, though we briefly present two images and cannot investigate them all in full detail. 〇

### Difficulty <note>original: *Tun* (屯), pronounced *zhūn*</note>

According to this, we are using the <term>Najia method</term> <note>a system of matching hexagrams with celestial stems and earthly branches</note>, specifically the <term>Nazhi method</term> <note>the system of assigning the Twelve Earthly Branches—time and direction markers—to the specific lines of a hexagram</note>. By assigning the <term>Twelve Earthly Branches</term> <note>Zi, Chou, Yin, Mao, Chen, Si, Wu, Wei, Shen, You, Xu, Hai</note> beneath the Eight Trigrams:
* **The Force** (Qian) receives <term>Zi</term> <note>North/11 PM–1 AM</note> and <term>Wu</term> <note>South/11 AM–1 PM</note>. 
* **The Field** (Kun) receives <term>Chou</term> and <term>Wei</term>. 
* **The Shake** (Zhen) is the same as **The Force**. 
* **The Ground** (Xun) is the same as **The Field**. 
* **The Gorge** (Kan) receives <term>Yin</term> and <term>Shen</term>. 
* **The Radiance** (Li) receives <term>Mao</term> and <term>You</term>. 
* **The Bound** (Gen) receives <term>Chen</term> and <term>Xu</term>. 
* **The Open** (Dui) receives <term>Si</term> and <term>Hai</term>. 

Each trigram receives two branches. Why is it that **The Shake** and **The Ground** are the same as **The Force** and **The Field**? This is because in the <term>Later Heaven</term> <note>the "King Wen" arrangement of trigrams representing the manifested world</note> positions, **The Force** and **The Field** retire from active use, while **The Shake** and **The Ground** take over their duties. This is the meaning of what **Master Shao Yong** meant by: "Placing **The Force** in the northwest and retiring **The Field** to the southwest; the eldest son [Zhen] manages affairs, and the eldest daughter [Xun] stands in for the mother."

Now, taking the two hexagrams **Difficulty** (Tun) and **Enlightenment** (Meng), they are assigned to the dawn and dusk of the first day of the lunar month. Regarding the method of matching: the inner trigram of **Difficulty** is **The Shake**. Its outer trigram is **The Gorge**. The <term>Heavenly Stem</term> matched to **The Shake** is *Geng*. The branch matched to **The Shake** in the inner trigram is *Zi*. Thus, the first line of the **Difficulty** hexagram is *Geng-Zi*. The Stem matched to **The Gorge** is *Wu*. The branch matched to **The Gorge** in the outer trigram is *Shen*. Thus, the fourth line of the **Difficulty** hexagram is *Wu-Shen*. This is why the text says "Difficulty at Zi and Shen." 

For **Enlightenment** (Meng), the inner trigram is **The Gorge** and the outer trigram is **The Bound**. The Stem for **The Gorge** is *Wu* and its branch in the inner trigram is *Yin*. Thus, the first line of the **Enlightenment** hexagram is *Wu-Yin*. The Stem for **The Bound** is *Bing* and its branch in the outer trigram is *Xu*. Thus, the fourth line of the **Enlightenment** hexagram is *Bing-Xu*. This is why the text says "Enlightenment at Yin and Xu." **The Bound**...
