<meta>This page continues the biography of the author/commentator, specifically focusing on Master Yunxiazi and the origins of the text. It then moves into a rhythmic summary (the "songs") of how the Seal of the Unity of the Three integrates the I Ching (divination/governance) and the Yellow-Lao tradition (internal alchemy).</meta>

Master Yunxiazi <note>Literally "Master of Clouds and Rosy Clouds," a Daoist sobriquet</note> was a man from Shangyu in Kuaiji. He was originally a son of a noble house, born into a lineage of high officials who wore the traditional tassels and robes of office. However, he alone chose not to serve in the government. Instead, he lived in seclusion to maintain his simple, unadorned nature, finding joy in the Way and cultivating the Truth. It is not known who his teacher was, but he obtained the subtle mysteries of the "Great Elixir." When his path was complete and his virtue established, he summarized the *Book of Changes* (I Ching) and composed the *Seal of the Unity of the Three* in three chapters to pass down to the world. For this reason, he called himself "a lowly man from Kuaiji" and "a decaying scholar of the hidden valley." He held fast to his simple and honest character, finding no pleasure in the superficiality of power and glory. He preferred to linger in remote and humble places, ignoring profit and fame. By holding fast to the tranquility within his own nature, he hoped for peace in his era. In the quiet leisure of non-action <note>the Daoist principle of *wu-wei*</note>, he composed the *Seal* to form this text. Although Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang</note> was exalted in his path and overflowing with virtue, he nonetheless referred to himself with these humble terms.

### The songs narrate the legacy of the three sages <note>the traditional authors of the I Ching: Fuxi, King Wen, and Confucius</note> of the Great Change; examining their purpose, unifying them in a common discussion, the focus is on harmony with—

# —principle, radiating the essence; divine transformations circulate through the four seas in peace. Presented as a calendar for ten thousand generations to follow, a sequence for governing, practiced without complexity.

<gloss>The songs within the *Seal* narrate the Way of the "Great Change" <note>the I Ching</note>, following the legacy of the three sages. By examining the purpose of their words and meanings, the text unifies the exchange of symbols into a single discussion. The focus is on following the principles of numbers and further radiating the spiritual essence, allowing divine transformations to circulate throughout the world so that the four seas may achieve peace. The *Book of Changes* says: "Observe the divine path of Heaven, and the four seasons do not err. The sage establishes his teachings through this divine path, and the world submits." This is what the text refers to. Furthermore, if one can truly master this Way and present it as a "calendar" <note>a set of laws or a framework</note>, then ten thousand generations can follow it without change. By using this sequence to manage governance, its practice becomes simple and easy rather than burdensome and complex. This section explains the effects of narrating the Way of the *Changes* within the *Seal*.</gloss>

# Incorporating internal nourishment, the natural Way of Yellow-Lao; the thickness of contained virtue returns to the root and origin. It is near in my heart, not separate from the body; embrace the One and do not abandon it, and one can live forever.

<gloss>The character for "Do not" <note>母</note> is pronounced like *wu* <note>無</note>. The character for "Abandon" <note>舍</note> is pronounced like *she* <note>捨</note>. The study of "incorporating internal nourishment" <note>neiyang</note> within the *Seal* emerges from the natural Way of Yellow-Lao <note>the philosophy of the Yellow Emperor and Laozi</note>. Therefore, those who contain a high and thick degree of Dao and Virtue return their breath/energy to the "root" and return their spirit to the "origin." Then, the hundred parts of the body are all harmonized, proving the state of non-action. The *Dao De Jing* says: "One who contains the thickness of virtue is comparable to an infant. Poisonous insects do not sting him, fierce beasts do not seize him, and birds of prey do not strike him." It also says: "Returning to the root is called stillness; stillness is called returning to life. Returning to life is called the Eternal." This is what the text refers to. The Way of internal nourishment is found close by in one's own heart and nature, not separated from one's own physical body. If one simply takes the Three Treasures—Essence, Breath, and Spirit <note>Jing, Qi, and Shen</note>—and embraces them into One, holding them fast without abandoning them, then one can achieve long life and exist forever. This section explains the effects of incorporating internal nourishment within the *Seal*.</gloss>

<gloss>The *Seal of the Unity of the Three* is written in three, four, and five-character verses, occasionally using prose. However, writing is used to carry Virtue, and words are used to transmit the "True Transmission." Therefore, the text states that these are not just stacked sentences or harmonized couplets; there is a "True Way" that exists within them. It is like a pile of common stones and pebbles that contains a hidden beauty within for those who can see it. Those who succeed me in this Way should follow it faithfully and not lose it. Wandering the world of men, spreading feathered wings to fly. East, west, and south, all things incline and shift. In the third part, when King Tang encountered the drought, there was 'no water' <note>removing the water radical 氵 from the character *Tang* 湯</note>, leaving the component *Yang* <note>昜</note>. The 'edge of hardship' provides the 'ear' radical <note>卩/阝</note>. Combining these creates the character *Yang* (陽)." Lord Wei’s intention was truly secretive! 

This is what Master Yu says. However, I currently find these sixteen lines of text quite obscure. It seems there is more hidden within them than just these three characters. Furthermore, there are errors in the text itself. The general meaning, however, refers to the purpose of achieving the Dao and composing this book. Since I have not yet grasped the exact meaning, I do not dare to force an interpretation, lest I lead others astray. I will wait until my own cultivation is complete and the "thorns are cleared" from my mind before providing a supplementary explanation.</gloss>

### Right, Chapter Seven

<note>The "Right" refers to the text preceding this heading in traditional vertical layout.</note>

Some say this chapter and the previous one are the original text of the *Seal*, while others claim they are Lord Wei’s own preface. It is difficult to verify the truth of this, so one need not search too deeply into the matter. He lists the effects of the *Great Change* <note>the I Ching</note>, the path of *Huang-Lao* <note>Taoist internal cultivation</note>, and the *Stove Fire* <note>external alchemy</note>. Although these three have different names, they actually emerge from the same "Gate of the Dao." This reinforces the meaning of the previous chapters. He further explains that the book is written in rhythmic, rhyming couplets not for the sake of beauty, but to encourage students to examine the clues closely and realize the Great Way. Finally, he uses a riddle to conclude, encoding his name and his purpose in achieving the Way and writing this book.

### As for analyzing Yin and Yang, matching their precise weights <term>weights <note>original: *zhuliang* (銖兩), ancient Chinese units of measurement; a *zhu* was 1/24th of a *liang* or tael</note></term>, the waxing and waning of the sun and moon, and the formation of images by the Eight Trigrams; the transformation of male and female, the movement and stillness of the firm and yielding—these are distinguished as clearly as rice from salt, with the *Book of Changes* as proof. The intent behind this is vigorous! Thus, a method is established to be passed to later sages. By deducing and understanding the Great Image, long life must be attained. As for the mechanism of analyzing Yin and Yang within the *Seal*, matching the numbers of their precise weights, the fullness and emptiness of the sun and moon’s phases, and the manifestations of the Eight Trigrams forming images—it uses the Kan <note>☵, the middle son</note> and Li <note>☲, the middle daughter</note> trigrams to bestow and transform their essence and qi. Its phrasing and intent are what is called "vigorous." 

Thus, while it is difficult to express these theories in words, they are established as a law to be passed to later worthies. By deducing and understanding the "Great Image" <note>the fundamental patterns of the universe</note>, the way of long life is almost within reach. As for strengthening oneself and benefiting the body—how could that be all there is to it? Those who wish to follow my Way should apply themselves with redoubled effort and investigate it deeply. 

According to Yu Quanyang, who quotes Shi Qizhen: "The great scholars of old first broadly read the alchemical books, then widely consulted with fellow practitioners of the Way. They compared the words of the Way, and found no discrepancy in what they studied. They contemplated the Way through people, and found no madmen among their teachers. How can later students claim that the secret oral instructions are 'not on the paper' and then pay no attention to the books? If someone says, 'I have a secret transmission from my master that speaks of the ingredients and the "fire times" <note>the timing of the alchemical heat</note> in a way that exists in no ancient or modern alchemical book and is not mentioned in the *Seal of the Unity of the Three*,' then they are simply a deluded person." 

How profound these words are! For in the literature of internal cultivation, since the *Seal of the Unity of the Three* was composed, students have known the source of the Great Way. Following that, Master Shi’s *Chapters on Returning to the Source*, Master Xue...

# The Preceding is Chapter Eight

Some call this chapter the "praise-preface" of the *Seal*, while others call it the "postscript to the commentary." However, neither can be definitively proven, so we simply follow the old arrangement. The *Seal of the Unity of the Three* uses subtle words with profound meanings. It aligns the Way of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors <note>the legendary sage-rulers of China’s high antiquity</note> with the methods for governing the state and governing the self. 

If one cannot follow its laws and standards, or if one is inconsistent and lacks a benchmark, then the three paths—governance, internal nourishment, and the ingestion of elixirs—will all fall into ruin. As for the mechanisms of Yin and Yang’s transformation and the flow of the *Book of Changes*’ imagery within the book, they are all verified by the *Zhou I Ching* <note>the *Book of Changes*</note> and passed down to later worthies so they may fully understand the principles of cultivating the body and nourishing one’s nature. Therefore, students should apply their hearts to investigating it deeply.

Old Man Gang said: Since I was forty-six or forty-seven years old, I have studied and sought the method for settling the heart <term>settling the heart <note>original: *an xin* (安心), a fundamental practice in Chinese philosophy and meditation aimed at achieving an undisturbed, peaceful state of consciousness</note></term>. 

Whenever matters of joy, anger, sorrow, pleasure, toil, or fear arise, I respond to them only with my five senses and four limbs. In the middle, however, there is a space only a "square inch" in size <term>square inch <note>original: *fang cun* (方寸), a traditional Chinese metaphor for the heart or the mind, considered the central command post of the self</note></term>. I keep this space constantly empty and hollow, yet bright and alert. I absolutely never allow those external emotions to enter it. Because of this, I always feel that this place is spacious, clean, and pure. 

I have envisioned this area as a city. I keep the city gates tightly closed and constantly stand guard, fearing that those various emotions might slip inside. Sometimes the "thieves" <note>a common alchemical and meditative metaphor for intrusive thoughts or distracting emotions</note> are very sharp, or the city gates are slightly neglected, and they occasionally manage to slip in. As soon as I notice them, I immediately drive them out of the city and half-close the gates, ensuring that this place remains spacious and clean once more. 

Over the last ten years, I have gradually felt that the times they slip in are fewer, and I do not have to exert much effort to drive them out. However, disturbances outside the city are unavoidable. But with the Master <note>the "Master" refers to the true self or the original spirit dwelling within the heart</note> dwelling in the center, I still possess the joy of never forgetting my heavenly nature.

He also said: Sages, worthies, immortals, and Buddhas—none of them are without the principle of joy. Those in this world who spend their entire lives in distress and grief, or who are suddenly unhappy, are certainly people who lack the spirit of the Way <term>spirit of the Way <note>original: *dao qi* (道氣), the refined temperament or "breath" of a person who has made progress in spiritual cultivation</note></term> and have no sense of life’s true meaning.

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the unity of sciences, specifically transitioning from the general classification of natural philosophy and metaphysics into a specific inquiry regarding the nature of Logic. It concludes the previous argument about how knowing many things as "one" constitutes perfection in science.</meta>

<header>**BOOK II.**</header>

...if it were, there will be no perfection in it, except insofar as it were one thing: and therefore to know things, is to know them as they are one thing. Thus says he.

In the same way <term>Aristotle</term> <note>original: *Aristoteles* (384–322 BC), the foundational Greek philosopher whose works formed the basis of medieval and Renaissance curricula</note> says in the first book of *On the <term>Heavens</term>* <note>original: *De Caelo*, a treatise on cosmology</note>, text 1:
> The science of all <term>nature</term> is almost entirely concerned with <term>bodies</term>, and <term>magnitudes</term>, and their properties, and their principles.

Where <term>Averroes</term> <note>original: *Averrois* (1126–1198), an Al-Andalus Muslim polymath known as "The Commentator" for his extensive work on Aristotle</note> remarks:
> He means to say that the science which considers all <term>natural</term> entities is a single science in its <term>genus</term> <note>a broad category or classification</note>, which is <term>Natural philosophy</term>.

From this it follows that the <term>science</term> which deals with <term>all</term> beings simply is a single science—namely, <term>Metaphysics</term>. And from this it likewise follows that <term>Logic</term> is a single science, because it deals with all syllogisms <note>logical arguments where a conclusion is drawn from two premises</note> and modes of knowing, and consequently with all <term>beings</term>, insofar as the <term>second intention</term> <note>original: *intentio secunda*; a term in logic referring to concepts that the mind forms about its own internal concepts (like "genus" or "species") rather than about external things</note> applies to them.

# ARTICLE IV.
### Whether logic is a speculative science, or a practical one.

<margin>1. The opinion denying that Logic is a speculative science.</margin>
This **QUESTION** is usually raised regarding <term>Logic</term> more than other sciences, because <term>Logic</term> seems to be ordained not only toward the <term>contemplation</term> of truth, but also toward <term>operation</term>—namely, toward <term>syllogizing</term> and <term>discursive reasoning</term>, which are certain operations of the mind.

In this question, the first opinion is that <term>Logic</term> is in no way a <term>speculative science</term> <note>a science pursued for the sake of knowledge itself</note>, but purely <term>practical</term> <note>a science pursued to guide action or production</note>. <term>Averroes</term> seems to think so in his commentary on the first book of the <term>Physics</term>, where he says <term>Logic</term> is the instrument by which the <term>intellect</term> is guided in its development. <term>Saint Thomas</term> <note>original: *D. Thomas* (Thomas Aquinas, 1225–1274), the highly influential Doctor of the Church</note> seems to follow this opinion in his first lecture on the <term>Ethics</term>, where he calls <term>Logic</term> a productive <term>art</term>, and it is expressed in these words:
> Just as the art of building is the <term>rational principle</term> <note>original: *ratio*</note> of order in stones, so <term>Logic</term> is the <term>rational principle</term> of order in the <term>acts of reason</term>.

This opinion is held by <term>Egidius</term> <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316)</note> in logic question 1; and <term>Maurus</term> <note>Sylvester Maurus (1619–1687), a Jesuit theologian</note> in the first question of the preface.

<margin>2. The affirmative opinion.</margin>
The second opinion is that <term>Logic</term> is a purely <term>speculative</term> science. This is held by <term>Scotus</term> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Scholastic philosopher</note> here in question 2, <term>Antonius Andreas</term>, <term>Tartaretus</term>, <term>Gabriel</term> in the preface to logic question 3, <term>Fonseca</term> in the first book of the <term>Metaphysics</term>, chapter 1, question 3, <term>Sonnas</term> in the fourth book of the <term>Metaphysics</term>, question 1, article 3, <term>Suarez</term> <note>Francisco Suárez (1548–1617), a leading figure of the School of Salamanca</note> in the preface to logic chapter 2, and many other <term>more recent authors</term>.

They argue for this opinion thus: Because <term>Logic</term> is not directed toward an external <term>work</term>, such as a house or health; nor to the <term>end</term> of a work, but toward knowing the <term>truth</term> in the <term>syllogism</term>, and in other <term>operations</term> of the mind: therefore it is <term>speculative</term>.

<margin>3. The middle opinion.</margin>
The third opinion is that <term>Logic</term> is partly <term>speculative</term> and partly <term>practical</term>: not that <term>one</term> part is practical and <term>another</term> speculative, but that the same part, and the whole of <term>Logic</term>, has the character of both, just as <term>Theology</term> does. <term>Bartholomew Mastrius</term> <note>Bartholomaeus Mastrius (1602–1673), a Franciscan philosopher</note> seems to think so here in disputation 2, question 2, article 1, number 22.

<meta>catchword: Fourth</meta>
<sig>O 3</sig>

<summary>This page discusses whether Logic should be classified as a speculative science (knowledge for its own sake) or a practical science (knowledge as a tool for action). It presents three viewpoints: that it is purely practical (following Aquinas and Averroes), purely speculative (following Scotus and Suarez), or a hybrid of both.</summary>

## Author’s Preface to the Elucidation of the *Seal of the Unity of the Three in Accordance with the Book of Changes*

The Way of the <term>Immortals</term> <note>original: *Shenxian*; refers to enlightened beings who have achieved longevity or transcendence</note> and the <term>Returned Elixir</term> <note>original: *Huandan*; the "Golden Elixir" created within the body through meditative practice</note> is as simple and easy as this, and nothing more. What is "this"? It is the <term>Supreme Ultimate</term> <note>original: *Taiji*; the ultimate source and principle of the universe in Chinese philosophy</note> of the *Book of Changes*. When the Supreme Ultimate moves, it produces <term>Yang</term>; when movement reaches its limit, it becomes still and produces <term>Yin</term>. When stillness reaches its limit, it moves again. One movement and one stillness act as each other's root. This is the mystery of <term>Creation</term> <note>original: *Zaohua*; the transformative power of nature</note>, the working of the divine, and the natural state of the Way. The *Book of Changes* is a book of vast and complete scope, containing the Way of Heaven, the Way of Humanity, and the Way of Earth. The benevolent see it and call it benevolence; the wise see it and call it wisdom. Its myriad transformations are applicable everywhere. Therefore, <term>Wei Boyang</term> <note>The legendary 2nd-century author of the *Cantong Qi*, often called the "ancestor of alchemical texts"</note> of the Eastern Han dynasty used it to discuss the intention of "making the elixir" and titled his book the <term>*Zhouyi Cantong Qi*</term> <note>The title translates roughly as "The Seal of the Unity of the Three in Accordance with the *Book of Changes*"</note>.

"To Join" <note>original: *Can* (參); also meaning to participate or investigate</note> is to join with this; "To Unify" <note>original: *Tong* (同); meaning to make identical</note> is to unify with this; "The Seal" <note>original: *Qi* (契); a tally or contract used to prove authenticity</note> is to seal with this. To receive a teacher’s transmission and then join, unify, and seal with this text is the <term>Orthodox Way</term>. Anything contrary to this is merely vague and groundless talk, a school of baseless speculation, or a "side-door" minor method; it is not what I call the Way.

Everything described in this book consists of <term>allegories</term> <note>original: *yuyan*; metaphorical or symbolic language</note>. When speaking of the Way of Heaven, it mentions the Sun and Moon, or Cold and Heat. When speaking of the Way of Earth, it mentions Mountains and Marshes, or <term>Lead and Mercury</term> <note>In internal alchemy, these are symbols for energies within the body, not literal minerals</note>. When speaking of the Way of Humanity, it mentions Husband and Wife, or Male and Female. Could there truly be literal suns, moons, lead, mercury, or husbands and wives involved? They are nothing but metaphors.

Whether the text speaks of "three and five," or "two and eight," or the <term>Four Images</term> <note>Symbolic groupings of the trigrams representing the cardinal directions and elements</note>, or the two "bowstrings" <note>Refers to the upper and lower halves of the lunar cycle</note>—though the names differ and the metaphors are winding, they are nothing more than the interplay of a single Yin and a single Yang. To sum up Yin and Yang, they are nothing more than one Supreme Ultimate. Expanded, they become ten thousand things; retracted, they become One. How vast! How expansive! It is infinite, and it communicates with the creative power of the *Book of Changes*. This is why it is called the *Seal of the Unity of the Three*.

When I first read this book, I tried to guess its principles and theories, leaving no stone unturned in my speculation. Someone said to me, "If you wish to cultivate the elixir, you must obtain the oral instructions from a master. To seek eternal life merely by studying words on a page is a waste of effort." But I remained devoted to this book and could not bear to put it down. Lord Wei <insert>Wei Boyang</insert> had stated that after a thousand readings and ten thousand repetitions, the divine would grant a spiritual realization in the heart. I felt that the words of an <term>Attained Person</term> <note>original: *Zhiren*; a perfected being</note> surely would not deceive me. 

Thereupon, I studied with great fervor and diligence for many years. Suddenly, one day, my spirit was indeed awakened, and I found the door to enter. From there, I traced the stream to find its source, and the principles became harmoniously aligned, as if a god were speaking to me. However, because I had not yet received a formal lineage transmission, I did not dare to immediately claim I was correct. I continued my deep search and profound inquiry, forgetting to sleep through the night. My faith grew even firmer, and I eventually moved an "extraordinary person" to point out the great essentials of the <term>Pre-Heaven</term> <note>original: *Xiantian*; the primordial state before physical form</note> True One, and to reveal the subtle details of the <term>Post-Heaven</term> <note>original: *Houtian*; the manifest, physical world</note> <term>Fire-phasing</term> <note>original: *Huohou*; the timing and intensity of meditative focus in alchemical practice</note>. This shattered the mysteries of the Mysterious Cavern...

<summary>In this preface, the author argues that the complex metaphors of alchemical texts actually point to the simple principle of the Supreme Ultimate (Taiji). He describes his personal journey from intellectual frustration to spiritual awakening and his eventual meeting with a mysterious teacher who confirmed his insights.</summary>

<keywords>Zhouyi Cantong Qi, Wei Boyang, Internal Alchemy, Taiji, Yin and Yang, Lead and Mercury, Pre-Heaven, Fire-phasing, Meditative Realization</keywords>

...without doubt. I returned to the source ten thousand times and took from it again. When I read this book thereafter, it was like **splitting bamboo**—it was resolved the moment the blade touched it. I also compared it with <term>Liu Haichan's</term> <note>A legendary 10th-century figure in internal alchemy, often associated with the "Golden Elixir"</note> *Returned Gold*, <term>Zhang Ziyang's</term> <note>Author of the *Wuzhen pian* (Understanding Reality), one of the most important alchemical texts</note> *Understanding Reality*, <term>Zixian's</term> <note>Refers to Xue Daoguang, an internal alchemist of the Southern Lineage</note> *Restoring Life*, and <term>Chen Niwan's</term> <note>Also known as Chen Nan, a master of the Thunder Rites and internal alchemy</note> *Emerald Void*. I found that everywhere I looked, they were identical; there was nothing that did not perfectly match.

Despite my mortal bones, I have been diligent in the study of the <term>Immortals</term>, and I privately felt I had gained much. I am fortunate that due to a connection from a previous life, I was able to hear the secrets of this Way. I have personally tested the true application of the <term>Elixir</term>, and I have personally witnessed the true visions of the Elixir. When I compare these to the scriptures of the Immortals, they match like two halves of a tally. 

I have observed that many today who study the Way of the Immortals without the <term>Orthodox Transmission</term> are often stubborn and rigid. They do not strive for a thorough understanding of the underlying principles. They are satisfied with minor insights and do not seek the complete Way. They form factions to attack one another, twisting meanings and making baseless interpretations. In this way, they mistake the false for the true, dressing up errors and never investigating the original intent of the ancient Immortals. Not only do they delude themselves, but they also delude others.

Because of this, I could not bear to remain silent. I have respectfully added a "footnote" <note>A humble way of referring to his entire commentary</note> to this book. Within it, I reveal the <term>True Mechanism</term> <note>original: *Zhenji*; the hidden workings of nature and the body</note> without any reservation. Whenever I discuss Heaven, Earth, Yin, and Yang, I refer to the words of the former <term>Confucian scholars</term>. When I describe the creation of the "Medicine" and the "Fire" <note>The internal energies and the meditative heat used to transform them</note>, I verify it with the sayings of various Immortals. Through repeated discourse, I strive to clarify Lord Wei's <insert>Wei Boyang</insert> original intent. I certainly do not dare to hide the mysterious mechanisms to shut others out, nor do I dare to mix in nonsensical words to confuse people.

If future seekers who share my aspirations will carefully recite and ponder this book, there will surely be a divine revelation; the effect of a spiritual realization in the heart is beyond doubt. 

However, why should my words alone be trusted? Clear-headed scholars should place their trust in Lord Wei's words. By investigating the mechanism of movement and stillness, unifying with the movement of Yin and Yang, and contemplating the mystery that existed even "before the hexagrams were drawn," you will see that my descriptions are indeed true and not false. I hope you will not let preconceived notions dominate your mind, nor hastily dismiss the *Seal of the Unity of the Three* as mere "words on paper."

->Preface by Yu Yan, styled Yuwu, also known as Quan-yang-zi, the Man of Linwu Mountain.<-

->Written on the 14th day of the 4th month of the *Jiashen* year of the *Zhiyuan* era [May 29, 1284 CE].<-

# Ruan’s Preface to the *Exposition of the Seal of the Unity of the Three*

The *Seal of the Unity of the Three* (*Cantong qi*) is the ancestor of all <term>Alchemical Classics</term> for ten thousand generations. Its language is ancient and obscure, subtle and dense; it is nearly impossible to measure or fathom. However, it is also true that one who lacks true knowledge and practical experience, or who has not received the <term>Orthodox Transmission</term>, will never be able to master it. If someone’s theories contradict this book, yet they claim, “I have a secret transmission and use it as my rule,” they are merely deluded individuals.

In the past, Master Zhu <note>Refers to Zhu Xi (1130–1200 CE), the most influential Neo-Confucian scholar, who took a deep interest in this alchemical text</note> spread the Way during the Chunxi and Qingyuan eras. He was well-versed in a hundred schools of thought. Even when there were views that differed from his own, he never followed along blindly just to agree. He particularly loved Lord Wei’s <insert>Wei Boyang</insert> book and studied it with great intensity and thoroughness, never considering his fascination a mere obsession. He produced a commentary and a textual critique of it. 

Master Zhu once said: “Master Shao <note>Shao Yong, a famous philosopher of the Northern Song</note> received his teachings from Chen Xiyi <note>Chen Tuan, a legendary hermit and progenitor of internal alchemy</note>, and Xiyi’s lineage originated from the *Seal of the Unity of the Three*.” He also said: “I can see it clearly with my eyes, yet I have no place to set my hand <note>Meaning he understood the theory but lacked the practical starting point for the internal work</note>.” He further remarked: “I have finally found the thread, but I have not yet obtained the raw materials for the work.”

When Master Cai Xishan <note>Cai Yuanding, Zhu Xi's closest disciple and a polymath</note> was exiled to Daozhou, Master Zhu saw him off at the Cold Spring Study. Together, they spent the whole night without sleep, correcting and refining this book. After Master Cai passed away, Master Zhu obtained further oral instructions, and he regretted that he could no longer discuss them with Cai. 

Not long after, Master Zhu also passed away. The commentary on this book was published after Master Cai’s death, and at that time, none of his disciples had reached his level of understanding in this matter. Therefore, there was no one left to ask for further clarification, and it is true that there are parts of that work that remain not fully satisfactory.

Master Yu Yan <note>The author of the current commentary</note>, also known by the name Shijian, has shown me the three volumes of his *Exposition*. It serves to fill the gaps left by previous Daoist scholars and to clarify what Master Peng, Master Chen, Master Guo, and Master Wang <note>Earlier commentators on the text</note> failed to explain. He has searched far and wide, and more importantly, he has received instructions from a <term>Perfected Person</term> <note>A fully realized Daoist master</note>. This is not comparable to the mere textual analysis of minor scholars.

I am old now. My "cauldron and vessel" <note>A metaphor for the physical body in alchemy</note> are decayed, and my "medicine" <note>The vital energies of the body</note> is exhausted. I no longer have any hope for myself. Reading Master Yu’s commentary on this book, how could I not sigh with heavy emotion? 

If seekers living in mountain retreats—whose breath is pure and whose spirit is whole—can obtain this book and use it to verify their path, they may perhaps live as long as the heavens and avoid the decay that eventually claims even the sun, moon, and stars. Therefore, I have written this preface at the beginning of the work, so that I may attach my name to his immortal legacy.

->Written by Ruan Dengbing, at age seventy-seven, Gentleman for Court Audience, Director of the Palace Library, and concurrent Official of the Left and Right Offices of the Department of State Affairs.<-

<summary>Ruan Dengbing provides a secondary preface, framing Yu Yan’s commentary as a necessary completion of the work begun by the great philosopher Zhu Xi. He emphasizes that this book contains practical secrets that even famous scholars like Zhu Xi struggled to fully grasp without a master's guidance.</summary>

# Lord Huang Zhongjie’s Remarks

Lord Huang Zhongjie <note>The posthumous name of Huang Daozhou (1585–1646), a famous Ming dynasty polymath, calligrapher, and statesman known for his unwavering integrity and eventual martyrdom.</note> said: 

Among the afflictions that plague scholars, none is more serious than the **desire for fame**. Before I reached the age of thirty, I read books without ever being truly sincere or practical; this was entirely due to this desire for fame. 

The Way of the <term>Gentleman</term> <note>Junzi: An idealized person of high moral character and self-cultivation.</note> is to follow the **Standard** without relying on intimidation. This "Standard" <note>Original: *fa*. In this context, it refers to a lived principle, law, or internal rhythm of conduct.</note> is the very "flavor" of the Way. 

The ancients encountered wealth and honor, poverty and low status, exile among <term>barbaric lands</term> <note>Yi-Di: Historically used to refer to non-Chinese tribes; here it symbolizes living in uncivilized or hostile environments.</note>, and times of great adversity—yet they handled them all as one and the same. This was simply because of the Standard. 

If one possesses the Standard, then dwelling in wealth or poverty, or living through exile and hardship, becomes a singular experience. In every situation—be it prosperity, destitution, life among outsiders, or catastrophe—the "flavor" of the Standard remains exactly the same.

<summary>Lord Huang Zhongjie reflects on his youthful vanity and explains that a true scholar must find an internal "Standard" or principle that remains constant and "flavorful" regardless of whether they are rich, poor, or in exile.</summary>

# Inscription for the Elucidation of the Seal of the Unity of the Three

Since the book *The Seal of the Unity of the Three* <note>Original: *Cantong qi*. This is considered the "Ancestor of Alchemical Classics," using the symbols of the *I Ching* (Book of Changes) to explain the secrets of longevity and alchemy.</note> was completed, the Great Scholar of Kaoting <note>A respectful name for Zhu Xi (1130–1200), the most influential Neo-Confucian philosopher, who wrote a famous commentary on this Daoist text under a pseudonym.</note> in recent times also provided a commentary for it. Now, I have observed the *Elucidation* written by **Quanyangzi** <note>The Daoist name of Ruan Dengbing, the author of this specific commentary.</note>. He has researched with precision and pondered deeply, "hooking the depths and reaching the distant" <note>An idiom meaning to uncover profound secrets and grasp far-reaching principles.</note>. It can truly be said that he has provided "wings" to this book.

Even Master Zhu Xi at that time harbored the hope of becoming "one of Liu An’s chickens or dogs" <note>A reference to a legend where the Prince of Huainan, Liu An, ascended to heaven after drinking an elixir; his livestock licked the remaining drops and flew up with him. It implies a sincere desire for immortal transcendence.</note>. In the poems of his later years, his spirit was so unburdened that he seemed ready to "cast off his shoes" <note>A metaphor for leaving the physical body or the mortal world behind.</note> and depart. Was this not because of what he gained from this book?

Quanyangzi has set his date; when his work is complete, he will "shed the husk like a cicada" <note>A Daoist term for death as a form of liberation/ascension.</note> and follow the Master Boyang <note>Wei Boyang, the legendary Han-dynasty author of the *Cantong qi*.</note> among the peaks of Langfeng and the Hanging Gardens <note>Mythological locations in the Kunlun Mountains where immortals dwell.</note>. They will surely say to one another: "This is indeed the *Seal of the Unity of the Three*."

In the third year of the Zhi Da era, the year of the Metal Dog, in the twelfth lunar month <note>Approximately January 1311.</note>, inscribed by the Successive **Celestial Master Zhang Yucai** <note>The 38th Celestial Master of the Zhengyi Daoist tradition.</note>.

***

Master Zhu <note>Zhu Xi.</note> remarked that the literary style of the *Seal of the Unity of the Three* is exceptionally fine, its word choices rooted deeply in ancient texts. He also said it was crafted with exquisite subtlety and precision. Consequently, he worked with **Cai Jitong** <note>Cai Yuanding (1135–1198), a mathematician and close collaborator of Zhu Xi.</note> to correct the text and compose a commentary.

When people see Master Zhu's commentary, they notice many points where he "left gaps in his knowledge" or did not explain in detail. They then assume that if even a man like Master Zhu could not explain it, how could anyone else? They do not realize that the alchemical books of the Immortals all use "internal scenery," "methodical imagery," and **coded language** <note>Metaphors used to hide the actual physiological or chemical processes of alchemy from the uninitiated.</note>. These are the so-called **"secrets of the oral instructions"** <note>Koujue: Secret instructions passed verbally from teacher to student that are not written in the main text.</note>. These must be received from a teacher; they absolutely cannot be understood through the ordinary academic study of glossaries and philology.

As for Master Zhu's work on this book, how could it be that he failed to investigate the literal meaning? It was simply that the "Great Teaching" has a "special transmission outside of words" <note>A phrase borrowed from Zen Buddhism, suggesting that the ultimate truth is an experience beyond written text.</note>. Now, observing Quanyangzi’s *Elucidation*, his analysis of chapters and sentences reveals things previous men never praised. He is one who has received the teacher's oral instructions and then set them down in words. His phrasing is direct, much like that of **Xiao Liaozhen** <note>Xiao Tingzhi, a famous 13th-century alchemist of the Southern Lineage.</note>. His arguments flow like a surging river, and he provides many citations. If a student glances at this, they will not only gain a glimpse of the **Way** <note>Dao.</note>, but this one book can simultaneously clarify the principles of other classics like the *Understanding Reality* or the *Purity of Emptiness*.

I once reached out to **Nanguzi, Du Daojian** <note>A prominent Daoist scholar and advisor to the Mongol Yuan emperors.</note>, and saw him reveal these heavenly secrets without the slightest stinginess. I deeply admire the universality of his mind and continue to sigh in respect. Thus, I have written this preface and followed it with a song:

# Elucidation of the Seal of the Unity of the Three according to the Book of Changes

## Narrated by Yu Yan, the Golden Yang Disciple, Man of Mount Linwu

### Part One

**Qian** and **Kun** <term>Qian and Kun: The primary hexagrams of the I Ching representing pure Yang (Heaven/Creative) and pure Yin (Earth/Receptive). In alchemy, they represent the "cauldron" and "furnace" or the vertical axis of the body.</term> are the gate and door of the *Changes*. They are the parents of all hexagrams.

The closing of the door is called **Kun**. The opening of the door is called **Qian**. One closing and one opening is called **Transformation**. Passing back and forth without end is called **Permeation**. This is why **Qian** and **Kun** are the gate and door of the *Changes*. **Qian** produces three sons; **Kun** produces three daughters. When male and female join their essences, the ten thousand things are transformed and born. This is why **Qian** and **Kun** are the parents of all hexagrams. Within a single human body, one models the Heaven and mirrors the Earth; the body shares the same **Yin and Yang** <note>The complementary forces of dark/light, passive/active, and female/male that balance the universe.</note> as the cosmos. If a person knows that this body shares the same Yin and Yang as Heaven and Earth, then they may discuss the **Way of the Returned Elixir**. <note>The "Returned Elixir" (Huandan) refers to the process of refining internal energies back to their original, primordial state of purity.</note>

**Kan** and **Li** <term>Kan and Li: The hexagrams representing Water/Moon and Fire/Sun. In alchemy, these represent the internal energies that must be "cooked" or circulated.</term> are the outer walls. They turn the hub and align the axle.

**Kan** is the Moon. **Li** is the Sun. The Sun and Moon travel along the **Yellow Path** <note>The Ecliptic, or the apparent path of the Sun across the celestial sphere relative to the stars.</note>, coming and going day and night, cycling without end like the surrounding of an outer wall. The "hub" is like the body. The "axle" is like the mind. When the hub turns, its axle must be aligned. In practicing the **Returned Elixir**, one moves the Sun and Moon within one's own body to travel the same path as the creation and transformation of Heaven and Earth. If one does not align the mind, how could this be possible?

The four male and female hexagrams act as the **bellows and pipes**. <note>A classic metaphor for the rhythmic breathing and energy circulation in internal alchemy, where the body acts like a blacksmith's bellows—hollow but inexhaustible.</note> They encompass the Way of Yin and Yang, just as a charioteer holds the reins and bit. There are standards and measurements; they follow the rules and keep to the tracks. The center controls the exterior. The numbers are found in the calendars and pitch-pipes. The record of a month's divisions consists of five and six <note>Referring to the 30-day lunar month (5 times 6).</note>. Longitude and latitude honor the Sun, making a total of sixty. **Firmness and Yielding** <note>The active and passive qualities of the hexagram lines.</note> have their internal and external aspects. At the dawn of the new moon, the hexagram **Zhun** <term>Zhun: Hexagram 3, representing "Sprouting" or "Difficulty at the Beginning," signifying the initial stirrings of energy.</term> takes charge; by evening, **Meng** <term>Meng: Hexagram 4, representing "Youthful Folly" or "Obscurity," signifying the cooling or containment of energy.</term> should be received. Day and night each have one hexagram, used according to their sequence. This continues until the darkness of the old moon and the light of the new, ending only to begin again.

**Qian** is pure Yang; <note>The original text notes the hexagrams Gou and Zhuang as stages of Yang growth.</note> **Kun** is pure Yin. <note>The original text notes the hexagrams Pin and Kuai as stages of Yin.</note> **Kan** contains Yang within Yin; **Li** contains Yin within Yang. These are the hexagrams where male and female intersect. In the methods of the Elixir, **Qian** and **Kun** are established at the top and bottom, while **Kan** and **Li** are arranged to the East and West. The opening and closing of **Qian** and **Kun**, and the back-and-forth of **Kan** and **Li**, resemble the shape of the **bellows and pipes**. Therefore, it is said that these four hexagrams act as the bellows and pipes. The "pipes" are hollow...

...is the vessel. The **bellows** <note>original: "tuo," referring to the leather bag of the bellows.</note> is the wind-bag; the **pipes** <note>original: "yue," referring to the flute-like tubes.</note> are the air vents. As Laozi says in the *Classic of the Way and Virtue*:

->The space between Heaven and Earth is like a bellows and pipes. It is empty yet inexhaustible; move it and even more comes out.<-

The vastness of the Great Void is the physical form of the bellows and pipes. The opening and closing, the coming and going of the **Qi** <note>The vital breath or energy that animates the body and the universe.</note>, is the function of the bellows and pipes. If one understands this, then more than half of the **Way of the Returned Elixir** has been grasped. However, regarding this Way: "Grasp it and it persists; let go and it is lost." Therefore, one must be cautious with what is internal and close off what is external. This is like what the *True Classic of Perfect Virtue* <note>The "Liezi," a foundational Daoist text.</note> describes as "The Charioteering of Master Tai Dou." Only then can one engage in this work. In Master Tai Dou’s driving, there is a perfect harmony between the reins and the control; the speed is balanced by the breath. The standard is set within the heart, and the rhythm is held within the hands. Internally, he attains it in his center; externally, it accords with the will of the horses. Thus, he can advance and retreat as if following a straight line and turn in perfect circles. The method of **Refining the Elixir** is exactly like this.

The "numbers found in the calendars and pitch-pipes" refers to the movement through the twelve positions, corresponding to the twelve tones of the pitch-pipes, the twelve months of the calendar, and the twelve years of a cycle. "A month’s divisions consist of five and six" because the thirty days of a lunar month are divided into six segments. The "longitude" refers to the fixed positions of **Qian and Kun** in the North and South. The "latitude" refers to the wondrous application of **Kan and Li** in the East and West. "Honoring the Sun" means following where the Sun leads. Its timing moves in union with Heaven, rising and setting with the Sun without the slightest difference.

"Making a total of sixty" refers to the hexagrams of the *Book of Changes*. If you set aside the four primary hexagrams of **Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li** <note>Because these four represent the fixed structure (the cauldron and directions), they are not part of the moving cycle.</note>, exactly sixty hexagrams remain. Each day has twelve double-hours, and two hexagrams are used to manage these. Each line of the hexagrams corresponds to one hour. Since two hexagrams total twelve lines, they match the twelve hours of the day. Over a thirty-day month, this totals sixty hexagrams. When these sixty are spread across the month, then on the dawn of the new moon, the hexagram **Zhun** <term>Zhun: Hexagram 3, representing "Sprouting," the first movement of Yang energy.</term> is used, and in the evening **Meng** <term>Meng: Hexagram 4, "Youthful Folly," representing the containment of that energy.</term> is used. The twelve hours of day and night exactly match the twelve lines of these two hexagrams. From then on, one uses **Xu** in the morning and **Song** in the evening, **Shi** in the morning and **Bi** in the evening, following the sequence. This continues until the end of the month with the final hexagrams **Jiji** <term>Jiji: Hexagram 63, "After Completion."</term> and **Weiji** <term>Weiji: Hexagram 64, "Before Completion."</term>. This cycle of the new and old moon repeats endlessly. 

As for the hexagram images—whether the lines are **Firm or Yielding**, whether they are reversed or paired—one must not be stubbornly literal. As Zhang Ziyang says in his *Chapters on Understanding Reality*:

->In this, capture the meaning and stop seeking images; if you investigate every line, you merely exhaust your spirit.<-

This means it is not that one literally spreads sixty hexagrams across thirty days. Some fail to realize this principle and stubbornly cling to the theory of hexagram images. They claim that using two hours a day constitutes the **Fire Times** <term>Fire Times (Huohou): The precise timing and regulation of internal heat/energy during meditation to "cook" the elixir.</term>. They follow written records to calculate the atmospheric cycles, anxiously watching the sundial by day and the water clock by night. Is this not a great delusion?

Master Chen Niwan <note>Chen Nan (d. 1213), a famous Daoist alchemist of the Southern Lineage known for his "Thunder Magic" and medical skills.</note> says in his *Chapters of Emerald Emptiness*:

->**"In the heavens, the twelve hours are clear; in the human world, they are divided into the schedule for refining the elixir."**<-

This refers to using the "days and hours" as the standards and measures for practice. The "day" represents the **Fire** <term>Fire (Huo): In internal alchemy, this refers to the concentrated intention and metabolic heat used to transform energy.</term>, and the "hour" represents the **Timing** <term>Timing (Hou): The specific moments or stages during meditation when the intensity of focus should change.</term>. If a person can take the hours and days of the heavens and seek them instead within their own body, then the position where the Sun resides becomes the present moment in their own internal clock.

The *Chapters on Understanding Reality* <note>The "Wuzhen pian," one of the most important texts in the history of Chinese internal alchemy.</note> says: "In refining the medicine, one must know the dusk and the dawn." This refers to the fact that there is an early and a late stage to **Movement and Stillness**. Movement is like the sun rising to begin the day's work; stillness is like the sun setting to begin the night's rest. Within my own body, there is naturally a dawn and a dusk, a sunrise and a sunset. The movement and stillness of the "Fire Times" each secretly correspond to the degrees of the heavens. This is not a matter of using the movement of the stars or the timing of the tides as the moment to begin one's work.

**In Spring and Summer, rely on the internal essence, moving from the hour of the Rat to the hours of the Dragon and Snake. In Autumn and Winter, correspond to the external application, from the hour of the Horse until the hours of the Dog and Pig.**

A hexagram has six lines. The bottom three lines are the "Internal," and the top three lines are the "External." Let us clarify this using the two hexagrams **Zhun** <term>Zhun: Hexagram 3, "Sprouting."</term> and **Meng** <term>Meng: Hexagram 4, "Youthful Folly."</term>. 

In the morning, one uses **Zhun**, which is the time when the **Yang Fire** is ascending. The first line of Zhun corresponds exactly to the **Hour of the Rat** <term>Hour of the Rat (Zi): 11:00 PM – 1:00 AM, the time of the first "spark" of light/energy.</term> within the body. Because it moves from the inside to the outside, it is called "Spring and Summer," and it relies on the "internal essence" from the hour of the Rat through to the hours of the Dragon and Snake <note>The sequence from Zi (Rat) to Si (Snake) represents the increasing growth of light and heat (Yang).</note>.

In the evening, one uses **Meng**, which is the time when the **Yin Talisman** is descending. The top line of Meng corresponds exactly to the **Hour of the Horse** <term>Hour of the Horse (Wu): 11:00 AM – 1:00 PM, the peak of heat and the beginning of the descent into darkness/coolness.</term> within the body. Because it moves from the outside to the inside, it is called "Autumn and Winter," and it corresponds to the "external application" from the hour of the Horse through to the hours of the Dog and Pig <note>The sequence from Wu (Horse) to Hai (Pig) represents the gathering and storage of energy as it cools (Yin).</note>. 

However, these terms—Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter, the hours of the day, and the talk of "internal essence and external application"—are all merely metaphors. If one stubbornly clings to the literal images and follows the written text as a rigid schedule for the "Hexagram Breath," they will merely exhaust themselves with hard labor. What benefit could there be in that?

### Diagram of the Internal Alchemical Cycle

->The diagram illustrates the circular flow of time and energy:<-

- **The Center:** The hexagrams **Kan (Water)** and **Li (Fire)** are at the core, representing the fundamental ingredients of the elixir.
- **The Rings:** The twelve **Earthly Branches** (Rat, Ox, Tiger, etc.) are arranged in a circle to show the progression of the twenty-four hour day.
- **The Seasons:** **Spring and Summer** are mapped to the left and top (East/South), associated with the **Internal Essence** and the rising of energy. **Autumn and Winter** are mapped to the right and bottom (West/North), associated with **External Application** and the storage of energy.
- **The Application:** The diagram serves to map the "Fire Times" (the intensity of meditation) onto the natural cycle of a single day, showing that the practitioner's internal state should mirror the cosmic cycle.

**Reward and punishment correspond to Spring and Autumn. Dusk and dawn follow cold and heat. Written words contain benevolence and righteousness. Joy and anger are expressed according to the time. In this way, one responds to the Four Seasons; the Five Elements obtain their sequence.**

**Yang** <term>Yang: The active, warm, and creative principle.</term> energy arises during the Spring to bring about growth, while **Yin** <term>Yin: The receptive, cool, and contracting principle.</term> energy arises during the Autumn to perform the "solemn killing" <note>This refers to the natural seasonal cycle where life grows in spring and retreats or dies in autumn.</note>. The "reward and punishment" used in the alchemical method is exactly like this. On a long day, the sun rises in the East at the **Hour of the Tiger** <note>3:00 AM – 5:00 AM.</note>; on a short day, it sets in the West at the **Hour of the Monkey** <note>3:00 PM – 5:00 PM.</note>. The "dusk and dawn" of the alchemical method is exactly like this. 

As for the phrases "written words contain benevolence and righteousness" and "joy and anger are expressed according to the time," these refer to the stages of **Submerging, Leaping, Advancing, and Receding** <note>These are specific technical stages of meditative focus based on the "Book of Changes."</note>. Whether one increases or decreases the "Fire," it must follow the proper timing. The *Chapters on Returning to Life* by Master Zixian <note>Xue Daoguang (1048–1121), an influential figure in the Southern Lineage of internal alchemy.</note> says:

> **"In the Fire Times, adding and subtracting requires a mind free of worldly dust; with one poke of the stir-rod, a person is reborn. Follow the increase and decrease of the Yin civil and Yang military fires, and the single pearl of the Returned Elixir will be formed within the flames."**

Are there truly literal "hexagram lines" inside the body? No. Concepts like reward and punishment, benevolence and righteousness, joy and anger, as well as the talk of the Four Seasons and Five Elements—these are all merely metaphors.

### Heaven and Earth establish their positions, and the "Changes" act within them.

One high and one low: these are the positions of **Heaven and Earth**. One Yin and one Yang: this is the **Change** <term>Change (Yi): The dynamic process of transformation described in the I Ching (Book of Changes).</term> of Heaven and Earth. 

**Yang** is born at the **Hour of the Rat** <note>Midnight.</note>. It moves through the hours of the Ox, Tiger, and Rabbit, reaching its peak at the **Hour of the Snake** <note>Late morning.</note>. After 180 units of time have accumulated, **Yin** is born. Yin is born at the **Hour of the Horse** <note>Noon.</note>. It moves through the hours of the Goat, Monkey, and Rooster, reaching its peak at the **Hour of the Pig** <note>Late night.</note>. After another 180 units, Yang is born again. 

Yang gives birth to Yin, and Yin in turn gives birth to Yang. This mutual generation of Yin and Yang cycles without end. This is what we call "The Changes." This process exists in the universe, and it also exists within the human body. Have you not heard what the *Chapters on Understanding Reality* says?

> **"First take Heaven and Earth (Qian and Kun) as the tripod and vessel, then take the Sun and Moon (the Crow and Rabbit) as the medicine to be cooked."**

Does this refer to a literal Heaven and Earth outside the body? Or a literal Sun and Moon outside the body? The practitioner should seek these within their own frame. 

Now, consider that Heaven is positioned above and Earth below. The "Two Energies" (Yin and Yang) circulate between them, one rising and one falling, coming and going without end. This is just like a **Bellows and Pipes** <term>Bellows and Pipes (Tuoyue): A famous metaphor from the Daodejing (Chapter 5) describing the void-like but productive nature of the universe or the lungs/breath.</term>. 

Humans receive the energy of central harmony and are born between Heaven and Earth; from the very beginning, we are not a separate substance from the universe. If one can realize the mystery of the "Bellows and Pipes" of Heaven and Earth, their heart will become empty, serene, and crystal clear. Naturally, the "Single Breath" will circulate up and down. When it opens, the breath goes out; when it closes, the breath comes in. The outgoing breath is like the rising of Earthly energy; the incoming breath is like the descending of Heavenly energy. By following this, one can endure as long as Heaven and Earth. Master Zihua <note>A legendary Daoist figure associated with the text "Zihuazi."</note> said:

> **"The ancients who knew the Way built ramparts to ward off evil and cleared the source to nourish the Truth. They lived in deep stillness, undisturbed by external things. Whether moving or resting, breathing in or out, their Spirit and Qi remained together. Their souls maintained discipline, guarding the 'Child' (the Elixir) in the inner banquet. With focus undivided, the True Qi remains. It pours through the upper and lower reaches, and the breath flows like running water or the tireless movement of the Sun and Moon. Fortify the storehouse and strengthen the palace of Yang."**

# The Way of the Great Elixir

Heaven and Earth are the images of **Qian** <term>Qian: The hexagram representing pure Yang, Heaven, and the creative principle.</term> and **Kun** <term>Kun: The hexagram representing pure Yin, Earth, and the receptive principle.</term>. "Establishing their positions" refers to the arrangement of the positions where **Yin** and **Yang** match. The *Changes* mentions **Kan and Li** <note>Kan (Water/Moon) and Li (Fire/Sun) are the two primary functional energies in alchemy.</note>. Kan and Li are the two "functions" of Qian and Kun. These two functions have no fixed positions among the hexagram lines; they circulate throughout the **Six Voids** <note>The six directions (North, South, East, West, Up, and Down), representing the entirety of the internal space of the body.</note>. Their coming and going is never fixed, and their rising and falling is without constant routine.

Qian is Heaven and Kun is Earth: these are the **tripod and vessel** <note>The "tripod and vessel" are the internal energetic structures—often the head and lower abdomen—where the elixir is refined.</note> of my body. Li is the Sun and Kan is the Moon: these are the medicinal ingredients of my body. In the **Pre-celestial Eight Trigrams** <term>Pre-celestial (Xiantian): The primordial state of the universe before physical manifestation.</term>, Qian is in the South and Kun is in the North; Li is in the East and Kan is in the West. North and South arrange the positions where Heaven and Earth pair together; East and West divide the "gates" through which the Sun and Moon emerge and enter. If one turns inward to seek this within their own body, the principle is exactly the same. Qian and Kun provide the "body" (the structure), while Kan and Li provide the "use" (the process).

These two, Kan and Li, circulate, rising and falling through the Six Voids. They move up and down without staying in any one hexagram position. The Kan and Li of my body operate within the tripod and vessel. When they submerge into "Heaven," they become Heaven; when they submerge into "Earth," they become Earth. How could they be confined to literal positions?

# Hidden and Submerged, They Transform Within

"Hidden and submerged" means the **Spirit** enters the **Qi**, the Qi enters the navel, and they sink back down to the **Bottom of the Sea** <note>A term for the lower dantian or the perineum area, the lowest point of the body's central energetic channel.</note>. "Transforming within" means that when the time comes, the Qi transforms itself; when stillness reaches its peak, the "inner mechanism" triggers itself, and the "Sun" (the refined spirit) emerges from the head. Master Chen Xiyi’s <note>Chen Tuan (c. 871–989), a famous Daoist sage and hermit of Mount Hua.</note> *Chapters on Pointing to the Mystery* says:

> **"Far off without a trace, it returns to the Dark Warrior; hidden within is the mechanism that forms the Sacred Embryo."** <note>The "Dark Warrior" (Xuanwu) refers to the North/Water element. The "Sacred Embryo" is the metaphorical result of internal alchemy—a new, immortal self.</note>

This is exactly what the text means.

# Encompassing All Things, It Is the Discipline of the Way

The *Chapters on Understanding Reality* says:

> **"The Way arises from the Great Void to produce the Single Breath; from that Single Breath, Yin and Yang are produced. When Yin and Yang combine, they produce the Three Bodies; when the Three Bodies generate further, the myriad things are spread out."**

The "Mother of the Golden Elixir" is nothing more than this **Pre-celestial Single Breath**. It splits into two, divides into three, and scatters into the myriad—yet all of them come from this one Breath. Therefore, it is said to "encompass all things" and serve as the "discipline and bond of the Way."

By using "Nothingness" to control "Being," the usefulness of the vessel lies in its emptiness.

<meta>This page continues Yu Yan’s commentary on the *Zhouyi Cantong Qi* (The Kinship of the Three), moving from the structural roles of the trigrams to the fundamental Daoist principle of "Emptiness" (Void). He uses the classic metaphors of the hub, the vessel, and the room from the *Tao Te Ching* to explain how the internal alchemical "furnace" must be empty to be functional.</meta>

The *Tao Te Ching* says:

->Thirty spokes share one hub;<- 
->where there is nothingness, the carriage has its use.<-
->Molding clay to make a vessel;<-
->where there is nothingness, the vessel has its use.<-
->Cutting out doors and windows to make a room;<-
->where there is nothingness, the room has its use.<-
->Therefore, what is "being" provides benefit, but what is "non-being" provides utility.<-

The commentator Lin Luyi notes: "The hub is what receives the axle of the carriage. The spokes are the 'legs' of the wheel. The hub is only able to move the carriage because it is **empty at its center**. 'Molding clay' refers to the potter's craft. The vessel can be completed because it is empty and capable of holding contents. Doors and windows are the openings that allow light into a room. These three examples are all metaphors for how **emptiness** is the source of function."

Therefore, it is said that "being" provides benefit (the physical object), while "non-being" (the void within) provides the actual utility. The carriage, the vessel, and the room all require physical existence to be beneficial, but their purpose is defined by the emptiness at their centers.

Now, Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the legendary 2nd-century author of the *Cantong Qi*, the "Ancestor of all Alchemical Texts."</note> says that the Way uses "Nothingness" to control "Being." This "utility of the vessel" specifically uses Laozi’s teachings on the empty and the solid. In the methods of the Elixir, we take the **Great Void** <term>Great Void (Taixu): The boundless, formless state of the universe, which in alchemy represents the state of mind required for the work.</term> as our tripod and furnace. Within this Great Void, a natural and wondrous utility arises. How marvelous! How marvelous indeed!

*Guan Yinzi* <note>A classic Daoist text attributed to the Guardian of the Pass who received the *Tao Te Ching* from Laozi.</note> says:

> "When clothes are shaken in the air, wind is produced. When breath is blown upon an object, water (moisture) is produced."

The commentator Chen Baoyi notes: "If you understand that shaking clothes in the void produces wind, then you understand that by 'pumping the bellows and pipes' <note>A metaphor for the breathing and energetic work within the body's central channel.</note> one can generate **Qi** (energy). If you understand that blowing on an object produces water, then you understand that by 'nurturing the breath' one can transform energy into **Essence** <term>Essence (Jing): The foundational physical/sexual energy that is refined into Qi during alchemy.</term>."

If one is ignorant of this and seeks the "Tripod and Vessel" elsewhere, they have strayed from the Way of Emptiness and Nothingness.

### Therefore, Deducing the Ebb and Flow, Kan and Li Disappear

*Xi* (Flow/Waxing) refers to the timing of advancing the fire; it is the stage where the **Kun** (Earth) hexagram changes three times to become **Qian** (Heaven). <note>This represents the growth of Yang energy from the winter solstice toward the summer.</note> *Xiao* (Ebb/Waning) refers to the timing of withdrawing the "tally" (the cooling phase); it is where the Qian hexagram changes three times to become Kun. 

From the first day of the new moon, when the **Zhen** (Thunder) hexagram takes charge, we pass through **Dui** (Lake) until we reach the full moon of **Qian**. Once the full moon passes, the **Xun** (Wind) hexagram takes charge, and we pass through **Gen** (Mountain) until we return to **Kun**.

During this cycle, we do not see the positions of the lines for **Kan** (Water) and **Li** (Fire). Does this mean Kan and Li have "disappeared"? No. It means Kan and Li are the ones *operating* the cycle; they move throughout the **Six Voids** and their coming and going is not fixed.

***

Speech is not created carelessly, and theories are not born in vain. They are drawn from evidence to show results, and weighed against the movements of the spirits. By deducing categories and forming the characters, the original principles serve as proof. **Kan** is **Wu** <term>Wu: The 5th Heavenly Stem, representing "Yang Earth."</term>, the essence of the Moon. **Li** is **Ji** <term>Ji: The 6th Heavenly Stem, representing "Yin Earth."</term>, the light of the Sun. Sun and Moon form the **Changes** (*Yi*); Hard and Soft match one another. Earth rules the four seasons, connecting the beginning to the end. Green, Red, White, and Black <note>Representing the four directions and elements: Wood/East, Fire/South, Metal/West, and Water/North.</note> each reside in their own quarter, yet all rely on the power of the **Central Palace** of Wu and Ji Earth.

Kan is Yin on the outside but Yang on the inside—this is the image of the Moon. Li is Yang on the outside but Yin on the inside—this is the image of the Sun. Kan contains Wu, which is Yang Earth. Li contains Ji, which is Yin Earth. When these two "Earths" intersect and combine, Yin and Yang assist one another, and Hard and Soft are balanced. This is just like how the characters for "Sun" (日) and "Moon" (月) are joined to form the character "Changes/Brightness" (易). Green, Red, White, and Black are simply Wood, Fire, Metal, and Water. These four elements...

<meta>This page continues Yu Yan’s commentary on the *Zhouyi Cantong Qi* (The Kinship of the Three). It expands on the previous discussion of the "Central Palace" and "True Earth," explaining how the element of Earth serves as the essential mediator for all other elemental transformations in internal alchemy.</meta>

Each [element] resides in its own direction, but only Earth occupies the center. It distributes its flourishing power through the periods of **Chen, Xu, Chou, and Wei** <note>The four "Earth" branches of the zodiac—Dragon, Dog, Ox, and Goat—which represent the transition periods at the end of each season.</note>, weaving together the beginning and the end of the year. Therefore, Wood relies on Earth to flourish, Fire relies on it to rest, Metal relies on it for birth, and Water relies on it for its foundation. These four elements all receive their efficacy from the power of Earth.

Yet this "Earth" permeates the entire universe; it has no single fixed location. Within the **Kan** (Water) trigram, it manifests as **Wu Earth**; within the **Li** (Fire) trigram, it manifests as **Ji Earth**. In the Central Palace, it is the combined **Wu-Ji Earth**, and within the four seasons, it is the Earth of the four branches. All of these are essentially the same substance.

How profound indeed! The poems of the *Wuzhen Pian* <note>The "Chapters on Understanding Reality," a seminal 11th-century alchemical text by Zhang Boduan.</note> state:

-> "The Four Images and Five Elements all rely entirely on Earth." <-

The text further says:

-> "It is only because both sides harbor **True Earth** <term>True Earth (Zhen Tu): In alchemy, this represents the "True Will" or "Central Sincerity" that allows the disparate energies of the body (Yin and Yang) to fuse.</term>, that the Golden Elixir can undergo its cyclic return." <-

Without the harmonizing influence of True Earth, **Yin and Yang** would be blocked and separated (**Pi**) <note>Referring to Hexagram 12, "Stagnation," where heaven and earth do not communicate.</note>, and Hard and Soft would be pulled apart, making it impossible to form the Elixir.

Alas! Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang</note> composed this book to reveal the mysteries of this Way. His words are nothing other than a record of verified results and personal attainments. Fearing that his teachings might not gain the trust of later generations, he measured the divine brilliance of the Sun and Moon to establish his method and traced the principles of the *I Ching* hexagrams to provide proof. His presentation is both profound and luminously clear. How could he have fabricated baseless claims or given birth to useless theories merely to deceive and mislead those who come after?

# The Changes are but images. Among the suspended images that shine with brilliance, none are greater than the Sun and the Moon. By exhausting the spirit, one comes to know transformation. If the author did not employ these "images" and borrow the names of physical objects, how could he illuminate the path and allow people to "exhaust the spirit and know transformation"?

By showing people what is clearly visible, he enables them to perceive the Yin and Yang of the universe and silently realize the subtle mystery of spiritual transformation. They circulate through day and night like a wheel turning, never-ending. If a person can turn their attention inward and reflect, extending these principles by analogy, they will find that their own body possesses its own Sun and Moon, no different from those of Heaven and Earth.

How could one possibly need to seek this outside oneself?

### The Changes consist of 384 lines; based on these lines, one selects the talismans. "Talismans" refers to the sixty-four hexagrams.

The entirety of the *I Ching* consists of 384 lines (*yao*), and one pound of the **Great Medicine** <note>The internal elixir.</note> consists of 384 *zhu* <note>An ancient unit of weight; there are 24 *zhu* in a Chinese ounce, and 16 ounces in a pound, totaling 384.</note>. This is where the Way of Alchemy and the Way of the Changes intersect, and it is the reason why the *Cantong Qi* was written. 

The "lines" are the individual strokes of the hexagrams; the "talismans" are the completed structures of the hexagrams. While the *I Ching* has sixty-four hexagrams, the Alchemical Method uses **Qian** (Heaven) and **Kun** (Earth) as the **Vessel** <term>Vessel (Dingqi): The internal 'cauldron' or energetic container in which the elixir is refined.</term>, uses **Li** (Fire/Sun) and **Kan** (Water/Moon) as the medicinal ingredients, and uses the remaining sixty hexagrams to track the **Fire Phasing** <term>Fire Phasing (Huohou): The precise timing and intensity of internal heat/focus required during meditation.</term>.

If we look at the sequence starting from **Qian** and **Kun**, beginning with the hexagrams **Tun** (Sprouting) and **Meng** (Youthful Folly) and ending with **Jiji** (Already Fords) and **Weiji** (Before Fording), we see that throughout the entire process, every inverted or opposing hexagram matches perfectly. Here we see that "one Yin and one Yang constitute the Way." The ancient immortals based their work on these lines and selected these talismans to serve as metaphors for the Vessel, the Medicine, and the Fire Phasing. Their system can be called truly ingenious and complete.

# When the darkness reaches the dawn of the new moon, it refers to the interval between the end of one lunar cycle and the start of the next. "Zhen (Thunder) arrives to receive the talisman" means that Qian (Heaven) has coupled with Kun (Earth) to produce Zhen. This represents the birth of the "One Yang" within the human body. 

At this precise moment, the Spirit and the Breath (*Qi*) intersect and harmonize, much like the coupling of the essences of Heaven and Earth, or the perfect alignment of the Sun and Moon. Therefore, it is said: "At this time, Heaven and Earth couple their essences, and the Sun and Moon support one another." In this context, "Heaven and Earth" refer to the **Qian and Kun** within the practitioner's own body, while "Sun and Moon" refer to the internal **Kan and Li** <note>Kan (Water/Moon) and Li (Fire/Sun) are the primary energetic components in internal alchemy.</note>. Just as the macrocosmic Heaven, Earth, Sun, and Moon intersect at specific times to nurture all things and complete the cycle of the year, the internal Qian, Kun, Kan, and Li must intersect at the proper time to "seize the creative power of nature" and form the **Sacred Embryo** <term>Sacred Embryo (Shengtai): The spiritual or energetic "seed" developed through alchemical practice that eventually leads to enlightenment or immortality.</term>. 

Lord Wei <note>Wei Boyang, the author.</note> feared that students would not understand the internal workings of Yin and Yang within their own bodies, so he borrowed the timing of the lunar conjunction as a metaphor. He was not suggesting that one can only practice during the actual new moon once a month.

> As the *Chapters on Understanding Reality* <note>The *Wu Zhen Pian*, a seminal text of Southern Lineage Taoist alchemy.</note> states: "The Sun and Moon meet once every thirty days. If you can exchange 'days' for 'hours,' you will master the divine work."

If the student understands the subtle mystery of "exchanging days for hours" <note>This refers to a practice where the practitioner undergoes a full cycle of internal circulation (the "alchemical month") within a much shorter period of time, such as a single day or meditation session.</note>, they can steal the secret mechanism of Heaven and Earth to complete the **Great Elixir**.

### Virile Yang sows the dark seed; Feminine Yin governs the yellow transformation.

"Virile Yang sows the dark seed" describes the Breath of Heaven descending to reach the Earth. "Feminine Yin governs the yellow transformation" describes the Earth receiving the Breath of Heaven to bring forth life.

> The *Chapters on Understanding Reality* states: "When the Sweet Dew falls, Heaven and Earth must unite. When the **Yellow Sprout** <note>A poetic term for the first sign of the internal elixir's growth.</note> grows, Kan and Li must intersect."

The generation of the Elixir is identical to the way Heaven and Earth generate life. It is nothing more than the two energies of Yin and Yang—one sowing and one transforming—intermingling until they are unified.

> Thus Confucius praised the Primordial Chaos; Qian and Kun’s virtue penetrates the void. Examining antiquity, one hails the Primal Sovereign; the "Ospreys" poem establishes the beginning. A "Talisman" (*Fu*) means a conjunction or a matching. As the Moon travels through the heavens, it completes one degree each day and enters a conjunction with the Sun; therefore, it is called the "Heavenly Talisman." 

Regarding "advancement and retreat, expanding and contracting to respond to the seasons": After the first day of the lunar month, the light gradually advances. The <term>Hun</term> <note>The "heavenly" or "yang" soul associated with light and movement.</note> grows while the <term>Po</term> <note>The "earthly" or "yin" soul associated with darkness and stillness.</note> diminishes. Yang expands and Yin contracts. This corresponds to the internal hours from *Zi* (midnight) to *Si* (late morning). 

After the sixteenth day, the light gradually retreats. The *Po* grows while the *Hun* diminishes. Yin expands and Yang contracts. This corresponds to the internal hours from *Wu* (noon) to *Hai* (late night). 

The Perfected Ones of antiquity observed the Way of Heaven and maintained its operations.
